Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.
The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.
“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.
The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”
The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.
While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.
“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”
Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict.
Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine.
Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.
A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.
The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.
Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”
Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.
Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”
So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.
With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.
Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.
“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”
Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”
Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”

L.A. Rams fans and TV executives are both smiling today about the same thing.
Aaron Donald, the all-world defensive tackle who led the Los Angeles to a Super Bowl victory in 2022, announced today that he will come out of retirement this season.
The team confirmed the news by sharing a letter on Rams letterhead addressed to NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, ostensibly from Donald, which read simply, “Dear Commissioner Goodell: I’m Back.” It was signed by Donald.
DraftKings Sportsbook had the Rams as favorites to win the Super Bowl even before Donald’s announcement. The 2027 championship will be played on the Rams’ home turf at SoFi Stadium.
	What’s more, a one-of-one defensive superstar returning to a team in the country’s second-largest media market is a boon to networks and streamers that carry NFL games. 
The 35-year-old Donald retired prior to the 2024 season, but announced earlier this summer that he was considering a comeback, leading to a couple of workouts with the team in August under the supervision of head coach Sean McVay.
Watch on Deadline
The Rams did not disclose details of his contract, but ESPN and the NFL Network both reported that it was a one-year, $20 million deal with playoff incentives that could raise the total value of the deal to $30 million.
Donald was one of the most dominant defensive lineman in NFL history during his 10 seasons with the Rams, recording 111 sacks, 24 forced fumbles and seven fumble recoveries.
He is one of three players in NFL history to have won the Associated Press NFL Defensive Player of the Year Award three times — 2017, 2018 and 2020.
If Donald can even approach his previous level of play, his return could give the Rams a devastating pair of pass rushers. The team acquired reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett on June 1.
Garrett, 30, set the NFL’s single-season record for sacks last year with 23, and was voted the NFL’s Defensive Player of the Year for the second time. He added a league-leading 33 tackles for loss.
According to ESPN, that makes L.A. the only team with two active players who won multiple Defensive Player of the Year awards.
The Rams’ next game is Thursday against longtime NFC West rivals the San Francisco 49ers on Netflix. Donald could play, but no announcement has been made as of yet.

The two sons of a police officer killed in a crash on Teesside will lead out the Manchester United team as mascots for Sunday's Premier League match against Ipswich at Old Trafford.
PC Matthew Blades, described as a "proud Red" by United, was a regular at Old Trafford. The club have paid tribute to him in Sunday's match programme. His widow will attend the game with their children.
PC Blades and his colleague PC Tom Clough died in a head-on collision between their police car and a vehicle going the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough early on 22 August. Five people in the other vehicle also died.
United said they learned of the deaths of the two officers "with great sadness".
"Matthew was a proud Red, a devoted family man and a police officer who dedicated his life to helping others," said the club, in a tribute in the programme.
On Saturday, there was a minute's applause in memory of PC Blades and PC Clough before Middlesbrough's Championship encounter with West Brom at Riverside Stadium. Pictures of the two men were displayed on a screen.
People also gathered to pay tribute at Seaton Carew FC's game against FC Hartlepool. PC Blades had been a junior football coach at both teams.
Earlier this week, 17 people were arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash bringing the total number of arrests to 24.
The occupants of the other vehicle, a Passat - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17, also died.

Lake Ontario now called ‘Lake America’ on Google Maps for US users after Trump order
The move echoes what Google did in 2025 when Trump issued an order to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America
Google has updated its maps application to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for users in the United States, reflecting a recent order by US President Donald Trump that changed the name of the lake, the global technology giant says.
The Google Maps update comes days after Trump’s order amid an escalating trade war with Canada that has led both countries to impose billions of dollars in added tariffs on each other’s goods. It echoes what Google did in 2025 when Trump issued an order to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
Google said in a blog post on Saturday that the decision was based on its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System, also known as GNIS.
“People using Maps in the US will see ‘Lake America’, those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’, and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said in a brief statement. “These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now.”
Trump’s decision on Thursday to rename the lake was met with mockery and indifference in both Canada and the United States. On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded to Trump’s order with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shore: “Lake Ontario. Now and forever.”
The White House, the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ford’s office did not immediately comment on Sunday on Google’s decision.

Gwyneth Paltrow Is Very Sorry to Postpone Her Dinner
Is controversy not all the more reason to take a conversation alfresco?
Special and invited guests,
I’m sorry to inform you that after intense public scrutiny, I have decided to postpone the Hamptons dinner I had planned this weekend to celebrate Sam Altman, whom you all doubtless know as the billionaire co-founder of OpenAI. I was so excited for you to get to know him the way I do: as a friend.
I met Sam last summer in a Sardinia beach bar, where, over a few rounds of espresso Sardinis (if you know, you know!), I asked him all about artificial intelligence—the sorts of questions heard at kitchen tables across the country: What does AI mean for beauty? What does AI mean for lifestyle brands? What does AI mean for being able to appear in additional Marvel movies without actually needing to be on set?
I knew you all would have questions too—the same ones, but possibly also additional ones—hence our little dinner. As the invitation promised, I had hoped to discuss these matters in an environment that was “private,” “off-the-record,” and “al fresco.” Now none of that is possible, except for the “al fresco” part; the lawn remains immaculate.
When commentators learned of the dinner, they immediately cast me—an artist!—as a “technofascist.” They made hurtful jokes about “consciously uncoupling” from the party, as if that is something that could be done without the assistance of a Kabbalist. They accused me of ignoring the risks of artificial intelligence and “sucking up to our new A.I. overlords” instead.
Of course I recognize that AI and its brilliant, visionary, amazing makers may be controversial—but I know firsthand what it’s like to court controversy with your devotion to making the world a better place; I see something of my own mood-enhancing stickers and bee-sting facials in Sam’s art. There’s but a hair’s breadth between slop and goop.
Besides, I believe that controversy is all the more reason to take a conversation al fresco. Is this so misguided? Is complete off-the-record privacy really so high a price to pay for open dialogue? I will use this lonely weekend to reflect, I suppose.
For those who have already traveled to the Hamptons, I am happy to provide for your return trip on my jet, the Jetney. Take some flowers too. I’d hate for the water to go to waste if it’s suddenly so precious. At least I’ll see you all at the Montecito house for the costume ball this fall. You are going to just die when you see Jeff’s getup as Daddy Warbucks.
Please also fill out the Google poll for a possible rescheduling of this dinner; I will endeavor to work around everyone’s Sardinia dates.
I think it’s only appropriate to close this note with a few words from ChatGPT on the value of dialogue: Talking to each other is not just a skill—it’s a superpower. Dialogue builds empathy, and empathy allows people to truly feel rather than to—OKAY, now that any reporters have tuned out, the dinner is STILL HAPPENING! Please meet me at my Amagansett DECOY HOUSE (you know the one!) for cocktails at 6 p.m., from which we will take the Jetney to my OTHER DECOY HOUSE (this one’s new!) for a seated dinner at 6:45 p.m. The flowers are already on their way!
Genuinely,
 Gwyneth

Villages of Keralam, namely Kanan Devan Hills, Kuttampuzha, Chittar, Mankulam, Padavayal, and Peechi, have been identified as persistent hotspots for both elephant mortality and human casualties.
As many as 21 villages have also been classified as areas of high incidence of human-elephant conflicts (HEC), where 20 or more human casualties were reported.
The villages that are prone to HEC were listed in a recent report, ‘HEC in the State of Keralam 2008-2025, trends challenges and insights,’ released by the Wildlife Institute of India.
Of the 214 villages from where human mortality and injury incidents occurred during the study period, 175 were classified as low incidence (0-10 incidents), 18 as medium incidence (10-20 incidents), and 21 villages as high incidence (more than 20 incidents).
Most impacted division
Ranni was identified as the most impacted forest division with records of 169 HEC cases. Munnar division followed with 144 cases, while Munnar Wildlife and Nilambur North divisions each reported 138 and 108 cases respectively.
Although HEC affected many villages, the majority experienced relatively few incidents with only a small proportion of villages being identified as high-conflict hotspots, it noted.
Nilambur, Palakkad-Mannarkkad, Munnar-Mankulam, and Kothamangalam-Periyar landscapes have been identified as major hotspots of HEC, with a high concentration of incidents occurring in and around these forest divisions.
The highest number of human deaths was recorded in Nilambur South (78), followed by Palakkad (57), Mankulam (57), Munnar (50), Periyar East (42), Nilambur North division (27 cases). Kothamangalam accounted for the highest number of human injuries (164), followed by Marayoor (102), Nilambur North (63), Periyar East (64), and Thiruvananthapuram (58). The period also saw 1,781 incidents of HEC leading to 581 human deaths and 1,200 injuries in the State.
Elephant deaths
Electrocution was found to be the major anthropogenic factor contributing to elephant deaths as 154 elephants died after coming into contact with live wires. While explosive baits killed 12 elephants, retaliatory killing took the lives of 11 elephants. Poisoning (5), poaching (7) and snare/trap incidents (4) accounted for 16 deaths, according to researchers.
Solitary adult males were found responsible for the highest proportion of HEC incidents, especially raiding crop lands and causing damage to properties. Translocation of conflict elephants rarely provided a long-term solution, as many of them attempted to return to their original home ranges or continued to cause conflict in new areas after release, quoting a study from Sri Lanka, the report concluded.
A similar pattern was observed in Keralam during the translocation of the elephant Arikomban from Chinnakkanal in 2023, where it moved into human-dominated areas after release, requiring further management interventions. Repeated translocation of conflict elephants often provided only temporary relief, it was reported.

As Germany's far right gains ground, coded symbols are hiding in plain sight
Supporters have co-opted everyday brands to signal their beliefs while skirting the law
As Germany's far right gains political ground in some parts of the country, researchers say some supporters are getting more comfortable showing their views in public — albeit sometimes without displaying an explicitly political symbol.
At recent rallies for the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, that coded language was visible on things as ordinary as a pair of sneakers or a T-shirt.
Researchers say logos for brands including New Balance and Lonsdale are increasingly used as dog whistles for nationalist and Nazi symbolism — something that is especially significant in Germany, where the display of Nazi symbols is restricted by law.
"What we noticed in the last couple of years is that frequently at these events, you see a lot of people who have different signs which relate to the extreme right," said Gideon Botsch, head of the Emil Julius Gumbel Research Unit on Antisemitism and Right-Wing Extremism at Potsdam University.
"Some are clear and open right-wing and neo-Nazi symbols ... others are opaque or playing the game a little bit."
Some have co-opted New Balance, taking the large "N" on the side of its sneakers to mean "nationalist" and "NB" for Nationale Bewegung, or "national movement," Botsch said.
Likewise, Lonsdale has seen renewed use of its sportswear by the far right in part because, he says, when worn a certain way the logo spells out NSDA — the abbreviation for Germany's National Socialist Party.
"Those who know will know; those who don't know will think this is harmless," Botsch said.
The ambiguity is significant because Germany's law against Nazi symbols "expressly covers flags, badges, uniform items, slogans and forms of greeting,” said Sophie Scheuble, digital policy and counter-extremism manager at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.
So "most of what is worn at far-right events is therefore lawful, and this distinction is well understood within right-wing extremist scenes.”
Those restrictions have led to an increase in the use of symbols recognizable only to those who know what they mean, without crossing legal lines.
When the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt's domestic intelligence service updated its handbook on far-right symbols in May, Scheuble said, its director noted that most extremists avoid prosecutable symbols and instead rely on codes and catchwords.
What has changed, researchers say, is the political environment where those styles are appearing.
Changing political climate
The Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has grown from a fringe party in 2013 into the likely winner of an upcoming state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The party has been legally designated a far-right extremist group in the state.
If it wins, it would mark the first time a far-right party has had an absolute state majority in Germany since the Second World War.
Fabian Wichmann, an expert at the EU Knowledge Hub on Preventing Radicalization, said there is a growing "grey zone" between Germany's hardcore neo-Nazi movement and the broader populist right.
Members of neo-Nazi groups attend AfD rallies and meetings and have encouraged their supporters to vote for the party, he says, seeing its success as a step toward their own political goals.
"The AfD has a widespread and diverse group of followers," Wichmann said. At its election events and marches, "you will see people who look very normal in their clothing," wearing things like New Balance and Lonsdale.
He said not everyone wearing those brands is a neo-Nazi, but there are "also a lot of neo-Nazis who wear this kind of stuff because they have some typical symbols, some typical narratives they share."
But the bigger change researchers say they're seeing isn't in the clothing itself. It's in the willingness to display those signals openly.
Wichmann says that shift matches the growing strength of Germany's far right and the AfD.
"They feel like ... the culture, the temperature of a society is changing. And now it's possible to wear something like this without getting into conflict,” he said.
"There's a feeling of, 'OK, we are on the winner's side right now,' and that's the reason why they are so openly wearing it."
Lonsdale's decades-long battle
New Balance has no affiliation with Germany's far-right movement. The company did not respond to requests for comment, but in the past has said it "does not tolerate bigotry or hate in any form."
Likewise, Lonsdale has spent decades fighting its appropriation by the far right with anti-racism initiatives since it became popular among German skinhead and neo-Nazi subcultures in the 1980s and '90s.
But the British boxing and sportswear company says the phenomenon is returning.
"We have noticed that since around summer 2024, the Lonsdale brand has once again been increasingly worn by far-right extremists,” spokesperson Ralf Elfering said. "This earlier misuse of the Lonsdale brand — and the fact that we are seeing it again today — is very frustrating.”
Elfering said the company stops supplying retailers when it discovers Lonsdale is being sold in a clearly extremist context.

Other brands, however, carry considerably less ambiguity, according to experts.
Botsch points to Thor Steinar, a brand known for Nordic and runic imagery that has long been associated with Germany's far-right scene.
"Thor Steinar … maybe is a clearer sign than New Balance or Lonsdale that somebody is part of the scene," he said.
The company's original rune logo prompted police seizures after German authorities argued it resembled banned SS symbolism. Higher courts ruled in 2008 that displaying the logo was not punishable, according to Scheuble, and the company had by then introduced a replacement logo.

Nick Jonas has been on plenty of road trips — but none quite like this.
The actor and musician plays a prominent role in what is expected to be a significant and long-running campaign for sports-wagering giant DraftKings. In a new ad, Jonas and comedian Kevin Hart appear to take a massive road trip, visiting many different parts of the country. And while Jonas is no stranger to traversing the nation, often on a tour bus, he may not have been accustomed to the way it was done on the commercial’s set.
“When you’re shooting like that, the vehicle that you’re in is on a practical trailer. It can’t be on. Therefore, the air conditioning can’t be on at all,” Jonas recalls, even though he and Hart felt they were working during “one of the hottest days in New York, New Jersey, of the year.”
Popular on Variety
“We were both kind of kind of dying in the car, and the windows had to be rolled all the way up for it to look the right way for the camera shot,” Jonas recalls. “But we survived.”
And now, the payoff. Fans of NFL and the NBA are likely to see the commercial in various iterations for weeks. The campaign will continue throughout the football and basketball seasons, and DraftKings will also run additional creative featuring Chad Ochocinco and Carmelo Anthony. In addition to the national advertising, DraftKings expects to make promotional forays into local markets as well.
With sports wagering gaining approval in the bulk of the nation, except for 11 states including California, Texas, Georgia and Minnesota, companies like DraftKings and rivals such as FanDuel and BetMGM continue to move aggressively to court sports fans. Football aficionados are likely to encounter the DraftKings pitch week after week, so Jonas and Hart need to demonstrate winning chemistry.
Sports fans by this time expect to hear a lot from DraftKings during game time. The company spent approximately $69.5 million to advertise during NFL games in 2025, according to data from iSpot, a tracker of ad spending, and approximately $12.8 million to run commercials during NBA games last year. Some of the company’s most likable commercials in the past have relied on celebrities, according to iSpot, including Hart.
The goal of the ad effort is to help consumers understand that they can interact with DraftKings across the U.S., says Stephane Sherman, DraftKings’ chief marketing officer, during a recent interview. Thanks to the rise of prediction markets, DraftKings now offers services throughout the nation, not just in states that allow sports wagering.
“It is a real change for us from a business standpoint,” she says. The campaign will “invite more fans to be a part of the DraftKings experience.”
Entertainment fans have seen Jonas and Hart work together before, in two of the recent “Jumanji” movies. But the bet (no pun intended) here is that the push-and-pull of Hart, who often comes across with high energy and Jonas, who plays more of a straight man, will get audiences to focus more intently.
“We were trying to boil the ocean a little bit,” acknowledges Chaucer Barnes, chief marketing officer of Translation, the marketing agency that helped devise the commercials. DraftKings wants consumers to understand that the company now offers a broader array of services. “We need you to lean in because we actually have big news to deliver,” he says.
The hope is the actors keep things cool on screen, even if they navigated a little warmth behind the scenes.

A study by researchers from NIMHANS has found that peripheral inflammation may play a significant role in triggering brain inflammation and neurodegeneration in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP), a rare neurological disorder for which there is currently no disease-modifying treatment.
The findings, recently published in Frontiers in Immunology, provide fresh insights into how the disease develops and raise the possibility of identifying blood-based biomarkers that could improve diagnosis and potentially guide future therapeutic strategies, researchers said.
Understanding PSP
PSP is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by loss of balance, difficulty in walking, swallowing and speaking, as well as impairment of eye movements. Because many of its early symptoms overlap with Parkinson’s disease, it is frequently misdiagnosed during the initial stages. Although previous research has suggested that abnormal immune responses contribute to neurodegenerative diseases, the mechanisms through which inflammation outside the brain influences brain pathology have remained poorly understood.
The study, led by Monojit Debnath, professor of human genetics at NIMHANS, sought to bridge this knowledge gap by investigating inflammatory pathways both within the central nervous system and in the peripheral immune system.
Multi-pronged investigation
The researchers examined three major inflammatory pathways — the NLRP3 inflammasome, NF-κB pathway, and Th17 pathway — all of which are known to regulate immune responses. Using a multi-pronged approach, the team analysed inflammatory markers in peripheral blood and cerebrospinal fluid while simultaneously employing PET-MRI imaging to assess inflammation in the brain. The combined analysis demonstrated a clear association between inflammation in the peripheral immune system and neuroinflammation in patients with PSP.
The findings add to a growing body of evidence suggesting that several neurodegenerative disorders may not originate solely within the brain but may also involve immune processes occurring elsewhere in the body.
Hope for better diagnosis
Explaining the significance of the findings, Dr. Debnath told The Hindu that the study is the first to establish a direct connection between peripheral inflammation and brain inflammation in patients with Progressive Supranuclear Palsy. “Finding a definite and reliable biomarker in peripheral blood is the need of the hour for the accurate diagnosis of various neurodegenerative diseases, including PSP. Our study raises hope in that direction,” he said.
Dr. Debnath said the findings strengthen the hypothesis that the immune system outside the brain plays an active role in the disease process, especially in the ongoing neurodegeneration.
Ravi Yadav, professor of neurology at NIMHANS and a senior author of this study, emphasised that understanding the relationship between systemic inflammation and brain pathology could help researchers develop simpler and more accurate diagnostic tools based on blood samples. This reduces dependence on neurological investigations, which don’t have 100% diagnostic accuracy and sensitivity, Dr. Yadav said.
Disease mechanisms
The researchers said PSP is caused by degeneration of nerve cells in brain regions that control movement and cognition and is characterised by abnormal accumulation of tau protein. While rogue immune cells are believed to contribute to this process, the factors that trigger these abnormal immune responses have remained unclear. The present study suggests that inflammatory changes occurring in the peripheral immune system may influence immune activity within the brain, thereby contributing to neuronal damage and disease progression.
Further studies involving larger patient groups would be required to validate the findings and determine whether the identified inflammatory pathways could be targeted for future therapies, Dr. Debnath said.
The study adds to the growing body of research highlighting the role of systemic inflammation in neurodegenerative disorders and offers new directions for understanding, diagnosing and eventually treating Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, he added.

A new Man Utd era - but Fernandes still sets the standard
- Published
As Manchester United's home game with Ipswich Town drew to its conclusion, the skies went dark grey and the heavens opened.
Thunder and lightning accompanied a torrential downpour, followed by the obligatory pictures of rain pouring into the stadium through a leak in the roof.
It would have been a fitting metaphor for an awful afternoon for the Old Trafford hosts.
But this wasn't awful for United in the end, and for that a lot of credit must go to skipper Bruno Fernandes.
On a day when Marcus Rashford started his first Premier League game for the club since December 2024 and Kobbie Mainoo was also part of Michael Carrick's starting line-up, it was Fernandes who took centre stage.
A hat-trick in United's 5-2 win made the day all about him.
"What else can I say?" said head coach Carrick.
"We've said quite a lot about him already - and I've only been here six or seven months."
To sum up, the season started pretty badly for Fernandes, who was one of many players well below par in a shock 2-0 defeat at Hull City.
Matters improved significantly on Tuesday, as Fernandes collected the PFA Players' Player of the Year award for his phenomenal contribution to United returning to the Champions League after a two-year absence.
Last season, he totted up a Premier League record of 21 assists.
Before the Ipswich game, he walked on to the pitch with the sons of PC Matthew Blades, who was tragically killed in a recent head-on collision on the A66 near Middlesbrough.
Once the match began, Fernandes was largely anonymous as the home side went a goal down to Gary O'Neil's side.
But, when opportunity presented itself, Fernandes stepped up.
First, the 31-year-old fired home a blistering equaliser after Marcelino Nunez slipped under no pressure, presenting Matheus Cunha with a clear run at the Ipswich goal, which allowed him to set up his captain.
Fernandes then kept his cool to smash home a penalty in front of the Stretford End to make it 3-1 after an hour. Bearing in mind Fernandes missed two penalties in pre-season, there must have been a sizeable amount of personal pressure on the shot.
Fernandes completed his third United hat-trick seven minutes after that, although arguably all his previous efforts would have been overshadowed had he managed to find the net with an audacious 55-yard effort after Ipswich lost possession straight after the restart.
Goalkeeper Kjell Scherpen was backpedalling furiously and was relieved the ball ended up on top of his net rather than in it.
"He means a lot," said Carrick, when asked to sum up Fernandes' contribution.
"I mean, he's the captain. He's been here for a good number of years now and experienced a whole load of different emotions.
"Times like today, when you're looking towards certain players to give us that little bit of something else, he did particularly well."
'Huge hole at Man Utd without Bruno'
Not everything is straightforward around Fernandes, though.
He has entered the final year of his contract – United have the option to extend by another year – and while it is clear that interest from elsewhere in Europe, including from Turkish club Galatasaray, will not result in him leaving this month, he could justifiably say he should be the highest earner - a status that now belongs to Rashford.
The idea of Fernandes leaving, even at the age of 31, is not something many United fans would be comfortable with.
"He is the one that gets Manchester United ticking," former United and England wide man Ashley Young told Sky Sports. "There is a reason why he was voted player of the year by his fellow professionals and it's performances like this.
"He wants to be the best and he wants to win. He is huge for his club. If they don't have him, there is going to be a huge hole in this team."
At the final whistle, Fernandes' initial reaction was to talk to substitute Benjamin Sesko about a technical point around a pass he had been trying to find the striker with during injury time.
Fernandes then shook hands with opposing players and the officials and was heading off to find more opponents to greet when he realised he had forgotten to collect the match ball, his hat-trick reward.
He swiftly turned, asked, and referee Craig Pawson handed it over.
Without his contribution, Manchester United may well not have won this game - but then, you could have said that about a lot of games over the past couple of years.
"Obviously it was a huge week and to end with a win at home today was massive," Fernandes told BBC Sport.
"I said before the game to be honest; there are certain days you feel it. It is one of those days when everything comes to you and you have to take it.
"I hate losing and it is difficult to be positive when you lose games. It is very difficult for me to control the emotions.
"At this club you want to be on top of everything."

Salmonella is often linked to food poisoning, diarrhoea and typhoid. But the infection can range from mild gastroenteritis that gets better on its own to a serious bloodstream infection, and therefore, say experts, deserves more attention than it is currently being given. Typhoid also remains a major health burden in India. A Lancet study published this year, estimated 4.9 million typhoid cases and about 7,850 deaths in India in 2023. About 730,000 people were estimated to have been hospitalised, with fluoroquinolone-resistant infections accounting for 82% of these hospitalisations.
Salmonella is a group of bacteria that can cause different infections. Typhoid and paratyphoid or enteric fever, are caused by Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi. Unlike common food poisoning, typhoid can spread from the gut into the bloodstream, causing prolonged fever and, in severe cases, intestinal bleeding or perforation. It usually spreads through food or water contaminated with faeces The problem, however, is broader than typhoid. Non-typhoidal Salmonella infections, which often cause gastroenteritis, may go undiagnosed because many people recover without testing. At the same time, antibiotic resistance is making serious infections harder to treat.
Why infections turn serious
Non-typhoidal Salmonella commonly causes gastroenteritis, with diarrhoea, stomach cramps, fever and sometimes vomiting. It is often linked to poultry, eggs and other animal-based foods. Most healthy people recover with supportive care, but the infection can become serious and spread to the bloodstream, particularly in young children, older adults and people with weakened immunity.
“Salmonella should not be seen as only a cause of diarrhoea,” said Sweatha Kumar, associate consultant, infectious diseases, Rela Hospital, Chennai. “In some patients, especially young children, older adults and those living with other illnesses or weakened immunity, it can become invasive and life-threatening.”
Suresh Kumar D., senior specialist in infectious diseases, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, said the actual burden of non-typhoidal Salmonella is difficult to estimate as many mild infections are never diagnosed.
Contaminated water, food chain
Both typhoid and non-typhoidal Samonella infections spread through the faecal-oral route, but their sources are different.
For typhoid, humans are the reservoir. Someone with the infection, including someone who has no symptoms but carries the bacteria, can contaminate food or water. This makes safe drinking water, sanitation and hand hygiene central to prevention. Lack of access to safe water and adequate sanitation are major risk factors for typhoid.Non-typhoidal Salmonella has a wider ecology, involving animals, food and the environment. Poultry, eggs, meat and other animal-derived foods can be sources. Transmission can also occur when raw meat contaminates ready-to-eat food during preparation.
“Contamination can occur at multiple points, from farms, slaughterhouses and food processing to transportation, storage, restaurants and finally the household kitchen,” Dr. Sweatha said. “That is why Salmonella is very much a One Health problem involving humans, animals, food and the environment.”
Food handlers can play an important role in transmission, as those carrying the infection can contaminate food and potentially expose many people to the bacteria. But food safety cannot depend only on individual food handlers. The wider system needs better training, sanitation, refrigeration, monitoring and enforcement. While the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has surveillance and testing systems, gaps remain, particularly in the large informal food sector.
At the household level, it is important follow: washing hands, using safe water, cooking poultry and eggs thoroughly, refrigerating perishable foods appropriately and keeping raw meat separate from ready-to-eat food.
Challenges and way forward
The major concern is the growing antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella.
India has seen a major shift in the resistance pattern of S. Typhi. A recent study in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases said, culture-confirmed isolates from 1977 to 2024 found that fluoroquinolone resistance rose sharply, reaching 85% in 2015-19, and remains high despite a subsequent decline.
“The emergence and spread of extensively drug-resistant typhoid shows what can happen when resistance accumulates across multiple antibiotic classes,” Dr. Sweatha said, “It can leave clinicians with very limited treatment options.”
A study published in Indian Pediatrics found of an enteric fever outbreak in Thane between April and July 2025 found that 44 of 167 culture-proven cases 26.35% were resistant to ceftriaxone. Tanker-water supply was significantly associated with ceftriaxone resistance in the outbreak.
Researchers have also documented carbapenem-resistant S. Typhi carrying the blaNDM-5 resistance gene in India, highlighting the possibility of resistance emerging even to antibiotics generally reserved for difficult infections.
Experts say the answer is not to simply use stronger antibiotics. Blood culture is the main test for suspected typhoid and should ideally be done before antibiotics are started. The Widal test has limitations and should not be used alone to diagnose typhoid. For uncomplicated non-typhoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis, treatment mainly involves adequate fluids and electrolyte replacement. Antibiotics are usually reserved for severe or invasive infections and people at higher risk of complications.
“Giving an antibiotic for every fever is not harmless,” said J.S. Kumar, professor and head of general medicine, SRM Medical College Hospital & Research Institute, Chennai. “Unnecessary antibiotic use is one of the things that drives antimicrobial resistance.”
For typhoid, antibiotics are necessary, but the choice should be guided by the local resistance pattern and, where possible, culture and susceptibility results.
Prevention remains as important as treatment. The World Health Organization recommends typhoid conjugate vaccines for children from six months of age; however, this not yet part of India’s universal immunisation programme.
The challenge is to treat the infections that genuinely require antibiotics while preventing the infections that can be prevented in the first place.

Three years after a closely watched research misconduct investigation of Stanford’s then-president, Marc Tessier-Lavigne, led to his resignation, the prominent neuroscientist revealed new details this week from his research and travel in an attempt to refute allegations that he published fraudulent results and orchestrated a cover-up.
These allegations found new life this year with the release of “How to Rule the World,” a book by former Stanford Daily reporter Theo Baker, who presents Tessier-Lavigne as a case study in Silicon Valley’s culture of corner-cutting. A key part of that story revolves around a major paper on neurodegeneration that Tessier-Lavigne co-authored in 2009, while he was a top scientist at the South San Francisco biotech Genentech.
The former university head on Wednesday posted a more than 3,000-word response to the book on his Stanford lab website, alongside emails with former colleagues meant to bolster his defense of the study, published in the journal Nature.

FC Barcelona has reportedly agreed on a deal to sign Gabriel Jesus from Arsenal, with the Brazilian forward set to sign a two-year contract that includes an option to extend for an additional year, taking the deal through to 2029.
According to reports from the UK and Spain, his medical is scheduled on August 31 ahead of the permanent transfer.
Under the terms agreed upon, Arsenal is due to receive a 10 million euro package plus add-ons for the deal.
Gabriel Jesus made an immediate impact after joining Arsenal from Manchester City in July 2022, having previously worked under Mikel Arteta. He scored twice on his home debut, but a knee injury at the 2022 World Cup hampered his first season before he returned in April 2023 to net twice against Leeds.
In the 2023-24 season, despite having a knee surgery days before the Community Shield, he contributed eight goals and eight assists, shining in the Champions League with standout performances against Sevilla and RC Lens.
He also extended his remarkable record of never being on the losing side when scoring in a Premier League match (60 games: 55 wins, five draws at the start of the season).
In the 2024-25 season, Jesus hit form in December with five goals in four days against Crystal Palace, including a Carabao Cup hat-trick and two Premier League strikes. Another knee injury against Manchester United in the FA Cup third round, after scoring on New Year’s Day versus Brentford, ended his campaign early.

Medical expenses in Japan for fiscal 2025 rose 2.6% from the previous year to a record ¥49.2 trillion ($308 billion), reflecting the country’s aging population and advances in medical technology, according to preliminary data.
The expenses paid to medical institutions to treat diseases and injuries in the year through March 2026 increased for the fifth consecutive year, according to the data released by the health ministry Friday.
The pace of growth accelerated after slowing for three years in a row.
“The increased use of high-cost medications, such as anticancer drugs, was one contributing factor,” a ministry official said.
The data covered payments from the public health insurance system, other public expenses and out-of-pocket costs shouldered by patients. The preliminary figure accounted for roughly 98% of the total medical expenditures in the country.
Expenses for inpatient treatment climbed 2.3% to ¥19.6 trillion, while those for outpatient treatment rose 1.6% to ¥16.5 trillion. Costs to treat dental patients gained 3.5% to ¥3.5 trillion and drug-dispensing costs grew 3.9% to ¥8.8 trillion.
Per capita medical expenses amounted to ¥400,000, up 3.1%. Medical expenses for those age 75 or over averaged ¥989,000 — four times the average of ¥261,000 for those under 75.

Every Love Island cycle produces the same predictable arc: a finale, a flood of brand deals, and a cluster of influencer careers that rise fast and often fade faster. Season 8 of Love Island USA is breaking that pattern. As the cast heads into Monday's reunion special, several Islanders have used their newfound platforms to build something more durable than a sponsored post, moving into media ventures, entertainment deals, and campaign work that reads more like a career launch than a victory lap. Here are the standout marketing moves so far.
Melanie Moreno’s Substack Launch
Of everyone to come out of the villa this season, Melanie Moreno has made arguably the most unconventional play. Rather than defaulting to the usual influencer route, brand partnerships stacked on Instagram, she launched a Substack. It is a choice that runs against the grain of reality TV monetization, and it is a smart one.
A newsletter lets Melanie build a direct relationship with her audience rather than renting attention on platforms she does not control. She owns the list. She owns the data. And she is not at the mercy of an algorithm change or a platform outage that could sever her from her audience overnight, a real risk for creators whose entire businesses live on borrowed real estate. It also lets her go deeper than a 30-second clip allows, giving fans a more intimate, long-form view of who she is beyond the villa edit. In an ecosystem where most contestants chase the same short-term influencer churn, Melanie's Substack is a bet on longevity over quick engagement, and it is the kind of move other reality alumnae should be studying closely.
Jen Terry’s Playfully Provocative Photoshoot With Gal
Jen Terry and Gal Tshnieder's Casa Amor connection fell apart almost as fast as it began, but the two turned their post-villa reunion into one of the season's smartest pieces of content. Rather than avoiding the drama or litigating it in interviews, they leaned all the way in: a cheeky, high-fashion photoshoot at Gal's coffee shop that played directly on their public breakup, complete with Jen tossing a drink in Gal's face and, in one shot, tying him to a surfboard.
The concept worked because it did double duty. It gave fans the closure and comedy they wanted around the storyline, while also positioning Jen as a legitimate style presence with real editorial range, someone who can hold a concept and a camera, not just a ring light. The post pulled hundreds of thousands of likes on TikTok, proof that turning a villa storyline into a controlled, stylized moment outperforms simply hoping the discourse dies down.
Gal Tshnieder's Coffee Shop Marketing
Gal's run in the villa was brief, but his marketing instincts back home have been the season's best case study in localized, community-first brand-building. His Venice coffee shop, Saba Surf and Coffee, became a pilgrimage site for fans within days of his elimination, and instead of treating the attention as a distraction, Gal and his team built directly on top of it: watch parties, free drinks tied to storylines from the show, and a dunk tank that let fans literally dunk him during the finale watch party.
It is a sharp example of how to turn reality TV infamy into foot traffic rather than just follower counts. Gal's approach shows how a physical, local business can ride a viral moment without losing its identity, treating fans as customers to welcome into a real space rather than just an audience to broadcast at. The result was lines out the door, a local political commendation, and a business that converted attention into revenue in a way most post-villa deals never manage.
Kenzie Annis And Dylan Wrona's Use Of TikTok
Kenzie Annis and Dylan Wrona's relationship played out almost as much on TikTok as it did in the villa, and that visibility has carried directly into their post-show run. Their content together, appearances, red carpet moments, casual clips of them out in Los Angeles, has kept fans invested in their story past the finale, extending the shelf life of a couple that could otherwise have faded once the season ended.
What makes their approach notable is the consistency. Rather than treating TikTok as a place to post the occasional sponsored plug, they have used it to keep their relationship narrative alive in near real time, which is exactly the kind of ongoing engagement that brands look for when deciding which Islanders are worth a longer-term partnership rather than a single campaign.
Trinity Tatum's Verizon Campaign
Trinity Tatum's Verizon partnership is the clearest example this season of what patience can do for a personal brand. Rather than taking the first offer that came her way after her win, Tatum, who signed with WME shortly after the finale, waited for a global brand with the scale and creative ambition to match her platform.
The payoff was "Queen of Cash," a campaign built around Verizon's new rewards program and directed by Warren Fu, known for his work with major music artists. The spot reimagines Tatum as a modern-day queen, an extravagant, cinematic concept that gave her room to actually perform rather than simply hold up a product. It let her flex real acting range while still tying back to the glamorous, fashion-forward persona that made her a standout in the villa. Verizon's chief marketing officer, Leslie Berland, called the partnership central to the brand's launch of Verizon Dollars, and the selectivity behind it is the real lesson here: Tatum treated her first major deal as a brand decision, not just a payday, and it shows.
What We’re Waiting For, Heading Into The Reunion
Taken together, these moves suggest Season 8's breakout stars understand something that earlier casts have not always grasped: attention is only valuable if you know what to do with it. A Substack, a coffee shop dunk tank, and a Warren Fu-directed ad campaign have little in common on the surface, but each represents a deliberate choice to build something that outlasts the news cycle rather than chase it. As the cast reunites Monday for the first time since the finale, it will be worth watching whether these early moves translate into the kind of sustained careers that Love Island has historically struggled to produce, or whether they simply set the bar higher for the next season's Islanders to clear.

'That trust isn't there' - how does Iraola get best out of Isak?
- Published
During Liverpool's negotiations with Paris St-Germain for Bradley Barcola, the Anfield hierarchy were determined not to pay more than the club-record £125m they spent on Alexander Isak last summer.
When the £123m deal for Barcola is completed over the coming days, the France winger will become the 10th £100m player in Premier League history.
None have cost more than Isak, so the expectation on the former Newcastle striker is understandable, to say the least.
Isak scored 44 Premier League goals in his last two seasons at Newcastle, but in an injury-plagued first campaign at Anfield the 26-year-old found the back of the net just three times in 14 top-flight appearances.
For Andoni Iraola, who has drawn his first two games as Liverpool manager, a major part of success at Anfield will be the ability to get the best out of Isak, who - despite scoring - was largely ineffective in their 2-2 draw against Nottingham Forest on Saturday.
Unlike last summer, Isak has looked sharp in pre-season after some impressive displays for Sweden at the World Cup, but struggled on his return to Tyneside last weekend.
For 45 minutes against Forest on Saturday, those struggles continued with just six touches, one accurate pass and zero shots.
"It is clear that Liverpool haven't worked out how to play with Alexander Isak yet," said ex-England goalkeeper Joe Hart, who is a pundit on Saturday's Match of the Day.
"At Newcastle everything flowed through him. That was down to a trust thing that they had built up over time - their midfield knew exactly where he was and they didn't even need to look up as he'd be there waiting.
"At Liverpool that trust just isn't there at the moment - no-one is feeling it and he isn't that central point, which is leading to him looking lost and isolated."

'There's no doubting Isak's quality'
It would have been intriguing to be a fly on the wall in the directors' box at Anfield.
Iraola's first home Premier League game was watched by incoming Liverpool vice-chairman Amit Bhatia, principal owner John Henry, and sporting director Richard Hughes, who was integral in getting the deal for Isak done last summer.
Thankfully for them - and Iraola - Isak got Liverpool on level terms after the break. He managed just seven more touches in the second half but centre-forwards deal in goals and the Swede timed his run perfectly to meet Cody Gakpo's delivery for his first goal of the season. His smile after told a story in itself.
"That's the job ultimately as a striker [to score goals]. I am very happy to score the first one and hopefully it just keeps coming," Isak told TNT Sports.
Former Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard described the goal as "big" - for both the striker's confidence and the team's.
But, in Hart's opinion, Iraola still has a major conundrum.
"Andoni Iraola has some big decisions to make," said Hart. "Does he base his team round him [Isak] or does he try to find a different solution within his squad? In my opinion he's got to commit to what the club have done by investing so heavily in Isak.
"There's no point signing these players if you aren't going to use them properly and play to their strengths. There's no doubting Isak's quality - they are just at a bit of a crossroads at the moment."
During Isak's struggles last season, the belief inside the club was that he was a long-term signing and judgement would be reserved for once he was fully fit.
Only Erling Haaland, Mohamed Salah and Ollie Watkins have scored more Premier League goals since Isak's first season in England and, with Salah now out of the picture, the onus is on Isak to deliver - particularly with Hugo Ekitike out injured.
Iraola's possession problem
Liverpool's first two games of the season have finished 2-2 despite Iraola's side enjoying 60% of possession against Newcastle last week and 70% against Forest.
In both games, they have found themselves trailing and are yet to be ahead in the Premier League this season.
That has inevitably made things trickier for Isak, who was such a force in a counter-attacking Newcastle side. Against low blocks, the proposition is different.
It is also symptomatic of a wider issue Iraola faces.
Last season, his Bournemouth side won just four of the 19 Premier League games in which they had the majority of possession. They won nine of the other 19.
The Cherries, who were known for their counter-pressing style and effectiveness in transition, also failed to win a game in which they had more than 58.8% possession.
In essence, his side were more successful when they had less of the ball - something that will rarely happen now he is at Anfield.
"As an attacking force it isn't flowing for Liverpool," said Hart. "With the physical nature of the Premier League and with them not 100% sure on what they are doing at the moment, teams are stomping all over them.
"It's going to take a whole lot of work from Iraola and his staff on the training pitch, but he is a top coach and they have top players."
Asked about whether he sets targets for the season, Isak said: "Not really. I think every striker wants to score [in] every game he plays. Obviously that's difficult but [we take] each game at a time."
That is one way to look at it, and this was certainly an improvement on his showing against Newcastle, but deep down Isak will know he can - and must - do better.

Deaths reported after ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers capsizes off Cyprus
More than 172 people have been rescued, Northern Cyprus PM says.
BODRUM, Turkey -- At least seven people have died after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers and crew capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, Turkish media reported.
Some 237 people have been rescued, Northern Cyprus Prime Minister Unal Ustel told Turkish state-run TRT news channel. He said a search was underway for another 24 people.
Ustel said the ferry faced adverse weather conditions and began taking in water just 15 minutes after departure. A call for help was issued shortly after, he said.
The catamaran-style ferry was traveling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of ethnically divided Cyprus, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in Mersin province.
Kyrenia Mayor Murat Senkul said the ship belonged to the Filo Denizcilik ferry company and sank off the coast of Diana beach on Cyprus’ northern coast.
The ferry started taking in water about 7.5 kilometers (4 nautical miles) off the coast, TRT reported.
Video footage from the scene shows people with life-vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel.

Sir Billy Boston - 'the world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told'
- Published
When Sir Billy Boston was knighted in 2025, it was a unique moment for rugby league.
For the first time, this rebel sport from the north of England had been recognised in such a manner; one of its heroes had been acknowledged for their contribution to history through the game.
Sir Billy was a fitting recipient of the honour and a world class athlete, whose story deserved to be told.
You can tell the importance of someone by how many statutes have been erected in tribute, and Sir Billy Boston wasn't lacking.
His name was chosen as one of just five to grace Wembley's monument to rugby league's Challenge Cup, while years after his departure north, his home city of Cardiff also ensured his legacy remained cast-iron strong as he formed part of a three-man tribute along with Clive Sullivan and Gus Risman.
Unsurprisingly, Boston is also captured in bronze in his adopted home of Wigan; the place where his legend really came to life.
Born and brought up in Cardiff's ethnically-eclectic Tiger Bay district, he learned his rugby skills on the streets and with the talent factory-esque Cardiff International Athletic Club.
Like all Welsh lads he harboured dreams of playing for his local club Cardiff RFC and hopefully the national team.
Like others before and after for a time, Boston found those routes blocked, having to travel to Neath and Pontypridd to trial before his military service took him north.
It was here where the league scouts came calling, and Wigan persuaded Boston to turn professional in 1953, forever ending his union dreams in the time of 'sine die' penalties for liaising with league personnel.
The money was life changing.
£3,000 could easily buy a house at that stage, while it proved money well spent as he took to the new code like a duck to water, scoring with his first touch in a Wigan A team game.
This prime specimen of Welsh breezeblock had everything; he was quick, he could step and as former player and BBC commentator Ray French put it - his fend was like "being hit in the face with shovel".
The sepia footage and slow shutter speeds of the cameras that captured his magic during his playing days simply cannot dull his brilliance.
Whether it was bustling over for another try in cherry and white hoops at Wembley or crushing the Aussies at Sydney Cricket Ground, Boston was a blur of speed, footwork and power.
Having swiftly progressed to the first team at Central Park, he would go on to score 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan, and tales of his feats would be passed down through generations. There are very few down at the Brick Community Stadium these days who don't know of Sir Billy, young or old, his name carried a cache right until his last.
Great Britain gave him the international recognition denied to him by Wales, and he rewarded the selectors by racking up the tries, particularly against the Australians who would bear the brunt of his scoring ability.
He scored 36 tries alone on his maiden Great Britain tour, dazzling both Australia and New Zealand in 1954 under captain and fellow Welshman Dickie Williams.
Boston was a phenomenal rugby league player, but there is also a powerful message in how in post-war Britain a black athlete could become a hugely popular figure by communities adjusting to a new, more diverse world.
Others like Roy Francis beforehand, Johnny Freeman, and Colin Dixon, also became established names, but never quite sprinkled the same stardust as Sir Billy.
It paved the way for players such as Ellery Hanley and Martin Offiah to charm the public with their talents, while modern day talent such as Junior Nsemba and Kai Pearce-Paul continues to stand out in a sport which has broken down barriers for years.
Sir Billy had a unique unifying effect on a normally partisan and tribal rugby league community.
He was revered naturally in Wigan, his adopted home, but you won't hear a boo or jeer at mention of Boston anywhere - not even at sworn rivals St Helens where they appreciate a good footballer when they see one.
Still a regular visitor to Wigan games right up to his passing, it was always a beautiful moment when the cameras found him, the crowd spotting him on the screen bursting into cheer, and the realisation creeping over his face in the shape of a smile.
There was a photo of him and his wife Lady Joan, who had died just a few weeks previously, on her seat with flowers at Wigan's game with Wakefield last week. There is a poignancy that Sir Billy departed soon after her.
His seat will always be reserved at Wigan, and he will be dearly missed but certainly not forgotten.

A Ukrainian manufacturer developed a roving turret with two Kalashnikov assault rifles for its main armament, as Kyiv aims to build more cheap ground drones to fill dangerous infantry roles.
The uncrewed ground vehicle was recently used in combat by the Security Service of Ukraine's Alpha Group special forces to destroy a Russian ambush drone, said the country's defense tech incubator, Brave1, on Thursday.
"Why the Kalashnikov? The reason is simple: It's the most widely available small arm across our military units," the incubator wrote in a social media post, adding that using the assault rifle allowed its forces to "rapidly scale" the drones on the front lines.
Neither the drone nor the manufacturer was named, though Brave1 said the drone's creator is a member of its platform. The Kalashnikov design was built for a technical brief issued by Brave1.
More than five Ukrainian units are operationally testing the drone, Brave1 added.
Footage of the turret shows the two Kalashnikov rifles mounted closely to each other on a frame attached to a pan-and-tilt gimbal, which in turn rests on a four-wheeled platform.
Each rifle appears to be modified behind the grip and trigger guard to remotely receive fire commands, though no other significant tweaks are visible.
Notably, Brave1 showed clips of a person manually reloading one of the Kalashnikovs with a box magazine and then racking the bolt, indicating that the turret's current design still requires a soldier nearby to help it stay in a prolonged fight.
Ukraine has been developing uncrewed ground vehicles for all manner of tasks, including ground assault, artillery cover, casualty evacuation, mine-clearing, and logistics for years.
They've been a major, though not complete, solution for its shortage of soldiers on the front lines and forward areas, which have become saturated with drones and deadly to cross or navigate.
The new Kalashnikov turret points to a Ukrainian emphasis on building cheaper, simpler systems to be built quickly for the war.
"We are scaling cheap combat UGVs and robotizing the front line to reduce risks to our infantry," Brave1 said in its post.

MAS commits S$220 million to accelerate innovation in the fintech sector: Gan Kim Yong
The fourth iteration of the scheme will be implemented through six tracks spanning institutional innovation, AI adoption, infrastructure and platforms and talent development.
 
SINGAPORE: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will commit S$220 million (US$173 million) to accelerate innovation in the fintech sector, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong on Monday (Aug 31).
To be spread over three years, the investment is part of a renewed fourth iteration of the Financial Sector Technology and Innovation (FSTI) scheme aimed at strengthening Singapore's position as a vibrant and competitive fintech hub.
To this end, the scheme aims to develop technology infrastructure to position the financial sector to adopt new technology solutions and support talent development and attraction for the industry, MAS said in a press release.
MAS said the scheme will help build a "pipeline of young talent for Singapore's fintech ecosystem" by co-funding internship stipends, aiming to support at least 1,000 fintech internship opportunities over the next three years. Singaporeans can qualify for this scheme.
MAS also seeks to anchor and scale innovation activities in Singapore and accelerate financial technologies, with a focus on frontier technologies, the central bank added.
“Taken together, these efforts will help our financial institutions, fintech firms, and workers innovate, scale, and build the capabilities to seize the emerging opportunities,” said Mr Gan, who is also the Minister for Trade and Industry and the MAS chairman.
He added that the government has been consulting the financial industry and fintech companies to get feedback to identify gaps and needs, and will continue to engage the industry to refine and improve the scheme.
The first version of the scheme was started in 2015 by MAS. Since then, more than 350 fintech projects have been supported under the programme.
Mr Gan said the scheme has helped to build a “very strong ecosystem” for fintech and the financial industries.
He noted that Singapore has more than 1,800 fintech companies, many of which have already ventured into the region as well as served the world market.
The industry also employs some 10,000 people, he said.
“And last year, in 2025, we have already seen a total investment of close to S$3 billion in fintech alone. So I think the momentum will continue, and we hope that FSTI 4.0 will continue to provide that boost to the fintech industry,” he said.
MANPOWER SUPPORT
The latest iteration of the scheme, FSTI 4.0, will be implemented through six tracks spanning institutional innovation, AI adoption, infrastructure and platforms and talent development, MAS said.
Apart from co-funding internship stipends over the next three years, MAS announced a new FinTech Internship Portal, fintechinternships.sg, which is managed by the Singapore FinTech Association (SFA).
The portal will connect fintech firms with students from Institutes of Higher Learning for internships across business, technology and other roles.
Mr Gan said building a pipeline of talent is “particularly critical” in the fintech industry because it is emerging.
“Not only is it a new industry, it is also evolving very rapidly with the emergence of AI and frontier technologies," he said.
"You can imagine that the talent that we need, the capability we need to build, is going to be very critical for the growth of this sector, and that's why we want to invest in building our people, in giving them the skills and knowledge so that they are able, well-positioned to seize the opportunities where they emerge,” he said.
The fintech sector has been facing a talent crunch and high attrition rates.
SFA's 2025 talent report said the industry is facing “significant shortages” of talent in AI, data science, cybersecurity and cloud architecture. Issues include a long time-to-hire, high compensation expectations and high attrition when career development or compensation is insufficient.
FRONTIER TECH
Apart from manpower issues, other tracks in the scheme include the Institution Project Track, which will support Singapore-based financial institutions and fintech firms in developing and deploying innovative solutions.
MAS said it will focus on frontier technologies such as AI, distributed ledger technology and quantum technology.
The AI Pathfinder track will help accelerate adoption of market-tested AI solutions listed on PathFin.ai and drive sector-wide AI use across financial services, the central bank added.
The infrastructure and platform track supports industry-wide infrastructure and platforms that improve sector efficiency, productivity and innovation.
Meanwhile, the Centre of Excellence track aims to anchor high-value functions of financial institutions and fintech firms in Singapore.
It will bring together specialised talent and expertise, while supporting the growth of emerging technologies such as AI, quantum computing and digital assets.
The MAS FinTech Awards track aims to raise Singapore's global profile as a fintech hub through the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF) FinTech Excellence Awards and the Global FinTech Hackcelerator (GFH).
As a new enhancement, MAS will introduce the GFH Scale-up Grant to further develop and validate eligible finalists’ solutions after the competition and help them attract private investment, scale their business and strengthen their presence in Singapore.
Since the scheme's inception, more than S$3.8 billion of funding has been raised by GFH finalists, and more than 30 Centres of Excellence have been established, said MAS.
BUILDING A FINTECH ECOSYSTEM
In the previous iteration of the scheme, FSTI 3.0, MAS committed S$150 million over three years, between 2023 and 2026.
The scheme similarly comprised tracks that supported Centres of Excellence and introduced new tracks on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) fintech and quantum technology.
It also supported advanced capability development and adoption in areas such as artificial intelligence and data analytics, regulatory technology and industry-wide projects.
Under the Centre of Excellence track, MAS had provided up to 50 per cent and 25 per cent co-funding on manpower expenses for qualifying roles for Singapore Citizens and non-citizens, respectively, for a period of 24 months.
The second iteration of FSTI involved a commitment of S$250 million between 2020 and 2023, and broadened digital adoption across the financial sector. It also provided critical support during COVID-19 by helping smaller financial institutions pivot to remote working.
MAS committed S$225 million between 2015 and 2020 through the first iteration of the scheme.
It established the foundational ecosystem to build Singapore's reputation as a leading fintech hub, introduced tracks like Proof-of-Concept and Innovation Labs to kickstart early-stage innovation and laid the groundwork for public-good utilities and infrastructure.
Asked whether the upgraded version of the scheme can help Singapore better compete with other regional financial hubs such as Hong Kong, Mr Gan said the financial industry is not a “zero-sum game”.
"I think as we get better, Hong Kong and other financial centres will also get better. And as they get better, we want to make sure that we get even better. And I think this FSTI 4.0 will help to spur innovation in the local financial sector and FinTech sector," he said.
"And hopefully, with this, it will keep Singapore's financial sector and fintech industries continue to be very competitive, and as we do better, many of the innovation, many of the solutions will also benefit the financial industries in this region."

A Peaceful Detective Mystery to Watch
Culture and entertainment recommendations including The Sheep Detectives, the Hold Steady, and more
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Lily Meyer, a staff writer who has published stories about the wisdom of Holden Caulfield, why making America’s houses bigger may have been a mistake, and the Seinfeld theory of fiction.
Lily recommends watching The Sheep Detectives for a heartwarming mystery, listening to any song by the Hold Steady, and reading Brother of the More Famous Jack, by Barbara Trapido, if you want a good cry and a laugh.
— Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor
A good recommendation I recently received: My friend Eliza Brooke—a freelance culture writer who often covers movies—told me to watch The Sheep Detectives, which I had assumed was for children, but I trust her. I was absolutely charmed by the film and, at the same time, quite moved by its exploration of how we think and talk about death. Also, it’s a whodunit, and I love whodunits. Hollywood, could we please have fewer sequels and prequels and remakes, and more peaceful detective stories?
The upcoming arts event I’m most looking forward to: I can’t wait to see the Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock show opening at the Met this October. I love abstract expressionism, and ever since I read Mary Gabriel’s Ninth Street Women—an exceptional group biography of five abstract expressionist painters, including Krasner—I’ve been fascinated by the arc of her career, which included creating government-sponsored public art during the Depression, making mosaics in the Long Island house she and Pollock shared during their marriage (meanwhile, he got an entire barn as a studio), and the flowering of her own painting practice after his death. Of course I’m excited to see the Pollock paintings at the Met too, but I’m most eager to see the Krasners.
An actor I would watch in anything: Greta Gerwig. I saw Frances Ha, the gorgeous, bittersweet ode to female friendship that she starred in and co-wrote, a few weeks after I graduated from college—that is, at a moment when I was heartbroken about no longer living with my closest female friends—and I imprinted on her like a baby duck.
The best work of nonfiction I’ve recently read: Vivian Gornick’s The Romance of American Communism. Gornick, a “red-diaper baby” raised in the working-class Jewish Bronx, set out to interview former Communist Party USA members and militants about what their political activity meant to them, years after the party had lost most of its following. The result is a surprisingly beautiful and often wrenching reflection on belief, belonging, self-delusion, and sacrifice.
An author I will read anything by: Too many to name, so instead, I’ll give you a translator. I try to read—and believe I have read—everything that Megan McDowell translates. Her taste is impeccable, her style is flawless, and she works with some of the greatest Latin American authors writing today: Mariana Enríquez, Samanta Schweblin, Alejandro Zambra, and many more.
A quiet song that I love, and a loud song that I love: “It’s Gonna Be Easy,” by the Texas outlaw-country singer Doug Sahm, is a soft, melodic lament for a relationship the singer wishes would be easier to forget. (A recommendation to go with it: Callie Collins’s novel Walk Softly on This Heart of Mine, whose protagonist is loosely inspired by Sahm. Like the song, the book is a gentle heartbreaker.)
A loud song is “Waiting Room,” by my D.C. hometown heroes Fugazi. My husband and I asked the DJ to play it at our wedding, and the resulting mini–mosh pit is one of my favorite memories of the night.
A musical artist who means a lot to me: The Hold Steady. I’ve been going to their shows since I was 14, and seeing them live is the closest I’ve ever come to a religious experience. Hold Steady fans are real diehards, and the band’s lead singer, Craig Finn, believes fervently that—as he shouts at every single show—“we are all the Hold Steady.” He’s right: We are.
Something I recently revisited: I’m revealing a lot about my high-school self here, but one of my absolute favorite novels as a teenager was Chang-rae Lee’s Aloft, whose hero, Jerry Battle, is a New Jersey dad hiding from his emotions about family and aging by flying private planes. I revisited it before reviewing Lee’s new novel, A Tender Age, and was relieved that I loved it even more than I did at 15.
A favorite story I’ve read in The Atlantic: I’m not sure if “favorite” is the right word here, but Spencer Kornhaber’s essay about the singer Lizzo and her downward mobility has been haunting me since I read it. Spencer, I want you to know that introducing me to the concept of the Khia Asylum was not nice!
Something delightful introduced to me by a kid in my life: My toddler recently became obsessed with the book Chirri & Chirra, written and illustrated by Kaya Doi and translated from Japanese by Yuki Kaneko. It is so delightful. Doi’s illustrations are lovely, and the heroines’ sweet little adventure through the forest is a dream day. At the end, Chirri and Chirra go to a forest concert, and my daughter loves to sing “La-la-la” along with me as I read—it’s the best.
The last thing that made me cry: Brother of the More Famous Jack, by Barbara Trapido. It’s a sharp, generous tale of yearning and innocence, and its descriptions are my favorite kind, economical and precise. Its plot twist made me cry, but so did the intensity and joy of its narrator’s longing.
The last thing that made me snort with laughter: Also Brother of the More Famous Jack. I’m telling you, you need to read this book.

The Week Ahead

- Season 2 of The Gentlemen, a crime-comedy series about an aristocrat and his partner expanding their criminal empire into Italy (streaming Thursday on Netflix)

Essay
We’re Living in the World Dolly Parton Built
By Spencer Kornhaber
Dolly Parton’s death at age 80 comes at a time when her influence seems at its peak. Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences seem hungry for honest idiosyncracy—for figures who, like Dolly, transmit their inner truth to mass audiences in a voice that’s clear yet scraggly. But Parton’s greatest legacy is existential in nature. Piling on wigs and feathers, she showed that you can be yourself while playing a character.
