Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has defended her government’s highly controversial energy deal with Donald Trump, insisting the South American country will maintain ownership and sovereignty over its massive oil reserves.
Rodríguez, who assumed power in January after Trump ordered the abduction of the president, Nicolás Maduro, took to the airwaves on Saturday to push back against criticism of what the US president has called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
“The benefits are endless,” claimed Rodríguez, a former vice-president whom Trump backed after ordering Maduro’s capture during a special forces raid on the capital, Caracas.
During a six-minute television broadcast, Venezuela’s acting leader claimed the deal would help her resource-rich country develop its economy, earn revenues of more than $209bn (£154bn), and become “an energy powerhouse”.
Rodríguez said: “As everyone knows, our country has the biggest oil reserves in the world. But having resources underground isn’t enough. We need investment, technology, infrastructure [and] production capacity to convert this wealth into wellbeing for our people.”
She added: “It’s no use having our oil reserves underground, only to appear in statistics or bookkeeping … and for us not to be able to convert and translate them into development for Venezuela.”
Trump announced the “groundbreaking” deal on Friday, calling it a “historic transaction [that] more than doubles American oil reserves … while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity”.
On Sunday, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan Oil is fill up the Strategic National Reserves which, because of Sleepy Joe Biden, has been virtually emptied.”
Trump added: “The ‘topping out’ process will begin very shortly, and is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.”
Hours after seizing Maduro on 3 January, Trump warned Rodríguez she would face an even worse fate if she failed to toe the US line. “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” Trump said.
Details of the agreement – struck during months of secret talks – remain sparse but it will reportedly see Washington take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.
The South American country has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn. Rodríguez said the deal involved 17 “strategic oilfields” where it was hoped more than 1.5m barrels could be produced each day.
But the deal has provoked outrage, both among members of Venezuela’s opposition and within the Chavismo political movement of which Rodríguez is part.
Speaking on Friday, one prominent opposition figure, who asked not to be named, called the agreement “a massive land grab” by a “rapacious, mafioso United States”.
Writing on X, Rafael Ramírez, the former head of Venezuela’s state-owned oil company PDVSA, accused Rodríguez’s administration of “driving a dagger straight into the heart of the homeland” with the “neocolonial” transaction. “They are handing over 65bn barrels of our reserves to the United States. That has never happened in Venezuela, and I think nowhere else in the world,” Ramírez added in an interview with the newspaper El Nacional.
On Saturday, dozens of leftwing protesters marched through Caracas with banners reading: “We are neither a colony, nor a back yard” and “Yankees go home!”
Critics of the agreement shared an ironic meme on social media suggesting the state oil company’s name should be changed from PDVSA to “PDUSA”.
In her broadcast, Rodríguez, the daughter of a Marxist guerrilla who spent years denouncing “imperialist” attempts to snatch her country’s oil reserves, countered claims she was surrendering Venezuela’s natural resources to a foreign power. She thanked Trump and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, for striking the deal but added: “There is something that must be made absolutely clear: Venezuela retains the ownership and sovereignty over its resources.”
“We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” claimed the politician, whose country was plunged into authoritarian rule and one of the world’s worst peacetime economic crises during Maduro’s 13-year rule.
The deal represents an astonishing U-turn from Rodríguez and the socialist, anti-imperialist political movement she and Maduro inherited from Hugo Chávez after his death in 2013.
In one 2024 speech, footage of which circulated on social media after Friday’s announcement, Rodríguez lambasted the Venezuelan opposition, accusing it of seeking to surrender the country’s oil, natural gas and gold reserves to its “masters” in Washington.
Last September, as the US tightened the screws on Maduro, Rodríguez told the New York Times: “The Pentagon always had a strategic objective of obtaining Venezuelan reserves.”
The deal will reportedly involve the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, which channels funds into projects seen as important for national security. It will also involve a private company owned by Alejandro Betancourt, a controversial UK-based tycoon who has emerged as a key intermediary between the Trump administration and Rodríguez.
Opposition politicians fear the deal will scupper attempts to recover Venezuela’s democracy and hold fresh presidential elections. Maduro is widely believed to have stolen the last vote, in 2024, and Rodríguez has deflected questions about a future election, saying vaguely that it will happen “some day”. Trump has also said Venezuela is “not really ready” for elections.
Writing on X, the opposition leader Juan Pablo Guanipa, said: “The only way to truly reactivate the Venezuelan economy in the long term and make this agreement benefit both parties is through a free election that leads to a representative government, clear rules of the game, rule of law, and institutions that allow our resources to be managed transparently and for the benefit of the nation.”
Without that, the energy deal was like “a skyscraper [built] on pillars of clay”, Guanipa added.

WASHINGTON — Vaping company Juul Labs on Friday received federal permission to sell an updated version of its e-cigarette, which includes an optional age-verification system designed to prevent underage use.
The decision from the Food and Drug Administration allows the company to sell a new version of its top-selling vaping device for the first time since it launched more than a decade ago. In recent years, the company has had to lay off hundreds of employees while paying roughly $3 billion to settle government and private lawsuits over teen use of its products.
Juul plans to market the new device under the brand name Juul2, along with updated versions of its tobacco- and menthol-flavored cartridges. In 2019, the company discontinued several flavors, including mango, mint and creme, that drove most of its sales but were favored by teens.
In a statement Friday, Juul CEO K.C. Croswaite said the company plans to market its new system with “a portfolio of flavors — beyond tobacco and menthol — that are targeted to adult nicotine consumers.”
The latest announcement is not an approval or endorsement, and people who do not smoke should not use Juul or any other e-cigarettes, according to regulators. The FDA determination indicates that smokers who switch completely to Juul can reduce their exposure to deadly carcinogens and other chemicals found in traditional cigarettes.
According to company studies reviewed by the FDA, between 20% to 50% of smokers who used Juul products were able to stop smoking at the end of six weeks. The rates of quitting varied based on the flavors and nicotine strengths used.
The new device also gives users the option to require age verification via an online app before the e-cigarette can be unlocked.
The FDA has authorized a handful of e-cigarettes to help adult smokers quit or cut back on cigarettes. In May, the FDA OK’d the first fruit-flavored electronic cigarettes intended for adult smokers. The approval represented a major policy shift and came after months of appeals to President Donald Trump from the vaping industry.
Juul is no longer the top-selling e-cigarette brand in the U.S. and trails Vuse, which is sold by tobacco giant Reynolds American. Reynolds also makes Camel and Newport cigarettes.
Teens have shifted away from Juul as part of a wider drop in vaping, according to federal figures. Teens who continue to vape mostly use unauthorized disposable e-cigarettes imported from China, which come in fruit and candy flavors.

Why Chelsea need more than a new goalkeeper to be title challengers
- Published
Just five hours after having his much-anticipated signing confirmed by Chelsea, Emiliano Martinez was walking out at Stamford Bridge to play for his new team against Brighton.
Having been thrown straight into the starting XI by manager Xabi Alonso, however, it quickly became clear that he alone cannot solve their defensive problems.
The 33-year-old said he was "fit and ready" to play despite his £7.5m signing from Aston Villa being announced so close to kick-off.
In reality, the Argentina international had already trained with his new team-mates after completing his move before Friday's registration deadline, with public confirmation delayed for marketing reasons.
There was little blame attached to the goalkeeper for any of the three goals conceded in their 4-3 victory, unlike on Monday, when Robert Sanchez was clearly at fault for the first goal, and arguably the second, in Chelsea's 3-2 win at Fulham.
Either way, that is now five goals conceded in two games. Their impressive new-look attack is the reason, despite the leaky defence, they have a 100% record nonetheless.
"A win is a win," Martinez told Sky Sports after his debut. "I know it wasn't a perfect game. But in the end, winning and moving on is what we need.
"I am here for a reason. The front three is amazing. When we go forward, we can hurt teams. We had a lot of chances to finish the game. Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro had chances to kill the game. At the back, we need to bring the goals down."
Ex-Premier League goalkeeper Shay Given, who is a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, described Martinez as a "brilliant signing".
"Martinez is interesting," Given told BBC Sport. "He's only just signed but Alonso's thought 'I'm not messing about, I'm getting him straight in the team'. The manager clearly thinks he needs someone of that sort of stature."
It was, ultimately, victory in chaos, but Alonso will need to find a way to control matches if Chelsea are to become title challengers, with a trip to Arsenal next.
Will Martinez improve Chelsea?
Martinez is a two-time Fifa Best Goalkeeper winner and can point to those individual honours having helped Argentina win the World Cup in 2022 and, more recently, Aston Villa lift the Europa League in May.
"I am happy with his first impact," said Alonso after the win over Brighton.
"He has been in the building for 48 hours so now we will have the whole week to prepare for the next one and day by day we will feel his presence because he has this charisma, this aura to influence and to have a very positive connection with the rest of the team."
By contrast, Sanchez had not won any major silverware before joining Chelsea from Brighton for £25m in 2023.
Both statistically and through the eye test, Sanchez compares favourably with many goalkeepers, which is why Chelsea head of goalkeeping Ben Roberts retained faith in him for so long.
However, Sanchez has proved prone to errors, particularly during the 2024-25 season, and temporarily lost his place to Djordje Petrovic, now at Bournemouth, and Filip Jorgensen, now at Strasbourg, before regaining the starting role.
Despite making only one error leading to a goal last season, compared with three by Martinez at Villa, Sanchez is now considered available for transfer and has fallen to fourth in the goalkeeping pecking order at Stamford Bridge.
Asked what will happen to Sanchez, Alonso said: "We will see. Sometimes you have to take tough decisions."
It is a ruthless outcome for the Spain international, who was backed publicly by Alonso and privately by senior figures at the club before they changed course.
A closer look at last season's statistics suggests Martinez produced stronger underlying numbers than Sanchez despite making more errors leading to goals.
Martinez conceded fewer goals, recorded a higher save percentage, prevented more goals relative to the quality of shots faced and posted significantly better passing accuracy.
The Argentine has already won over a lot of supporters, asking John Terry for permission to wear the number 26 shirt at Chelsea.
"I spoke with Chelsea legends John Terry and Petr Cech," he said. "I know how big this club is and what we want to achieve this season. I came here to help.
"I have come here to challenge and to try and win the Premier League. I trained only one day with the team. The guys have treated me really well in the last day or two. I know the talent we have up front. I try to bring that solidity in the back."
Plenty to worry about for Alonso
Alonso will be concerned by his side's struggles to keep possession and their vulnerability from set-pieces.
Remarkably, Chelsea recorded 25.9% possession against Brighton, the lowest in a league match managed by Alonso across his spells at Chelsea, Bayer Leverkusen and Real Madrid.
They also completed just 146 passes, Chelsea's lowest figures on record (beginning in 2003-04) in a Premier League match.
That inability to keep the ball comes as Enzo Fernandez's exile from the first team entered a second match, with Manchester City expected to make a bid before Tuesday's transfer deadline.
The Blues also had concerns over Moises Caicedo's fitness, and he was forced off just 11 minutes into his substitute appearance.
Malo Gusto and Romeo Lavia started in central midfield, while Jordan Henderson was also unavailable through injury and Valentin Barco was seemingly not yet trusted to start a Premier League match.
It is no surprise Chelsea are exploring a move for Monaco's Lamine Camara and want to ensure a replacement is lined up should Fernandez join City in a deal expected to be worth more than £120m.
A lack of midfield protection, coupled with a switch to a back three after largely operating with a back four last season, left centre-backs Wesley Fofana, Maxence Lacroix and Levi Colwill looking vulnerable at times.
Chelsea have scored a remarkable seven goals in their opening two league matches but have also conceded five. They have now gone 18 games without a clean sheet, their longest such run since the 1960s.
In typical fashion, Alonso played down any concerns that his side almost threw away a three-goal lead.
"No, I would say it is quite normal," he said. "It happens in many teams, other teams that they have already worked for and they are together and they have more games together."

In Summary
- Instagram has announced a new feature for its app, called First Draft. Available only for iPhone users at the time of writing, it trims and blends selected videos, converting them into a reel within seconds.
- Although First Draft’s editing is on the basic side, it is nevertheless extremely useful for those newcomers (or even veterans) who are not comfortable with editing videos.
- Experts might find First Draft to be very basic, but its ease of use and speed make it perfect for content creators who feel held back by their lack of basic video editing ability.
Instagram has just rolled out a new feature, which it claims is going to make creating Reels easier. As its name suggests, First Draft basically gives users a quick “first draft” by turning all the video clips that they have selected into a quick Reel. The feature is an iPhone exclusive for now and only available on the main Instagram app, and not on Edits (the Reels editing app by Instagram), but an Android release is likely to follow soon.
Given all the AI hype and how much Meta is focusing on it, you might think First Draft is a new AI feature, but Instagram has confirmed that First Draft does not use Artificial Intelligence. Nevertheless, it has made people wonder if its ease of use could actually reduce the role of conventional, “manual” editing in the Reel world. Well, we have used the feature for a short while, and here is what we think.
How to use Instagram First Draft
Using First Draft is a pretty simple affair. Just follow these steps:
- Open the Instagram app on your iPhone (do remember to update it to the latest version), then tap on the “+” icon present on the top left side of the app to add new content.
- From there, swipe to Reels on the panel on the lower part of the app.
- Tap on the camera to record footage or select an existing video from your gallery, which will be displayed.
- Once you have selected all the clips you wish to add, look for the First Draft option, which will appear on the panel at the lower part of the app – it appears the moment you select a video. Tapping it will open a First Draft box, with a “Try it” button. Tap on this button.
- Hitting the button puts the selected videos into a processing phase where the app analyses the clips, identifies highlights, trims clips, and reduces the length.
- In a matter of ten seconds, the feature will present a pretty basic edited version of your videos, trimming them and cutting out awkward pauses, with preview frames beneath the result, which you can move back and forth to reorder.
- If you like the results, tap on the Next button in the bottom right corner of the app to go to the Instagram Reels posting page (you can also take your results to Edits), make more changes, if need be, and hit Publish.
How First Draft works
Instagram has stressed that the new editing feature is just a “starting point” on which creators can then build their final Reel. The social media platform says the feature can identify silences, awkward pauses, and other such moments. It then removes these moments, trims the video, and gives a first draft that highlights what it assumes are important parts of the video. It allows creators to select or record, edit, and share all without leaving Instagram.
Instagram has been ensuring that users know that all that is done by the feature is reversible, and does not come as an attempt to replace a creator’s creativity, but actually offers ‘early video trimming’ so users can move their focus from the technical part of editing to its creative part. Instead of using AI (which comes as a surprise), First Draft actually uses internal processing and audio detection to find moments of silence in selected videos. We have fiddled with the feature for a short while and can say that it actually works,serving up a very basic edit of videos (or of a single long video), even while leaving the “creative work” to the user.
Going by our first encounter with First Draft, it cannot really replace manual editing. It is not a very creative feature and only offers what can be termed as the ‘bare-bones’ of what your edited Reel might look like. We found the feature does eliminate pauses and silence, but when it trims videos, there seems to be no method to its madness, which basically means you can end up with some of the important bits removed from the video. In its current form, it might come in handy for people who create piece-to-camera video formats, but you would still need to revise and re-edit the whole thing on your own.
Also See: Instagram Edits vs CapCut: Best Video Editing App for You
First Draft: Who is it for (and who might not like it)
It is rather basic, but those who are new to creating videos and struggle with editing might find First Draft useful. It offers a very quick, hassle-free edit of videos. This can be helpful for creators who are not as skilled when it comes to editing their content, or are intimidated by the task. First Draft can be a very simple, quick-fix solution for them. But it is unlikely to appeal much to those creators who have been in the game for a while, are good at editing, and have their own style and flair in the editing field. We can already see them skipping this new feature.
But given that a large number of Instagram users do not really know much about video editing, First Draft seems to be an extremely handy tool, especially for those who do not want to get into the hassle of going through all their videos one by one and trimming out stutters and pauses. The fact that one can do so right from within Instagram, without having to open an additional app, is a huge bonus. As mentioned by the platform itself, First Draft is just a starting point and nothing more. Even in its current form (and we think it will get better in clip selection), it will help new creators start their content journey and feel more comfortable without getting knee-deep in editing hassles from the get-go.
Experts might shake their heads at how basic the feature is, but then remember how DSLR photographers shook their heads at 0.3 MP cellphone cameras? First Draft might be the first step to breaking down the editing barrier that holds back many content creators, and if it gets better (maybe with even options to automatically choose background audio or add subtitles in other languages, and so on), who knows, even experts might find it a handy tool to save them some time. But that’s in the future (and we bet AI will come into it at some stage). As for now, First Draft is mainly for Instagram newbies who want Reel creation with zero hassles. And that actually is a bigger deal than some of the pros might admit.

Kobe shifts extracurriculars from municipal junior high schools to private clubs
The Kobe program is part of the central government’s effort to push for afterschool activities to be operated by local private teams, clubs and coaches to reduce the burden of teachers, who currently work overtime and weekends to oversee them.
| AFLO
The city of Kobe will shift the entire operation of extracurricular activities from municipal junior high schools to private clubs on Tuesday, becoming one of the first in the country to do so as local governments aim to reduce teachers’ overtime and schools struggle to have enough students on a team.
The Kobe program is part of the central government’s effort to push for after-school activities to be run by local private teams, clubs and coaches to lessen the burden on teachers, who work overtime and weekends to oversee them.
Under the new program, called Kobe Katsu, local private organizations — such as sports teams, universities and nonprofits — register with the city to provide activities, including sports, the arts and academics.

'Moonies' church leader jailed for two years over bribery offences
- Published
The leader of the controversial Unification Church has been sentenced to two years in prison for bribing South Korea's former first lady and other political funding offences.
A court found that Han Hak-ja's church gave Kim Keon Hee, the wife of ousted president Yoon Suk Yeol, two Chanel bags and a diamond necklace, together worth 80 million won ($57,900; £42,500).
Earlier this year, Kim was sentenced to 20 months in jail for accepting bribes from the church.
Han, the 83-year-old widow of the Unification Church's founder Sun Myung Moon, had repeatedly denied the allegations, calling them "false".
A special counsel team appointed to the case said Kim received the luxury products from the church between April and July 2022, in exchange for business and political favours.
The prosecutors said the probe was the first time the authorities have confirmed the church's attempt at buying influence in politics, and released photos of $19m (£14m) worth of cash found in Han's personal safe.
South Korea's former first lady admitted to receiving Chanel bags, but said she later returned them without using them.
Kim made a public apology when she appeared for questioning last August: "I am truly sorry that a nobody like me has caused concern to the people."
The Unification Church, known formally as The Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, was founded in South Korea in the 1950s by Moon Sun-myung, who proclaimed himself the messiah.
The church is probably best known for the mass weddings where thousands of couples were married by Han and her late husband and founder Sun Myung Moon in a stadium.
Critics have described the group as "cult-like". Lawyers have accused it of coercing devotees, known colloquially as "Moonies" after its founder, to donate large sums of money. "Moonies" is a term used by critics that many church members find offensive.
The Unification Church had come under the spotlight in Japan after the assassination of the country's former leader Shinzo Abe. The alleged assassin blamed the group for bankrupting his family and held a grievance against Abe for allegedly promoting it.
The church has boasted extensive links to politicians in Seoul, Tokyo, and even in Washington. Various politicians sent video message to its 2021 event congratulating the church's new think tank.
The list included US President Donald Trump, former US Vice-President Mike Pence, Shinzo Abe, as well as the mayors of Seoul and Busan.
The group is banned in parts of the world, including Singapore. In Japan, it has been ordered to dissolve.

In August 2026, Republican and right-leaning social media accounts shared posts attempting to tie Michigan Secretary of State and gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson, a Democrat, to the Ku Klux Klan.
These posts claimed Benson held a leadership role at the Southern Poverty Law Center — a prominent civil rights group known for tracking extremist groups — while it supposedly funneled money to the KKK.
"Secretary of State @JocelynBenson must explain to the people of Michigan her involvement with the Southern Poverty Law Center while it funded radical groups like the KKK and others that committed acts of racism against Americans," said one X post from the official Michigan House Republicans account.
Similar posts circulated on Facebook. A conservative dark money group, America Next, ran an attack ad tying Benson to the KKK. Snopes readers searched the website for information about whether Benson was involved with the KKK or if she funneled money to it.
These claims are missing significant context. It is true that Benson once served on the Southern Poverty Law Center's board. However, Snopes previously determined that there was no evidence the SPLC funneled money directly to extremist hate groups. The U.S. Department of Justice has alleged that the SPLC improperly funneled donor money to individual informants in extremist groups, including the KKK.
Benson is not named as a defendant in that case, nor is there any evidence she was involved in the SPLC's now-defunct practice of paying informants.
We have not rated this claim as the Justice Department's court case against the SPLC is ongoing as of this writing.

We reached out to Benson for additional information about her time at SPLC and await a response.
Conservative groups have long criticized the SPLC for allegedly targeting right-wing groups. In 2025, during President Donald Trump's second term, the FBI severed ties with the SPLC, claiming it "long ago abandoned civil rights work and turned into a partisan smear machine."
Legal experts have called the Justice Department's case against the SPLC "not a valid indictment" and potentially a "targeted attack."
Benson and the SPLC
Benson's relationship with the SPLC started when she was a 19-year-old unpaid intern who worked as a researcher and undercover investigator. She posed as a freelance journalist to uncover and expose the plans of white supremacist leaders and groups, according to reports of 
According to Detroit Legal News, Benson moved to Alabama after college to work at the SPLC full time, which reportedly inspired her to go to law school.
In 2014, Benson joined the SPLC's board of directors in an unpaid role, where she remained until 
"Jocelyn Benson has spent her career advancing the unfinished work of the civil rights movement and expanding economic opportunity, including helping dismantle white supremacist and neo-Nazi extremist networks," Benson campaign spokesperson Alyssa Bradley reportedly said to Bridge Michigan, a nonpartisan news outlet.
In July, Michigan House Republicans said 
If the emails included information about the informant program or the Justice Department's indictments, Michigan Republicans certainly would have shared that in their news release. They didn't.
DOJ indictments against SPLC
The indictments allege the SPLC secretly paid informants within various extremist groups more than $3 million in total to supposedly defraud banks and donors from 2014 to 2023, overlapping with Benson's time as a board director.
However, as of this writing, Benson's name does not appear in any of the Justice Department's SPLC indictments.
Contrary to a claim from John James, Benson's Republican opponent for governor, the indictments also did not claim that the SPLC funneled millions to the KKK, specifically.
According to the indictments, more than $3,500 allegedly went to one KKK member, more than $70,000 went to a former KKK member and more than $160,000 was funneled to an informant who "then sent funds to various violent extremist group leaders including the former Grand Wizard of the Knights of the Ku Klux Klan."
The SPLC has not contested the existence of the informant program, instead stating it had a "long history" of assisting law enforcement using its informants.
"The government is blatantly mischaracterizing our efforts to successfully fight hatred and violent extremism, something we have done for decades," SPLC's interim president and CEO, Bryan Fair, said in an April statement. "At one moment, they are appreciating our work in destroying the Klan and now, they are saying the SPLC funded and promoted the Klan."
The bottom line
It's true that Benson worked for the SPLC and it's true that the Justice Department accused the prominent civil rights organization of defrauding donors by secretly paying informants in extremist groups, including the KKK.
However, it's misleading to claim that Benson has connections to the KKK, particularly because the Justice Department did not name her in the indictments. Furthermore, contrary to the framing of this claim, the SPLC has a long, documented history of fighting white supremacist ideology and filing lawsuits against the Ku Klux Klan. Meanwhile, the Department of Justice has not proven its allegations against the SPLC in court.
That's not to say the SPLC hasn't received its fair share of criticism from both sides of the aisle — just that there's far more evidence the SPLC is anti-KKK than pro-KKK.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an integral part of healthcare and is here to stay, but the skills, judgement and critical thinking of medical practitioners will remain central to patient care, experts said at a webinar on "The Future Doctor: Balancing Clinical Experience with Technology" organised by SRM Institute of Science and Technology, in association with The Hindu.
The panellists comprised R. Jayanthi, Dean, SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre; Vivek N, Dean (Dental), SRM Kattankulathur Dental College and Hospital; Ritubhan Gautam, Head – Global Health, Deep Tek.ai; and K. Ganapathy, Honorary Distinguished Professor, IIM Jammu, Distinguished Professor, Tamil Nadu Dr. M.G.R. Medical University, and Emeritus Professor, National Academy of Medical Sciences.
Dr. Jayanthi said AI has become an important part of healthcare and medical education, and doctors and institutions must adapt to the AI era. She stressed the need for medical students to develop AI literacy and a strong “verification reflex”, ensuring that AI-generated information is checked against trusted sources and does not undermine clinical reasoning and critical thinking.
AI comes with responsibilities
AI should support clinical decisions, but doctors should never outsource their responsibility to the technology, said Dr. Ganapathy. He underlined the importance of strengthening judgement, empathy and accountability, and of asking the right clinical questions while assessing how reliable an AI prediction is for a particular patient and setting.
In dentistry, Dr. Vivekpointed to the growing role of AI in automating several aspects of diagnosis and treatment. At the same time, he said, the technology remains a decision-support tool and cannot replace the dentist, who must continue to make the final clinical decision.
From a public health perspective, AI can act as a force multiplier in areas where specialist clinicians are scarce, said Mr. Gautham. He said it could make screening more accessible in rural and underserved settings and help prioritise patients requiring urgent attention, while accuracy, bias and clinical oversight remain important considerations.
The session was moderated by Geetha Srimathi, senior reporter, The Hindu. The webinar can be viewed at https://newsth.live/THSRMFY.

Social Transformation in the Sands
The afforestation project around Inner Mongolia's Malan Lake has grown into a fine example of how ecological engineering, economic incentives and institutional cooperation can reinforce one another
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
On the southeastern rim of the Tengger Desert, where dunes can rise 30 metres high and advance significant metres a year, a private afforestation effort is attempting something larger than tree planting. At Malan Lake in Alxa, Inner Mongolia, founder Mr YUEN Shu Wah is testing whether desert restoration can succeed by redesigning not only landscapes, but also livelihoods and governance.
Battling Moving Sand
“Countries, cities and villages have been annihilated by the desertification,” Yuen says, describing the stakes in stark historical terms and adding the spread of desert conditions affects communities “very, very much” and must be stopped.
Malan Lake lies along an ecological corridor where unchecked expansion can intensify sandstorms and push degradation outward. Greening this frontier, Yuen argues, helps “hold the desert expansion” at a critical point. His aim is afforestation, which is the process of planting trees where there have not been any for a long period of time, as opposed to reforestation where new trees are planted to replace old or missing ones in existing forests.
Yuen began exploring desert restoration in the late 2000s and formally established Alxa League Springfield Forest Limited in 2011 to scale the Malan Lake initiative. When he first surveyed the site around 2010, he encountered moving dunes up to 30 metres high, advancing roughly 12 metres a year.
Early planting efforts revealed how technically complex the terrain was: seedlings on the windward side could be uprooted, while those on the leeward side risked burial. After more than two years of experimentation and hesitation, Yuen committed significant capital in and around 2013–2014, shifting from small-scale trials to systematic afforestation.
The project has since expanded dramatically. At its most intensive recently, it reported planting up to 150,000 mu—approximately 100 square kilometres—of desert in a single year. Planting density is intentionally low, at about 50 plants per mu (roughly 750 per hectare), reflecting dryland forestry practices designed to maximise survival under limited rainfall.
Yet Yuen is quick to temper any sense of triumph. Against the vastness of the Tengger Desert, he says, even these gains remain “a drop in the bucket”. Nevertheless, what began as a cautious pilot has evolved into a structured operation involving partnership between full-time staff, seasonal workers, university, research organisations and government, demonstrating both scale and organisational maturity.
What distinguishes the Malan Lake model is not only its scale but its structure. It is largely privately funded, operating with the discipline of a business while pursuing public ecological objectives.
“The unique point is, firstly, it comes from a private source of funding,” Yuen explains. In addition, the emphasis is very much on keeping costs down and maintenance needs low. The team focuses on planting indigenous, drought-resistant species capable of surviving harsh conditions with little or no irrigation. “The plant needs to survive on its own,” Yuen says, adding that the aim is to tackle “the most harsh conditions” at minimal cost.
This technical discipline is matched by a social one. For Yuen, desertification cannot be separated from human behaviour. Overgrazing has long contributed to land degradation, but simply restricting herds without offering alternatives risks undermining livelihoods. “We try to green the desert and keep the people happy,” he says. “We need people to look after the land.”
That philosophy has led to the development of what he calls a “sand industry” - economic activities adapted to arid conditions. Cultivating Tremella mushrooms, using local shrubs as a growing medium, has become one example of an alternative income stream. The initiative also promotes indigenous plant propagation and cultivating medicinal species suited to desert environments. These ventures are designed to reduce dependence on expanding herds while giving residents a stake in ecological recovery.
“In order to let people stay there without relying only on overgrazing, we developed a sand industry,” Yuen says. “Since we're able to develop the Tremella industry, this is an innovative sort of livelihood for the local people.”
He acknowledges that policy efforts to curb overgrazing face limits if livelihoods are not addressed, pointing out that without viable alternatives, behavioural change is difficult to sustain. Yuen has called on enterprises and educational institutions to help develop more desert-based industries that align economic incentives with conservation.
“The government also knows that they need to change the herdsmen’s habit of overgrazing. But if they cannot find a good livelihood for the herdsmen… their achievement is limited,” he says.
Participation extends beyond local communities. Universities have reserved plots of land where students can take part in greening efforts over several years. Corporate partners contribute not only funding but also procurement support, for example by purchasing desert-grown products as gifts. In this way, ecological restoration is woven into supply chains and ESG strategies.
Technology is increasingly central to the project’s governance model. In its early years, operations relied heavily on field experience and practical experimentation. Now, in collaboration with City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK), the team is introducing environmental sensors and exploring satellite assessment to monitor larger areas. The goal, Yuen says, is to improve predictive capability, to understand better what can and cannot be done under volatile desert conditions, and to make the project more productive.
“We always wish to make better predictions of what we can do, what we cannot do. I think it helps to make the project more productive,” he explains.
He situates the work within a broader ESG and SDG framework. Environmental gains include biodiversity restoration and carbon sequestration; social benefits include employment and education about sustainable land use; governance innovation lies in cross-sector collaboration between private funders, public institutions and research partners.
“To find out ways and means to do this is by itself an achievement,” he reflects.
A Model for All
The project has made considerable progress, but Yuen acknowledges its limitations and emphasises that the ambition is not to conquer the desert single-handedly, but to demonstrate that restoration is possible—and replicable.
“We want more companies, enterprises, foundations, individuals to realise it is possible to forest the desert land,” he says, “and hopefully they can chip in and do the same.”
After more than a decade of work, Yuen believes the team has gradually found its way. Malan Lake now stands as more than a green patch against a shifting horizon: it is a test case for how ecological engineering, economic incentives and institutional cooperation can reinforce one another.
In a landscape defined by wind and sand, the project suggests that the more durable force may be governance—the careful alignment of people, capital and purpose towards a common environmental goal.

For most urban Indians, catching up with friends is practically synonymous with ordering coffee or booking a table at a restaurant — “Milna hai toh pehle decide karo coffee kahan peeni hai.” Somehow, this fairly common practice irked a NRI woman visiting from Australia, who highlighted that this routine social habit is like an unavoidable “social tax”—cabs, drinks, cover charges, dining out, and incidental spending just to share the same space as your friends—adding up invisibly in the moment, only to hit like a ton of bricks once you look at the total. This sparked a social media debate about why metro cities make you a “customer before you can simply just be a person”. In a viral Instagram Reel, Smidha, a desi expat from Australia, noticed that meeting friends in India always comes with a bill. “I realised how much money I spent just trying to hang out (in India),” she said. “I was in Mumbai and generally wanted to explore the city, and somehow every plan either became about a cafe, restaurant or a mall.” She said that before moving to Australia, she never even noticed this cafe culture because, like every Indian, it seemed normal to her. The contrast becomes stark for Smidha because she had experienced a culture with functional public infrastructure in Australia, where simply sitting in a park or wandering by the beach came without a mandatory transaction. “In Australia, you can meet a friend for a coastal walk, sit in a park for hours, or spend an afternoon in a public library without spending a dollar. You don’t need a receipt to justify your presence,” she said. But in India, Smidha said, “Milna hai to pehle decide karo coffee kahan peeni hai.(Decide where to have a coffee if you want to meet).” “Somewhere along the way, a lot of our cities became places where you have to be a customer before you can simply just be a person.” “Saans lene ke bhi paise lagte hai,” she captioned her viral reel. Later in the comment section, Smidha asked if consumerism is an Indian problem, or “did we just get so used to cafes and malls that we forgot how to hang out for free?” The viral post struck a chord with social media users who felt frustrated by socialising, which felt more like an expensive transaction than a meaningful connection. “India is about malls and shops .. no community spaces left anywhere,” a user said. “Going out to eat or drink is somehow the only concept of socialising nowadays (in India),” added another user. Another added, “Indian cities are not built for quality of life. They are built to mint money.” “Summer heat, non-existent nature and public infrastructure in the cities force us to limit ourselves to indoor spaces only!” a user said. “Public spaces, Infrastructure is such that only money can give you a space to sit with someone outside your home. India needs to work upon this, but wait, politicians do have their farmhouse, and they don't care about this issue at all,” added another user. Google Pixel phones are our favorite Android phones here at WIRED and have been for a few years. They have industry-leading cameras, get speedy software and security updates directly from Google (like iPhones do from Apple), and are priced competitively. But now with so many models in the lineup, which Google Pixel phone should you buy? The new Pixel 11? The affordable Pixel 10a? What about the crazy-expensive Pixel 11 Pro Fold? Don’t fret—we break down the differences between the best Pixel phones and sort out the right one for you.
You'll also find Pixel-exclusive tips to help you get the most out of your new phone, along with some accessory and case recommendations for added protection. For more, read our other guides, including the Best Pixel Phone Settings to Change, Best Pixel 10 Cases, Best Pixel 9 Cases, Best Samsung Phones, and Best Android Phones.
Updated August 2026: We've added the new Google Pixel 11 Series, Pixel Watch 5, and a few new Pixel software features.
The Best Pixel for Most People
Google’s Pixel 10a is all the phone most people need. It remains the best smartphone for the money, even if it isn't drastically different from the Pixel 9a (although Google just released the new Pixel 11 series, don't expect a Pixel 11a until 2027). The 6.3-inch display is brighter, and it's sharp, colorful, and smooth with a 120-Hz refresh rate. Google also got rid of the plastic ring around the camera module, so now the back is flatter than ever, a true boon for anyone who hates camera bumps.
Google's Tensor G4 chipset powers this phone, the same as in 2024's flagship Pixel 9 series and Pixel 9a, rather than the Tensor G5 inside the Pixel 10 series. Comparing the Tensor G4 and G5 chips, performance is pretty much identical—smooth and fast, whether gaming or multitasking. (That also means you should consider the Pixel 9a if you can find it on sale.) Keep in mind the Pixel 11 series introduced Google's new Tensor G6 processor, so the G4 is two generations behind.
The Pixel 10a has only 8 gigabytes of RAM, and it won't support some of the exclusive smart software features of the flagship Pixel devices. But the important ones are here, notably the feature that lets you send files and photos to iPhone owners using Google's Quick Share to AirDrop.
The 48-megapixel main camera is joined by a 13-MP ultrawide and a 13-MP selfie cam on the front, and they're all reliable. The camera system is mostly identical to the Pixel 10, except the 10a lacks the 5X optical zoom that makes close-ups look much better, and the selfie camera isn't as sharp because it doesn't autofocus. However, like most Pixel phones, the camera is terrific, and most of the pictures you snap with the Pixel 10a will look great.
The 5,100-mAh battery ably lasts a full day, but heavy users may still need to tote a power bank to top up in the evenings. There's faster Qi wireless charging in this model, but it's the only Pixel in the lineup without Qi2 Pixelsnap magnets. An IP68 water-resistance rating rounds things out, not to mention secure face unlock in addition to fingerprint unlock, giving you two biometric authentication methods to unlock your phone and quickly access sensitive apps.
The Pixel 10a also gets seven years of software support—the longest you'll find on an Android phone under $500. It's one of the best smartphone bargains around.

A Step Up
The Pixel 11 isn't as big a step up from the Pixel 10 as it was from the Pixel 9. It brings iterative improvements, including a slightly better camera, a more efficient chipset, and slightly faster Qi2 25W wireless charging, alongside fresh, AI-infused software. This is the Pixel for anyone who wants to enjoy Google's unique features but doesn't want to spend $1,099 on the Pixel 11 Pro.
It has the same screen size as the Pixel 10 and 10a and 3,000 nits of peak brightness, making it easy to read the display in broad daylight. The Tensor G6 chipset offers a tasty mix of upgrades, promising 20 percent gains in power efficiency, 25 percent faster browsing, and 15 percent faster app loading. It broadly matches the Pixel 11 Pro models on performance, and you'll find it silky smooth for everything but the most demanding games (hardcore gamers might prefer something else).
Google has finally upgraded the base model to 256 GB of storage, though that means the starting price is $100 higher than last year's Pixel 10. You can also snag it with 512 GB for an extra $120, and both use speedy UFS 4, enabling faster app load times, quicker file saves, better gaming performance, and even better battery life.
The Pixel 11's battery will easily last you a full day, but much depends on what you're doing; if you're playing Wuthering Waves for more than an hour, that'll sap juice fast. That's why the Qi2 charging system is so great. You can easily attach a magnetic battery pack to the back of the phone and wirelessly charge it—faster and more efficiently than traditional Qi chargers. Just make sure the power bank is Qi2.
Like the Pixel 10, the Pixel 11 has a triple-camera system, but Google upgraded the main camera's image sensor. You can expect detailed shots with rich colors, and the new Camera Looks feature lets you tune the aesthetic you prefer. The telephoto camera offers the same 5X zoom as the Pixel 10, which is great for capturing distant subjects. You can even get decent results at 10X zoom, and it now goes all the way up to 30X (versus 20X in the Pixel 10), though things get fuzzy. The selfie camera has autofocus, ensuring sharper selfies than the Pixel 10a can muster, especially at night.
The Pixel 11 doesn't just have camera tricks. You also get Rambler to improve the Pixel’s voice-to-text, cutting ums and ahs and letting you draft messages conversationally. AI overviews pop up in the Messages app when someone texts with a meet-up request, and you can add it to your calendar. (You'll find more of Google's special Pixel features listed below.)
The US models of the Pixel 11 are eSIM-only, so you can no longer use a physical SIM card. This change brings security benefits, and US carriers have made it easier to switch eSIMs than it used to be.
The Pixel 11 is the way to go if you can spend a little more. To me, the convenience of Qi2 and the 5X zoom camera are worth the price bump alone, but you'll also enjoy better performance, a brighter screen, louder speakers, and sharper selfies. That said, it's not a huge leap over the Pixel 10, so the older model may still be worth considering if you want to save some money (it's still part of Google's lineup).

Best Pixel Upgrade
If you want the best Google has to offer, go for the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL. The Pixel 11 Pro XL has a few minor differences that put it a step ahead of the Pixel 11 Pro, but these devices are largely the same and have a few hardware and software improvements over the Pixel 11.
New is the HiLight feature, a cluster of LEDs in the flash module on the camera bar. It swirls through a rainbow of colors when you are engaging with Gemini or lights up in specific colors when your favorite contacts call. The OLED displays can adjust the refresh rate from 1 to 120 Hz, which makes them more efficient and helps conserve battery life, and they offer a peak brightness of up to 3,600 nits for HDR highlights.
The higher storage options (512 GB and 1 TB) come with more RAM (16 GB), so you can expect better performance, especially if you're juggling multiple tasks, though the entry-level 256-GB models have the same 12 GB of RAM as the regular Pixel 11. The Pro models also boast Wi-Fi 7 and ultra-wideband (UWB) connectivity.
The cameras are a big step up from the Pixel 11, even though they have a similar triple-camera system. All the sensors across the board are different; specifically, they're larger. Larger sensors can capture more data, and the end result is a brighter, sharper image. That rings true in my testing. Compared to last year's Pro models, there's a new 50-megapixel main sensor and a new 48-MP telephoto zoom with 30-percent better light sensitivity.
The Pixel 11 Pro models are the only ones to support Google's new, frankly ridiculous, 120X zoom. But you should be aware that Google's AI will add what it thinks should be in the image to fill in some of the gaps. Regardless of how you feel about that, the result is spectacular and shockingly sharp, but it's downright tricky to keep your subject in view when you zoom in this far because the slightest movement will drop it out of the viewfinder. Most folks will be content with the results at 50X zoom.
Another exclusive camera feature is Instant Night Sight. It's not quite instant, but it lets you snap impressively bright photos in low-light environments, and you're less likely to end up with a blurry snap if your subject moves. Google has also added Camera Looks to let you choose the level of contrast and color temperature you prefer, Magic Capture to automatically snap shots and record video at events, and Creator Suite to provide tools like a teleprompter for content creators.
Both models have Qi2 25W support, meaning they can charge wirelessly up to 25 watts instead of 15 watts, provided you use a Qi2 25W wireless charger. The Pro XL has the fastest wired charging speeds, supporting 45 watts (as opposed to 30 watts on the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro). Battery runtime averages a full day, and both Pro models have similar stamina, but power users will want a Qi2 power bank.
The best of Google is the Pixel 11 Pro XL, but if you prefer a smaller phone, the Pixel 11 Pro will satisfy. You'll save some cash, too.

A Folding Pixel
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a couple of folding phone standouts: an IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating and Qi2 25W wireless charging for easy magnetic mounting. Google also claims it can withstand 10-plus years of folding due to the gearless hinge. It may well be the most durable foldable you can currently buy, and that's important when you're looking at dropping $1,900 on one.
Sadly, unlike folding phones from Samsung and Honor, this book-like device is hefty. Despite a slight shave and weight loss compared to last year's 10 Pro Fold, it is still quite heavy and a little cumbersome to use. Google also calls it a “Pro” phone, but it doesn't actually have many of the advanced features of the Pixel 11 Pro. For example, the triple-camera sensors aren't as good, and you don't get access to 120X Pro Res Zoom or Instant Night Sight. It can still capture excellent photos, but at this price, I expect parity with the Pro phones.
There are some handy new software features. Bubbles gives you a floating circular profile picture from an open chat that you can open or minimize with a tap, enabling even more multitasking, since it can sit on top of two split-screen apps. There are also more contextual AI pop-ups, such as links to suggested restaurants from chats, which you can easily open in Maps.
If you want a folding phone, the new passport-sized Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 is thinner, lighter, and easier to use, and its sibling, the Z Fold8 Ultra, boasts a more impressive spec sheet. However, if you prefer Google's software experience and camera quality, you'll likely enjoy the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—if you can stomach the price.

The 2025 Pixels
You don't need to buy the latest and greatest! Purchasing a previous flagship phone is a great way to save some cash while still enjoying newish tech. Just make sure you're spending a good bit less than the MSRP—otherwise, you may as well buy one of the latest Pixel 11 phones. The previous Pixel generation from 2025 includes the Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, and Pro XL, as well as the Pixel 10 Pro Fold (the Pixel 10a is still current).
The Tensor G5 chipset in these phones is perfectly capable. The displays still get very bright, and the cameras are very similar to their respective successors. While the new chipset and modem in the Pixel 11 are slightly better—most notably at improving battery life—there aren't any truly compelling hardware reasons to upgrade. Google will also likely roll out some of the new software features from the Pixel 11 series to the Pixel 10 phones in due time.
The Pixel 10 regularly dips to $550, the Pixel 10 Pro to $699, and the Pixel 9 Pro XL to $899, while the Pixel 10 Pro Fold has been on sale for $1,499. I wouldn't buy these devices unless they were at those prices again or lower.
How Long Is Your Pixel Supported?
The Pixel 11 series, Pixel 10 series, Pixel 9 series, and Pixel 8 series will get 7 years (from their release date) of Android OS upgrades and security updates. The Pixel 7 series, Pixel 6 series, and original Pixel Fold will receive five years of Android OS upgrades and security updates from their launch dates. The Pixel 5 series and older are no longer supported. Google has a page you can check to see exactly what month your Pixel phone will stop receiving updates. Security updates reduce the risk of malware, keep your phone bug-free, and make it more secure. Android version updates introduce new features—cosmetic and functional—that improve the OS as a whole.
Pixel phones are also the first to receive Android updates, so as soon as Google releases a new version, like Android 17, you can download it immediately by heading to Settings > System > System Update > Check for Update. You can also test beta versions of Android, but you'll need to enroll your device. (Make sure to back up your phone first!) Pixels also get the feature drops Google releases every few months, including the ones introduced in newer Pixels that trickle down to older models, plus completely new features for the latest devices.
What Is Qi2?
Qi2 is the next-gen wireless charging standard, following the Qi wireless protocol. It uses magnets embedded in the backs of smartphones to align perfectly with magnets in Qi2 wireless chargers, delivering faster, more efficient charging with less heat. It's practically the same as Apple's MagSafe technology (Apple helped develop the Qi2 standard), and all MagSafe iPhones now support Qi2, starting from the iPhone 12. However, not all phones that claim Qi2 functionality are actually Qi2 phones. Samsung's Galaxy S26 series is notably Qi2 Ready, meaning the phones don't have magnets inside, and the only way they can achieve Qi2's charging speeds and efficiency is with a magnetic case.
You don't have to worry about that with the Pixel 11 phones. They're all proper Qi2 devices with magnets inside. Google calls it Pixelsnap, and that's also the name it's using for its suite of accessories. The Pixel 10 Pro XL was the first and only phone from Google to support the newer Qi2.2 25W standard, which bumps charging speed from 15 to 25 watts, but all four Pixel 11 series phones do. That means they'll wireless charge the fastest, provided you use a compatible charger.
If you have an older Qi wireless charger lying around, it may not work well with the new phones. Qi2 is backward compatible, but we've run into issues with older chargers not recharging devices consistently. You'll probably need to upgrade to a Qi2 charger. If you get a case, make sure it's Pixelsnap- or Qi2-ready with magnets inside.
What About Older Pixel Phones?
Several Pixel phones are worth considering if you don't want any of the above choices. The Pixel 9 and Pixel 9 Pro XL are available through official channels and third-party retailers (until supplies last). But if they're not heavily discounted, you may as well put that money toward the Pixel 10 or Pixel 11 series.
We do not recommend you buy any older Pixel devices. Several Pixel A-series phones have been put under a battery performance program to mitigate the risk of overheating or swollen batteries. These software updates have crippled battery life on those phones, and Google had to offer customers battery replacements or Google Store credit for a new Pixel phone. These potential issues mean it's just not worth the risk of buying a Pixel 7a or Pixel 6a. We also don't think the Pixel 8a is worthwhile anymore as the price hasn't come down much; you're better off buying the Pixel 9a or Pixel 10a.
Pixel A-Series Battery Issues
In 2025, some Google Pixel 4a and Pixel 6a owners received mandatory updates that intentionally degrade battery performance to prevent overheating. Their phone may have been working fine before, but Google issued these updates as a preventative measure, even if not every device was affected. Similarly, some Pixel 7a devices may experience battery swelling.
If your Pixel 7a has been affected, you can get a free battery replacement through Google's registration page. Unfortunately, the programs for the Pixel 4a and 6a have been discontinued.
These issues seem to have only affected some batteries in the A-series phones, suggesting it's likely a supplier issue. What about the Pixel 9a? Here's a statement a Google spokesperson provided to WIRED: “Google continuously improves Pixel testing based on user feedback and thoroughly investigates reported incidents for all components, including batteries. With Pixel 9a, we delivered the largest and longest-lasting battery of any A-series yet. We’ve been encouraged by its reception so far and are confident in the phone’s longevity and durability.”
As for the Pixel 10a, Google continues to include the Battery Health Assistance feature by default, which will lower the battery's maximum charge after you hit a certain number of charge cycles. It's designed to protect the battery over several years. We'll be monitoring it over the next few years.
What Does Pixel Care+ Include?
When you purchase a Pixel from Google, you'll see the option to add Pixel Care+ for protection. It's only available in the US through the Google Store and Google Fi. The monthly option lasts up to 60 months, whereas the fixed pricing is for a two-year term. Here's what you get.
Pixel Care+ starts at $10 per month or $199 for a two-year plan for the latest Pixel 11 series and includes unlimited accidental damage protection, $0 screen and battery repairs, replacements that ship in a day, and priority support from Pixel experts. That pricing is for the Pixel 11, and it goes up for the pricier devices. For example, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold will cost $19 per month, or $319 for the two-year term. The cheapest Pixel Care+ option is for the Pixel 8a, 9a, or 10a is $6 per month or $119 for two years.
Pixel Care+ with Loss and Theft starts at $11 per month or $219 for the Pixel 11 and includes the same protections as mentioned above but includes two claims of loss and theft every 12 months. Weirdly, Loss and Theft coverage is not available in New York state.
You Can DeGoogle Your Pixel Phone
Love Pixel phones but want to get away from using Google services? It's a little odd, but you can actually use a different operating system with the Pixel instead of the built-in Android. We've tested and really like /e/OS, a privacy-first operating system that's based on the Android Open Source Project. While you can install it yourself, it requires a bit of technical know-how; Europeans can buy a refurbished Pixel from Murena with /e/OS installed already (not available in the US currently). If you're interested, we have more details about /e/OS here.
The Best Pixel Cases and Accessories
We'll have a Pixel 11 case guide for you soon. In the meantime, there are guides on the Best Pixel 10 Cases and Best Pixel 9 (and 9a) Cases, but here are a few selections for your perusal. We've highlighted cases for the current Pixel lineup, but you can easily find the same versions for prior models by browsing the case maker's catalog. There will likely be versions for the Pixel 11 series, but note that cases are usually not interchangeable.
These official Google cases for the Pixel 10 series are Qi2-certified with Pixelsnap magnets built in, so you can attach the phone to compatible magnetic accessories without losing strength or wireless charging capabilities (without magnets, the strength is reduced and the feature won't work). The soft silicone feels pleasant to the touch, and you can color-match it to your Pixel 10 to highlight the phone's color. We also like Google's official Pixel 10a case ($30), which is similar, but it doesn't have the magnets inside, as it's not a Qi2 phone.
Mous cases are Made for Google certified, and that's especially important with the Pixel 10 series, as it ensures the best compatibility with Pixelsnap. The Limitless is a great all-rounder, with raised edges over the display, clicky buttons, reliable magnets for Qi2, and several design aesthetics you can choose from, including a walnut back or speckled fabric (pictured).
Dbrand's Grip case lives up to its name. It has clicky buttons and incredibly grippy edges. It feels robust yet fairly slim, and you can choose a snazzy design. Just know that you have to apply this “skin” to the back of the case. There's a lot of room for error, so be careful and watch Dbrand's installation video for tips. There's Pixelsnap support, so you can use your Pixel with Qi2 and even MagSafe accessories, and it worked exceptionally well in our testing.

After more than a year of testing, we've never had a phone fall off a ride using this mounting system. The company also has several other magnetic accessories, like a car vent mount. The case itself is nice; I just wish the edges were raised more for better screen protection. You can choose to have it with the loop, which acts as a grip, or without it.

The company technically doesn't make it for the Pixel 10, just the Pro models, but because the dimensions are the same, the 10 Pro case fits perfectly on the Pixel 10.

You can also twist it to put the phone in landscape or portrait orientation. Make sure you take it off before placing the phone on a wireless charger; you're not supposed to attach magnetic accessories or chargers to the Ring Stand itself.
You don't need to spend this much for a decent Qi2 charger, but these are what Google is officially selling, and they're great (if overpriced). The stand version is actually the same Pixelsnap charger, just with a robust stand to keep it propped up. The stand is stable, doesn't shift around, and you can charge the phone in landscape or portrait orientation.
