Serial killers and child abductions. Trippy science-fiction stories about alternate realities. A courtroom drama starring an anthropomorphic coyote with more than a passing resemblance to Who Framed Roger Rabbit? Screwball comedies, dark horror flicks and so much more await in this weekend’s edition of your friendly neighborhood streaming guide.
Movie night this past week was Taylor Sheridan’s Wind River, an absolutely devastating neo-Western that examines the injustice many Native American women face on and off the reservation. Jeremy Renner and Elizabeth Olsen star and put on tremendous performances. I think this is my favorite of Renner’s roles and his best performance, though he has quite a few. Jon Bernthal has a small role that he really knocks out of the park as well (all these Marvel actors showing us what acting chops they have in a serious movie).
Lots of Yellowstone actors were in this movie first, including Kelsey Asbille, Hugh Dillon, Ian Bohen and Gil Birmingham (to name a few). Birmingham is on fire in this movie. Graham Greene also stars. If you haven’t seen this one yet, please do yourself a favor and give it a watch on Netflix. It’s tremendous, but not an easy watch. It reminds me that Sheridan can write (and direct) really great material. He just puts out way too much content now and it’s never even close to as good as this film or Sicario or Hell or High Water.
As I do every week, I’ve scoured the internet for the best TV shows and movies streaming on Netflix, Prime Video, Apple TV, Disney+ and beyond for you to watch this weekend. I haven’t watched all of these (some aren’t out by the time this gets posted and others are just not in my review schedule), so some of these are my own personal recommendations while others are just things to keep on your radar.
If you have any recommendations, tips or other thoughts feel free to shoot me a note. Let me know what you’re watching these days, or if you’ve enjoyed any of my recommendations, on Twitter, Instagram, or Facebook. Be sure to also check out last weekend’s streaming guide below:
Alright, there’s a bunch to get through so let’s dive right in!
New TV Shows To Watch This Weekend
Adults – Season 2 (Hulu)
What It’s About: FX’s Gen-Z comedy hangout comedy returns with Samir (Malik Elassal), Billie (Lucy Freyer), Issa (Amita Rao), Anton (Owen Thiele) and Paul Baker (Jack Innanen) still sharing Samir’s family home in Queens and stumbling their way through relationships, jobs and the increasingly messy business of adulthood. Ben Kronengold and Rebecca Shaw created the series, and Season 2 brings in guest stars including Susie Essman, Raven-Symoné, Gaten Matarazzo, Zosia Mamet and Julia Fox. All eight Season 2 episodes dropped on Hulu Thursday, August 27, so this is a binge release and the finale is already available. FXX is also airing two episodes each Thursday, which puts the linear finale on September 17.
Why You Should Watch: This isn’t one I’ve watched yet, but the reviews are through the roof. Critics give Season 2 a 100% score and audiences are almost right there with them at 98%. If you’re looking for something funny to kill some time this weekend, give it a look.
Dark Matter – Season 2 (Apple TV)
What It’s About: Joel Edgerton returns as physicist Jason Dessen alongside Jennifer Connelly as Daniela and Oakes Fegley as their son Charlie, with Alice Braga, Jimmi Simpson, Dayo Okeniyi and Amanda Brugel also returning. After the first season’s multiverse chaos, the Dessens attempt to settle in a seemingly safe reality while Jason’s obsession with the Box threatens to drag the family straight back into trouble. New episodes drop Fridays, though on Apple TV this actually means Thursday evenings, with the finale October 30 (or 29, as the case may be).
Why You Should Watch: It’s very rare for an author to adapt and show-run their own novel, but such is the case for Blake Crouch’s Dark Matter. Now Crouch moves into uncharted territory, taking his own story further in TV format than in book format, which is kind of cool and unique and hopefully means we’re in for a great second season. The good news? Season 2 has much higher ratings than Season 1 so far.
The Simpsons: Yellow Mirror (Disney+)
What It’s About: A fun new Disney+ exclusive Simpsons special that very deliberately riffs on Black Mirror (if that wasn’t totally obvious by the title). It consists of two dark (but still humorous) sci-fi stories: one in which a defective lamp forces Homer to question his reality, and another where an AI-powered tablet befriends, and begins controlling, Maggie. Demi Moore and Patti Harrison guest star.
Why You Should Watch: I suppose if you’re a fan of both The Simpsons and Black Mirror, this is a no-brainer. I always liked The Simpsons Halloween episodes and this is kind of the same vibe. I haven’t really watched The Simpsons in ages, and I can only do Black Mirror in very small doses but I might still check this special out.
Revival – Season 1 (Netflix)
What It’s About: This supernatural mystery is based on the Image Comics series by Tim Seeley and Mike Norton and was adapted for TV by Luke Boyce and Aaron B. Koontz. Melanie Scrofano stars as Wisconsin deputy Dana Cypress, whose small town is thrown into chaos when recently deceased residents suddenly return to life—not as shambling zombies, but apparently as the same people they were before they died. The series originally aired on Syfy back in 2025 and just dropped all 10 episodes on Netflix.
Why You Should Watch: This one has two things going for it. First, the first season basically tied up the storylines from the comics, meaning that even if there’s never a second season, you have a pretty complete story here. Second, the reviews are very strong: 90% critics and 85% audiences on Rotten Tomatoes.
The Undeclared War – Season 2 (Peacock)
What It’s About: The British cyber-thriller returns with Simon Pegg as GCHQ operations director Danny Patrick and Hannah Khalique-Brown as Saara Parvin. Following the devastating Russian cyberattack of Season 1, the GCHQ team discovers evidence of a mole while a new Chinese cyber threat begins targeting the British government. Siân Brooke joins a returning cast that also includes Adrian Lester, Alex Jennings and Danny Sapani.
Why You Should Watch: The entire season is out now on Peacock so if you haven’t seen Season 1 yet, you could just binge both seasons all at once. It’s an interesting premise, though reviews peg (get it?) the show at around 67% on RT – a passable, if not tremendous, “Fresh” score.
New Movies To Watch This Weekend
The Whisper Man (Netflix)
What It’s About: Adam Scott stars as Tom Kennedy, a widowed crime novelist whose 8-year-old son is abducted, forcing him to seek help from his estranged father, Peter Willis (Robert De Niro), a retired detective whose decades-old serial-killer investigation may be connected to the disappearance. Michelle Monaghan plays detective Amanda Beck, with Hamish Linklater and Owen Teague also starring.
Why You Should Watch: Adam Scott, Robert De Niro, Michelle Monaghan, Hamish Linklater, Owen Teague. I mean, that’s one helluva cast! And the premise is certainly intriguing. I’m a sucker for serial killer mysteries and Adam Scott is always a joy to watch. This is definitely going on my weekend watch-list, though I’m so busy this weekend I’m not sure I’ll have time to watch anything I’m not already reviewing!
The Woman In The Yard (Peacock)
What It’s About: Danielle Deadwyler stars as Ramona, a grieving mother recovering from the accident that killed her husband while trying to raise their two children alone in an isolated farmhouse. Then a mysterious woman dressed in black simply appears in the yard—and begins moving closer to the house.
Why You Should Watch: It sounds spooky and everyone loves a good horror movie these days, but the 41% RT score is a red flag, and I’m not sure it’s my cup of tea. But maybe it’s yours!
Borderlands (Peacock)
What It’s About: The infamous video-game adaptation stars Cate Blanchett as Lilith, Kevin Hart as Roland, Ariana Greenblatt as Tiny Tina, Jamie Lee Curtis as Tannis and Jack Black as the voice of Claptrap. Eli Roth directed the film, which follows the mismatched group across Pandora while searching for the missing daughter of powerful corporate magnate Atlas.
Why You Should Watch: I might watch it just because it’s streaming now, but this movie has looked terrible from the very first time I saw stills. Things were far more grim than even I predicted, and the movie currently has a 10% Rotten Tomatoes score! 10%! It was a huge critical and financial failure despite the big names attached and earned less than $16 million at the box office on a budget topping $110 million. Talk about a flop! Flop slop! I kind of want to watch it with some friends MST3000 style.
M3GAN (Netflix)
What It’s About: Allison Williams stars as roboticist Gemma, who suddenly becomes guardian to her orphaned niece Cady (Violet McGraw) and decides that pairing the girl with her experimental AI companion doll M3GAN will solve both her parenting and work problems. Predictably, an AI whose overriding directive is protecting a child begins interpreting “protection” rather aggressively. Amie Donald physically portrays M3GAN, with Jenna Davis providing the voice.
Why You Should Watch: This movie is a few years old now and there’s already a sequel and probably three more movies planned and the eventual reboot is already a twinkle in some movie producer’s eye, but I liked this little comedy-horror picture when it came out and you should give it a watch if you’re looking for something light and a little weird.
Venom: The Last Dance (Netflix)
What It’s About: Tom Hardy returns for the third and supposedly final outing as Eddie Brock and his symbiote alter ego Venom. This time they're being hunted simultaneously by government forces led by Chiwetel Ejiofor's Rex Strickland and a monstrous Xenophage sent by symbiote god Knull, voiced/performed by Andy Serkis. Juno Temple, Rhys Ifans and Stephen Graham round out the cast.
Why You Should Watch: Talk about a stacked cast for what is almost certainly a mediocre movie. I’ve only seen the first of the Tom Hardy Venom movies, unless I’ve simply forgotten watching the second one. Audiences liked this quite a bit more than critics (79% Popcornmeter vs 40% critic score). I liked the first Venom movie more than I expected but not really enough to continue following the series.
The Last Sunrise (Prime Video)
What It’s About: Maia Reficco stars as Oriah “Ry,” a young American dancer who travels to Mallorca with her mother (Eva Longoria) and falls for local fisherman Julián, played by Fernando Lindez. Their Mediterranean romance becomes complicated when Ry's mother becomes involved in a resort development threatening Julián's family's land.
Why You Should Watch: I mean, Mallorca sounds nice this time of year. I’d like to go. This film sounds about as far from something I’d actually watch as you can get, but I know some of you enjoy this kind of romance, so here you go. Have at it!
New Movies In Theaters This Weekend
Coyote vs Acme
What It’s About: Wile E. Coyote (of Looney Tunes fame) finally decides he’s had enough of being maimed by defective ACME products and hires ambulance-chasing attorney Kevin Avery (Will Forte) to sue the company. John Cena plays ACME’s attorney. It’s a courtroom comedy involving an anthropomorphic coyote, basically.
Why You Should Watch: This is a bit of a miracle movie. Warner Bros. finished the movie and decided to not release it in order to claim a tax write-off, a practice they did with a number of movies and shows (along with other studios, including Disney). There was major backlash and Warner Bros. sold the film to Ketchup Entertainment. It now sits at 95% on Rotten Tomatoes with critics and 92% with audiences, making it one of the best-reviewed entries in this guide, and hopefully makes a bundle of cash for its rescuers.
The Dog Stars
What It’s About: Ridley Scott directs this post-apocalyptic adaptation of Peter Heller's novel, starring Jacob Elordi as Hig, a pilot surviving after a pandemic alongside hardened survivalist Bangley (Josh Brolin). A mysterious radio transmission sends Hig beyond their isolated compound, eventually bringing him into contact with characters played by Margaret Qualley and Guy Pearce. Allison Janney and Benedict Wong also star.
Why You Should Watch: Ridley Scott, a stellar cast, a cool post-apocalyptic setting and . . . well, Ridley Scott. Scott has been putting out dud after dud after dud, and this one appears to be yet another, with just a 40% RT score. Actually, when I saw the trailer for the first time I thought “Wow, this looks really cool” and then I saw who directed it and immediately was reminded of how much I hated Gladiator II. What a shame.
TV Shows Currently Streaming Weekly
Reacher – Season 4 (Prime Video)
What It’s About: Season 4 of Reacher adapts Lee Child’s Gone Tomorrow: a distraught woman’s death on a Philadelphia subway pulls Jack Reacher (Alan Ritchson) into a conspiracy involving the Pentagon and an international terror cell. Three episodes dropped August 12, with weekly releases through the September 16 finale. Amazon will release all eight episodes of the spinoff Neagley (starring Maria Sten) the same day as the finale.
Why You Should Watch: Season 1 remains the gold standard when it comes to Reacher, but at least Season 3 was a lot better than the truly atrocious second season of this action-crime-mystery-ish adaptation of the over-the-top Lee Child books (of which I’ve read about nine or so). I finally posted my review of the season (so far) and . . . the verdict is not pretty. I’m not even getting much pushback on my criticism, with many fans very unhappy with how the season is shaping up. You can watch my video discussion of the season right here.
Lanterns – Season 1 (HBO Max)
What It’s About: DC’s True Detective-style take on Green Lantern: rookie John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) and veteran Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) investigate a Nebraska murder that opens onto something much larger, told across two timelines. Kelly Macdonald is Sheriff Kerry, Ulrich Thomsen plays Sinestro, Laura Linney a Guardian of the Universe, and Nathan Fillion reprises Guy Gardner from Superman. Co-created by Chris Mundy (Ozark), Damon Lindelof, and Tom King. Premieres Sunday, August 16 at 9pm, then weekly across eight episodes, with the finale on October 4. See the full release schedule and time zones right here.
Why You Should Watch: I’ve watched the first two episodes of Lanterns so far and it’s fine. Nothing special but not bad, and I’m curious about the various mysteries and fan theories. I think they did a pretty terrible job at actually setting the stakes for those of us less familar with Green Lantern, but it still has potential and the cast is terrific. You can read my review of the Season 1 premiere and my review of Episode 2, and I’ll be recapping and reviewing episodes weekly on Sunday evenings, though as I note in that second link, I think this probably should have just been a binge release. I’ll also be posting video reviews on my YouTube channel.
Furious – Season 1 Finale on Monday (Hulu)
What It’s About: An eight-episode crime drama created by Elizabeth Meriwether, loosely inspired by the 1987 film Black Widow. FBI agent Alice Black (Emmy Rossum) hunts a calculating female serial killer played by Lola Petticrew (who I first saw in Say Nothing, I believe). As their paths converge the line between justice and revenge gets blurry. Scoot McNairy, Quincy Tyler Bernstine and Jake Lacy also star. If you’re enjoying this show, the good news is that Season 2 has already been greenlit ahead of the Season 1 finale.
Why You Should Watch: I have decidedly mixed feelings about Furious as we approach the finale. I think part of this is marketing. The show is described as a rookie FBI agent hunting down a female serial killer, but it’s really about a revenge killer and abuse and sex trafficking and I guess I was just hoping it wouldn’t be so predictable. I don’t love how often modern shows and movies give female serial killers a “pass” by justifying their murders because of past abuse. I purely evil female serial killer would be a nice change. Men shouldn’t get to have all the fun. Still, cat-and-mouse serial killer detective shows are one of my guilty pleasures so I’ll be watching this on Monday nights. The finale will arrive furiously on August 31.
It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia – Season 18 (FX / Hulu)
What It’s About: The Gang — Charlie Day, Glenn Howerton, Rob Mac, Kaitlin Olson and Danny DeVito — return to Paddy’s Pub for a 10-episode run that includes inheritance scams, tent encampments, workplace automation, neurodivergence, conspiracy theories, a Renaissance Faire, and a Little League sponsorship. What could go wrong? The season premiered this past Monday, August 17 with a two-episode drop. Weekly episodes land on Mondays with the finale airing on October 12. Season 18 is currently sitting at 100% on Rotten Tomatoes.
Why You Should Watch: To be fair, I’m late to the game on Always Sunny, so I’m way way behind on this show and just put on episodes whenever I need a dose of hilarity in my life. Sometimes I end up binging three or four or five because life is filled with tragedy and the Gang always lifts my spirits. So why should you watch? First, because it will bring you joy. Second, because you’ll be like “there but for the grace of God go I.”
The Shards (Hulu)
What It’s About: Ryan Murphy (Glee, The Politician, etc) adapts the Bret Easton Ellis novel of the same name for FX/Hulu. Set in Los Angeles in 1981, The Shards follows a 17-year-old fictionalized Bret Easton Ellis (Igby Rigney) through his senior year at the elite Buckley prep school, where the arrival of enigmatic transfer student Robert Mallory (Homer Gere) coincides with the killings of a serial murderer known as The Trawler. The show drops new episodes on Wednesdays with a September 9 finale.
Why You Should Watch: I’m not really sure, if we’re being honest. The promo images of young people in the 80s in swimsuits make this look like a show for young people and I’m not a young man anymore. The reviews aren’t great (55% / 35% audience and critic scores) and I suppose I’m not really a big Bret Easton Ellis guy. I mean, I enjoyed the movie American Psycho, but I never read the book! Maybe I should do that instead of watching this show.
The Walking Dead: Dead City – Season 3 (AMC+)
What It’s About: The Walking Dead: Dead City returns with an eight-episode season 3, with Lauren Cohan as Maggie Rhee and Jeffrey Dean Morgan as Negan returning, now working alongside Perlie Armstrong (Gaius Charles) to build a "functioning" community in post-apocalyptic Manhattan. The fragile alliance is tested by newcomer Renata (Aimee Garcia), her doctor brother Luis (Raúl Castillo), and loner Dillard (Jimmi Simpson of Westworld fame). New showrunner Seth Hoffman, a Walking Dead veteran writer and former co-executive producer on the original series, is taking over this season. New episodes drop Sundays, running through September 13.
Why You Should Watch: I don’t think this show should exist, quite frankly, and after watching the Season 3 premiere, I not only wrote a scathing review, I made a scathing video to go with it, which you can watch here. It’s not good, folks, but I genuinely hope that it gets better because there are other ways I could be spending my Sunday evenings. Update: I watched about five minutes of the second episode and turned it off and I haven’t been able to come back. I think maybe you need alcohol to enjoy this show, or to even enjoy hate-watching this show, and I don’t drink anymore.
Fightland (Starz)
What It’s About: On the night Maduka "Duke" Kilroy (Howard Charles) becomes world heavyweight champion, an assault leaves his brother dead and lands him in a U.S. prison for eight years. Out and back in London, he sets out to destroy the empire of criminal kingpin and former promoter Kingsley Marshall (Nicholas Pinnock), the man he blames — complicated by the fact that Kingsley has vanished and his wife Joy (Deborah Ayorinde) is the love of Duke’s life. Charles Babalola and Anita-Joy Uwajeh co-star. New episodes drop Fridays with the season finale landing on September 25.
Why You Should Watch: I’m a few weeks late to this – it premiered on Starz on July 31. In any case, it’s co-produced by rapper Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson, marking his first international series. It’s a pretty compelling plot and has a reasonably strong 73% on Rotten Tomatoes. Also, boxing. Boxing is fun especially when the boxer in question is beating up criminals in East London.
Ted Lasso – Season 4 (Apple TV)
What It’s About: Ted Lasso (Jason Sudeikis) returns to Richmond to coach a second-division women’s football team in this reboot of the popular Apple TV sports comedy series. Jack Burditt (30 Rock, Modern Family) takes over as showrunner for this new, more estrogen-charged spin on the fish-out-of-water TV show. New episodes drop on Wednesday (Tuesday evening for Apple TV) with ten episodes running through October 7.
Why You Should Watch: Honestly, the reason that Ted Lasso worked so well in the first season was precisely because it was a fish-out-of-water comedy. But a fish can only stay out of water for so long before, well, RIP fish. Ted was an adorable lead and head coach and despite his lack of experience or knowledge of soccer, his remarkable way with people took everyone off guard, including viewers. That affable, mustachioed man was the epitome of “I am rubber and you are glue” and nothing stuck to him. He made you want to believe (like Fox Mulder did back int he day, only about aliens and whatnot). 
That rarest work of optimism and hope in a sea of cynicism was perfect in its first season. But it should have been a one-and-done series because it ran out of steam in Season 2 and I didn’t return for Season 3. Let me know if you think Season 4 is worth it or a misfire. I’ve heard mixed things.
Monsters of God (HBO Max)
What It’s About: A five-part HBO documentary series directed by Eric Goode (Tiger King, Chimp Crazy), produced by Goode Films, A24, and Central Pictures. Goode dives into the underworld of exotic animal smuggling, a billion-dollar criminal enterprise driven by obsession over rare species. The docuseries is inspired by and draws from the 2008 nonfiction book, The Lizard King, by Bryan Christy (oddly, not about The Doors frontman, Jim Morrison). New episodes drop Mondays with a September 3 finale.
Why You Should Watch: I really think Lizard King would have been a better name for this series, since it would so quickly evoke Goode’s hit Tiger King, but maybe that name was taken or maybe they worried about the link to The Doors. Either way, with a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score (based on just 10 reviews) this one might be worth checkikng out. 
Conan O’Brien Must Go – Season 3 (HBO Max)
What It’s About: Conan travels overseas to meet listeners he first connected with on his podcast, experiencing local traditions while spending time with the fans who invited him — this season to India, the Philippines, the Netherlands and Morocco. Premieres Friday, August 21 at 9 pm ET on HBO and HBO Max with four episodes airing weekly on Fridays, and the finale on September 11.
Why You Should Watch: Conan O’Brien is just one of the funniest, most likable people in Hollywood and basically anything he does is worth watching just because he’s such a fun guy. If you like humorous travel shows, check it out. The series holds 88% critics / 84% audience and has won two Emmys.
Star Trek: Strange New Worlds – Season 4 (Paramount+)
What It’s About: The crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise is back for another round of adventures as Captain Christopher Pike (Anson Mount) continues leading his crew across the final frontier. Season 4 picks up after last season’s cliffhanger and sends Pike, Spock, Number One, and the rest of the Enterprise crew on a series of dangerous new missions, from mysterious alien encounters to impossible scientific mysteries, while continuing to build toward the events of Star Trek: The Original Series. The new season is comprised of 10 episodes airing Sundays through September 24
Why You Should Watch: I actually gave up on New Star Trek some time ago, having doggedly tried my best with the JJ Abrams films, Discovery and Picard. And while I’d heard some very positive things about Strange New Worlds, I just couldn’t find the energy to catch up. Maybe someday. I do really like the casting in this series, and Anson Mount is the perfect Pike (though I thought he looked more handsome in the very first episode before he shaved and cut his hair). However, it should be noted that Season 4 has a stellar 100% on Rotten Tomatoes, higher than any previous season. If there is a show that could lure me back to Star Trek, it’s this one.
Silo – Season 3 (Apple TV)
What It’s About: Set in a dystopian future, 10,000 people live in a massive, self-sustaining underground "Silo" comprising 144 levels. Residents are strictly governed by regulations and believe the outside world is toxic, but the protagonist, an engineer named Juliette Nichols, begins to uncover secrets about the Silo’s history and the truth behind their world.
Why You Should Watch: I thought the first season was a bit slow but ended up being a really compelling mystery. For whatever reason, I couldn’t get into Season 2 and still need to catch up. I keep looking at this and Sugar and thinking, I need to watch these shows! But then something else is out that I have to watch. Time is my enemy, and yet the only thing that can defeat my enemy is more of it, which I cannot get. What a conundrum! Season 3 airs weekly on Thursday evenings for a total of 10 episodes, with the finale dropping on September 4.
Lioness – Season 3 (Paramount+)
What It’s About: Taylor Sheridan's Lioness returns for a third season with Zoe Saldaña back as CIA operative Joe McNamara, who finds herself caught up in her most dangerous mission yet. As a sprawling conspiracy threatens both national security and the people she cares about most, Joe is forced to balance her loyalty to the mission with her responsibilities at home. Nicole Kidman, Morgan Freeman, Michael Kelly, Laysla De Oliveira, Genesis Rodriguez, and Dave Annable all return for another season of high-stakes espionage and military action.
Why You Should Watch: You know, I thought the first season of Lioness was pretty excellent military spy thriller fare, and I’m a sucker for that kind of stuff. I’m okay with shows that make Islamic radical terrorists and South American cartels the bad guys and I’m okay with shows that point out that often the bad guys can be right here in the West, too. Taylor Sheridan is a bit more “red-blooded” than a lot of contemporary Hollywood and that’s fine, but I just got kind of sick of the characters in Season 2, so I’m behind. New episodes drop Sundays with the finale landing on September 20.
Ghost in the Shell (Prime Video)
What It’s About: Ghost in the Shell has been around forever, but it’s always fun to see a new take on an old classic. The new series, which debuted on Prime Video this past Tuesday, was created by Science Saru (aka Science Monkey), the studio behind the hit Devilman Crybaby and Danadan. The new series is based on the 1989-91 manage of the same name and takes place in the distant future (well, 2029) in a futuristic Japan replete with elite cyborgs, tactical anti-terrorism forces and mysterious hackers. You can also watch the old 1995 movie on Prime Video. A total of 10 episodes will comprise the first season, with the finale airing on September 8.
Why You Should Watch: If you like this anime series, or you’re just into anime in general, this is probably your thing. I found that even though I’ve seen the movie, I was totally lost and confused after the first episode and so I haven’t continued. Maybe someday.
Stuart Fails To Save The Universe (HBO Max)
What It’s About: Stuart Fails to Save the Universe stars Kevin Sussman, reprising his Big Bang Theory role as Stuart. Comic book store owner Stuart Bloom is tasked with restoring reality after he breaks a device built by Sheldon and Leonard, accidentally bringing about a multiverse Armageddon — and as the title implies, things don't go well. Along the way he meets alternate-universe versions of familiar Big Bang Theory faces.
Why You Should Watch: First, a confession: I have never watched even a single episode of Big Bang Theory. Sure, I’ve seen the odd clip here or there, but I really couldn’t even tell you what it’s about. And yet, this show sounds like a really clever spinoff. It takes the sitcom into an entirely new genre, and even though I’m sick of multiverse stuff, this sounds really fun. It has a 71%/78% critic/audience split on RT. New episodes land Thursdays and the finale drops on September 24.

Tottenham make Ndiaye move with Richarlison set for Everton
- Published
Tottenham are in advanced talks to sign Iliman Ndiaye from Everton, with Richarlison set to move in the opposite direction as part of separate negotiations.
Although a deal for Nidaye is largely agreed between the two clubs, it remains unclear whether he will make the switch to north London, with Manchester City among the clubs to have expressed an interest.
City have also held talks to sign Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, another Spurs target, although the Reds would need to secure a replacement before sanctioning any move.
Everton are open to selling Ndiaye, 26, after he rejected multiple contract offers and held talks with Saudi club Al-Hilal earlier this summer.
Meanwhile, Everton have agreed terms in principle to re-sign Brazilian striker Richarlison after he told Spurs head coach Roberto de Zerbi "too many times that he wants to leave".
The Brazil international has entered the final year of his Tottenham contract and would provide competition for first-choice striker Thierno Barry, with uncertainty surrounding Beto's future at Hill Dickinson Stadium.
Everton are also growing increasingly confident of completing a loan deal to bring Jack Grealish back from Manchester City, although the precise terms of any agreement remain complicated as the England international enters the final year of his contract at Etihad Stadium.
Grealish has prioritised a return to Everton, where he spent last season on loan, over the option of rejoining his boyhood club Aston Villa, who have also expressed an interest.
The club are also targeting a right-back, with talks over a move for Fulham's Kenny Tete reopened after he came close to joining last summer.
Fulham are already assessing potential replacements and have entered talks to sign Andrei Ratiu.
It is part of a chain of interconnected Premier League deals before Tuesday's transfer deadline.
Richarlison, Danso and Sarr ask to leave Spurs
Richarlison is one of three players who De Zerbi says have asked to leave Tottenham.
He, Kevin Danso and Pape Matar Sarr have all been linked with moves away from Spurs and none were included in De Zerbi's matchday squad as Tottenham lost 2-0 at home to Newcastle on Saturday.
Asked about their status after the loss, De Zerbi said: "Richarlison, I don't know. He said too many times he wants to leave.
"Danso came to me two days ago and he said wants to leave and Pape Sarr the same, but he suffered a small injury, but he is almost ready to train.
"I have very good relationships but if they want to leave, they have to bring the solution, the economic solution, to the club, and they can go."
Spurs have spent more than £300m this summer in an effort to restore their competitive edge following back-to-back 17th-place Premier League finishes.
But Tottenham are bottom of the table, having lost their first two games to Brentford and Newcastle and failing to score a goal.
With 11 goals, Richarlison was Tottenham's top scorer last season, and a key figure during their struggle for Premier League survival, which was secured on the final day.
Earlier in August, De Zerbi said that the Brazilian was uncertain about his future, noting that, "it's not easy to find another striker like Richarlison".
Last week, Manchester City striker Omar Marmoush joined Spurs on loan and he replaced Richarlison in De Zerbi's starting XI against Newcastle.
Danso's first-team opportunities may be limited this season as Marcos Senesi and Jan Paul van Hecke arrive to challenge for his place in central defence, where Micky van de Ven's spot was secured by the signing of a new contract and the award of the captaincy.
Sunderland made an offer to take Danso, who has 36 Austria caps, on a season-long loan - but Spurs rejected it.
In midfield, Sarr's chance to play has been impacted by the arrivals of Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali early in the window, as Tottenham kicked off their a statement summer of transfers by breaking their club record fee twice in one week.
The Senegal international, 23, has attracted interest from a number of clubs, including several in the Premier League and Turkish side Besiktas.
However, Juventus are understood to be confident of winning the race for his signature on a loan deal that includes a conditional obligation to buy.

Apple increased the price for a monthly subscription to Apple TV by $2, to $15, today.
Annual prices increased by 20 percent from $99 to $119. Current subscribers will receive one month’s notice before paying the new prices, Apple said, per Variety.
Apple’s most recent price hike was in August 2025, when monthly prices went from $10 to $13. Monthly prices also increased in October 2023 and October 2022. Apple TV (then called Apple TV+) started in 2019 for (a seemingly financially unsustainable) $5/month.
Apple TV doesn’t have commercials and is still cheaper than many of its biggest rivals, like Netflix (ad-free plans start at $20/month) and Disney+ (ad-free plans start at $19/month). However, Apple TV has a much smaller library than many subscription-based streaming services.
Apple also increased the cost of a monthly individual subscription to Apple One—which bundles the Apple TV streaming service with Apple Arcade, Apple Fitness+, Apple Music, Apple News+, and iCloud+—from $20 to $22 today. The price bump tracks somewhat logically, considering new higher fees for Apple TV, as well as Apple Music, whose monthly price increased from $11 to $13 last month.
Last month, Apple also increased the prices of Apple One’s Family (from $26 to $28) and Premier (from $38 to $40) plans.

In mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by helicopter to a small settlement in a rural area of southern Colombia where they lined up and, one by one, handed their weapons to government officials: rifles, pistols, machine guns and grenade launchers.
They also stripped off their heavy tactical vests, field packs and camouflage uniforms, which were each piled into a bonfire to mark the beginning of a new life away from an armed conflict that has claimed nearly half a million lives in the last six decades.
That was precisely what the former president Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” plan had sought to achieve: negotiating with and disarming all of Colombia’s criminal groups, which are estimated to have nearly 30,000 members.
But the group of just 99 people was the only one to disarm, and did so just three days before the presidential runoff, which was won by the far-right millionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who had campaigned on a promise to end “total peace” and return to a full-on strategy of jailing or killing criminals.
Now, several weeks after the new president took office – and amid efforts to deal with the aftermath of the 7.4-magnitude earthquake, as his government has already begun the promised airstrikes against criminal groups – the 99 do not know what will happen to them.
“We’re in limbo,” said Natalia Bríñez, 29, one of 13 women among the group staying in the temporary location zone, or ZUT by its Spanish initials, a government-controlled zone where, under surveillance and unable to leave, they were supposed to make the transition to civilian life over the following months.
The former guerrillas are housed in beige brick buildings decorated with drawings they painted themselves, including doves of peace, with a communal dining hall where three meals a day are served. No weapons are allowed inside and soldiers guard the ZUT from a perimeter less than a mile away.
One former combatant built a makeshift gym with weights made from metal pipes and tins filled with cement and sand, and there is an improvised football pitch, but most of them spend their days on their phones.
De la Espriella has repeatedly said his government will no longer negotiate peace agreements and has yet to announce what he intends to do regarding the people at the ZUT. The president has not responded to requests for comment.
In theory, any arrest warrants against the group are suspended, and they remain under state protection until 25 December, when Petro’s decree establishing the ZUT expires. But De la Espriella could revoke the decree at any time.
Armando Novoa, the former government official who led peace negotiations with the group, said “the worst-case scenario would be for the new government to close the ZUT, launch a military operation and try to capture or kill them. That would be a crime against humanity, because these people are unarmed.”
Between 2 and 4 August, days before De la Espriella’s inauguration, Novoa led journalists including the Guardian through the ZUT. The Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, where he worked, has since been absorbed into the newly created National Security Commission – a move expected to result in more than 200 job losses – and Novoa has resigned.
For now, at least, the ZUT remains in operation and has a small library run by Bríñez, who has a phoenix tattoo on her left shoulder as a symbol of her rebirth away from the armed conflict.
“The hardest thing for me has been being away from my children,” said Bríñez, who has a seven-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old son and speaks to them on video calls, but will only be able to see them in person once her “transition” is complete, a process that includes vocational training and psychosocial support.
They were also supposed to receive financial support of about £425 a month, which had not yet been paid. In the meantime, some of them were planning to start a chicken-rearing business.
The 99 made up a small part of a group of about 1,000 combatants called Commandos of the Frontier – most of whom remain armed – and are part of the National Coordinator of the Bolivarian Army (CNEB), a former dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) with about 2,500 members which controls the border with Ecuador.
The Petro administration said negotiations were also under way with other members of the CNEB, who published an open letter addressed to De la Espriella saying they were willing to continue talks with him. It is not known whether the president responded.
The CNEB’s chief “peace negotiator”, Geovany Andrés Rojas, known as “Araña” (Spider), had been in custody since February under a US extradition request for drug trafficking, which Petro had delayed. Last Wednesday, De la Espriella ordered extradition.
Although such groups emerged in the 1960s as leftwing rebels fighting government abuses and seeking revolution – followed soon afterwards by far-right paramilitary groups – ideology has long since been overtaken for most of them by economic interests, above all drug trafficking (Colombia is the world’s largest producer of cocaine) and illegal mining.
“Here in the ZUT, the vast majority were not in the group because of any ideological commitment, but for economic reasons,” said Novoa. “It even surprised us that most of them simply called the group ‘the company’.”
Petro repeatedly tried to negotiate peace agreements with larger groups. The armed factions took advantage of temporary ceasefires to continue expanding, a process that had already begun before he took office. They also clashed among themselves for control of territory and illicit economies, which many security experts say contributed to a rise in homicides, kidnappings and massacres.
“Total peace” was an attempt to address what the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc failed to resolve, as other armed groups and Farc dissidents remained active.
Petro’s administration failed to reduce violence, which instead reached its worst levels in a decade, and to reach the disarmament stage with any of the gangs, apart from the 99 former combatants – who handed over their weapons only on the eve of an election that every poll indicated the government-backed candidate would lose.
“They [the government] told us: ‘If this works, you’re opening the door for other groups and will set an example,’” said Bríñez.
Some security experts saw the agreement as rushed.
“It was a somewhat irresponsible decision,” said Paula Tobo, a senior researcher at the thinktank Ideas for Peace Foundation, which published an extensive report on why Total Peace failed.
Tobo said the 99 were now in a “legal limbo” because their protection rested on decrees that could be revoked and there is no legal framework for their transition to civilian life. All of the Petro administration’s proposals to regulate surrenders failed in Congress and, under current law, anyone who has committed crimes such as kidnapping or drug trafficking is not eligible for amnesty.
“It’s positive that these people wanted to lay down their arms, but it really wasn’t the right time for the government to take that decision … The previous administration clearly put them at risk of this government suddenly deciding to abolish the ZUT and arrest them,” said Tobo.
The group wrote a letter to De la Espriella reaffirming its “irreversible decision to commit to peace” and inviting him to visit the ZUT. At the time of publication it had received no response.
The youngest member of the group, a 19-year-old who asked to be identified only as Adrián, said they wanted “to have a home, a family”.
However, he knows what he will do if things do not go according to plan. “Honestly, I’d take up arms again, because we’re keeping our side of the bargain and the government should do the same, shouldn’t it?” he said.
Daniela Díaz travelled to Valle del Guamuez at the invitation of the Colombian government’s former Office of the High Commissioner for Peace.

The story so far: On August 26, 2026, Meta agreed to an approximately $18 billion settlement with dozens of U.S. states in annual instalments over 10 years, and announced stricter controls in its apps for teen users. The settlement is the culmination of a lawsuit brought by California and 28 other U.S. states alleging that Facebook and Instagram are harmful for children and that they illegally collect personal data. While several parents and child health advocates welcomed the new child protection controls, enforcing them will be a lot more challenging.
What child protections is Meta rolling out?
The social media giant is both rolling out new features and building on existing features designed to create a safer and less addictive experience for Facebook and Instagram users under 18.
These measures are set to automatically apply in participating U.S. states and territories. 52 attorneys general covering U.S. states, territories, and the District of Columbia have joined the agreement.
Arguably, the biggest win for parents and the biggest concession by Meta is a default two-hour daily time limit across Facebook and Instagram. Teens can only turn this off with a parent’s permission.
Furthermore, a ‘Night Mode’ will block app users between 12 AM and 6 AM, so teens cannot post or view their Feed, Stories, Reels, or the Explore section. Similarly, the School Mode between 8 AM and 3 PM will mute notifications by default.
However, these limits do not apply to direct messages (DMs).
Teens are set to receive multiple prompts after every 15 minutes of continuous screen time on Facebook/Instagram, apart from prompts that come after their total daily usage reaches 60 minutes and 90 minutes.
To directly address addictive video features, Meta is giving teens (and their parents) the ability to choose a non-algorithmic feed as their default, as well as the ability to turn off Autoplay.
As for steps to combat unhealthy comparisons and anxiety over appearances and popularity, teen users will no longer see the number of likes and reactions on posts by default. Meta is also expanding its policy to block teens from using “extreme makeup filters,” adding to a previous block against cosmetic surgery filters for teens.
Meta reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening existing controls in order to catch underage account users, as well as teens falsely entering adult birthdays. The company claimed it will continue placing teens into private accounts on Instagram and activating private default settings on Facebook, apart from restricting “potentially suspicious adults” from reaching out to them.
Meta also said it would encourage parents to set up its supervision tools, and give them new controls and insights.
Can these safety controls be effectively enforced?
This is the crux of the matter. Safety controls for teens work only as well as the technology that verifies users’ ages and detects rule-breakers.
Take Australia, for example; the country was the first to enforce a strict blanket ban on social media for children under 16. While many parents lauded the idea and Meta reported this month that it removed over 750,000 accounts that it suspected were held by under-16s, a study by the University of Newcastle there reported that the ban did not appear to have significantly impacted under-16s who were using social media.
As other platforms and administrations explore age restrictions, critics have pointed out how easily children can fake their ages — even in video selfies and live camera tests. What’s more, these data collection tactics raise additional questions about how children’s private information is being harvested.
In its settlement announcement, Meta pointed out that all platforms — and not just its apps — should have teen safety measures in place to prevent children from moving to less restricted apps. So as to not be held back in isolation, Meta called on rival social media apps YouTube and TikTok to adopt the “new standard.”
Meta stated that around 30% of its settlement, or $5.3 billion, would be released only after rival apps YouTube and TikTok implement similar controls and pay a stipulated amount of money. To sweeten the deal, Meta said that if industry peers signed the agreement, it would further reduce the daily limit to one hour per app and expand night mode limits. In other words, this increases the incentive for U.S. regulators to also bring Meta’s rivals in line with the new policies.
Separately, the social media giant said it supported laws requiring app stores to verify the users’ age and obtain parental approval before teens can download an app. This shifts the responsibility of age verification to companies such as Apple and Google.
How can parents elsewhere make Facebook and Instagram less addictive?
Even without Meta’s new controls, parents and educators can work with children to fight social media addiction. Most smartphones come with built-in parental controls that allow adults to set time limits for individual apps, as well as curtail overall device use.
Furthermore, many of Meta’s existing safety controls — such as Teen Accounts on Instagram — can be used by children across borders who enter their ages correctly.
For more advanced settings, adults can research and download parental control apps that allow them to set up different usage limits for multiple children and monitor their activity remotely. Some apps allow parents to remotely lock devices and apps during sleeping hours and/or school hours.
Meanwhile, teachers can communicate with their students via email, or send alerts through non-addictive digital forums during daytime hours. Students should be strongly discouraged from conducting school assignments or group projects via social media apps.
Enabling parental controls for teen social media users is a constantly evolving challenge. After all, these young internet and AI-native users are often more tech-savvy than the very adults trying to restrict their time online

South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.
A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.
The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.
Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.
The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”
Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.
The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.
South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.

Here at Ars, we’re intimately familiar with data leaks surrounding Valve’s games, hardware, and the workings of Steam itself. But nothing could have prepared us for this weekend’s “terarelease” encompassing more than 12TB of content related to seemingly every title available on Steam between 2003 to 2013.
What’s being sold as an “as-complete-as-possible … content server dump” of Steam’s defunct “Steam2” server architecture from that time period is now circulating around via a BitTorrent tracker that Valve seems unlikely to ever completely purge from the Internet. The massive collection includes thousands of “depots” representing what seems to be every version of every game uploaded to those old Steam2 servers. That includes public release builds, of course, but in many cases also covers previously unseen pre-release, prototype, and playtest versions of popular titles published by Valve and third-party Steam publishers.
Steam2: Electric Boogaloo
The reason this weekend’s leaked content cuts off abruptly in 2013 is because that’s when Valve updated its content distribution system from “Steam2” to the current SteamPipe system. In moving from a proprietary file distribution format to standard HTTP file trees, the new system removed various update approval bottlenecks on Valve’s end and streamlined update and patch downloads so they only reflected file differentials.
Publicly accessible early versions of some games released before this SteamPipe transition had been considered lost content by archivists, no longer accessible from Valve itself and living on only as local downloads on aging machines. Apparently all that content wasn’t as lost as many thought, though. Longtime Valve watcher and data miner Gabe Follower (previously) wrote on social media this weekend that he had “verified that everything in Steam2 Teraleak was obtained via a publicly accessible [API] endpoint. It’s Valve’s fault…”
Spanish-language Valve streamer and analyst Scolcer also said on social media (via machine translation) that the teraleak was “obtained from a site that was 100% accessible to the public. It was there for everyone to download. No passwords. Nothing. Hidden in plain sight, but with no protection whatsoever.”

Don’t be fooled by the question mark in the title of an article published this month in the Journal of the American Medical Association. When the authors, including medical superstar Ezekiel Emanuel and venture capitalist Vinod Khosla, asked, “Will Autonomous AI Exceed AI-Physicians as the Best Medical Care?” they were being rhetorical. Their answer is an emphatic YES. Many in the medical world are begrudgingly coming to terms with the premise that patients can get the best treatment by a hybrid approach where doctors work in consultation with well-trained bots. But this article’s thesis is that AI alone can deliver the best outcomes.
“Review of all published articles on AI in medicine since January 1, 2024, shows that medicine is rapidly approaching the transition point at which AI alone will exceed physicians and physician AI-hybrids in providing the best care at five fundamental medical tasks,” they write. Those tasks include taking medical histories, establishing a diagnosis, identifying what tests are needed, prescribing treatment, and managing chronic diseases. You know, doctoring. AI is now so good, they argue, that clinicians should refrain from meddling, because “humans in the loop degrade AI performance.” Stand back, doc, and let AI do its thing. Which used to be your thing.
Lead author Emanuel—brother of Ari and Rahm, chair of the Department of Medical Ethics and Health Policy at Penn and a renowned oncologist—told me that for many years, he’d dismissed the idea that AI could perform core medical functions. He would run into Khosla at conferences in the 2010s, and the VC would bend his ear about how AI would be doing 85 percent of what doctors did by 2035. It was a hobbyhorse Khosla had been riding for years, writing a 2012 piece in TechCrunch asking, “Do We Need Doctors or Algorithms?”(again, rhetorical) and penning a 101-page treatise in 2016 to that effect. “I said bullshit, there’s no way,” says Emanuel. “What doctors do is too complicated.”
But about a year ago, Emanuel’s friend Robert Wachter sent him galleys of his book A Giant Leap, where Wachter, who is head of medicine at UCSF, outlined a world where first-class medicine would be a collaborative process between AI and doctors, but the masses in “economy class” would mostly make do with AI alone. Emanuel began to think that Khosla might be right. He suddenly flashed on a frightening question: “If AI takes over, what’s left for doctors to do?”
First he needed to validate the premise. He asked Khosla to collaborate, and the VC suggested that his son Neal Khosla join the effort, along with Emanuel’s researcher. Neal runs Curai Health, an online company that uses AI to treat patients, with a staff of doctors to prescribe medicine and handle more complicated issues. (This conflict of interest is disclosed in the paper, along with Vinod Khosla’s relevant investments and Emanuel’s various grants and consultancies.) The coauthors set out to look at all the studies on AI medicine that they could find from January 2024 to the present and concluded that, in many cases, a “superior autonomous AI” will likely surpass humans using AI by 2030. That prediction, they admit, is “unsettling but seems probable.”
Unsettling is an understatement. One of the loudest dissenting voices is John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association, which represents all those doctors who will be worrying about what’s left. When I talked to him, Whyte began by noting what he saw as the paper’s shortcomings, including that some of the studies it surveyed are simulations, not blind experiments, and they don’t all support the article’s conclusion. Notably, a February 2026 Nature article found that in real-life cases, most patients were unable to effectively converse with large language models to access their expertise. Whyte unsurprisingly bristled at the idea of removing humans from the clinical loop. “The AMA does see the potential in these tools, but they have to be utilized in the context of a care plan that’s governed by a physician,” he says.
Emanuel countered that he and his coauthors were careful in their conclusions. “It’s been less than four years since ChatGPT was introduced,” he said to me. “We’re making a prediction for four years from now. You don’t think that [AI is] going to be way more advanced than a doctor?”
Seeking a second opinion, I consulted Wachter. He’s singled out in the paper’s first paragraph as the guy who wrongly argues that AI-only treatment will be “economy class.” (I know Wachter personally.) Surprisingly, Wachter concedes that the authors of the paper have a point. “The argument they’re making is important,” he says. AI is good, he says, and right now AI and humans together are better. “But that can no longer be chiseled into a tablet. There will be times when humans will muck up the performance.”
Wachter is insistent, however, that the unique human attributes of trained physicians are vital and irreplaceable. AI may never be as effective in breaking the news of a grim prognosis than a human, and a patient may well be more likely to be guided to the best path of treatment by a real-life clinician.
Wachter invokes what he calls the doorman fallacy, named after the fear that people who opened doors for tenants in apartment buildings would be out of work once doors could open automatically. In fact doormen perform myriad tasks and are still an invaluable presence in white-glove buildings. Like accepting Amazon packages, feeding pets, and sometimes lending a sympathetic ear to a tenant sharing a gripe. “We’re going to find a version of the doorman fallacy for doctors,” says Wachter. “I can imagine a world where a doctor accepts the AI diagnosis but also performs a lot of other functions that have value.”
What’s being displaced here, though, isn’t something as straightforward as opening a door. It's the hard-won expertise that comes from years of training. You know those scenes in The Pitt where Dr. Robby relentlessly puts his residents on the spot by asking them to come up with instant assessments? That won’t be necessary when AI has the answer on demand. Physicians are on a path to relying so much on AI that their own judgment and knowledge will become less relevant. This “de-skilling” process could accelerate the takeover of medicine by AI, especially as new generations of doctors won’t find it necessary to spend years learning stuff that they can find out by querying an always-on AI expert in the pocket of their lab coat. The AMA’s Whyte admits that this is a concern for him. “A lot of medical schools and residency programs are debating whether physicians in their training can utilize these tools, because if you’ve never learned how to take medical history and do a physical, how will you ever learn?” On the other hand, there’s an argument that ignoring such a compelling tool is a form of malpractice.
So what’s the future for doctors? Vinod Khosla says that we’ll need them, at least in the short term, for surgery and in the emergency room. But in terms of providing expertise and judgment, he says they’re largely expendable, except maybe as debaters with AI to improve those systems. Neal Khosla tells me that the shift is already underway and that he expects that in coming years we will give AI the regulatory permission to prescribe medicine.
Remember the TV series House, where a dyspeptic and rude diagnostic genius decoded baffling conditions while insulting patients and humiliating his hapless acolytes? In the world of AI medicine, a Dr. House would be rendered homeless, because AI will routinely and freely apply its vast knowledge base to the most obscure ailments. The value of human clinicians will be the elements where House was most lacking, like empathy and high-EQ communication. Of course those who perform hands-on procedures are safe from AI encroachment—until the robots figure that out.
Health care is a huge part of our lives, but the debate here goes beyond that sector. The question, “What’s left for doctors to do?” may well be “What’s left for humans to do?” Bill Gates suggests in his recent jeremiad on AI that society might designate some tasks—like doctors counseling patients on how to deal with AI’s prognoses—“human-reserved,” to stave off economic ruin and a run on pitchforks. (Try to sell that solution to corporate shareholders who question the funding of make-work jobs.) At least the misery of the unemployed masses will be mitigated by one bonus: first-class medical advice that’s one click away.

Did Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lie to lawmakers about vaccines?
Another day, another headline related to health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his position on vaccines.
Kennedy insisted to lawmakers that a 2019 visit to Samoa before a deadly measles outbreak had “nothing to do with vaccines.” New documents obtained by AP and The Guardian question that testimony.
Kennedy preceded the visit with a letter to the Samoan prime minister (above, at right, greeting Kennedy and his wife, actress Cheryl Hines) requesting to study the Pacific island nation’s measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines after the deaths of two children who had received them. In the letter, he used the words vaccine or vaccination eight times. Critics have blamed Kennedy for fueling anti-vaccine sentiment and sparking an outbreak that killed 83 people, mostly children under 5.
What’s in these letters? Who are the Democratic senators accusing the secretary of lying? Read more.
Speaking of vaccines …
… Vaccines took center stage at a federal autism advisory committee meeting yesterday, with committee members explicitly naming vaccines as a cause of autism.
The link between autism and vaccines has been routinely debunked, but Kennedy reshaped the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee in January with people who closely hew to his views on vaccines. Which is why nobody on the committee challenged those statements.
The committee spent the day discussing and then voting to approve a plan that would radically reshape the prevailing genetics-first approach to understanding autism, opting instead to fund research into areas with significantly less scientific evidence for their relevance — diet, inflammation, metabolic stress, and folate (remember leucovorin?).
The plan and its rollout received a ton of backlash, but the meeting was relatively tame — until the end. I’ve got the latest IACC drama, including the testy exchange between the committee chair and an autistic federal employee.
Former Stanford president responds to cover-up allegations
Three years ago, a closely watched research misconduct investigation led to the resignation of Stanford University’s then-president, Marc Tessier-Lavigne. Yesterday, Tessier-Lavigne revealed new details from his research, including nine emails, in an attempt to refute allegations that he published fraudulent results and orchestrated a cover-up. His self-defense is a direct rebuttal to charges made in the book “How to Rule the World: An Education in Power at Stanford University” by former Stanford Daily reporter Theo Baker.
As a Stanford undergraduate, Baker wrote a series of stories detailing concerns around studies co-authored by Tessier-Lavigne. In his book, he presented the former president as a case study in Silicon Valley’s culture of corner-cutting. “I believe it’s important to set the record straight,” Tessier-Lavigne told STAT’s Jonathan Wosen in an interview. Read more on the new details and how they line up with Baker’s account.
We quit the CDC. Here’s how to fix it
One year ago, Debra Houry, Daniel Jernigan, and Demetre Daskalakis jointly resigned from their posts at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest the Trump administration’s spread of misinformation and dismantling of the agency. The problems haven’t changed, they write.
As Erica Schwartz enters office as the new CDC director, the former federal health leaders have suggestions for Congress about fixing the CDC and restoring the agency as a bulwark for public health: shield science from politically driven policies, protect scientific publications, restore independent expert advice, and administer funding as directed by Congress.
“The answer is not simply to restore the CDC to what it was, but to build a stronger and more resilient public health institution for the future,” they write. “That requires safeguards so that no administration, Republican or Democratic, can replace independent public health decision-making with partisan ideology.” Read more.
The false hype of a new Medicare billing code
In a perfect world, primary care offers so much. Physical examinations, mental health check-ins, medication adjustments, vaccine suggestions. Two years ago, Medicare tried to enshrine this ongoing, relationship-based care and allow doctors to collect an additional $16 per visit with a specific billing code: G2211.
Unfortunately, early research suggests the code may not work as hoped, writes Ishani Ganguli, an associate professor of medicine and internal medicine primary care physician at Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women’s Hospital.
In reality, the physicians using the code the most? Specialists, not primary care physicians. Read more from Ganguli about her team’s research and the gaps in our current “fee-for-service” system.

The day after Donald Trump won the 2016 election, the conservative political operative Roger Stone was among the lucky few to get through to him on the telephone. The president-elect reminisced about the long-dead friend who had introduced him to Stone: “Wouldn’t Roy love to see this moment? Boy, do we miss him.”
“Roy” was Roy Cohn, who became notorious in the early 1950s as chief counsel to Senator Joseph McCarthy and then built a career as a lawyer and fixer for New York City’s rich and powerful. His roster of clients, many of whom doubled as his friends, included Cardinal Francis Spellman, George Steinbrenner, the media mogul Si Newhouse, and a host of famous mafiosi, including “Fat Tony” Salerno and John Gotti. Trump met Cohn in 1973, when the young developer sought advice about a federal lawsuit alleging racial discrimination by his family’s real-estate company. Cohn proposed countersuing the feds for defamation—even though the company had been marking the applications of prospective Black tenants with a large C, for “colored,” and then telling them no apartments were available. The countersuit, for $100 million, failed as a legal tactic—the company settled with the Justice Department, without admitting wrongdoing, after two years of litigation—but it made headlines, which was the real point. Trump and Cohn had the same attitude toward the law: It was not a system of rules, but a way of getting what you wanted.
For a generation of liberal Manhattanites, the mere mention of Cohn’s name produced a visceral loathing. They saw him as a self-serving and unprincipled social climber whose crusade against communism had ruined lives. In documentaries, profiles, and the play Angels in America, he has been portrayed as a villain in the vein of Shakespeare’s Richard III, whose monstrousness can be traced back to his own sense of social exclusion. When Cohn contracted AIDS, he kept his illness and his sexuality secret to the end. He died in 1986 insisting that he had liver cancer, even while enrolled in a clinical trial to receive AZT, an early AIDS medication.
In American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey From Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump, Kai Bird—writing with his wife, Susan Goldmark, whom he credits with contributing significant research—aims to bring Cohn into focus as a progenitor of Trump. Bird’s previous work as a biographer has focused on distinguished statesmen and scientists of the mid-20th century, most notably the left-leaning nuclear physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, whom he and Martin J. Sherwin wrote about in American Prometheus, the book adapted by Christopher Nolan for the movie Oppenheimer.
Cohn, like Trump, had nothing but contempt for the norms and ethos of that mid-century elite. But Bird argues that this hatred was driven less by a coherent politics than by “dishonesty, narcissism, careless cruelty, and vengefulness.” Both men were avatars of the glitzy New York of the ’70s and ’80s, sharing an obsession with sex, a love of celebrity, and a hatred for expertise. Bird quotes the New York Times reporter Sam Roberts on the lessons Trump learned from Cohn: “1. Never settle, never surrender. 2. Counterattack, counter-sue immediately. 3. No matter what happens, no matter how deeply into the muck you get, claim victory and never admit defeat.” (Bird also implies that Cohn may have had a crush on Trump, blond and blue-eyed men being his ideal type.)
In Bird’s telling, the parallels between Cohn and Trump begin with their childhoods. Both grew up in New York’s outer boroughs, in families that were prosperous but resentful of those in the real inner circle. Cohn, born in 1927, lived in the Bronx as a young boy, the only child of a loveless marriage. His maternal grandfather, a wealthy banker, founded the Bank of United States, whose clients were primarily Jewish immigrants. Cohn’s father, active in the Bronx Democratic machine, agreed to marry his mother in return for being made a judge, which her father could promise thanks to his political connections. But the family was plagued by a scandal: The bank collapsed in the early years of the Depression, and Cohn’s maternal uncle, who had taken over as its president, was convicted of fraud and sent to prison at Sing Sing.
Cohn grew up without many friends; one of his cousins said that he was the kind of kid who would have enjoyed keeping a snake as a pet and feeding it live mice. His social life didn’t improve when the family moved to the Upper East Side in 1935. Few Jews lived in the area then, but the collapse of real-estate prices in the Depression made it possible for the Cohns to get a place on Park Avenue. Cohn was educated at elite private institutions: the Ethical Culture School and then the more traditional and uptight Horace Mann School, followed by Columbia for college and law school.
Thanks to his father’s influence, Cohn quickly got a job in the U.S. Attorney’s Office. He was soon working on high-profile cases against alleged Communists, including the writer Dashiell Hammett and the State Department official Alger Hiss. In 1951, Cohn was a key member of the team that prosecuted Julius and Ethel Rosenberg for conspiring to pass atomic secrets to the U.S.S.R. He intimidated Ethel’s brother David Greenglass, who’d worked on the Manhattan Project, into testifying against her. After the Rosenbergs were convicted, Cohn helped press Judge Irving Kaufman to give both of them the death penalty, hoping that Ethel would feel forced to talk. She did not, and the Rosenbergs’ two children were orphaned.
Cohn’s ferocious investment in anti-communism, Bird argues, reflected the fears of New York’s “Park Avenue Jews,” who worried that Jewish Americans would be suspected of disloyalty because of Lower East Side radicals like the Rosenbergs. It also made him a natural choice when McCarthy, then at the height of his anti-communist campaign, needed a new chief counsel. Cohn was hired at age 25, beating out Robert F. Kennedy for the job. He advised McCarthy as the senator oversaw more than 110 closed-door hearings and subpoenaed hundreds of people, many of whom lost their job or faced public humiliation.
Cohn was especially nasty toward gay men. Hundreds of federal employees were fired not for being Communists but because they were suspected of being gay. Not that the two were entirely separate in his view; Cohn, like many others, believed that homosexuals were prime “prey” for spies. At the same time, he was the target of homophobic rumors himself, especially about his relationship with David Schine, a wealthy, Harvard-educated young man whom Cohn persuaded McCarthy to hire as an unpaid consultant. When Schine was drafted into the Army as the Korean War was ending, Cohn tried to get him excused from basic training. After these efforts were rebuffed, Cohn called the Army’s general counsel and threatened to “teach the Army what it means to go over my head.” A month later, Army representatives were called before McCarthy’s congressional committee for the first time, setting up a confrontation that would eventually lead to McCarthy’s downfall. Bird argues that Cohn’s willingness to say and do anything to get what he wanted—no matter who might suffer along the way—provided a model for Trump’s approach to political life.
Cohn may have entered American political history because of his role in the Red Scare, but American Scoundrel emphasizes the career he went on to build in New York, where he showed an amazing capacity to escape legal repercussions for his misdeeds. Over the course of the 1960s, the liberal U.S. Attorney Robert Morgenthau unsuccessfully brought charges against Cohn for perjury, obstruction of justice, mail and wire fraud, conspiracy to bribe a city official, extortion, and blackmail. Cohn claimed that he was being targeted by Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, his old rival: “A few people are out to get me,” he declared. During Cohn’s second trial, his attorney suffered a heart attack. Instead of getting a new lawyer, Cohn gave the summation of the case on his own behalf, and when he was acquitted of all charges, he told the press: “Thank God we put juries between the type of tyranny that Morgenthau perpetrates on his enemies!”
Cohn could be charismatic. Ayn Rand fawned over him when they met at a party: “You’ve always fascinated me so much and I believe in so much of what you stand for.” Still, he comes off in this book as smarmy and unappealing, a cheat from start to finish. Bird gives us a litany of Cohn’s pettier sins. In the summer of 1968, he invited Cardinal Spellman and the Democratic politician Carmine De Sapio onto his yacht (named Defiance) to discuss judicial nominations, then wrote it off as a business expense. He and Barbara Walters were good friends and he hinted to gossip columnists that they were romantically involved, using her to hide his sexuality. Cohn had a lifelong habit of eating off the plates of his dining companions without asking their permission. He regularly stiffed his creditors. When one hapless small-business man sent him a memo reminding him of a $10,000 debt, Cohn scrawled a characteristic response: “Dear Louie: Fuck you. Roy.”
For Cohn, being gay was a private matter—his business, nobody else’s. Drawing on an unpublished memoir by Cohn’s cousin, Bird details sex parties at Cohn’s townhouse on East 68th Street; apparently the house was also used as the set for a pornographic film (Cohn owned two X-rated-movie theaters in New Jersey). He went out regularly to gay establishments, and the gossip columnist Liz Smith wrote that he “owned a number of successful gay bars around Manhattan.”
But Cohn remained intensely homophobic in public, telling people that he believed “gays shouldn’t be schoolteachers.” He lobbied against gay-civil-rights legislation for New York City in the 1970s and early ’80s. In 1978, he told an interviewer that anyone “who knows the way my mind works or knows the way I function in active life, would have an awfully hard time reconciling that with any kind of homosexuality.” The playwright Tony Kushner drew on this idea for the famous monologue that his version of Cohn delivers in Angels in America: “Homosexuals are not men who sleep with other men. Homosexuals are men who in fifteen years of trying cannot get a pissant antidiscrimination bill through City Council. Homosexuals are men who know nobody and who nobody knows. Who have zero clout. Does that sound like me?” the Cohn character asks. “No. I have clout. A lot of it.”
American Scoundrel offers an effective portrait of Cohn’s role in New York society in an era when sleaze and respectability were not clearly delineated. There is a great deal of salacious gossip; readers will learn far more than they ever wanted to know about Cohn’s sexual habits. Yet despite the extent of Bird and Goldmark’s research, the portrayal of Cohn as an unbounded narcissist misses some of what his life might tell us about the right-wing politics of his era. Earlier accounts have been more sensitive to the irony that Cohn was undone by the same political forces he rode to prominence. The repression of the McCarthy era—the frenetic demands for loyalty, patriotism, normalcy—helped bolster the sexual secrecy and homophobia that compounded the devastation of AIDS in its early years, cloaking the disease in fear and shame.
What Bird does give us is a new way to think about Cohn, Trump, and the legacy of McCarthyism. Cohn always presented himself as an outsider facing down a hostile, arrogant establishment, a stance that Trump adopted as he moved into politics. But Cohn’s career depended on being an insider, connected to New York’s media empires, real-estate developers, politicians, law firms, and private schools. Looking at the long arc of Cohn’s career shows how much of McCarthyism was about ambition and careerism, rather than ideology. His friends and clients were obsequious to him because they thought he could get them things no one else could: money, divorce settlements, political influence.
Cohn’s commitment to his clients kept him in rarified company until the end. In March 1986, Trump threw a bash for Cohn at Mar-a-Lago, inviting guests such as Lee Iacocca of Chrysler and Manhattan Borough President Andrew Stein. Cohn attended, his skin blotchy with sarcoma; afterward, housekeeping staff was instructed to disinfect the silverware with bleach. In late June, a little more than a month before Cohn died, he was disbarred in New York State for offenses including perjury, misappropriation of funds, and coercing a mentally incapacitated client into signing a will that appointed Cohn executor. A blue-chip roster of Cohn’s friends testified in his defense, including William F. Buckley Jr., William Safire, Barbara Walters, and Trump.
Cohn insisted he didn’t care about being disbarred. Recalcitrant and self-righteous, he always claimed to disregard other people’s opinions of him. He would have responded the same way to the conclusion Bird reaches in American Scoundrel, that he was an “empty vessel” with “no coherent personal philosophy unless you count his shallow mirroring of Ayn Rand’s celebration of unadulterated selfishness.” But he would surely have been bothered by the epitaph that was included on the AIDS Memorial Quilt—especially the last word: ROY COHN. BULLY. COWARD. VICTIM.
