England's Dean storms to British Masters title
- Published
British Masters final leaderboard
-14 J Dean (Eng); -11 JS Olesen (Den), N Norgaard (Den), N Elvira (Spa), D Hillier (NZ)
Selected: -10 M Penge (Eng), T McKibbin (NI); -9 F Zanotti (Par); -8 M Wallace (Eng), E Ferguson (Sco)
Former supermarket delivery driver Joe Dean fired a sensational bogey-free nine-under-par 63 to snatch the British Masters title at The Belfry.
It is a first DP World Tour victory in his 70th event for the 32-year-old Englishman who is ranked 292nd in the world.
He collected the trophy and about £440,000 in prize money, more than he had earned in total from his previous 19 tournaments in the 2026 season.
"All those painful hours and all the work, it's finally led to something," said Dean, who two years ago was delivering groceries to help fund his golf.
"It was a rare day when everything felt right and the putts were dropping and I couldn't do anything wrong."
It caps a busy summer for the Sheffield golfer who won the inaugural Last Chance Qualifier on the Monday of Open Championship week in July to earn the final spot in the field at Royal Birkdale.
He then married Emily, who carried his bag that week and this.
"I can't thank her enough," said Dean on Sky Sports. "I hope I made her proud."
Dean started Sunday's final round seven shots behind leader Dan Hillier and made a move with four birdies in his opening six holes. Five more followed on the back nine, including a 10-footer at the last to set the target at 14 under par.
He then had to wait about 90 minutes to be crowned champion as challengers came and faded.
Dean eventually won by three strokes from four players, including 2023 champion Hillier, at a tournament that was disrupted by stormy conditions in Warwickshire.
More than nine hours of play was lost on Thursday and Friday, leaving organisers scrambling to complete the event before more forecast inclement weather returned.
Marco Penge, who had a breakthrough year in 2025 with three wins, led on 10 under after a sparkling 65 in round two.
He also started the final round on that total after completing a third-round 72 on Sunday morning.
Five birdies and two bogeys in his first nine holes of round four catapulted Penge into a one-stroke lead with nine to play.
However, a third bogey of the round, on the 11th, halted his momentum and five more pars followed to leave him 12 under with two to play.
Penge compounded the error of a wild drive into trees on the par-five 17th by hitting a branch with his second shot and then had to chip out sideways with his third.
That led to a bogey and with his challenge over, he dropped a shot at the last too to finish with a 72 and 10-under total.
A double-bogey six on the sixth hurt Hillier's tilt at winning a second title. And while the New Zealander had two birdies on his back nine, he closed with a one-over 73 to finish on 11 under.
That left him joint second alongside the Danish pair of Niklas Norgaard and Jacob Skov Olesen who both signed for 71s, and Spain's Nacho Elvira who carded a 69.
Paraguay's Fabrizio Zanotti threatened to trouble Dean's lead late on after firing four birdies in five holes during a purple patch on his back nine to get to 12 under, but he had a triple bogey on the last after taking two shots to get out of a fairway bunker and then finding water.
The British Masters was the first event in the race to qualify for the European team to take on the United States at next year's Ryder Cup in Ireland.

Nasa's powerful next-generation telescope has blasted off into space from its launchpad in Florida, with a mission to explore dark energy, black holes and other mysteries of the Universe.
The Nancy Grace Roman telescope will capture vast panoramic views of space, with a field of vision 100 times larger than both the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, Nasa says.
The mission begins with a 100-day journey to a vantage point roughly one million miles from Earth, where the telescope will then start charting planets outside our solar system, known as exoplanets.
"Roman is going to change the way we look at the Universe," said Nicky Fox, a Nasa administrator.
"It is going to discover tens of thousands, maybe even 100,000 new exoplanets."
US President Donald Trump dialled in to Nasa's news conference on Sunday morning to congratulate the scientists working on the project.
"You're the hottest in space, and we have the hottest country anywhere in the world. So, let's keep it all going. You're a big part of it," Trump said.
The successful launch of the telescope took place on Sunday morning local time from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
"What a glorious dawn launch," Jackie Townsend, a project manager on Nasa's Roman telescope, said at the news conference after liftoff. "The ride was magnificent. It put us right where we wanted to be."
About 30 minutes after launch, Roman separated from its SpaceX rocket and is now heading towards its orbiting point around a million miles away.
Astronomer Jenifer Millard said the telescope will be four times further from Earth than the Moon is, where a lot of infrared space cameras - made to pick up what she describes as "heat light"- operate.
She told the BBC this is to make sure infrared light from the Moon and Earth don't interfere with the cameras.
Nasa's James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, also orbits the Sun around one million miles from Earth, but its field of vision is not as expansive. Nasa's Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits at about 300 miles above Earth's surface.
While Roman will look outward into the Universe, Millard said scientists are also anticipating it will find thousands of new worlds in our own galaxy.
The telescope is named after physicist Nancy Grace Roman, who was Nasa's first chief astronomer in the 1960s and its first female executive.
During her career, she was instrumental in getting the Hubble Space Telescope approved by US Congress and later said its most interesting discovery was dark energy.
The new telescope is similarly expected to revolutionise our understanding of the Universe, including through investigating dark energy. It has a five-year primary lifespan with a goal to operate for 10 years.
Nasa says its "crisp, sweeping surveys will help scientists investigate dark energy and dark matter, discover and characterise exoplanets, map billions of galaxies, study black holes, and explore objects from our own solar system to the edge of the observable Universe."
Dark matter, which is invisible, acts as a kind of gravitational glue, while dark energy is believed to be a repulsive force driving the Universe's expansion. Together, they are thought to make up about 95% of the Universe.
"One of our main goals at Nasa is answering the question: are we alone in the Universe?" Fox said at a Sunday morning news conference.
"With Roman, we are going to make this giant leap forward... that is going to allow us to look at these distant, distant worlds and start to really resolve the atmosphere around them to let us know: could they be habitable?"
Millard said, through the work of telescopes like Roman, scientists are hoping to create "enormous cosmic maps" of the Universe at various stages.
"They'll be almost like an onion, so you can peel back layer upon layer... and see how the distribution of galaxies changes through cosmic time," she said.
"What we want to do is use this distribution to try and figure out dark matter and dark energy because we know they exist, we see their effects, but what they are is a real mystery."

They fell in love - then had to check they weren't brother and sister
- Published
For years, Arthur Kermalvezen, the child of a sperm donor, saw possible fathers everywhere he went. "I imagined it might be my teacher, the people I saw on the bus... and I was very angry because it's impossible to live like this."
When, as an adult, he fell in love with Audrey, another sperm donor baby from Paris, the question became even more pressing.
Audrey describes the moment they met at a gathering for donor conceived activists in 2010 as "love at first sight" - but was this connection a romantic or genetic attraction?
When they were born, there were only two sperm banks in Paris and many men had made multiple donations - so there was a real possibility they could be half-siblings.
Before building a life together, Arthur and Audrey needed to know whether they were related. But in France, laws governing genetic testing and donor anonymity made finding the answer extremely difficult.
In France, only a research scientist, doctor or judge can order and supervise a genetic test, and people can be fined more than €3,500 ($4,288; £3,191) for possessing a home testing kit. As a result, companies such as 23andMe, Ancestry and MyHeritage don't make their kits available in France.
Supporters of the law, in place since 1994, say it stops sensitive genetic data being given to commercial companies, and prevents family disputes being caused by unexpected results.
But Arthur points out that France is the only country in Europe that criminalises the use of such tests.
Immediate chemistry
Even before her parents told her as an adult that she was donor-conceived, Audrey had qualified as a lawyer, specialising in bioethics law. Because of this, she fully understood that French law had guaranteed donor anonymity, even after a donor's death.
But Audrey had been conceived in 1979, before any such legislation existed.
While searching for other donor-conceived people born before 1994, Audrey came across Arthur. He had written a book detailing his desire to learn more about his biological origins.
Audrey says she was struck by how precisely he expressed feelings she herself had struggled to articulate. Both had loving families, yet both found themselves drawn to questions about the unknown people who had helped to create them.
When they met in person the chemistry was immediate. So was the problem.
Before they could move from platonic friendship to a romantic relationship, and even build a life together, they had to know the truth about their fathers. But no one in authority was willing to tell them.
In search of the truth
After months of searching, they found a doctor in southern France who, for €900 ($1,028; £764) in cash, conducted a genetic test which found that they were not related. But their unease remained as the doctor was breaking the law in sharing that result with them.
"We were worried he was a charlatan," Audrey says.
They considered using a home-testing kit to confirm the result, but as a lawyer, Audrey was determined to act within the law.
So, from 2010, she launched a series of legal challenges to the French system.
She wanted to know whether her donor was still alive and, if so, whether he still wished to remain anonymous. Could she access non-identifying information about how many times he had donated and whether Arthur could be among her half-siblings?
Her efforts failed.
After three years of legal challenges, the couple took a 'leap of faith' and got married.
In 2015, France's highest administrative court rejected Audrey's final appeal.
Shortly before the birth of their first child, a doctor agreed to investigate what information might exist about their respective donors. Under French law, a medical practitioner has access to this information about their patients, but is not allowed to share it with them.
The doctor found that their donors were born in different years - and so could not be the same man. A life-changing piece of information, but one they only gained because a doctor agreed to break the rules.
"It's completely weird," Audrey says, "because it means that the doctor can know more than me... about me."
Even with this new information, Arthur still worried they could be related, so after years of resisting it, they finally took a home DNA test.
Campaigners say the French ban has done little to stop people taking home tests, with the advocacy group DNA Pass estimating that well over a million French people have taken one. Many order them via friends in countries where they are legally obtainable - or by using forwarding services in neighbouring countries.
The test said they weren't related.
DNA shock
The DNA results soon opened more doors. After 30 years of imagining who his father might be, Arthur finally made contact with his sperm donor on Christmas Day in 2017.
But Audrey had the greatest shock. Among her DNA matches was a woman named Sophie whom she'd represented in court. The two women had been fighting for similar legal rights.
"I discovered that Sophie - a woman whose case I had pleaded in court - was my biological sister," Audrey says.
Audrey and Arthur had taken their DNA test alongside eight other donor-conceived activists campaigning for access to their origins.
Of the 10, four turned out to share the same donor: Audrey, her brother Peter, Sophie and Sophie's brother David - highlighting how real the risk of a shared donor had always been.
Many years later, a genetic match with an American led Audrey to her donor - a man called Philippe - but he had already died.
Audrey's mother wrote Philippe's family a letter, thanking them for his "gift" which she described as "immeasurable".
His family welcomed Audrey for a visit. "Everybody had tears in their eyes," recalls Audrey. Philippe's sister had never known he was a donor.
The discovery gave Audrey answers that she had sought for decades. She learned details about her biological family's medical history. She saw photographs and video footage of Philippe. "I can watch him, see how he moved and hear his voice."
Audrey's legal campaign and Arthur's book together helped drive changes to French donor-conception laws, allowing people conceived after April 2025 to access identifying information about their donors when they reach adulthood.
For now, however, France remains one of the few countries in Europe where at-home DNA testing is still prohibited.
Which means, for Audrey, the wider fight continues.
"Every person has the right to know their origins and the right to know their history," she says.
Based on an episode of The Gift on BBC Radio 4

Boreham Wood accept Vardy-beating record fee for Abdulmalik

Swedish club Djurgardens have agreed a National League record fee thought to be in excess of £1.5m to sign winger Abdul Abdulmalik from Boreham Wood.

The agreement also brings to an end a long-running transfer saga, with the Hertfordshire club having rejected bids of £1m and £1.5m for the former Millwall academy player earlier this summer.
Abdulmalik said: "I'm ready for the next challenge. I'm ready to prove to myself and those around me that I'm capable of reaching the top."
He scored in his final appearance for Boreham Wood in mid-August but subsequently made himself unavailable for selection in an attempt to secure a move.
Clubs in England, including Peterborough United, had also expressed an interest.
Abdulmalik was previously an England Under-17s international but was released by Millwall in 2024 and had an unsuccessful trial at Portsmouth.
Stockholm-based Djurgardens are currently fifth in the Allsvenskan - which runs from April to November - but have two games in hand on the majority of their rivals and remain in contention to qualify for Europe.

The Trump administration is considering ending employment authorisation for some spouses of H-1B visa holders, changing a policy that has allowed eligible H-4 spouses to work legally in the United States for more than a decade. The move could impact working families and household incomes. The proposal, posted on the website Reginfo.gov, under the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, is titled “Removing H-4 Dependent Spouses From the Classes of Noncitizens Eligible for Employment Authorization.” It says, “DHS [US Department of Homeland Security] is proposing to remove from its regulations certain H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B nonimmigrant workers as a class of aliens eligible to request employment authorization under the (c)(26) category.” H-4 dependents are the legal spouse and unmarried children under the age of 21 of a primary temporary worker in the United States, such as an H-1B visa holder. Simply put, a spouse and unmarried children under the age of 21 are eligible to come to the US as the H-4 dependents of an H-1B worker. According to Murthy Law Firm, H-4 status must be separately extended for each family member by filing an application with USCIS. It says that H-4 status is not automatically extended when the spouse or parent receives an extension of H1B status. Persons in H-4 status are permitted to live in the US and to attend school, but are not permitted to work. But certain H-4 spouses can work if they apply for and receive an Employment Authorization Document (EAD). "You will not be authorized to work until USCIS approves your Form I-765," says the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). As per reports, this proposal would reverse the changes made in the 2015 final rule, “Employment Authorization for Certain H-4 Dependent Spouses.” It will restore DHS's long-standing policy of not extending eligibility to request employment authorization to H-4 dependent spouses. It proposes to remove H-4 dependent spouses from the category of foreign nationals eligible to receive Employment Authorization Documents, or EADs. The change has not taken effect, and nothing has changed for H-4 EAD holders yet. This is not a proposed rule yet. The item has been classified as a “Long-Term Action” and, significantly, the date for a proposed rule is listed as “To be determined." There is no draft text available, and no deadline has been set as yet for the rollout of a draft proposal. Before an H-4 EAD could actually be eliminated, DHS would to publish a proposed rule, invite public comments, consider and respond to those comments, publish a final rule and establish an effective date. This could take months. The current US Citizenship and Immigration Services rules continue to allow certain H-4 dependent spouses to apply for an Employment Authorization Document, or EAD. The H-4 EAD program was created in 2015. The Federal Register said the rule would allow certain H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B workers who were pursuing employment-based lawful permanent residence to apply for employment authorization. USCIS currently says an H-4 spouse may file for employment authorization if the H-1B spouse meets specified requirements, which include: 1. Is the principal beneficiary of an approved Form I-140, Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers; or 2. Has been granted H-1B status under sections 106(a) and (b) of AC21. Under AC21, H-1B nonimmigrants seeking employment-based lawful permanent residence (green card) may be eligible to work and remain in the United States beyond the six-year H-1B period of admission limitation. So, this means a change to H-4 employment eligibility would affect not only immigration status but also the ability of qualifying spouses to remain in the US workforce. According to the Times of India, the significance of H-4 EADs cannot be understood without looking at the US employment-based green-card backlog. A recent analysis by the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP) estimated that more than a million Indians, including dependants, were waiting in the first three employment-based green-card categories as of December 2025. Also, the work permit can serve as a source of income for H-1B families. The potential financial impact, therefore, depends on whether a household currently relies on the H-4 spouse’s earnings. If the proposal eventually becomes a final rule that removes that employment authorization, affected spouses could no longer continue working under an H-4 EAD. Nearly a lakh Indian spouses are estimated to hold H-4 EADs. If the programme were eventually abolished, these families could face a major disruption to their lives. An NBC News team is safe in Tel Aviv after being attacked on camera by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
On Sunday’s episode of Today, foreign correspondent Matt Bradley revealed that his team is “recovering well” after they “all took hits” during an interview the day before with elderly Palestinian woman Aida Ahmed Abdullah, who was knocked unconscious in Saturday’s attack.
“I’m safe, I am recovering,” Bradley told Willie Geist. “I got hit twice on the arm. Actually, every member of my team, including a producer, the cameraman and one of the drivers we were with, they all took hits. But we’re all recovering well.”
While interviewing Abdullah, whose home has been occupied by Israeli settlers, a group of masked men in a car with Israeli license plates descended on them with sticks and stones, beating them. One of the attackers could be seen swinging a stick at the cameraman before the camera fell to the ground.

Not long ago, a diagnosis of advanced cancer left doctors with little more than symptom control and hope. Over the course of a few of decades, however, that picture changed dramatically. Chemotherapy delivered the first meaningful survival gains, though at a steep cost in side effects, a cost later softened by a new generation of supportive drugs that made treatment safer and more tolerable. The mapping of the human genome then opened up an era of precision medicine, as whole-genome sequencing revealed mutations that could be directly targeted. Survival improved again, but a cure remained elusive: tumours kept finding new, resistant mutations to evade each targeted drug. It took a deeper understanding of the immune system to breach the next frontier: immunotherapy taught the body’s own defences to attack cancers once thought untreatable.
Now, a new contender has emerged that could rewrite the story once more: personalized mRNA tumour vaccines. Recent trial results suggest that the next chapter of the cancer treatment story may already be unfolding.
Evolution of treatment
Cancer treatment has advanced in successive waves. In the 1970s and 80s, chemotherapy became the cornerstone of oncology, improving outcomes across the board and curing diseases such as Hodgkin’s lymphoma and testicular cancer. The sequencing of the human genome and subsequent advances in molecular biology then enabled targeted therapies aimed at specific genetic abnormalities — HER2 in breast cancer, EGFR mutations in lung cancer, and many others.
The most dramatic transformation of the past two decades, however, came with immunotherapy. Checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab (drugs that block certain proteins on T-cells of the immune system, helping to attack cancer cells) changed the outlook for metastatic melanoma, a disease that had previously carried a dismal prognosis. What began in melanoma soon spread to lung, kidney, bladder, liver and head-and-neck cancers, reshaping treatment paradigms worldwide.
Immunotherapy has greatly impacted the management of blood cancers as well. Once primarily managed by chemotherapy, cancers like multiple myeloma and lymphoma, have entered the immunotherapy era through CAR-T cell therapy and bispecific antibodies (lab-made proteins that can attach to two different targets), producing outcomes unimaginable just a decade ago.
Today, personalised mRNA vaccines are poised to build on that foundation.
The melanoma breakthrough
The recent excitement around mRNA vaccines stems from the Phase III INTerpath-001 trial, which evaluated intismeran autogene (mRNA-4157/V940), a personalised mRNA vaccine. The study enrolled roughly 1,100 patients with high-risk melanoma who had undergone complete surgical removal of visible disease. They received either immunotherapy through pembrolizumab alone, or pembrolizumab combined with an individualised vaccine designed, using artificial intelligence, from the genetic profile of each patient’s own tumour. This vaccine essentially trained the patients’ immune systems to recognise and destroy unique mutations (neoantigens) on their tumour cells
The results were striking: the combination significantly improved both recurrence-free and distant metastasis-free survival compared with pembrolizumab alone. Earlier studies of the same strategy had already shown roughly a 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death, and a 59% reduction in the risk of distant metastasis or death, compelling evidence that a personalised vaccine can amplify the effect of existing immunotherapy.
For the first time, a personalised neoantigen-based mRNA therapy has succeeded in a large, randomized Phase III trial, validating a concept researcher have pursued for years.
How does it work?
Unlike traditional vaccines, which prevent infection, these are therapeutic vaccines, developed after a disease has been diagnosed, to help trigger the body’s immune system. Once a tumour is sequenced, sophisticated algorithms pick out the mutations unique to that patient’s cancer (neoantigens), providing the necessary information for production of customised mRNA constructs encoding these tumour-specific neoantigens. When injected, these mRNA constructs train the patient’s immune system, particularly the T cells, to recognise and destroy cancer cells carrying those exact mutations. In effect, every patient receives a vaccine made exclusively for their own cancer.
Cancer is increasingly understood as an ecosystem, shaped by interactions between tumour cells, the immune system and the surrounding microenvironment. Immunotherapy works by altering that ecosystem, changing the ‘immune soil’ in which cancer grows. Personalised mRNA vaccines may be the next step: directing the immune response with even greater precision.
Following on, from immunotherapy
The current moment resembles the early days of immunotherapy. When checkpoint inhibitors first showed unprecedented benefit in melanoma, many assumed the impact would stay confined to a handful of cancers. Instead, immunotherapy became a universal oncology platform, transforming treatment across tumour types.
mRNA vaccines appear to be following a similar trajectory. Melanoma, with its high mutational burden and strong response to immune-based approaches, served as the ideal proving ground. Researchers are now studying personalised vaccine strategies in lung, gastrointestinal, genitourinary and several other cancers.
If these trials succeed, the implications could be enormous. Future treatment may routinely involve genomic sequencing after surgery, followed by the rapid design of a patient-specific vaccine given alongside immunotherapy — aiming to wipe out microscopic residual disease before it can return. This is the essence of personalised cancer treatment.
The path ahead
Further automation of neoantigen discovery through AI and manufacturing techniques refined during the COVID-19 pandemic have demonstrated the capacity to generate sophisticated mRNA therapies at scale. Together, these advances are moving personalised cancer vaccines from concept to clinical reality.
Oncology has moved from supportive care to chemotherapy, from chemotherapy to targeted therapy, and from targeted therapy to immunotherapy. Personalised mRNA vaccines may mark the next great leap.
The battle against cancer is far from over. But history offers an encouraging precedent: melanoma announced the arrival of immunotherapy, and it may now be announcing the arrival of another revolutionary treatment platform. If the promise of mRNA tumour vaccines holds across multiple cancers, future generations may look back on this moment as the beginning of the next major transformation in cancer care.
(Dr. Harish P. is a consultant in medical oncology at Manipal Hospital Yelahanka. harish.p1@manipalhospitals.com)

Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
- Published
Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday.
Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital.
One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges.
Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year.
The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder.
Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials.
The motive behind the attack is unclear.
Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."
Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing".
Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.
He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.
Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.
He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.
After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended.
Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world.
According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day.

The Food and Drugs Administration (FDA), Jammu & Kashmir, has prohibited the sale, storage, distribution and display of 10 identified brands and batches of ghee across the Union Territory after laboratory analysis found the products to be sub-standard, unsafe or misbranded.
The action has been taken under the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, following examination of samples by notified food analysts at the National Food Laboratory, Ghaziabad, and the Food Testing Laboratory, Kashmir.
The affected products are Dairy Mohan Desi Ghee (Batch No. 05), Apna Dairy Milk Desi Ghee (Batch No. DM-06), Milk Bite Cow Ghee (Batch No. 137), Nandni Desi Ghee (Batch No. ND-28), Shahi Taj Desi Ghee (Batch No. 134), Daawat Fresh (Batch No. VT09), Nand Krishna Cow Ghee (Batch No. PC-05-26), Vandu Cow Ghee (Batch No. D143), Dairy Milk Desi Ghee (Batch No. OM12), and Mohan Dairy Ghee (Batch No. 06).
Samples of the affected products were collected from different parts of Jammu and Kashmir, including Anantnag, Shangus, Larnoo, Bijbehara, Samba, Kathua, Jammu, Tral and Pampore.
Laboratory findings included the presence of beta-sitosterol or foreign vegetable fat, a positive Baudouin test, abnormal fatty-acid profiles and deviations from prescribed physicochemical parameters.
The FDA has directed all Food Business Operators (FBOs), wholesalers, distributors and retailers to immediately stop the sale, distribution and display of the affected batches and ensure that the products are withdrawn from circulation.
The concerned FBOs have also been directed to submit details of the stock of the affected batches to the concerned Designated Officer within 48 hours. Enforcement authorities have been instructed to maintain strict vigil and take necessary action to prevent further circulation of the prohibited products.
The Administration reiterated that, under applicable food safety standards, ghee must be derived exclusively from milk or milk products, and ghee containing any added matter not exclusively derived from milk fat is not permitted for sale.
The prohibition has been imposed with immediate effect across Jammu and Kashmir in the interest of public health and consumer safety. The FDA has urged consumers to remain vigilant and check the brand name, batch number and date of packing while purchasing ghee.
Consumers and retailers have also been advised to report the sale or availability of any of the prohibited batches to the concerned Food Safety authorities.
The FDA clarified that the prohibitory action is a precautionary measure taken in the public interest and does not affect the statutory right of the concerned FBOs to seek re-analysis through an FSSAI-notified Referral Laboratory in accordance with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the rules framed thereunder.

Zomato bans analogue paneer on its platform, asks restaurants to switch to dairy
With immediate effect, dishes that restaurant partners have declared as containing analogue dairy have been removed from Zomato.
Zomato has announced a zero-tolerance policy against the sale of dishes containing analogue dairy products on its platform, saying restaurants that fail to comply could be delisted.
With immediate effect, dishes that restaurant partners have declared as containing analogue dairy have been removed from Zomato, the food delivery platform said in a release on Monday.
Under the new policy, restaurants have been asked to take corrective measures, including switching to natural dairy products and removing items containing analogue dairy from their menus where an immediate transition is not possible.
Zomato has also asked its restaurant partners to review product labels and ingredient declarations provided by suppliers to verify the ingredients being used and ensure that products listed on the platform are accurately represented.
“At Zomato, our core mission is better food for more people, and that means safeguarding customer health and upholding clear standards for what's listed and served by our restaurant partners. This policy reflects that commitment, one we're taking together with partners who share it,” Aditya Mangla, CEO, Zomato, said.
The company said restaurants that remain non-compliant will be delisted from the platform.
What are analogue dairy products?
Analogue dairy products are non-dairy alternatives in which some or all milk constituents are replaced with ingredients not derived from milk. Analogue paneer, for instance, can be made using vegetable oils, starches, plant proteins, emulsifiers and other additives instead of milk fat.
The issue has come under increased scrutiny in recent months. In April, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) clarified that while analogue products can be sold when accurately labelled, selling or serving a cheese analogue as “paneer”, or listing dishes made with analogue products as paneer, violates the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
Maharashtra subsequently announced a one-year ban on the manufacture and sale of artificial or analogue paneer, citing public health concerns.
The state said its enforcement drive between April 2025 and March 2026 found that 109 of 308 analysed samples, or 35.4%, failed to meet prescribed standards. Of these, 79 were classified as sub-standard and 30 as unsafe.

Meta Platforms agreed to pay a maximum $16.68 billion as part of a settlement to resolve claims brought by states across the country that the company designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children, misled consumers about their safety, and improperly collected personal data of children who used its platforms, court papers show.
The settlement was reached during a California federal trial over claims brought by 29 states, averting one of the highest-profile tests yet of allegations that social media companies harmed young users.
Meta also agreed to make changes for teenage users of Facebook and Instagram nationwide, including daily usage limits and nighttime blocks, court papers show. The Menlo Park, California-based company denied wrongdoing in agreeing to settle. Shares of Meta rose 4.4% in pre-market trading.
The claims were part of a broader wave of litigation brought by states, local governments, school districts and individuals alleging Meta and other social media companies fueled a nationwide youth mental health crisis.
The federal trial covered claims from California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey that Meta violated their state laws protecting consumers. It also covered claims from 29 states that Meta violated the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting personal data from users it knew were children without parental notification or consent, and using the data to train machine learning and generative AI models.
Meta has denied the allegations, saying it has worked hard to protect children on its platforms. The company had argued it could not have misled consumers about whether its services were addictive because “social media addiction” is not a recognised psychiatric condition.
In a filing before the trial, Meta said California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were seeking up to $1.4 trillion in penalties. The states suggested before the trial began that the figure would be closer to $200 billion. The states were also seeking additional monetary damages, plus an order directing Meta to make major changes to its platforms and to bar children from creating accounts.
A mental health crisis
Meta, Snapchat and its parent Snap, YouTube and its parent Alphabet, and TikTok and its parent ByteDance still face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts over claims they knowingly designed their platforms to have features that are addictive to children and teens, fuelling a mental health crisis.
The federal cases were consolidated before U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, and include lawsuits brought by individuals, school districts and state governments.
Thousands more cases against the companies are pending in state courts. A judge in Los Angeles is overseeing thousands of lawsuits brought by individuals who say they or their loved ones were harmed by the platforms’ designs.
Around 30 states have filed lawsuits against the companies in state courts, court records show. A trial has been ongoing in Nashville since July over claims brought by the state against Meta. The settlement comes after Meta lost both phases of a landmark lawsuit brought by New Mexico.
A jury in March ordered it to pay $375 million after finding it had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms. On August 6, a judge found Meta had created a public nuisance and ordered it to pay an additional $567 million and implement youth-safety measures. Also in March, the first trial over an individual’s claims against Meta and Google ended with a verdict in the plaintiff’s favor. A Los Angeles jury found the companies liable for plaintiff Kaley G.M.’s depression and anxiety and ordered them to pay a combined $6 million in damages.
The companies have said they will appeal those verdicts. All four companies settled the first case set for trial in federal court, where a Kentucky school district alleged they were liable for harm to students. Breathitt County School District was set to receive a combined $27 million, public records showed.

In one Nepal district, flood catastrophe is measured in bodies and burial trenches
The devastating flash floods in the Himalayan region swept so many people downstream that authorities in one Nepalese district have begun burying bodies in temporary graves before they can be identified
KATHMANDU, Nepal -- The devastating flash floods in the Himalayan region swept so many people downstream that authorities in one Nepalese district have begun burying bodies in temporary graves before they can be identified, prompting accusations that Hindu funeral traditions are being ignored.
In south-central Nepal's Chitwan district, the scale of the catastrophe was evident in some 250 bodies awaiting identification and the hastily dug trenches for their temporary burial following Wednesday’s catastrophic floods and mudslides, which killed at least 800 people and left more than 3,000 missing in Nepal and Tibet.
The bodies were carried hundreds of kilometers downstream by the Bhotekoshi River from the flood's epicenter before being recovered in Chitwan.
Authorities carried out a temporary burial of about 100 victims on Saturday, officials said, as forensic teams struggled to cope. A convoy of vehicles carrying bodies entered a lush, forested area as an excavator dug a wide trench in the red earth while officials and media looked on.
Anil Thapa, a police inspector coordinating the handling of the bodies, said another 50 bodies were having DNA samples taken ahead of their likely burial Sunday.
Authorities preserve the DNA samples, photograph distinguishing facial features and record other identifying details, Thapa said. The bodies are assigned a reference number to help families claim them later.
Thapa said many of the bodies had remained submerged in floodwaters for about four days and were already decomposing by the time they were recovered.
Across the region, homes, vehicles and farm tractors still lay partially buried in mud.
Limited forensic infrastructure and inadequate morgue capacity in the district further strained efforts to manage the overwhelming number of bodies recovered from the disaster, officials said.
High humidity and sweltering heat accelerated decomposition, compounding the challenges as health experts warned that leaving the remains exposed could increase the risk of disease.
Fresh landslides in the area on Sunday closed the main highway linking the capital city of Kathmandu and Chitwan, a day after it partially reopened, complicating efforts to move bodies and relief supplies.
As survivors grappled with the aftermath, criticism of the burials mounted. Some residents said the dead had waited days for their last rites and were denied dignity in death. Families still waiting to locate missing relatives and some public figures questioned whether authorities moved too quickly.
The issue is particularly sensitive in Nepal, a predominantly Hindu nation where the dead are traditionally cremated.
Ruby Chaudhary, who has two missing relatives, said the burials should not proceed without families’ consent.
“The dead deserve to be treated with dignity,” she said. “Our tradition is to cremate them on the riverbank, surrounded by their immediate family.”
A former prime minister, Baburam Bhattarai, said it was inappropriate to dispose of unidentified bodies before search and rescue operations were complete and without broader consultation with families of the missing.
If morgues were insufficient, authorities could have mobilized emergency resources to set up temporary morgues or secure cold storage facilities, he said in a social media post Saturday night.
Officials said the burials were a temporary measure necessitated by health concerns and limited capacity.
“People are worried that this could be a permanent burial, but it is only temporary management,” Thapa said. “If someone is able to verify the identity later using the available information, they can take back the body and perform the appropriate funeral rites.”
Amrit Bahadur Rai, Nepal’s foreign secretary, said the temporary burial of unidentified bodies was carried out in line with internationally accepted disaster-management protocols, including those of the International Committee of the Red Cross.
“Families can match records later, and will be allowed to exhume (the remains later) for necessary rituals,” Rai said at a press briefing in Kathmandu.

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

Wrexham complete signings of Ekomie and Kabore
- Published
Wrexham have completed the signings of Issa Kabore from Manchester City and Jacques Ekomie from Angers.
Burkina Faso international Kabore featured 32 times across all competitions during a loan spell with Wrexham in 2025-26 and has now signed a three-year deal with the club.
"I'm very happy to be back. It feels good to be here again," said right wing-back Kabore.
"Everybody knows our ambition is to get to the Premier League, and I'm here to fight for that promotion."
The deal for Kabore is worth up to £4.75m - with City having a 20% sell-on clause and matching rights.
Left-back Ekomie was in the final year of his deal with Angers and reportedly attracted interest from Wrexham's Championship rivals West Ham United and German side Hamburg.
On signing for Wrexham, Ekomie - who has put pen to paper on a four-year contract - said: "I'm excited to be here. It is a very big and interesting project for me - I'm here to progress, and I'm very happy to be here.
"I want to achieve great things at Wrexham. I think it's an ambitious project and I want to bring all my experience to help the team achieve our goals."
The Red Dragons recruited Liberato Cacace from Italian side Empoli during the 2025 summer transfer window, but the New Zealand international has been plagued by injuries since moving to north Wales.
Ekomie - signed for an undisclosed fee - will bolster Phil Parkinson's left-sided options, with the Gabon international joining right wing-backs Kabore and Danny Imray, goalkeeper Anthony Patterson and midfielder Ben Whiteman in moving to the Racecourse Ground this summer.
Kabore made a dream start to life with Wrexham last season as he registered a pair of assists on his debut to help the Welsh side earn a 3-2 win over Norwich City at Carrow Road.
His eight assists in the Championship were more than any other Wrexham player.
He was a mainstay under Parkinson before sustaining a hamstring injury while on international duty during the November break.
Kabore made his long-awaited return to action for Burkina Faso in the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations before again featuring prominently for Wrexham in the second half of the season.
The 55-cap international moved to Man City from Mechelen in 2020 before immediately returning to the Belgian club on loan.
He went on to have loan stints with Troyes, Marseille, Luton Town, Benfica and Werder Bremen prior to joining Wrexham on transfer deadline day in September last year.
He leaves Man City having failed to make a senior appearance for the club.
On Kabore's return, manager Parkinson said: "We're delighted to welcome Issa back to the football club.
"He had a successful loan spell with us last year, and we're looking forward to working with him again and watching him really develop as a player this coming season."

Donald Trump has downplayed a visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, as “semi-routine” after he turned up in the Russian capital unannounced, triggering a wave of speculation about the reasons for his trip.
Ratcliffe was reported to have flown to Moscow on a government transport plane on Tuesday in a rare visit after taking off from the Andrews air force base in Maryland.
The White House, CIA, Pentagon and the US air force all declined to comment on the visit, which was confirmed on Wednesday by the Kremlin spokesperson, Dimitry Peskov.
Interviewed by the conservative radio host Glenn Beck, Trump poured cold water on speculation that Ratcliffe had travelled in response to fears that Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, was planning to “test Nato resolve” or to win Moscow’s cooperation for intensified US sanctions on Iran.
“None of the above,” the US president said in response to Beck, who referred to the speculation as “crazy”.
“He’s there, you know, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said.
“John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things that you said. Now something may come … out of it. We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point.”
On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the visit, that the reason for the spy chief’s surprise visit was to warn Russia not to attack Nato countries.
Ratcliffe’s visit was the first from a CIA director since his predecessor Bill Burns travelled to Moscow in November 2021 to warn Putin of the consequences of attacking Ukraine.
The Russian leader went ahead with the attack regardless in February of the following year. Trump’s efforts to end the war – which he once vowed to bring to a conclusion on “day one” of his second presidency – have proven unsuccessful, despite his friendly personal relations with Putin.
Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Ratcliffe did not meet Putin during his visit.
Washington and Moscow have found themselves on opposite sides following Trump’s decision last February to go to war with Iran, with Russian satellite technology said to have been used to help Iranian forces with precise targeting of US and allied bases in the Gulf and beyond.
With military hostilities at an impasse, the US treasury department this week unveiled a new program of economic warfare against the Tehran regime involving secondary sanctions against countries that trade with it. To be effective, it would need the cooperation of allies of Iran such as Russia and China, experts say.
Peskov did not give a reason for Ratcliffe’s visit, but described forecasts that it would lead to an upturn in US-Russian relations as “premature”, the Washington Post reported.
“Contacts through intelligence-service channels are in themselves a positive phenomenon, a positive process. These contacts often continue even in the most difficult moments of bilateral relations,” Peskov told reporters. “But whether this will affect, on the whole, the process of bringing our bilateral relations out of the deep crisis they are in – it’s premature to say at this point.”
In recent days, Ukraine has targeted Russia’s energy infrastructure and online retail facilities in long-distance strikes, while Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Kyiv.

World number one Scheffler claims second Fedex Cup title
- Published
Tour Championship, final leaderboard
-16 S Scheffler (US); -13 V Hovland (Nor); -12 R Gerard (US); -11 A Fitzpatrick (Eng), C Gotterup (US), R McIlroy (NI), R Henley (US), MW Lee (Aus), J Bridgeman (US)
Selected others: -10 T Fleetwood (Eng), C Young (US), A Scott (Aus), L Aberg (Swe); -9 C Morikawa (US); -7 J Rose (Eng); -5 M Fitzpatrick (Eng), W Clark (US); E R MacIntyre (Sco)
At times it felt like there was a certain inevitability about Scottie Scheffler collecting his second Fedex Cup title on Sunday.
As those around him began to falter, the world number one, who started the day three strokes adrift of overnight leader Viktor Hovland, produced a typically metronomic performance with the winning cheque in sight.
And what a prize. Scheffler's reward for his 22nd career victory at the PGA Tour's season-ending Tour Championship in Atlanta will see his bank account credited to the tune of $10m (£7.4m).
The 2024 champion also joins Tiger Woods (2007 and 2009) and Rory McIlroy (2016, 2019 and 2022) to have won the event on multiple occasions.
"To come from behind and be able to win tournament is a really cool feeling," Scheffler said.
"There were a lot of talented guys in front of me on the leaderboard. I was fortunate to get off to a good start and put myself in the mix. It's a gift to be out here on tour. Each and every day I'm going to try to give it my best."
Across the final three pairings, Scheffler's four-under 66 was the only round to break par with his superb ability to find green after green giving him a substantial edge over his rivals.
Hovland, whose driving became more erratic, also found that his putter had gone cold when he most needed it, and the Norwegian signed for a two-over 72 as he finished three back in second place.
American debutant Ryan Gerard, who started one behind Hovland, ended the day in the same position and third overall on 12 under par after also taking 72 shots.
McIlroy was unable to rediscover the rhythm that rocketed him into contention on Saturday, with his topsy-turvy round of 69 containing four birdies and an eagle mixed with five bogeys.
Aside from the Northern Irishman there were few moments of sparkle on show elsewhere among the potential contenders, albeit Justin Rose's hole-in-one on the ninth was an obvious exception.
While Rose was unable to gather any momentum from that to seriously challenge, ending the day at seven under overall, another Englishman Alex Fitzpatrick matched Scheffler's 66, the lowest round of the day, to catapult himself up the leaderboard to conclude the tournament alongside six-time major winner McIlroy at 11 under.
It earned the 27-year-old a tie for fourth on his debut to cap a remarkable season in which he won his first DP World Tour event at the Indian Open before teaming up with his elder brother, the 2022 US Open champion Matt, to win the Zurich Classic of New Orleans pairs event.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday (August 30) launched another attack on the news media, targeting NBC’s Meet the Press moderator Kristen Welker and calling on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to take action over what he described as “fake polls” and inaccurate political commentary.
Trump made the remarks in a series of posts on Truth Social, objecting to Welker's description of his record of endorsing Republican candidates as producing “mixed results.”
Trump called Welker the “Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press,” which he renamed “Meet the Fake Press.”
He accused her of deliberately misrepresenting his record of political endorsements.
“Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment,” Trump wrote.
Trump claimed his endorsements had achieved a 99% success rate overall, including a 100% success rate for Senate endorsements and a 98% success rate for House endorsements.
He cited the victories of Republican candidates Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei as examples of his successful endorsements.
Trump strongly defended his record of backing Republican candidates, arguing that his endorsements had played a decisive role in several unexpected victories.
“Their new weapon is to say that my 99% SUCCESS Rate on Endorsements, 100% on Senatorial Endorsements... is either a mixed result, or not very good,” Trump wrote.
“In actuality, it is, without question, the strongest Endorsement in the History of Politics,” he added.
Trump also highlighted Darline Graham's Senate victory, saying she had not been expected to win before receiving his endorsement.
“Darline Graham’s run for the Senate was the biggest story in all of Politics, because she wasn’t expected to win, and then, when I Endorsed her, and she easily won,” Trump said.
He also pointed to an Oklahoma gubernatorial candidate whom he said was trailing in polls before receiving his endorsement and subsequently winning.
In a separate Truth Social post, Trump intensified his criticism of polling organizations and news outlets.
“THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE!” he wrote.
Trump has repeatedly attacked polls that show weak approval ratings or unfavorable political prospects for his administration.
He also urged FCC Chairman Brendan Carr to take his complaints seriously.
“I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” Trump wrote.
The President accused news organizations of deliberately targeting him and said the media was attempting to undermine his political record.
“Unfortunately, she is not the only one,” Trump wrote of Welker. “The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP.’”
He concluded his post by calling the press “a Disgrace to our Nation” and described the issue as a matter of “Fake Polls and Commentary.”
NBC defended Welker following Trump's attack.
“Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her,” an NBC spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
Trump's criticism comes amid already strained relations with Welker. In June, he abruptly ended an interview with her following a tense exchange, during which he became irritated by questions about the war against Iran.
The confrontation with Welker is part of a broader campaign by Trump and his administration against media organizations he accuses of unfair or hostile coverage.
Earlier in the week, Trump attacked New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman over a report that he would skip New York's annual September 11 commemoration because he would not have a speaking role.
Trump has also sued major news organizations, including The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times, while his administration has pursued restrictions on journalists and cut federal funding for public media.
Several major news organizations and broadcasters have pushed back, including through lawsuits. The latest dispute puts renewed focus on the limits of presidential influence over the nation's broadcast regulators—and the constitutional protections surrounding political journalism.

Hundreds attend funeral in Haiti for 4 victims of brutal gang attack that killed 47
Hundreds of mourners have gathered at a church near Haiti’s capital for the funeral of four victims of a brutal gang attack
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti -- Hundreds of people crowded into a church near Haiti’s capital on Sunday for the funeral of four of the 47 people killed in a recent gang attack so brutal that it shook a country that has long struggled with violence.
Mourners wiped away tears, raised their hands and cried out as coffins arrived at a church in the farming community of Kenscoff.
“We thank everyone who came in solidarity with the families that died and those who lost their loved ones,” Pastor Jean Robert Dorlus said. “God will open a space to receive them.”
Inside the church, people swayed to gospel music. Some wailed as their shoulders shook. The church was so packed that dozens had to stand outside, peering through the windows, as they honored those being laid to rest: a mother, father and their son, and a 70-year-old man whose body had been set on fire by the gang members.
“I’ve known them for a long time,” said Yvonne Marleus, a Kenscoff resident who lost a cousin in the attack. “These are people who are respected in the community.”
Gangs abducted more than 50 people during the attack, although they recently released six children and seven women following an intervention by community leaders and UNICEF.
It was one of the biggest mass kidnappings in Haiti in recent years, and survivors have organized protests and blamed police for not preventing the attack.
“They didn’t act in time to stop the carnage,” Marleus alleged.
Haiti’s National Police has said that it ordered an investigation to establish the truth about the attack, and whether it was "due to complicity or negligence.”
Outside the church, civilians stood guard with automatic weapons, ready to repel any potential new gang attacks with the help of police officers stationed nearby.
Kenscoff resident Jean Calixte Juste said he and two cousins survived the attack “by luck.”
"I almost died,” he recalled. “I almost fell into a ravine running. This is the worst and most terrible night I’ve ever experienced.”
He didn’t know the four people whose funerals were held Sunday, but he said he wanted to honor their memories.
It wasn't clear when funerals of the other victims might be held.
Marta Hurtado, a spokesperson for the U.N. Human Rights Office, said that some 150 heavily armed gang members participated in the Aug. 23 attack. She said they first killed 13 people who tried to flee and then pursued 50 more who had sought refuge inside a church.
“After forcing them out from the premises, they executed 22 of them on the church courtyard and 12 others behind the church,” she said.
Dozens of others were injured, and more than 2,600 people were left homeless.
Overall, gang violence has displaced a record of nearly 1.5 million people in recent years across Haiti, where more than 3,050 people were reported killed from January to June, according to the U.N.
Armed men control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and swaths of land in Haiti’s central region and beyond, and they are also seeking to seize territory in Kenscoff.
“I’m ready to leave," said Juste, one of the residents. "Because after this, I don’t think we’re going to survive another big attack.”

Zhao, a 30-something woman living in Beijing, says she lost over $100,000 in May to a romance scammer who claimed to be a researcher working for Microsoft. After initially chatting Zhao up on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohongshu, he asked to move their conversation to Microsoft Teams, where he was happy to provide her with an account and password she could use.
“I didn’t think much because I had used this app before. And since it was developed by Microsoft, I kind of trusted it,” says Zhao, who requested to use only her last name for privacy reasons.
Once they switched to Teams, the scammer began promising to build a future with Zhao when they eventually got together and introduced her to a cryptocurrency investment project, which he said would turn a profit much faster than trading stocks. Zhao says that at first, she was excited about the opportunity, and even took out loans from several banks so she could invest more.
Then the scammer disappeared with all of her money. Because she can no longer log into the Teams account he told her to use, she can’t share the chat logs with police.
After Zhao began talking about her experience on social media, she says she started hearing from dozens of other people in China who have fallen prey to the same scheme. They claim to have lost anywhere from $1,500 to $300,000, and only one reported that they were able to recover some of the funds—by tracking down the recipient’s bank account.
The victims all describe the same pattern. At some point, they were instructed to download Microsoft Teams and log in using credentials provided by the scammers. The tactic has become so common that some local law enforcement bureaus in China have issued warnings explicitly naming Teams as a tool used by scammers, with one even describing it as a “fraud-related app.” Maimai, a Chinese platform similar to LinkedIn, told Chinese media outlets last year that if it detected high-risk keywords in messages like “Teams” and “Skype,” it would automatically warn users about how to avoid getting scammed.
For years, alleged scam victims have been writing angry reviews of Microsoft Teams on Chinese app stores, some warning others not to download it. WIRED analyzed the past 18 months of reviews of Teams on Apple’s Chinese app store, and found that out of 500, 30 percent included explicit complaints about scammers. The oldest review calling out scams dated all the way back to 2022.
“The scammers had me register for this app so they could contact me, and they defrauded me of RMB 1.48 million [$220,000]. The police have opened a case,” reads one review from January of this year. “This was unquestionably a ‘pig-butchering’ scam. Beware of fraud—this was a bitter and costly lesson!”
Microsoft says scammers routinely exploit trusted brands and communication platforms to carry out social engineering schemes. As these tactics evolve, the company says it “investigates reports of abuse, takes action against accounts that violate our policies, and continues to strengthen protections designed to identify and disrupt fraudulent activity,” Steven Masada, the global head of Microsoft’s digital crimes division, said in a statement to WIRED.
In June, Microsoft started displaying a general warning banner to Teams users in China cautioning them about common scams and urging them to be careful when sharing sensitive information. The company also discontinued the personal version of Teams in China, and the service is now only available in the country through enterprise accounts.
On Chinese social media, people have also reported experiencing variations of the scam involving other corporate software apps, including Webex, a video conferencing platform owned by Cisco, and Cliq, a workplace communication app owned by the Indian software giant Zoho. Since February 2025, 71 percent of the over 150 reviews of Webex on Apple’s Chinese app store referenced being scammed on the platform, according to WIRED’s analysis. Cisco did not respond to a request for comment.
Sam Wunderl, a spokesperson for Zoho, says the company has identified “a limited number of instances involving scammers using Zoho Cliq to defraud victims.” The company says it uncovered the suspicious usage internally. As of August 27, Zoho says it disabled online payments to Cliq in China, suspended every account created by the suspected scammer it identified, and plans to discontinue the free version of Cliq in China going forward.
All Roads Go to Teams
According to dozens of victim accounts shared on Chinese social media platforms like Xiaohongshu and Douyin, the scammers look for new targets seemingly anywhere they can. They pose as job recruiters looking to fill open positions, prospective renters contacting landlords, potential dates on Tinder, and international buyers looking to source products from Chinese factories.
The scammers take advantage of Teams’ enterprise features by creating accounts for their targets and sending them pre-made login credentials. Because the scammers control the organization, they can deactivate the accounts once the scheme is over, wiping out victims’ access to chat histories that could be potentially used as evidence. To explain the unusual setup, scammers may tell victims they’re using work devices that only allow certain apps, or say they created a private Teams account just for the two of them to chat.
It turned out that some of the other victims who contacted Zhao had encountered the very same scammer she had. One was able to share Teams login credentials with her. This time, Zhao pretended to be a new potential victim in order to hopefully trick the scammer into providing more information about how his ruse worked.
She asked why he had to use Teams instead of WeChat, by far the most popular messaging app in China. The scammer claimed his colleagues could see his WeChat messages because he was on a work project, so Teams “is like our secret base together.” The account he gave Zhao, he said, was “for team members to contact family while on the project.”
“Can I ask a small question. What’s the special meaning about my account ‘joy20706905?’” Zhao asked, referring to the username he provided. “The account was assigned by the software when you purchase it from Microsoft,” he responded.
Zhao says when she was defrauded in May, Microsoft Teams didn’t alert her that the conversation she was having with the scammer might be dangerous. It was only when she talked to him again in August that the app started showing a banner that reads: “Don’t share confidential info or your screen with people you don’t know. Report anything suspicious.”
Why Teams?
In many ways, Microsoft Teams is an ideal app for fraudsters in China. Unlike Telegram or WhatsApp, it isn’t blocked by the government. And it has advanced tools like screen sharing and remote control that allow scammers to potentially gain more control over their victims’ devices. Most importantly, it’s a legitimate workplace communication app made by a trusted multinational tech company.
The same factors also apply to Webex. Tan Chenxin, a Chinese software engineer living in New York, says he was nearly defrauded earlier this week after he received a call from someone claiming to be working on a joint police investigation with US Customs and Border Protection and Chinese law enforcement. They asked Tan to download Webex and hop on a video call to discuss the situation. “I looked up Webex and found that it was developed by Cisco, a world-leading cybersecurity software provider,” Tan says. “I happen to know what Cisco is, so I convinced myself it was fine.”
Luckily, he realized it was a scam and hung up before transferring any money. Tan says he couldn’t find a way to easily report the scammer’s account to Webex.
Compared to Chinese messaging apps, which have had to deal with rampant investment fraud scams for years, Western platforms appear less prepared to combat the issue. Apps like WeChat and Xiaohongshu, for example, frequently flag scam risks to users when they detect keywords related to investments and payments, including in private conversations. Even WIRED’s chats with scam victims on Xiaohongshu triggered repeated warnings as they recounted how they had been defrauded.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is now on its way to study the 'dark universe'
Its first images are expected to arrive in early 2027.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has officially launched on its mission to explore dark matter, dark energy and other mysteries of the universe. NASA's new space telescope, which is able to image swaths of the sky 100 times larger than what Hubble could capture, launched this morning from NASA's Kennedy Space Center on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.
The space agency confirmed shortly after launch that Roman had successfully deployed its solar panels and lower instrument sun shade. Over the coming days and weeks, the rest of its instruments will deploy and activate. Once it's all up and running, NASA says Roman will send home 1.4 terabytes of data a day. We can expect to see its first images in early 2027.
"Roman will be a discovery machine that will bring us closer than ever before to answering humanity's most profound questions about our cosmic history," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator for NASA's Science Mission Directorate. "With its large field of view and fast survey speeds, Roman will usher us into a new era of discovery and make the invisible visible, setting the foundation for humanity's search for life beyond our solar system."
In addition to helping scientists investigate dark matter and dark energy, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will observe exoplanets and planet-forming discs. NASA says it may measure light from a billion galaxies over the duration of its mission.

A powerful flash flood tore through Arizona’s Grand Canyon, sending torrents of muddy water, boulders and debris through Bright Angel Canyon and into the Colorado River. The National Park Service (NPS) said at least 20 people may be missing or unaccounted for, prompting a public appeal for information.
The flooding happened on August 29, but the park reported aftermath on Sunday (local time) about the damage and the missing people.
Meanwhile, more than 60 people were evacuated from Phantom Ranch and Bright Angel Campground as the flood swept through the canyon. Footbridges were destroyed, the creek bed was dramatically reshaped and debris, including what appeared to be a bunkhouse, was carried downstream while campers seeked safety.
The NPS is asking for information about hikers and backpackers who were in the Bright Angel Creek corridor on August 29, including people who had reservations at affected campgrounds. Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground and the North Kaibab Trail remain closed.
The flood also damaged the Grand Canyon’s sole water pipeline, forcing the park to suspend overnight hotel stays from August 31 and ask residents to conserve water. The pipeline is already being rehabilitated as part of a $208 million infrastructure project.
The flooding followed roughly 0.5 to 1 inch of rain in about 30 minutes, with much of the water running off immediately through the steep terrain. More rain and thunderstorms are possible, raising the threat of further flooding.

USS Abraham Lincoln sails past Singapore on its way home from Middle East
The U.S. aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has sailed past Singapore as it heads home
BATAM, Indonesia -- The U.S. aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln sailed past Singapore early on Sunday as it headed home after a grueling deployment in the Middle East. It's expected to stop in Thailand for a port visit.
Associated Press journalists on the Indonesian island of Batam, across the Singapore Strait, spotted the massive vessel as it transited waters near Singapore just after 1 a.m. local time.
The Lincoln, one of the U.S. Navy's largest warships, was supporting the U.S. war against Iran. Its deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days. Concerns have grown about the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment following reports of deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies including food and hygiene products.
Thai officials have said the Lincoln will stop in Thailand for rest and recovery before returning to its U.S. base.

The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
