Making ice cream for friends is my way of spreading joy — and cultivating some for myself
Along the way, I found healing in learning a new skill
This First Person column is the experience of Elizabeth Hunt, who lives in Montreal. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
As she packed up her kitchen, my friend Alisha pulled a bright red appliance from the highest kitchen cabinet and turned to me: “Do you want this?”
“What is it?” I asked.
“An ice cream machine,” she said. “I’ve had it for years and literally never used it. If anyone can do something with this machine, it’s you.”
Over the past decade, Alisha and I had forged a friendship over feeding each other’s kids and supporting each other’s struggles. Alisha was dubbed the “Almond Mom” by our combined crew of five kids for how she describes food by nutritional value, not tastiness. I got a reputation for having “the good snacks,” mostly because I make a mean chocolate chip cookie and a buttery Nutella crepe.
I wasn’t sure if my baking and cooking skills extended to frozen treats, but moving homes can be stressful. I was more than happy to check “Figure out what to do with the ice cream maker” off Alisha's list.
So I shrugged and said, "Sure," as Alisha thrust the ice cream churner in my hands.
For the first couple of weeks, the appliance just sat on my counter as I debated whether to put it in storage, pass it on to someone else or try my hand at something new.
In one of my regular chats with my Matante Rose-Marie, I told her about the ice cream maker. My 82-year-old aunt immediately launched into a story from the 1960s when her sister (my mother) had run an ice cream shop in Old Montreal for a few years and how her grandfather had been a beurrier (butter maker) in Saint-Jean-de-Matha, Que. My aunt seemed convinced that I was simply accepting my lineage in the dairy arts.
So after some Googling and YouTubing, I attempted my first batch of ice cream. Vanilla was the simplest recipe. Plus, I’ve always heard that vanilla is the standard by which to judge any ice cream shop. If you can’t get vanilla right, don’t even bother with other flavours.
My first batch of vanilla ice cream was a little thin and soupy but surprisingly delicious. I was ridiculously proud of myself and wanted everyone to taste it.
So I made more. I experimented with flavours, sweeteners, types of milk and how many crushed cookies a batch of vanilla ice cream can handle (about 23) to make “cookies 'n' cream.” I learned that the right temperature and correct churning time are essential to making creamy (not soupy) ice cream.
When Alisha’s birthday came around, I promised to make any flavour ice cream she wanted. She was delighted that I was putting her neglected appliance to use. She chose raspberry and dark chocolate. I used real raspberries and chopped up squares of the intense dark chocolate that she and I often share after a glass of red wine and a long conversation.
Folded into the ice cream was also a message for Alisha: I have created something delicious and filled with love (and nutrients) because you deserve some joy.
Nicole was next. We have the kind of friendship where one of us can call the other at 4 a.m. because of a bad dream — or any worry, really — and be met with compassion and support.
One day when my daughter was 10 she noticed that I was sad and asked, “Mama, do you need parenting?” When I worriedly assured her that it was not her job to parent me, she rolled her eyes and responded, “Obviously! I was gonna call Aunty Nicole.”
Nicole hesitantly asked for rum and raisin ice cream. “This was my favourite flavour as a kid,” she said, “but the lactose in dairy doesn’t agree with me”.
I left her house with a mason jar full of raisins soaking in dark rum and a promise to figure out an ice cream she could eat with joy.
The ice cream, made with lactose-free cream, turned out creamy and smooth and the plumped-up raisins provided pockets of sweet booziness (even though they all sank to the bottom during freezing, because I hadn’t yet mastered the intricacies of timing and temperature).
And yet, Nicole declared it the best ice cream she'd ever had.
Motivated by Alisha and Nicole’s enthusiasm, I asked more friends to describe an ice cream flavour they’d like to savour.
I learned to bloom matcha to make a strawberry-matcha concoction for my daughter’s friend’s 14th birthday (kids these days are way more sophisticated than I was in 1989).
When one of my buddies asked for tiger tail, which is almost impossible to find in Quebec, I recreated a taste combination that I’d never tasted or even imagined could exist: orange and black licorice.
All of these flavours stretched my abilities and forced me to get creative about sourcing ingredients within my budget. Specials after Valentine’s Day and Easter made chocolate more affordable. A kind café owner agreed to sell me exactly three tablespoons of good-quality matcha when I balked at the price of a full package. Buying recyclable cardboard containers at a restaurant supply store proved more affordable and easier to manage than chasing down my Tupperwares loaned to friends all over Montreal.
Several batches and birthdays later, the unthinkable happened: my churner stopped churning. I stared at the little machine on my countertop. I turned it off and back on. It made a sad little noise and then stopped. For good.
After a few days of living with the burnt-out little Cuisinart on my kitchen counter, I packed it up, dumped it at the local recycling centre and informed my friends that my ice cream era had come to an end.
I was not prepared for the wave of sadness that hit me.
“This is ridiculous,” I thought to myself. “I’ve known real grief in my life. This is just a hobby.” And yet, this sadness was real.
Somewhere between a Greek tragedy and a ridiculous soap opera, I’ve had the kind of life that makes therapists wince and friends gulp down their glass of wine. And then ask for another.
However, like many other people laden with a heavy past, I’m sick of my own story and tired of my own trauma. I thought “healing work’ would be full of revelation and closure. Mostly, it’s been about repeatedly greeting old emotional reactions and worn-out fears like houseguests who’ve outstayed their welcome.
Slowly, I’ve been stitching together a lighter life for myself: weekly potlucks with friends, complimenting strangers’ outfits when I walk by, growing avocados and pineapples plants from kitchen scraps, learning Gen Z slang (to my kids’ dismay) and experimenting with ice cream flavours.
Within two days of my little Cuisinart being sent to recycling, Nicole had scoured the second-hand online markets, found the same churner model in another colour and dropped it off at my apartment. She didn’t want praise or repayment.
If you ask Nicole, she’d say that she had a vested interest in not losing her supply of lactose-free rum and raisin. But she understood something that I’m just starting to articulate: It’s not about the ice cream.
It’s about creativity and the joy of gifting a bit of pleasure. It’s about the conversations with friends who share their memories, tastes and wild inventions. It’s about the thrill of taking on a challenge and the sense of accomplishment from creating something delicious that makes people smile.
We need more pleasure and kindness in this world. I want to share my hopes and talents and the gifts I have to contribute.
Thankfully, there are lots and lots of people who value real connection, generously offer help and support, know how to look for and find joy and make space for the deliciousness of life.
And for them I make ice cream.

Tearful Federer inducted into Hall of Fame
- Published
Roger Federer has been inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame, describing the moment as "one of the greatest honours" of his life.
The 20-time Grand Slam singles champion, who retired in 2022, was tearful at the ceremony in Newport, Rhode Island, as he reflected on his glittering career in front of tennis greats including Billie Jean King and John McEnroe.
After make his debut in 1998 at the age of 16, Federer won a men's-record eight Wimbledon titles, six Australian Open crowns, five US Opens and one French Open.
"This is one of the greatest honors of my life," Federer, 45, said.
"They call this the Hall of Fame, but fame was never the goal. My goal was to spend my life doing something I love, with people who love it as much as I do."
Only Spain's Rafael Nadal, with 22 majors, and Serbia's Novak Djokovic, with 24, have won more men's Grand Slam singles titles than Federer.
He won his first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon in 2003 and spent 310 weeks as the world number one - a record until he was surpassed by Djokovic.
Alongside his 20 Grand Slams, Federer won Olympic doubles gold for Switzerland with Stan Wawrinka at Beijing 2008 and singles silver at London 2012.
He was also part of the Swiss team that won the Davis Cup for the first time in 2014.

How to Use AI to Prepare for a Job Interview
Before we get to the applications, which indeed make job interview preparation an easy affair, you must understand the importance of a solid foundation to begin with. After getting to know the details of the job interview, mainstream AI models, such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude, and more, can be directed to put you at an advantage from the very initial phase of your preparation. Below is what you must do first.
→ Understand the Role and Generate Role-Specific Interview Questions
Most, if not all, job descriptions are little more than a pile of technical and corporate jargon, often failing to clearly state the requirements. Misaligned interview expectations may already put you in a bad spot during the interview, so you must ensure that you are well-versed with the job description. AI models can help you do so with a few prompts, but you must include a few crucial elements to get the best results. With all this, don’t forget to upload your updated resume for a tailored response.
For starters, you cannot miss out on knowing the core competencies required for the job you’re applying for. AI can help you identify the top non-negotiable technical and soft skills that the recruiter expects of you. Such attributes are often not understood by many applicants, which prevents them from brushing up on existing skills or learning the required ones. Next, your prompt must include identifying the success metrics, or the key performance indicators of the role.
Because every hiring takes place to solve a specific problem of the organization, it’s crucial to have an idea about the performance expectations the recruiter may have from you. For tech roles, it usually revolves around solving existing issues, improving existing processes, and related tasks. In contrast, non-tech roles focus on increasing client retention, establishing business relationships, and related tasks.
Lastly, you must also ask AI to groom you based on your resume. It will help you determine whether your resume aligns well with the role and whether any specific skills need to be spotlighted. With this initial study of the role’s requirements, you can certainly answer questions and defend yourself with confidence.
→ Study About the Company
While most candidates think they know the company they’re applying to well, the truth is, not many perform a proper deep dive. It is an important part of interview preparation, as knowing the company helps you give more relevant answers instead of generic ones.
AI makes company research much easier, but don’t simply ask it to “tell me about the company.” Start with its current market position, products, competitors, recent announcements, and anything else directly relevant to the role.

Useful AI Prompts for Job Interview Preparation
Mainstream AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can be surprisingly effective for interview preparation if you give them enough context. A common approach among job seekers is to provide the actual job description and resume, then have the AI conduct the interview one question at a time instead of generating a generic list of questions. Here are a few prompts worth trying.
1. Analyze the Job Description and My Resume
I am preparing for an interview for the job below. Act as an experienced hiring manager and analyze both the job description and my resume.
Identify:
The five most important skills or requirements for this role
The parts of my resume that match them best
Important requirements where my experience looks weak or unclear
Questions an interviewer is likely to ask about those gaps
Technical or industry topics I should revise
Five achievements from my resume that I should make sure to highlight
Don’t invent experience or skills that aren’t present in my resume.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
2. Conduct a Realistic Mock Interview
Act as the hiring manager interviewing me for the role below. Use my resume and the job description as your primary context.
Conduct this like a real interview. Ask only one question at a time and wait for my complete answer before asking the next one. Ask natural follow-up questions based on what I actually say instead of following a fixed list.
Include a mix of behavioral, situational, resume-based, role-specific, and technical questions where relevant.
Do not give me hints or feedback while the interview is taking place. Once the interview is finished, score my performance on answer quality, relevance, clarity, confidence, and completeness. Then identify my five biggest weaknesses and tell me how to improve each one.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
3. Give Me a Difficult Mock Interview
Act as a skeptical interviewer who isn’t yet convinced that I am the right person for this role.
Use my resume and the job description to identify weak points, career gaps, vague achievements, missing skills, questionable claims, or areas where another candidate may be stronger.
Ask me one difficult question at a time. If my answer is vague, generic, evasive, or unsupported, push back and ask a follow-up question. Don’t compliment every answer or make the interview artificially easy.
At the end, tell me which answers could hurt my chances in the real interview and show me how I could make them stronger without exaggerating my experience.
4. Build My STAR Interview Stories
Help me prepare 5 reusable stories from my career for behavioral interview questions.
Use my resume and the experiences I provide to identify strong examples involving leadership, conflict, failure, problem-solving, teamwork, initiative, and working under pressure.
For each story, organize the answer using STAR:
Situation: What was happening?
Task: What was I responsible for?
Action: What specifically did I do?
Result: What changed because of my actions?
Keep Situation and Task brief and spend more time on Action and Result. Ask me for missing details rather than inventing them. Where possible, help me quantify the result.
Finally, tell me which common behavioral interview questions each story could answer.

AI has made preparing for job interviews a lot less daunting than it used to be. For most people, mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are already good enough for understanding a job description, researching a company, preparing likely questions, and improving answers.
Dedicated AI interview tools become useful when you want something closer to the real thing. Critique My Interview Answer
I will give you an interview question followed by my answer.
Evaluate the answer as a demanding hiring manager. First, tell me:
Whether I actually answered the question
What was convincing
What sounded vague or generic
Whether I gave enough evidence
Whether I spent too much time on irrelevant context
What follow-up question an interviewer would probably ask
If it is a behavioral question, also evaluate it using the STAR method.
Only after giving me this critique, provide a stronger version that retains my real experience and sounds natural when spoken aloud. Don’t turn it into a polished corporate script that nobody would actually say in an interview.
FAQs about AI Interview Tools
Can ChatGPT help me prepare for a job interview?
Yes. You can give ChatGPT your resume and job description and ask it to identify likely interview questions, evaluate your answers, conduct mock interviews, research the role, and point out gaps in your preparation. Voice mode makes the mock interview experience significantly more natural.
Are AI mock interviews actually useful?
They can be, especially when the AI asks follow-up questions and gives detailed feedback instead of simply generating a list of questions. They are particularly useful for repeated practice, although they shouldn't completely replace practice with another person when that is available.
Which AI interview tools are free?
Exponent Practice offers a limited number of free peer mock interviews, while Yoodli has a free tier. Huru AI provides free access to try its mock interviews, and Ophy AI offers free starting credits. The exact limits can change, so check each service before signing up.
What is the best AI interview tool for software engineers?
Interviewing.io and Exponent Practice are the strongest options on this list for software engineers. They focus much more heavily on coding, system design, algorithms, and other technical interview formats than general-purpose interview coaching tools.
Can I use AI during an actual job interview?
That depends entirely on the employer and interview rules. Some companies prohibit outside assistance during interviews and assessments. Unless the interviewer explicitly allows it, the safer approach is to use AI extensively during preparation and answer the actual interview questions yourself.
How many AI mock interviews should I practice?
There is no fixed number. Instead of repeating mock interviews endlessly, complete one, review the feedback, fix the weak areas, and try again. A few focused sessions with clear improvement between them are more useful than doing many interviews without reviewing your mistakes.

What Is MagSafe?
MagSafe is Apple's magnetic technology built into the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17 lineups, as well as the iPhone Air (the iPhone SE and iPhone 16e are excluded). It consists of a ring of magnets on the back of the phone designed for a faster, more precise wireless charging system. But these magnets also opened up the ability to attach different kinds of accessories, like wallets and power banks. It even makes docking an iPhone to a car mount easier.
If you use a case on your iPhone, make sure it comes with MagSafe support (you'll see a ring of magnets on the inside). That way, the MagSafe accessories will have a proper connection. Otherwise, if you use a non-MagSafe case, the accessories will likely slide off due to a weak connection.

If you want a magnetic grip, make sure it supports MagSafe or Qi2, or at least mentions magnets on the product page. All the recommendations here are MagSafe grips.

Most Android phones are incompatible with MagSafe grips. But there are magnetic cases available for top Android phone models enabling MagSafe-like functionality. You can find WIRED-tested magnetic cases for select Android phones here.
Over the coming years, thanks to the new Qi2 wireless charging standard that incorporates the Magnetic Power Profile, you'll start seeing more high-end Android phones embed magnets inside the device. Google already has Qi2 devices with the Pixel 10 range. That will allow greater compatibility with MagSafe accessories with or without a magnetic case. The road is bumpy, though. Samsung's latest Galaxy S26 range, for example, are “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can only access Qi2 charging speeds and features with a magnet case. Hopefully, manufacturers will add native magnet support soon.
The Different Types of Phone Grips
MagSafe grips are hardly the only type of phone grips available. There are four main other types of grips you can buy.
Cases with attached grips. These are cases with a grip attached to the back. You get a strong and durable grip that will never fall off, but the trade-off is a thicker phone, and these cases typically are incompatible with wireless charging and may not work with other MagSafe accessories.
Clamp-style grips. Also called universal phone grips, these clamp to a phone so you can easily take them on and off, and they're not limited to a particular kind of phone. The downside is they're not the fastest to take on and off, and they can sometimes slide up and down the phone.
Adhesive grips. You can stick a phone grip to the back of your phone or case, and while this will typically give you a well-attached grip that likely won't fall off your phone, the downsides are similar to cases with attached grips. It may block features like wireless charging and restrict you from using other accessories. These grips can also be difficult to remove when you're ready—some have swappable tops, but they don't necessarily allow for easy mixing and matching with different phone cases.
MagSafe grips. These grips are all about convenience. You can easily take them on and off, but they only work with devices or cases with built-in magnets. While you can dangle a phone from a MagSafe grip without issue, additional force could cause the magnets to separate and fling your phone to the ground.
How We Test MagSafe Grips
Each MagSafe grip in this guide is one we used as a primary phone grip for weeks or months at a time. We make sure they snap securely to an iPhone or MagSafe case, and we also ensure they provide a comfortable hold for long periods and are durable enough to withstand drops and heavy use. We use the phone as we normally would—scrolling through social media, FaceTiming with friends, and sending texts and emails—and evaluate the grip to see if it gets in the way or makes life easier.
Other MagSafe Grips We’ve Tested
Spigen OM104 MagSafe Phone Grip: The OM104 is a phone/grip combo accessory for MagSafe and Qi2 devices that comes with a flexible nylon strap to slide your finger through while holding your phone. Dual magnets and a robust metal construction make the OM104 feel like money well spent, and even after hours of sliding my finger in and out of the strap, it still feels soft, flexible, and most importantly, comfortable. It has one annoying design oversight. As you slide your phone in and out of your pocket, the nylon strap will start to droop down. The strap is longer than the grip itself, so when you close the kickstand, it’ll get pinched inside and won’t allow the stand to fully close. It’s comfortable to use, but that quibble knocks it down.
Casely MagRing: Unlike other metal grips we've tested, Casely's MagRing is made of soft silicone. We find it more comfortable on the fingers. It also has a 360-degree swivel, so you can position the grip at virtually any angle. This is strictly a grip, so you can't use it as a kickstand. Since the grip doesn't fold in, your phone won't lie fully flat on a surface. We also tested the MagRing+, which comes with a ring clip for attaching your keys. That comes in handy for quick trips to the grocery store or when you go to the gym and need a place to put your car keys and key fob. But Jacob prefers the standard MagRing, since he typically carries his keys in his pocket or bag. Casely has a few variations of the MagRing and MagRing+ in stock, but it appears to be on its last legs.
Smartish Wallflower: It isn’t perfect, but we still love it. The Smartish Wallflower comes with seven small suction cups that look like a flower, allowing you to attach your phone to a wall (or any other surface) and leave it be. It mostly works, but it largely depends on how heavy your phone is and what surface you’re attaching it to. We didn’t have issues with an iPhone 17 and drywall, but the iPhone 15 Pro Max attached to a particleboard cabinet was too heavy for the grip to manage.
Avoid These MagSafe Grips
OhSnap! Snap Grip: I like that this grip allows you to use other MagSafe accessories, but the point of a MagSafe grip (to me) is that you can remove it easily enough that it doesn't hinder accessories in the first place. So it seems like sort of a needless feature. More importantly, this grip doesn't feel secure to me. I have a harder time keeping a good handle on my phone when I use it, which negates the purpose. The lack of bulk is nice, but a phone ring can provide essentially the same thing with a bit more security. And this grip has a tendency to stick to your accessories rather than your phone when you remove it.
PopSockets Low-Pro Grip and Stand: All phone grip analyses are going to be subjective, but I'm not a fan of how flimsy this new PopSocket feels. It's quite floppy, so I feel like my hand has to do more work to compensate for holding my phone, in which case I'd rather not use a grip in the first place. It's also very difficult to open with one hand. I'm of the mind that accessories shouldn't require more work than you'd need to put in without them. This PopSocket fails that test. Finally, like the OhSnap grip, this sticks to accessories too well. It regularly pulls off or sticks to the car mounts I'm testing rather than sticking to my phone.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday (August 28, 2026) submitted in the Supreme Court a proposal to provide information relating to added sugar, fat and salt in pictorial form on the front-of-pack (FOP) of food products, in line with international regulations.
“The proposal is intended to provide a simple, prominent and easily comprehensible warning to consumers regarding food products which are high in specified nutrients of concern,” an FSSAI affidavit filed in the Supreme Court said.
The affidavit proposes an FOP warning label in red hexagonal shape for food products which are high in any two or more “nutrients of concern” such as added saturated fat, added sugar and salt, based on thresholds specified under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024.
The warning label would read ‘High Fat’, ‘High Sugar’, ‘High Salt’ or ‘Highly Sweetened Beverage’ and be displayed in a font one point larger than that used in the nutrition information table on the back of the pack to help customers readily identify at-risk foods.
The FSSAI said single-ingredient food products and those which are “inherently rich in fat, sugar or salt, like ghee, edible oil, jaggery, honey” are proposed to be exempted from FOP warning requirement.
Phased implementation
The affidavit said the FOP labelling mechanism is intended to be implemented in phases to “facilitate consumer acceptability and provide industry adequate time for reformulation”.
Phase I would cover products high in two or more specified nutrients and specified sweetened beverages. Phase II would extend the warning mechanism to products high in any one of these nutrients.
The affidavit in the Supreme Court came in a petition filed by NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi. Mr. Dvivedi said the NGO would file a comprehensive rejoinder to the FSSAI’s compliance affidavit in the apex court after inviting public comments.
The compliance affidavit by the food regulator follows scathing comments on August 13 from a Bench headed by Justice J.B. Pardiwala on the state’s obligations to protect public health. The court had observed that not only developed but even developing countries were adopting international standards of packaging food products.
Bringing awareness
“A positive step in that direction would further accelerate our country’s endeavour to be fully developed, by bringing awareness to the public in general of the ill-effects, emanating even from indigenous foods, despite our conviction that indigenous foods coming from diverse cultures in this country were never intended to be packaged,” the court had recorded in its August 13 order.
The court had noted that the Economic Survey has already suggested FOP labelling, and the Union government would not have any impediments in implementing the changes.
“We are doing this in public interest. Keep it in mind,” Justice Pardiwala had addressed the government on August 13.

PM Modi gets Uzbekistan's highest state honour, Order of Oliy Darajali Do‘stlik
PM Narendra Modi thanked his "brother" President Shavkat Mirziyoyev for the honour, saying India and Uzbekistan will work together for the welfare of humanity.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi was on Sunday conferred the ‘Order of Oliy Darajali Do‘stlik’, Uzbekistan’s highest state honour, by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, in recognition of the deep and enduring ties between India and Uzbekistan.
This happened during PM Modi's two-day state visit to the Central Asian country.
The prestigious honour was presented to PM Modi in Tashkent as the two leaders held delegation-level talks to expand cooperation between India and Uzbekistan across several key areas.
Last year, Uzbekistan conferred the same award on Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the President of Kazakhstan. Other notable leaders who have gotten the award are Turkmenistan President Serdar Berdimuhamedov, the chairman of the People's Council of Turkmenistan Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow, and United Nations secretary general António Guterres.
What PM Modi said
Prime Minister Narendra Modi thanked his "brother" President Shavkat Mirziyoyev for the honour, saying India and Uzbekistan will work together for the welfare of the Global South and humanity.
Expressing gratitude for the warmth extended to him and his delegation during his two-day State visit, PM Modi said the visit would remain memorable for him.
"My friend, the father of the economic revolution in Uzbekistan, who has served as a role model across this entire region in scaling new heights of development- this two-day visit of mine will always be remembered," PM Modi said.
"The warmth with which my delegation and I were welcomed made us feel right at home, and for this, I express my deepest heartfelt gratitude to the President," he added.
Reflecting on the honour, PM Modi said the words used by President Mirziyoyev captured India's heritage, its spirit of universal brotherhood and the efforts of its 1.4 billion people.
"The words you just used for me and the generosity you expressed--I believe you have captured in very few words India's thousands-of-years-old heritage, the identity of an India that lives by the spirit of universal brotherhood (Vishwa Bandhutva), and the enterprise of 1.4 billion fellow citizens," he said.
"I may only be a medium for all your words, but the true recipients are my thousands-of-years-old heritage, and the perseverance and hard work of 1.4 billion countrymen- they are the true deserving bearers of this honour," PM Modi added.
Calling the award a moment of "immense pride", the Prime Minister highlighted the significance of the word "Dostlik", meaning friendship, and said it reflected the core sentiment of India-Uzbekistan relations.
"Being conferred with Uzbekistan's highest award is a moment of immense pride for me. And you used a word with which the people of India are also very familiar--'Dostlik'," he said.
"'Dostlik' means friendship. This single word exquisitely captures and expresses the sentiment that lies at the very core of relations between India and Uzbekistan," PM Modi said.
PM Modi said the honour belonged not only to him but to the people of India, and dedicated it to the longstanding friendship and shared heritage between the two countries.
"This honour does not belong to just one individual; it belongs to 1.4 billion people of India. On behalf of all the people of India, I express my sincere gratitude to the people of Uzbekistan, its government, and my friend, the Honourable President," he said.
"I accept this highest honour with utmost humility and humbly dedicate it to the centuries-old friendship and our shared heritage between both nations," he added.
The Prime Minister also credited President Mirziyoyev's leadership and friendship with India for the steady strengthening of bilateral ties, noting that the relationship has now been elevated to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
"Excellency, under your visionary leadership and your friendship toward India, our relations have grown consistently stronger. They continue to successfully scale new heights at every step. As a result, our ties have today been elevated to the new level of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership," PM Modi said.
PM Modi said the honour also carried a greater responsibility and assured the people of Uzbekistan that India would remain committed to the friendship between the two countries.

68 tonnes of aid across 4 flights: PM Modi's love for Nepal reflected in swift aid delivery
Since August 26, India has sent four military flights carrying emergency relief material, temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps and more.
India, the first major nation to deliver aid to Nepal after devastating flash floods left over 700 dead and thousands missing, is stepping up its relief efforts.
New Delhi has now rushed more than 68 tonnes of emergency relief supplies to the neighbouring country, delivered across four military flights. The swift aid delivery is a testament to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's focus on the “Neighbourhood First” policy.
HT reported on Friday that India was the first country to physically deliver aid to Nepal after the disaster, reinforcing India's "first responder" tag and reflecting its growing record of delivering aid and assistance to disaster-hit countries such as Türkiye and Syria to Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Venezuela.
Deep Dive
Since August 26, India has sent a total of four flights carrying emergency relief material such as temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps, and medicines.
Other countries and international organisations have also pledged or begun providing assistance to Nepal.
HT has accessed details of how governments and global organisations are rallying around the disaster-hit country.
Nepal: By 29 August, more than NRs 5 billion has been collected in the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund operated by the government for flood victims.
India: India has sent a total of about 68.5 tons of emergency relief supplies across four military flights. On 26 August 2026, an IAF C-130J Hercules airlifted 10 tonnes of emergency relief material such as temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps, and medicines. On 27 August 2026, an IAF C-17 Globemaster airlifted 37.5 tonnes of relief items, including 28.5 tonnes of tents, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps, dewatering pumps, kitchen sets, gensets, 8 tonnes of medicines, and 1 tonne of food items. On 28 August 2026, a C-130J Hercules airlifted a 5-member Indian Army tunnel rescue recce team and a 6-member medical team, and another 10 tonnes of material, including portable gensets, dignity kits, food, water purification tablets, and medicines. The 4th flight carrying 11 tonnes of relief assistance landed in Nepal this morning. It consists of a tunnel technical contingent along with equipment for search & rescue operations; a team of forensics experts for DNA analysis and relief supplies, including blankets, sleeping bags, tarpaulin, plastic sheets & hygiene kits. India's contribution has been announced in physical tonnage rather than a cash figure. Additionally, 16 trucks carrying equipment for a 230-foot Single Lane Modular Steel Bridge have reached Nepal.
China: China has committed to providing both emergency supplies and cash assistance to Nepal. Chinese Ambassador Zhang Maoming has asked Nepal's Finance Ministry to begin the process for receiving these funds, but no confirmed amount has been made public yet. China's offer of a search-and-rescue team was declined by Nepal, which said its own security agencies could manage rescue operations. China’s Ministry of Emergency Management dispatched five tunnel experts to Nepal on 29 August. Two Y-20 transport aircraft of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Air Force carrying 50 tonnes of emergency relief supplies arrived at Tribhuvan International Airport this morning. The supplies include tents, blankets, sleeping bags, hard tack and first-aid kits. It is reported that Nepal has also asked China to supply Bailey bridges.
UAE: The UAE has allocated $10 million in assistance through the UAE Aid Agency, which is coordinating with local authorities and international organisations to ensure relief reaches all affected communities.
UK: The UK has pledged £5 million (approximately $6.8 million) along with emergency responders, to be disbursed through development partners in a coordinated manner. Like China's offer, the UK's search-and-rescue team offer was declined by Nepal.
Australia: Australia has pledged a $5 million assistance package, broken into three parts: $2 million to the World Food Programme (which has already dispatched food rations and logistics support), $2 million to Australian NGOs through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership (for shelter, hygiene kits, blankets, medical and psychosocial support), and $1 million to the Emergency Action Alliance for locally-led recovery efforts. Three Australian humanitarian workers are set to deploy within 48 hours, along with additional consular staff.
South Korea: South Korea has pledged $1 million in humanitarian aid to be channelled through international organisations. Its offer to send a search-and-rescue team was declined by Nepal.
Sri Lanka: Sri Lanka has pledged $1 million in direct financial assistance to support Nepal's relief efforts.
United States of America: The US State Department has committed $500,000 in immediate assistance for flood-affected communities, covering emergency shelter, relief supplies, clean water and hygiene needs - reportedly channelled through a global grant to Catholic Relief Services. The U.S. is also deploying a disaster-response adviser to support the relief effort. Catholic Relief Services, working through implementing partner Caritas Nepal, plans to deliver more than 2.5 metric tons of food supplies, 500 blankets, 500 mosquito nets, and 500 insulating foam sheets for temporary shelter flooring to two school locations in Rasuwa. The first shipment was delivered on 28 August. On 29 August, the U.S. announced that it is providing more than USD 3.6 million worth of humanitarian assistance, including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households.
Canada: Canada has announced C$ 5 million in humanitarian assistance funding to support emergency relief efforts in Nepal.
Countries which have expressed solidarity, but yet to announce aid packages
While many countries have pledged support and already rushed out aid packages to Nepal, many are yet to send in relief material despite pledging solidarity.
NGOs, international organisations come to Nepal's aid
World Bank: The World Bank's country director has informed Nepal's Finance Ministry that up to ₹25 billion (approximately $163.6 million) in emergency aid could be mobilised to support rescue and reconstruction efforts.
European Union: The European Union has allocated €2 million (USD 2.32 million) in humanitarian aid to support affected communities. This emergency funding will help address immediate needs, including food, healthcare, clean water and sanitation. EU-funded partners are already providing help on the ground.
UN Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF): The UN has released $2.5 million in emergency funds to support medical care, shelter and water needs for affected communities.
International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC): The IFRC has released an initial 1 million Swiss francs (about $1.24 million) in emergency funding to support the Nepal Red Cross Society's response, and has separately launched a larger Emergency Appeal for CHF 25 million (approximately $31 million) to sustain the Society's relief operations.
Welthungerhilfe (Germany): This German humanitarian organisation is providing €100,000 (approximately $110,000) from its emergency relief fund.
World Health Organisation (WHO): WHO has dispatched essential emergency medical supplies, including medicines and multipurpose tents - an in-kind contribution not assigned a specific dollar value.
Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF): This French humanitarian organisation has an emergency medical team already on the ground in Nepal, providing immediate care, and also an in-kind contribution without a quantified dollar figure.
On August 26, the Nepal-China border region saw devastating flash floods that are believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse—some reports point to an avalanche of ice and rocks—that sent a torrent of water, mud and debris down Himalayan river systems, destroying villages and sweeping away roads, bridges and other infrastructure. Officials and scientists are continuing to assess the precise sequence of events.
As of Sunday morning, the combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 750 dead and over 3,000 people missing. As per Nepal’s disaster agency, the death toll had climbed to 734 with 2,498 people missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, including over a hundred Nepalis and people from over a dozen countries.

The Madras High Court on Monday (August 31, 2026) reserved its orders on a writ petition filed by DMK president M.K. Stalin to order 100% counting of VVPAT slips of the Kolathur Assembly constituency, and to consequently declare him the returned candidate after nullifying the election of TVK MLA V.S. Babu.
The First Division Bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan deferred their verdict after hearing the arguments advanced by senior counsel Kapil Sibal for the former Chief Minister and senior counsel G. Rajagopal and Dama Seshadri Naidu for the Election Commission of India (ECI).
The ECI counsel contended that the writ petition was not maintainable at all in view of Article 329(b) of the Constitution and Section 80 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which categorically state that an election to a parliamentary or Assembly constituency could be challenged only by way of an election petition.
Entertaining a “cleverly and artfully” drafted writ petition to set aside an election would lead to the opening of a pandora’s box, and numerous such writ petitions may get filed in the High Court in the future for setting aside validly held elections to Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies, the counsel said.
Stalin’s argument
On the other hand, Mr. Sibal argued that the present case does not stem out of any constitutional or statutory provision but a 2024 Supreme Court judgment, in Association for Democratic Reforms versus Election Commission of India, which permitted either the runner-up or the third-place-holder in a parliamentary/Assembly election to make a request for the checking and verification of the burnt memory/microcontroller in 5% of the EVMs by a team of engineers from the EVM manufacturers.
Since the top court had ordered that any such application for verification must be made within seven days of declaration of the result, Mr. Stalin, who lost by a margin of 8,795 votes by securing 74,202 votes as against 82,997 votes garnered by Mr. Babu, had duly made such application within three days from the declaration of the election results on May 4, 2026.
However, the ECI began the verification of 14 out of 286 EVM sets used in Kolathur only on July 29, 2026, well after the expiry of the 45-day period for filing an election petition, and completed it on August 5, 2026. Highlighting that the writ petitioner had come across serious anomalies in the working of the EVM sets during the verification process, with one of the units not being able to identify the petitioner’s name, Mr. Sibal said: “Whether Your Lordships give me relief or not is another matter, but this must be investigated. What’s the explanation for this?”
Further, underlining that the writ petitioner could not file an election petition only because of the delay caused by the ECI in commencing the verification process, the senior counsel said that the petitioner could not be let go remediless because of the delay in which the he had no role to play.
Another writ petition withdrawn
Mr. Stalin’s counsel withdrew another writ petition filed by him, challenging certain provisions of the SOP framed by the ECI for the verification of 5% of the EVM sets. The petition was withdrawn, with liberty to file a fresh case, after the judges pointed out that the petitioner had wrongly challenged the 2024 SOP though that had been superseded by the 2025 SOP under which the verification was carried out this year with respect to the Kolathur constituency.

Dolly Parton was laid to rest Friday in a small, private service, per the singer’s wishes. The ceremony was confirmed by her great-niece, Lainey Parton, who posted a remembrance on social media.

An upcoming election could produce modern Germany's 1st far-right state governor
An election in eastern Germany on Sunday could produce the first far-right state governor in the country’s post-World War II history
MOESER, Germany -- An election in eastern Germany on Sunday could produce the first far-right state governor in the country's post-World War II history as Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his unpopular national government struggle to dispel what he calls “widespread moroseness.”
Several polls show a large lead for the anti-migration Alternative for Germany, or AfD, ahead of the election to the state legislature in Saxony-Anhalt. Taking control of a state government would be the biggest prize in the party’s 13-year history, a political shock to Germany and at least a symbolic blow to Merz.
“If AfD wins the election and forms the government, that would be kind of breaking a taboo in Germany,” said Wolfgang Merkel, a political science professor with the WBZ Berlin Social Science Center. Modern Germany so far has been “an exception” in Europe in having no radical right-wing party governing at the national, state or big-city level, he added.
Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union has led Saxony-Anhalt, a region west of Berlin that's among the country’s less prosperous and is home to 2.1 million of Germany's 83.5 million people, since 2002. But it faces strong headwinds.
In last year’s national election, AfD achieved the best postwar showing by a far-right party, with 20.8% of the vote. It became Germany’s biggest opposition party.
It was stronger in the ex-communist east, including Saxony-Anhalt. And with Merz's government struggling to convince voters it can turn around a stubbornly slow economy, it has gained in national polls as it harnesses discontent with issues beyond its signature theme of curbing migration.
In Saxony-Anhalt, AfD is seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature. That would overcome the so-called “firewall” of mainstream parties’ refusal to work with AfD, whose regional branch is one of several classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a proven right-wing extremist group. AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism.
AfD’s campaign slogan is “Everything is possible.”
“This is a historic opportunity that we have here in Saxony-Anhalt,” its candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, told The Associated Press at a campaign event in the small town of Moeser, where supporters lined up to meet the charismatic 35-year-old over beer and sausages. “We will write history here."
Among his top priorities, Siegmund lists “the deportation of people who are illegal, a deportation offensive and above all dropping the incentives for why people come here and exploit our social system.” He wants to initiate a long process to withdraw Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcaster, citing concerns about “disinformation.”
AfD’s first and so far only head of a county administration was elected in 2023 in neighboring Thuringia state. A state administration would be a far bigger prize, fueling the party's ambitions of further gains and one day governing at the national level.
Germany’s 16 states have extensive powers, for example in overseeing security matters and running the education system.
In Saxony-Anhalt, AfD wants to allow home schooling, which so far isn't permitted in Germany. It pledges to ban schools from officially raising the rainbow flag and ensure they fly the national flag. It opposes taxpayers' money being “given away” to Ukraine and says it would push to lift sanctions against Russia, but that isn't a matter state governments can decide.
“No one here needs to be afraid, quite the contrary,” Siegmund said. “Every honest person in Saxony-Anhalt will benefit from an AfD-led government.”
Siegmund's main opponent, incumbent governor Sven Schulze from Merz’s CDU, told the AP at his party's offices in Magdeburg, the state capital, that AfD “wants the past back” and the state would face “isolation” with AfD in power.
He pointed to major progress made in strengthening Saxony-Anhalt's economy and bringing down unemployment since Germany was reunited in 1990. The far right, he said, effectively “doesn't want to have anyone here who was born abroad and lives and works here.” With many immigrants working in hospitals and companies, for example, that would be “a huge problem for Saxony-Anhalt,” he said.
“AfD does one thing — it describes problems,” said Schulze, who said that he won't work with the party and his own CDU is “100%” behind him. “But it never has a solution for a problem.”
AfD's chances of governing are uncertain even if it does become by far the strongest party. If it doesn't win an absolute majority, Merkel said he doesn't see it governing for lack of any potential coalition partner.
That likely would leave Schulze trying to cobble together some kind of alliance with multiple smaller parties to his left. That would leave many people saying that “they are clinging to power,” Merkel said.
It remains unclear how an AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt would affect the national government, particularly if Merz’s CDU and its coalition partners, the center-left Social Democrats, fare poorly in elections Sept. 20 in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, another eastern state.
Merkel said he believes Saxony-Anhalt is too small to have “any particular impact.” But a significant loss of votes would amplify a narrative that the traditional big parties are in decline.
Merz's government needs to prove its ability to reform Germany and so far lacks “visible successes,” Merkel added, noting that “when the economy isn't running, basically all areas of politics are infected.”
Merz sought to spread optimism after his Cabinet met last week to underline its determination to push through reforms.
“We must get out of this climate of glumness and anger,” he said. “Together, we must shake off this widespread moroseness that has long paralyzed our country.”

Protests against reservations were held at Jantar Mantar and Connaught Place in Delhi on 21 and 23 August 2026. The protests were part of an online campaign called the ‘Reservation Hatao Andolan’, which has over 5.6 million followers on Instagram. The protestors primarily demanded that government jobs and opportunities in educational institutions be provided based on financial status and merit, rather than caste. They also demanded the withdrawal of the 2026 Equity Regulations, which were brought in by the UGC to control discrimination in higher educational institutions.
In this context, a video of a huge crowd blocking a road is being shared on social media, claiming to show the protest at Jantar Mantar on 21 August 2026, demanding the withdrawal of the UGC Equity Regulations, 2026. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of massive crowd at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, protesting against reservations and demanding a rollback of the UGC Equity Regulations on 21 August 2026.
Fact: The video actually depicts a July 2026 farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, demanding minimum support price (MSP) for their Moong crop. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to an identical clip (archive), which was uploaded on the Facebook page of Ramakant Dwivedi on 29 July 2026. The description states that it shows a farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. We found several other videos of this protest on social media, which can be seen here and here.
The protest site can also be identified on Google Maps as Narmadapuram Road in Bhopal. According to reports (here, here & here), the farmers were protesting to demand 100% procurement of their Moong (green gram) crop at the Minimum Support Price (MSP), among other issues. The farmers marched from Narmadapuram to Bhopal, demanding the abolition of the e-token system for procurement and fertiliser distribution. However, the protest ended after talks with the government.
To sum it up, the viral video depicts a July 2026 farmers’ protest in Bhopal and is falsely being shared as UGC roll back protests in Delhi.

For crores of Indian families, the financial shock of hospitalisation — especially in a private hospital — begins even before treatment is complete. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare, in its 176th Report tabled in Parliament on August 7, 2026, noted that the average cost of hospitalisation is ₹50,508 in a private facility, compared with ₹6,631 in a government facility. For childbirth, the average out-of-pocket medical expenditure in private facilities is ₹37,630, against ₹2,299 in public facilities.
Some of the contradictions
The committee has made 368 recommendations, including standardised package rates and mandatory pre-treatment cost estimates. Among the widely reported proposals is that basic room tariffs in metropolitan private hospitals should not exceed the average tariff of three-star hotels that are nearby. It has also suggested that large corporate hospitals earning from medical tourism, foreign patients and high-net-worth individuals should cross-subsidise poorer Indians and reserve beds for Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) beneficiaries at regulated rates. Yet, there is a contradiction. India wants more private and foreign capital in health care, particularly in Tier-2, Tier-3 and rural areas, while simultaneously asking the government to review foreign direct investment rules related to the acquisition and management of existing hospitals.
There is a strong case for continued investment in Indian health care. Hospitals require substantial capital. Land, equipment, intensive care units, digital systems, laboratories and trained personnel are expensive. Public hospitals cannot currently meet all demand for secondary and tertiary care. Private hospitals therefore fill an important gap. Foreign investors and private-equity funds can bring capital, managerial capacity, technology and the capacity to expand hospital networks. India also needs investment in pharmaceutical and medical-device manufacturing. If regulation becomes excessively restrictive or unpredictable, some investment may move elsewhere. This could slow capacity expansion and delay the development of better health-care infrastructure in cities and districts where need is genuine.
However, in all sectors, capital comes with expectations of returns. In health care, it creates a special concern because patients are not ordinary consumers. A patient rarely decides independently whether an MRI is required, whether hospital admission should continue for two more days, or whether a procedure is necessary. Health care is shaped by what economists call information asymmetry: the provider knows more than the patient. Therefore, when financial incentives become too strong, they can influence not just the price of care but also how much care is delivered.
A closer look at private care
This is where the role of private equity and venture capital in health care deserves closer attention. Corporate hospital groups increasingly compete for well-known specialists, sophisticated technology and premium infrastructure. These can improve quality, but also create a high-cost ecosystem. Hospitals that pay very high salaries to senior specialists and super-specialists, acquire expensive equipment and operate under pressure to increase revenue must eventually recover these costs. Revenue targets, procedure-linked incentives, higher occupancy expectations and higher revenue per bed can gradually influence institutional behaviour. Most doctors act in patients’ interests. Yet, systems shape behaviour. If hospitals and doctors are rewarded for doing more, the direction becomes predictable.
The result is not only higher cost but also a worrying medicalisation. Lab investigations may detect abnormalities that would never have caused harm. More screening can lead to unnecessary follow-up tests. A patient who could be managed as an outpatient may be admitted. Caesarean sections, angioplasties, intensive-care admissions, diagnostic packages and long lists of medicines must therefore be seen not only as individual clinical decisions but also within the incentive structure of the health system. This does not mean these interventions are usually unnecessary. It means that a system rewarding interventions and procedures needs strong safeguards against unnecessary prescriptions, surgeries, investigations and medications.
That is why a review of FDI in the acquisition of existing hospitals is justified. Domestic investors can be equally profit-oriented, while foreign investment can create valuable capacity. The more useful question is about what an investment does to the health system. Does it create new beds or simply acquire existing ones? Does it improve competition or lead to market concentration? Does it enter an underserved district or add another high-end facility in a metro? If an investor receives concessional land, tax benefits or other public support, are there enforceable obligations related to affordable beds or participation in public insurance schemes? India should encourage greenfield investment and manufacturing, while scrutinising acquisitions that reduce competition or raise the risk of excessive pricing.
Price regulation also needs to be approached carefully. The proposal to link hospital room charges to nearby three-star hotels is easy to understand, but cannot by itself solve the affordability problem. A hospital room includes nursing, infection-control and emergency support that a hotel room does not. More importantly, if one component of the bill is capped, hospitals may increase charges elsewhere. India’s experience with coronary stent price regulation showed that government intervention can reduce excessive mark-ups. But hospital care is more complex; what matters is the total cost of an episode. Package rates, transparent estimates, billing standards and audit mechanisms are therefore more useful than isolated caps on individual components. There is also an established approach to such payments: Diagnosis-Related Groups (DRG). A DRG is a patient-classification system that standardised hospital reimbursement by paying a fixed, predetermined amount for an inpatient stay based on the diagnosis and procedures, rather than reimbursing each service separately.
Focus on public health
There is a larger policy question. India cannot regulate its way out of weak public health care. If government hospitals remain overcrowded, understaffed or difficult to access, citizens will continue to depend heavily on private providers. Experience from OECD countries has shown that one effective form of regulation is a strong public health system that provides a credible alternative.
Public hospitals must therefore become a genuine option, not merely the last resort for those who cannot afford private care. Primary health care needs strengthening so that disease is prevented, detected and treated early. Insurance systems, including AB-PMJAY, should reward appropriate care rather than simply higher volumes of procedures. Clinical audits, evidence-based treatment protocols and transparent billing can protect both patients and doctors from commercial pressures.
The Parliamentary Committee is right to focus attention on affordability and to question whether the current pattern of investment in private health care aligns with public interest. Price caps and an FDI review are reasonable starting points, but India needs a wider conversation about the kind of health-care system it is building. Private investment will remain essential, and profit by itself is not the problem.
The problem begins when the pursuit of returns starts a key influence. A health-care system should attract capital, but its clinical priorities must still be set by medical need. The true measure of India’s health-care progress will not be how much money flows into hospitals or what is the annual compounded growth rate in medical tourism, but whether Indian citizens can enter them with confidence that they will receive what they need. No more, no less.
Chandrakant Lahariya is a practising physician specialising in preventive and cardio-metabolic medicine, whose upcoming book, Pill-Free: You Don’t Need Everything You Have Been Prescribed, will be released in September 2026

This past week, the top health story, without any doubt, is the huge crisis that is brewing out of proportions in Africa - the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. It was first announced as an outbreak on May 15, this year.As per latest data, it has reached over 5,000 cases, making this the one of the worst Ebola outbreaks in history. The outbreak has clearly outpaced response efforts.
Data from Congo’s Ministry of Health showed the outbreak had so far recorded 5,021 cases, including 2,378 deaths as of August 16, 2026, as it rages in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable fuelled by insecurity, displacement and intense population movements. It has officially infected and killed more people at a greater speed than any other outbreak in history. Starting from the first detected case, it has spread about three times faster than an outbreak from 2014 to 2016 across West Africa, which was the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record with more than 11,000 deaths.
The dire situation was underlined as World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced: “We must be frank: the epidemic is far from being under control.” Safety concerns have limited the response as health workers are targeted, particularly in Ituri, the province that has been hit the worst by the outbreak. Residents recently attacked a health team in the territory of Aru after a suspected case was reported there. A mob set fire to an ambulance and damaged two other vehicles, according to Michael Wani, president of the Union of Cultural Associations for the Development of Ituri.
Meanwhile, more than 16,000 doses of the new Ebola vaccine Ervebo arrived in the DRC. WHO experts still do not know whether Ervebo protects humans against the Bundibugyo strain, but early data, notably from animal trials, suggest it could offer some protection.The Ervebo vaccine “has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak”, Samuel Roger Kamba, the DRC’s Minister of Health, told the press.
The other big story in India was also about an infectious disease - H1N1. As the cases continue to surge, experts assure that there is no cause for alarm yet. However they do advise that a large number of children were being affected, and that children with asthma and other chronic conditions might require special intervention.
The H1N1 virus, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A, and can cause respiratory illness, with symptoms including fever or chills, cough, sore throat, a runny or blocked nose, headache, tiredness, and muscle or body aches. In some cases, patients may also experience vomiting and diarrhoea. Cases have been rising in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru and Kerala, and while there are a number of respiratory-like illnesses also about during this season, doctors have warned that early testing is key. Bindu Shajan Perappadan reports that union Health Minister J.P. Nadda reviewed the H1N1 situation, healthcare preparedness in Delhi.
With National Eye Donation Fortnight being observed across India every year from August 25 to September 8 to raise awareness about eye donation we did our bit to highlight issues relating to eye health a little ahead of schedule.
Athira Elssa Johnson writes about the Lazy eye in children, and about squints. In the former, she focuses on how many parents may miss lazy eye among their children. Often called lazy eye, amblyopia may have no obvious signs and can remain undetected during early childhood. Screening, timely treatment and sustained follow-up are important because visual development is time-sensitive. Squints are another condition that impact the development of vision, and therefore need to be addressed on time. Squint, medically known as strabismus, is a condition in which the two eyes do not align properly. It can affect children and adults and, when it develops during childhood, can interfere with the normal development of vision
In the modern age, the field of ophthalmology is among the earliest adopters of AI systems in health care, so here is an article on using AI systems in smartphones to help detect eye diseases. Kathleen Sherwin and Rishi Raj Borah make an impassioned case for more women to lead eye health care systems.
This week we looked at some little explored aspects of cancer care too. Shrabana Chatterjee writes an interesting story on a hardly-spoken about aspect- Navigating the challenges of fertility and breastfeeding after surviving cancer. This story has a positive message for women in this position - that with careful management and supervision, it can be done.
After a cancer diagnosis, women who have not yet started their families, must be given the option for fertility preservation, say doctors. Options such as embryo freezing before cancer treatment is begun may be considered under medical guidance. Other fertility preservations techniques including oocyte and ovarian-tissue cryopreservation may also be explored before treatment begins. When it comes to breastfeeding, doctors say that after surviving cancer it may pose difficulties, but it can be done under the right medical conditions and with guidance from doctors.
Dr. Siddharth Turkar turns the spotlight on sarcomas: Many soft-tissue sarcomas, which are rare types of cancers that form in fat, muscles and blood vessels, initially look like ordinary lumps. However, when a suspicious mass of this sort is removed without appropriate imaging, tissue diagnosis or oncological planning, the opportunity for the simplest and best-planned first operation may already have been lost.

Rupsy Khurana writes the truth: South Asians are missing from global health databases, and why this matters and what needs to change in this scenario. When scientists try to understand why diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease affect South Asians differently, they often have to rely on genetic data drawn from European populations. Advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning are allowing scientists to mine vast amounts of genomic and health data to detect disease earlier, predict risk, monitor patients and tailor treatments to individuals. But at the heart of this changing landscape lies an old, constant problem – the data used to build these tools lack diversity, she points out.

It’s safe to say Grand Theft Auto VI is the most anticipated game ever. Thirteen years after the last entry in the series, rampant fervor and speculation about what features the game will include have ratcheted up. Today, Rockstar Games divulged more details through an exclusive livestream event on Netflix called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look. The spectacle was a 26-minute-long collection of gameplay, cutscenes, and game mechanics.
And boy, does this sure look like a GTA game. The trailer featured Lucia and Jason, the two main characters, driving around Vice City, GTA’s fictional version of Miami. It highlighted all kinds of violence and shenanigans your characters can engage in, and it looks good doing it.
The livestream follows a week of gameplay leaks and story spoilers by the hacker group Cyberleek, which Rockstar called “heartbreaking.” A bevy of other details about the game emerged just a day before the event in a story published by the British magazine Dazed. The piece chronicles the extraordinary level of detail and effort Rockstar has put into GTA VI, including how players control the characters and the unprecedented realism that Rockstar put into its satirical sandbox version of Miami.
It’s bound to be a massive game; today’s reveal shows just how much of a monster it will be. Here are the big takeaways from the livestream.
It Sure Is Pretty
GTA VI is gorgeous. The cityscapes, nightclubs, and lush natural parks shown all seem vibrant and awash in color.
There is a noticeable difference between cutscenes and gameplay, though, as the gameplay clips looked a little flatter and more desaturated than the cinematic cutscenes. That’s kind of a nitpick, though it’s worth noting that in the very first scene—in the dark basement of a crack house—the lighting is so dim it washes out the features of several Black characters around the table.
You Play as 2 Characters Simultaneously
The player can control two characters, Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque couple who seem to be working out some lingering tension in their relationship as they go about their various criminal activities.
The voice acting for the main characters and other non-playable characters (NPCs) feels tightly written, though that’s based on the select clips Rockstar showed. According to Dazed, the relationship between the characters can change over time, and the player’s actions can affect how that plays out. Keep that in mind if you’re hoping for a particular ending.
GTA VI offers a plethora of options for changing the two main characters’ appearances. Eating too much or too little food affects their weight. Working out can make them swole. The Extended Look also showed off characters eating and working out in minigames. It was a feature in 2004’s GTA San Andreas and in a smaller way in GTA V. Now, that reactivity will be much more fully realized in GTA VI.
There’s also an array of clothes you can equip your characters with, which Rockstar has apparently coordinated with real-life fashion designers to put in the game. Some of these, however, may only come with the $100 Ultimate Edition that people are very mad about.
Maybe Don’t Hit and Run
The NPCs in the game appear much more responsive and interactive than in prior games. According to Dazed, Rockstar has an entire studio in Los Angeles dedicated to working on NPC pedestrian behavior alone.
In the Extended Look, gameplay segments with car chases pointedly avoided streamrolling over pedestrians. But NPCs wore yoga outfits, rode scooters, and seemed to have more personality than the cut-and-paste crowds of past games.
Driving seems greatly improved. When driving, you have a minimap that looks like an actual GPS map guiding you where to go. A car chase saw the main characters running from the police. The player can switch between Lucia and Jason and choose to either drive or shoot at the pursuers. Shooting out tires can cause a car to flip, crash into the sidewalk, and cause environmental destruction.
At one point, a character also body-slams a cop through a wall, which hints at potentially more destructive environments indoors as well. GTA games have been iffy about destructible environments before, though. Sometimes in GTA V you can easily crash through a large light pole but then get instantly stopped by a volleyball net. So we’ll see how reactive everything gets.
So Much Room for Activities
Vice City and the surrounding areas seem absolutely massive. It’s also fully Florida, allowing your characters to fanboat around the Everglades, kayak on the rivers, or scuba dive and jet ski in the Gulf.
One scene from the trailer shows Lucia accidentally kidnapping a livestreaming influencer, then carrying him along through a car chase from the police. Many of the characters use phones and communicate via text. It’s clear that GTA VI has some satirical takes on social media, but we’ll see how relevant it feels in a constantly shifting era.
You Can Pet the Dog
A dog is in at least one scene of the game. Can you pet it? Yes. Yes, you can.
User-Generated Content
In 2023, Rockstar bought the modding marketplace Cfx and reworked it into an official place to share and purchase user-created mods for the game. That service, along with GTA Online’s Rockstar Mission Creator, which lets users make custom levels and modes, indicates that Rockstar has long realized that GTA is fertile ground for user creativity.
The Extended Look didn’t show anything suggesting it would advance those user-creation capabilities, but that’s likely because the game is being released as a single-player title before any multiplayer elements are added.
