Footage of Tibet floods isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
- Published
The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives.
The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world.
Except here, in China.
Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin.
It has also been difficult to find the video on China's heavily censored internet. It is just as hard to even find posts describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday.
Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts.
But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever.
Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party.
China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist.
That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this.
There have been daily updates on the missing and the dead, and Beijing has also been posting updates on the rescue operations, as well as the dangers posed by a barrier lake that has been at risk of overflowing.
But there is little detail beyond that. There are no accounts from survivors in Tibet, and almost no user-generated footage showing the deadly moments or their aftermath.
We are yet to hear from anxious families of those missing. Trying to contact people there is near-impossible during regular times.
As a journalist who has covered North Korea, it has often been easier for me to contact interviewees in Pyongyang than it is in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa.
On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".
Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled.
Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.
Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.
This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.
China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.
The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.
The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it.
It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.
Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.
Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.
A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents.
The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".
It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.
That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.
The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".
To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.
There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.
They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long.
Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.
Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on falling robots and the US-China AI race, follow Robert Hart. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
China’s robots race ahead
Bots were breaking records and breaking down at Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games.
China’s robots race ahead
Bots were breaking records and breaking down at Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games.
How it started
I’ve admitted my fondness for robot fail videos on Stepback before, and let me tell you the World Humanoid Robot Games did not disappoint.
The five-day event, which wrapped this week in Beijing, brought high drama, and brought it well. One robot, made by smartphone maker Honor, lost a leg mid-sprint, while others tripped in a flurry of sparks. Another finisher ran straight into a crash mat, bounced off it, and promptly burst into flames. In the weightlifting, one robot lost its balance beneath a modest barbell and toppled inexorably into the judges’ table, arms cartoonishly aloft. Robotic cheerleaders tumbled and stumbled through routines, while a separate bot fell off a platform in circumstances that, had it been human, might have looked suspiciously like it was gawking at the performers.
This was only the second World Humanoid Robot Games, though it was already far bigger than the inaugural event last year. Unlike this year, last year’s records were paltry. The winning 100-meter sprint was a glacial 21.50 seconds and the highest standing high jump was just 0.95 meters. In keeping with China’s habit of turning robots into public spectacle — from intricate dances at a Spring Festival Gala to demos at major tech events — both this and last year’s games were staged in Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, a former Olympic venue.
And a spectacle it was. At most sporting events, contestants losing limbs, careening into walls, catching fire, and regularly being carried away on stretchers — oh, and did I mention catching fire?! — would probably be grounds to stop proceedings. At the Humanoid Robot Games, it was par for the course.
Fire aside, the games were unusual in other ways too. Alongside familiar events like sprinting, football, boxing, and weightlifting were more unusual competitions in bed-making, parcel delivery, shelf stacking, clothes folding, and hammering nails. Aptly, there was a firefighting contest too.
These less standard offerings spoke to the real purpose of the games: getting robots out of the lab and into the messy real-world environments their makers hope they will ultimately work in. And China is making no secret of wanting to lead the way.
How it’s going
For all the spectacle and drama, the games show there has been massive progress in robotics in recent years. Records fell, with one humanoid running the 100-meter sprint in 9.39 seconds, beating Usain Bolt’s 2009 world record. Another bot reached 2.88 meters in a standing high jump, nearly half a meter above the human high-jump record that has stood since 1993. Those performances are almost unrecognizable compared to robotics competitions a decade ago, when even the most advanced machines struggled to stay upright.
But the games also show how far there is to go before humanoids are actually useful in the real world. The flashy, video-friendly sporting events were impressive, but the more mundane tasks were less thrilling — I don’t see picking up soybeans with tweezers, block-building, or powder-weighing becoming Olympic mainstays anytime soon.
While many events required robots to operate autonomously — including gymnastics, football, tug of war, table tennis, and some track events — others allowed for human assistance via teleoperation, albeit with a scoring penalty. The dexterity being displayed certainly points to genuine and impressive hardware improvements, but seems like there is still a long way to go before these machines can operate reliably on their own in places like factories or homes.
What happens next
Beijing has not yet confirmed a third Humanoid Robot Games, but given the government’s enthusiasm for the industry, it would be surprising to not get another installment. The city has already confirmed another humanoid half-marathon for April, and the country plans to open its first robot-run hotel next year.
China was the undisputed champion of the games, and the country looks well placed to stay in top position moving forward — both at future competitions and in the humanoid robot industry as a whole. The medal table was almost entirely a Chinese affair, dominated in particular by AgiBot and Tien Kung, each scooping up more medals than nearly every other competitor combined, excluding the other.
In part, that asymmetry reflected the lack of international competition. Although the games were framed as a global affair, 641 of 666 teams were Chinese, domestically representing 157 companies and 200 universities, according to state-run China Daily. While there doesn’t seem to be a public breakdown of entrants, the biggest US humanoid players like Tesla, Boston Dynamics, and Figure were conspicuous by their absence.
Nevertheless, the sheer diversity of Chinese institutions represented in Beijing was a show of force, and a sign of how quickly the country’s robotics sector is maturing, even amid growing concerns about circular investment, thriving companies that lack viable products, and a possible humanoid bubble.
It’s not clear a stronger US showing at the games would’ve changed much. The US still has an edge in frontier AI and advanced chips, but China has been rapidly closing parts of that gap, while also making embodied AI a strategic national priority. The same cannot be said of Washington, which has for years paid much less attention to robotics and now trails China in nearly every regard, including manufacturing, deployment, and hardware. Some reports even suggest that recent efforts to ban foreign robots, a general policy squarely aimed at China, could backfire, given how dependent domestic firms are on Chinese components.
Catching up to China will take serious and concerted effort, but given how quickly the technology is moving, there’s still time to make up ground. Washington is already treating other areas of AI as strategic priorities in its competition with Beijing; robotics could be one of them. There will be plenty of stumbling along the way, and, hopefully, plenty more robot fail videos too.
By the way
- DARPA still runs robotics challenges, but they drew far more attention a decade ago.
- When the US government banned foreign robots, it didn’t just ban humanoids and quadrupeds. It banned Roombas too, reports The Verge’s own Sean Hollister.
- “The brains may come from the US, but the body could very well be Made In China,” writes Business Insider’s Lloyd Lee in a report setting out how the US could do with bolstering its hardware supply chain.
- Unlike language models, you can’t simply scrape the internet to build an AI capable of interacting with the real world. A lot of that data has to be generated, which is why companies desperately want to film you doing chores, or send someone to your house to film them doing them.
Read this
- The Atlantic and the South China Morning Post both have great sets of pictures showing highlights of the games worth checking out.
- Why do we keep laughing when robots fail? An old but still good exploration of that shared joy in vintage Vice.
- You can learn a lot about a robot by kicking it, says Verge alum James Vincent in an excellent Harper’s feature outlining the state of play in the humanoid industry.
- I’m not only about robot fail videos. I can hate them in real life too, as I did with Casio’s fluffy AI pet thing, Moflin.

Body odour is a normal part of life. Contrary to popular belief, sweat in itself does not usually smell. The familiar odour develops when bacteria and fungi that live on the skin break down substances in sweat, particularly secretions from glands in the armpits and groin. In most cases, body odour is harmless and may vary depending on factors such as heat, physical activity, diet and hygiene.
However, a new or persistent change in body odour should not always be dismissed as a hygiene issue, doctors say. In some cases, an unusual odour may be linked to an underlying health condition and may need medical evaluation.
Heat, food and hormones
Several everyday factors can alter body odour. Hot weather and physical activity increase sweating, while tight or synthetic clothing can trap moisture. Garlic, onions, spicy foods, alcohol and certain medicines can also affect body odour.
Hemanath M. J., consultant, internal and family medicine, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, says the apocrine glands in the armpits, groin and scalp contribute more to odour than the eccrine glands, which cover most of the body. Stress can stimulate the apocrine glands and intensify odour.
Hormonal changes can also play a role. Puberty, menstruation and menopause may temporarily alter sweating and body odour. Puberty is one common situations in which changes in body odour are routinely seen. An overactive thyroid, which can cause excessive sweating, may also make odour more noticeable.
A change is more likely to be temporary when there is a clear trigger and the odour settles after the trigger passes. “If somebody develops an odour after eating a particular food, drinking a particular drink, starting a medication or strenuous exercise, or during a period of hormonal change, and it returns to normal after some time, the context helps explain the change,” says Narayanan A., consultant, dermatology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai..
Body odour as a health clue
A persistent or unexplained change can sometimes be associated with a skin condition or an underlying medical problem. Skin infections in the armpits, groin or other moist areas can alter odour. These may be accompanied by redness, soreness, itching, peeling or discharge.
“An infection in the groin or axilla (armpit) or excessive growth of bacteria or fungi can alter the odour,” says Dr. Narayanan.
Dr. Hemanath says conditions such as erythrasma and fungal infections can produce a distinct smell, particularly in warm, moist areas. Excessive sweating, or hyperhidrosis, does not itself cause odour but can provide more moisture for bacteria to act on.
Certain metabolic conditions have also been associated with distinctive smells. Uncontrolled diabetes can produce fruity or sweet-smelling breath because of ketone build-up. A rare condition called trimethylaminuria can cause a fish-like odour because the body is unable to break down certain compounds properly.
Odour changes have also been described in advanced kidney and liver disease. But doctors caution against treating these smells as diagnostic tests.
“Some distinctive smells have been described with complications of diabetes, liver disease or kidney disease, but these are clues rather than reliable diagnostic tests,” says Dr. Narayanan. The overall clinical picture, including symptoms, examination and biochemical investigations, is what guides diagnosis.
Need for evaluation
The first step when there is a change in body odour is to look for an obvious trigger. Regular washing, changing sweaty clothes, washing clothes properly and using an antiperspirant can help determine whether the problem responds to routine measures.
But a sudden change in body odour without a clear cause is reason to consult a doctor.The physician would first consider what changed at the same time as the odour. If there is no obvious trigger and the change persists or keeps recurring, a deeper evaluation may be required.
A sudden unexplained increase in sweating, night sweats without an obvious reason, or sweating that interferes with daily activities should also prompt medical attention. Experts list other warning signs such as unexplained weight loss, excessive thirst or urination, fatigue, swelling, fever, night sweats or skin changes. A fruity odour with excessive thirst, frequent urination, nausea, vomiting or confusion requires urgent assessment.
Depending on the symptoms, a doctor may conduct a physical and skin examination and consider tests such as blood glucose and HbA1c, kidney and liver function tests and a thyroid profile. Skin scraping or culture may be considered if an infection is suspected.
Doctors say, body odour should not be used to self-diagnose a disease. Most changes have an everyday explanation, but a smell that is new, persistent, unexplained or accompanied by other symptoms is worth discussing with a doctor

Why is the GameCube controller so loved by gamers?
People still swear by this quirky controller, leading to Nintendo supporting it for 25 years and counting.
As the GameCube (GCN) turns 25 this year, there's no better testament to its legacy than the controller. Despite Nintendo experimenting with various input methods in the years since, every one of its ensuing home consoles has officially supported a GameCube pad. And the company has re-released it in new editions multiple times.
A combination of factors led to popularity long after the console left production. It was perfect for games designed for GameCube, became synonymous with one of Nintendo's biggest franchises, and its library was kept alive on future platforms. To this day, it's one of our top Nintendo Switch controllers.
It's not perfect — it has issues compared to the competition at the time as well as modern pads. Even though the design wasn't iterated on for future consoles like the PS2 and Xbox controllers were, it's still a delight to use. You should really give it a try if you never have. Thankfully, it's easy to do that today.
A unique layout and buttons
From your first look at the GameCube controller, you'll notice it's not like other pads. Instead of the four-button diamond layout most controllers have, it has an oversized green A button, a tiny red B button, and two kidney-shaped X and Y buttons. This has a few advantages. For newcomers, they'll immediately infer that the A button is the most important, and it's easier to feel which button your finger is on without looking. Also, this layout enabled you to easily press A along with any other button.
The L and R buttons are analog, meaning they react to how much force you use instead of being a simple on/off switch. Lots of titles on the system took advantage of this. For instance, in Super Mario Sunshine, pressing the R button partway allows Mario to shoot water while walking around, while fully pressing it locks Mario in place while spraying. In the Super Mario 3D All-Stars Switch port, it doesn't feel the same using separate buttons for these actions on a Joy-Con or Pro Controller.
In contrast to most controllers' circular control stick gate (the "guard" that restricts a stick's movement), the GameCube's primary thumbstick has an octagonal gate, just like the N64 controller that preceded it. This makes it way easier to input specific directions accurately, which is vital for some of the console's top games. The Super Monkey Ball titles require precision movements to move around narrow stages, while Soulcalibur II takes advantage of these to easily differentiate between inputs for the directional attacks common in fighting games.
The Super Smash Bros. tradition
It's impossible to separate the legacy of the GameCube controller from the Super Smash Bros. series. Super Smash Bros. Melee was the best-selling title on the console, offering an excellent casual party game experience that makes good use of the console's four controller ports. However, it also spawned a massive competitive scene. Melee has all kinds of hidden mechanics (like wavedashing) that give it an extremely high skill ceiling. It's fast-paced, which makes competitive matches enjoyable to watch. And its character roster is (mostly) balanced to allow for a variety of approaches.
Melee's sequel, Super Smash Bros. Brawl, was released for Wii in 2008. Since the Wii was backward-compatible with GCN discs and had four GameCube controller ports, players (competitive and otherwise) could use the familiar input method with the new game. It was also much better than using the Wii Remote. Ahead of Super Smash Bros. for Wii U's debut in 2014, Nintendo revealed an adapter that let you connect GameCube controllers to that system. This same accessory worked with the Nintendo Switch (and was sold again with updated branding) when Super Smash Bros. Ultimate, one of our favorite Nintendo Switch games, arrived in 2018.
Melee's success for both casual and competitive play meant tons of people built up muscle memory with it. Nintendo has kept this control method available with adapters, as well as GCN controller re-releases. A Smash edition GameCube controller arrived in 2014, with a near-identical one also going on sale in November 2018, shortly before Ultimate. To support the Switch 2's GCN titles available via Nintendo Classics, Nintendo now sells a revamped wireless GameCube controller with a few extra modern buttons, like ZL and Home.
A triumphant controller, though not a perfect one
While the GameCube received far fewer games than its contemporaries, the controller feels incredibly natural for exclusive games made with it in mind, like Luigi's Mansion and The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker. However, the gamepad isn't perfect, making it worse for certain genres. Its tiny D-pad and nub-like C-stick are two core flaws. The D-pad is mushy, which combined with its size means it's easy to accidentally push in more than one direction. The C-stick is OK for quick camera adjustments, but it's far worse than the now-standard two-stick setup. The irregular button layout also makes this one a poor choice when playing games made for other systems. For example, many SNES games have you hold the Y button to run and press B to jump, which is much more awkward with the unique GCN layout.
Another milestone was the 2002 release of the WaveBird, one of the first mainstream wireless gamepads. Older consoles had experimented with wireless connections before but relied on IR, which doesn't work without a clear line of sight. The WaveBird requires you to set a matching channel on the receiver and controller, lacks rumble, and is a bit bulkier at the bottom than the standard model. But it's a great option with excellent battery life and few wireless drops; I used a WaveBird for much of my time with the GameCube growing up.
Speaking of this, the GameCube controller has held up remarkably well over the decades. I still use my originals when playing multiplayer games with friends; they have few signs of wear and no annoying issues to work around. Contrast that with the Switch's Joy-Con, where stick drift has been such a pervasive issue that Nintendo paid a $40 million fine in France.

Ontario premier answers Trump’s ‘Lake America’ with giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has responded to President Trump’s “Lake America” decree with a billboard declaring “Lake Ontario
TORONTO -- Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered President Donald Trump’s “Lake America” decree Saturday with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shoreline — “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” — as Canadian leaders met the move with ridicule rather than outrage.
Wearing a Team Canada soccer jersey, Ford unveiled the sign near Grimsby, Ontario, and posed for photographs. The 24-by-12-foot (7.3-by-3.6 meter) sign stands on 6-foot (1.8-meter) legs, putting its top about 18 feet (5.5 meters) above the ground — roughly two stories high. The message is repeated in French, one
The display followed Trump’s executive order directing U.S. federal agencies to call Lake Ontario “Lake America.” After months of tariffs, threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state and personal attacks on its leaders, the reaction in Canada has mixed defiance with mockery.
Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves” and argued the name would outlast the president.
“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew compared Trump to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit
“You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago. I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now, Like he thought they had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico,” Kinew said, referring to Trump's executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. “And he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”
The mockery was not limited to politicians. Canadian historian Robert Bothwell was even more scathing.
“The greatest country on earth takes this moron seriously?” Bothwell said.
But Bothwell said the dispute was more serious than the jokes, arguing Trump’s broader aim was “to subordinate Canada and at best make it a colony, at worst absorb it into the United States.”
Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Trump “would like Canada to act like a vassal state, but it refuses to do so. That irritates him.”
The dispute comes as relations between the longtime allies worsen over trade. Negotiations collapsed last week, both governments accused the other of making late demands, and Canada announced retaliatory tariffs set to take effect next month.
Trump’s order also came amid an escalating war of words with Ford. In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this week, Ford said Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies and “disgusted with President Trump.”
Trump fired back by dismissing Ford’s comments as “bluster,” calling him Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “flunky” and mocking him as the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother” of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.
Trump continued promoting the new name Saturday, reposting a meme showing Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles as they “protected” Lake America.
Trump has repeatedly used maps to make political points. A “Gulf of America” map was displayed for a time beside the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, and Trump has posted images depicting Canada as part of the United States or as the 51st state.
The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The Canadian province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard, whose people historically lived from the St. Lawrence Valley to the Great Lakes and whose language gave Lake Ontario its name, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history.
“I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, noting the lake’s Indigenous roots and that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Trump cannot require Canada to adopt the new name.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Disha Lamba, 28, who lives in Gurugram, India. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
I was born and raised in India. As an introvert, I liked being in my comfort zone, but my dad dreamed of sending me to the US for my master's.
His friends' children went to the UK and the US and achieved so much. He wanted the same for me. In 2021, at 23, I went to NYU for a master's in computer engineering. I'd only seen New York in movies, but I quickly fell in love with it.
I had a great life in the US, but decided to move back in May 2026, primarily to be closer to family. I also wasn't OK with the restrictions that come with the H-1B visa.
New York transformed me
I owe a lot of my current personality to my five years in New York. Managing things on my own in a new environment made me really ambitious. I became more confident and had a high sense of individuality. In India, I never thought about traveling to another part of the country, and I didn't realize I loved hiking before coming to the US.
America exposed me to opportunities. In India, while studying information technology at undergrad, I was interested in data science, but lacked the confidence to pursue it. At NYU, I had good professors who spoon-fed me information about machine learning and data science, which really helped.
New York is a hub for conferences and meetups, and I attended many. At one event, I met a senior data scientist at CVS Health, who encouraged me to apply to his company. I landed a data scientist role there in 2024.
The job market was rough around that time, and a few of my friends moved to other countries because they couldn't find jobs or secure visa sponsorship.
Living away from family was hard
CVS sponsored my H-1B visa, and I was informed that I was selected in the lottery in March 2026. However, my plan had always been to eventually return to India, and by that point, I'd already decided.
I had a great life in the US — I was happy with my job and social life, and I had a six-figure salary, but I felt lonely.
When the clock hit 5 p.m., there wasn't anyone around to ask me how my day was. I had friends, but friends can't be your family. I kept having to organize my video calls with my mom — who's my best friend — around the time difference.
I missed my family and realized I was much happier and content around them. I wanted to be there for big celebrations and support my parents during good and bad times. I feared being far away if something bad happened.
My second reason for wanting to move back was the visa restrictions. Once you're on an H-1B, you need a new visa stamp to travel and return to the US, and getting a stamping appointment in India can be a pain. Since the H-1B is generally granted in three-year increments, I felt there'd be a lot of ongoing visa management.
The H-1B can also make it harder to change employers, pursue additional income streams, or take a career break.
The H-1B visa has its pros, but I wasn't OK with the cons.
I'm exploring options in India
I resigned from CVS and flew home to Gurugram, a satellite city southwest of New Delhi, to live with my parents and brother. I liked working in the healthcare industry, where I felt I could make an impact, and I liked my team and manager. I questioned my decision because I felt I was giving up a lot to move home.
In India, I can choose to build a startup, change employers, and do a side hustle without worrying about visa restrictions. I decided to take a two-month career break when I returned to India, relying on savings. It's a luxury that comes from not being on an employment visa.
I haven't got a job offer in hand yet, but I think India offers similar career opportunities to the US. Big companies like EY, Mastercard, and American Express have offices near me.
I'm embracing the little things
I miss certain things about the US. I used to love walking around after work and staring at the New York skyline, but where I am now, the sidewalks aren't as walkable, and the public parks aren't as clean.
But at home in India, we have house help, which means I don't have to cook or clean, so I have more time to pursue my passions. If you're earning well, you can live comfortably here.
I still get anxious about whether I made the right decision, but getting to hug my parents every morning reminds me it was worth it. Our family starts the day with a chat over a cup of green tea. The little things we take for granted are also the things that matter.
Business Insider confirmed she was employed by CVS. CVS declined to respond to a request for comment.
A State Department spokesperson told Business Insider, "Our embassies and consulates around the world, including in India, are prioritizing thoroughly vetting each visa case above all else."

A common way to deal with emotions is through food, says Lakshmi Venkatraman, consultant psychiatrist and assistant director of Psychosocial Rehabilitation Services at SCARF (Schizophrenia Research Foundation). Dieting and restrictions on food are also culprits. The vicious circle begins when people tend to eat more, end up feeling guilty at their act, reduce their self-esteem, because of which they binge eat and feel more guilty.
Simple measures such as eating regular meals with all foods, including favourites in moderation, helps. “When we realise emotions are pushing us (to eat), finding ways to tackle the emotions will help,” Dr. Lakshmi explains. “Be mindful while eating, focus on what we are eating, take it quite slow while eating which helps to prevent binge eating,” she points out.
R.M. Anjana, managing director of Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, cites the various studies done by the Foundation at various intervals of time, to explain the importance of regulating “what we put into our mouth”. When a person finds that they binge once a week and this persists for three months then it should trigger an alarm, she says. “Diet and physical activity alone can prevent 50% of diabetes,” she said and cited studies that state that binge eating contributes to about 15 to 20% of type 2 diabetes.
A bariatric surgeon aims to moderate the gut hormones, says P. Praveen Raj, consultant and head of the Department of Minimal Access Bariatric and Robotic Surgery in the Department of Surgical Gastroenterology, GEM Hospital and Research Centre, Coimbatore.
The first step is to take a thorough history of the person’s issues. There are various hormones in the gut that regulate satiety, trigger appetite and aid digestion. An imbalance in any one of them could be the cause for obesity. The aim is to treat the cause, he explains. “You rule out the psychological reasons, and the pathological abnormality. Once this is understood we can start to treat it (the condition),” he adds.
The specialists were panelists at a webinar on “The Binge: Learning to handle addictive behaviours,” organised on Sunday by The Hindu. The webinar can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cl4wxf7_HRI

Meta is rolling out an obvious fix to make its AI glasses less creepy amid backlash over the glasses’ non-consensual recordings that have flooded the Internet.
On Friday, The Verge reported that Meta closed a loophole that made it easy for smart glasses users to cover up an LED light that is supposed to alert bystanders that the device is actively recording. Meta had previously deactivated recording if a user attempted to start capturing video after placing a sticker over the light, but people quickly learned that they could get around that by reversing the order of the steps and covering up the light after they started recording.
In a post on Threads, Meta’s executive vice president of wearables, Alex Himel, explained that an update would be rolled out soon that ensures that “the camera will now stop working if the light is covered during a recording.” That way “the capture LED can reliably alert bystanders when photos or videos are being captured for someone’s gallery,” Himel said.
According to Himel, “only a tiny minority of people try to get around these protections, and the fact they have to go to these lengths shows our efforts are working. We’ll keep improving and evolving our approach.”
However, bad actors may still be able to modify the glasses or tamper with the light without affecting recordings. And it’s unclear if popular bypasses, like using semi-transparent stickers that make the light less noticeable, would block recording under Meta’s new safeguard.
Data regulators in the European Union are currently probing privacy concerns with Meta’s glasses and have suggested that Meta may not have properly field-tested the LED light to ensure that the public would understand its safety functionality. Germany is considering banning the glasses after a nonprofit filed a criminal complaint alleging that they breach Germany’s strict privacy laws, Politico reported. And Germany is not alone, as many countries in the EU mull a crackdown on the technology, which they see as invasive and carrying a risk of expanding mass surveillance. Another Politico report confirmed that the European Data Protection Board will release a report later this summer to decide what actions should be taken to ensure no one in the EU is recorded without their consent.

China teen with zero programming skills earns US$2,600 in 3 days selling AI study app
This development experience made me realise that as long as you have a great idea, AI can bring it to life, Shuhan says
A 13-year-old girl in China has earned 18,000 yuan (US$2,600) in just three days from an artificial intelligence (AI) product she developed to assist parents in supervising their children’s study habits.
Zhu Shuhan, a Grade Two student at a junior secondary school in Shanghai, has no programming background. She began using AI only last year, as reported by the Shanghai Morning Post.
At a national AI product marketing competition held in Hangzhou from August 21 to August 23, Shuhan secured the third prize of 5,000 yuan, competing against over 50 participants.
The contest did not include technical judges; instead, winners were selected based on their AI-generated apps’ income during the three-day period.
The app Shuhan created, called Zai Chang (translated as On Site in English), garnered 90 orders, resulting in total sales of 18,000 yuan, which helped her attain third place in the competition.
Once a parent uploads a photo of themselves using the app, the system assumes the role of a virtual parent, supervising their child while they complete homework.
Should the camera detect that the child is playing on a mobile device or leaving their seat, the virtual parent displayed on the screen will issue a voice reminder.
Upon completion of the homework, the app generates a “concentration report.”

Most people know that Labor Day is one of the best times of the year to buy tools (get it? Labor?), but if you’re a newly minted homeowner or DIY-er, the landscape can be intimidating. When I bought my first home, I owned only two screwdrivers, a pair of pliers, and a hammer; I had no clue what I was in for.
Now that I’ve been a homeowner for 17 years, I agree with WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson that unless you’re a professional tradesperson or really love large projects, you don’t need a garage full of specialty tools. Just the basics will do: a drill, a saw, a set of manual screwdrivers, and a stud finder, for example.
Luckily, early Labor Day deals are pretty decent this year. In fact, after examining all the major sales, I was able to find a rather encyclopedic house-repair kit for any new homeowner or DIY-er for under $375 (minus tax and shipping) with deals from Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Walmart. Any of these would also be great to stash away for a holiday gift.
Here’s what I chose:
Power-Tool Workhorses: Ryobi 4-Tool Kit for $199
Look, you’re not going to take Ryobi tools to a jobsite or use them to build a house from scratch (a former WIRED editor once deemed them “the Kia of tools”), but if you’re just using them for basic, casual home use, they’ll do the job. Ryobi’s 18V ONE+ batteries (this set comes with one) are fully backward compatible with all Ryobi tools ever made, and this set has a three-year warranty. I live in a DeWalt household, so I don’t have a lot of firsthand experience with Ryobi, but my brother, a contractor, says the brand is great for the average DIY homeowner and offers a much broader range of tools than competitor Bauer from Harbor Freight.
This set packs a ½-inch drill/driver, an impact driver (which WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson said had a profound 'I can't believe I didn't own one sooner' impact on him, though his is Milwaukee), a circular saw, and an LED light. The impact driver packs 1,800 pounds of torque, which is pretty decent for a consumer-level tool. If you need a sander, there's also another kit with a sander plus drill/driver and circular saw, which may be worth a look if this set sells out.
The Hand-Tool Essentials: Workpro 408-Piece Set for $144
I don't have this exact set, but I do have remnants of a similar one. Again, you're not going to bring these to a construction site, but this kit is a knockout deal for everything you get—pliers, screwdrivers, Allen keys, wrenches, sockets, bits, tape measure, knife, hammer, wire stripper … there's even a metal box in which to store everything. A lot of the “pieces” are doodads like screwdriver heads and drywall anchors, but it still contains pretty much any non-power tool you might need for light home repairs and even basic car maintenance. (There's no level, but you can always use an app on your phone for that.) However, note that this is a flash deal, so it's likely only live for a limited time.
Wall-Hanging Must-Have: Franklin Sensors Stud Finder for $22
No household repair kit is complete without a stud finder. (And if you're a dad, it will give you years of built-in dad jokes.) In fact, you can't—or, at least, shouldn't—hang anything even slightly heavy on your wall without one. I have a Franklin Sensors stud finder, though not this exact model, and it's done well to help my family hang pictures, shelves, mirrors, and pretty much everything else for the past decade or so. This is the best deal I could find, though it's not technically on sale. However, Lowe’s is having a sale on plenty of other tools, including outdoor furniture, appliances, and grills.

Quick Answer
You can customize websites without coding by using AI to create Tampermonkey user scripts or custom browser extensions. These tools can change fonts, remove clutter, tweak layouts, add features, and apply your changes automatically whenever you visit a site.
We are in the era of personal software. Thanks to AI, anyone can now build fully functional tools as good as existing high-end software for their workflows.
However, I really wish for the idea of personalizing the experience on existing apps and software, allowing users to add new features or customize them based on their needs.
Unfortunately, this isn’t the case for now, but hopefully someday someone will come up with this brilliant idea. While you cannot make changes to software and apps, you can make changes to websites, which many of us spend most of our time on now.
This is especially needed in times when plenty of websites are using AI for design and making changes to existing designs. I am not against using AI to develop websites; however, most AI designs in the first attempt look generic and offer a cluttered experience. Website owners should spend extra time tweaking to meet user needs.
Many websites that I personally follow and read have used AI to revamp their existing user interface, resulting in the same issues.
Fortunately, I found a way to easily customize website designs once the webpage is rendered. All changes I made to any website are temporary and can be easily reverted.
There are plenty of ways you can tweak website design; however, using extensions and user scripts are two best reliable ways. Those changes will auto-apply every time you visit the webpage.
In this guide, I am going to show you both methods, with step-by-step guides on how to tweak the design of any website.
How to Redesign and Personalize Any Website Without Coding
Just a heads-up: this might not work for every website. Some websites use hard-coded elements that are impossible to tweak, while others use completely different structures where you will need to try various approaches to get what you want without breaking anything.
Method 1: Customize Websites Using Tampermonkey User Scripts
The first method is using user scripts. You can run simple code snippets on your browser console once the web page is rendered. Since these user scripts only work once the website is fully rendered and stored locally on your device, once you refresh the page, everything goes back to normal. But to keep the changes permanently, you can use the Tampermonkey extension, which allows you to run multiple user scripts on any web page and every time you visit the site.
Tampermonkey is free to use. And since all the changes apply locally, you don’t need to worry about breaking everything. Even if it breaks, you can simply disable the added code.
You need to create a script that works for the specific site with all possible changes you want. I recommend using AI tools.
The best approach is to use an IDE where these AI models can directly inspect the website and analyze all the code. Alternatively, you can copy-paste the entire website HTML or the rendered code into any AI chat tool, such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude, and ask it to generate a user script.
You can use our simple website parser tool to get all the website code by just entering the URL. Once you have the URL or the HTML code, you can paste it into any chat and ask it to generate a specific type of user script.
I have already covered the best user scripts that you can run on a browser, but since you are using AI, the possibilities are endless. You can change the font size, remove ads or images if the site loads slowly, change the action of specific elements (such as auto-loading pagination), and much more
Remember that you can also ask ChatGPT or other AI tools to specifically build a script for a specific website, especially if you only want to make changes related to that specific site and don’t want to apply those changes to every website. Once the code is generated, follow the steps to add it to Tampermonkey.
How to Use Tampermonkey on Mobile
Step 1: First, go to the Google Chrome Web Store, search for the Tampermonkey extension, and tap on Add to Chrome.
Step 2: Now, pin the Tampermonkey extension.
Step 3: Next, you can tap on the extensions icon in the top toolbar and tap on the pin icon next to the Tampermonkey extension.
Step 4: Now tap on Tampermonkey and tap on the plus icon.
Step 5: From here, you can paste the user script that you have generated,
Step 6: Tap on the file option and tap on save.
Step 7: Now, the changes should be automatically applied to your browser. If not, you can tap on Tampermonkey again and click “Run Script” if it is not working by default.
You can also use Tampermonkey on your mobile browser; you can use a browser with extension support. Our favorite is the Quetta browser. You can see the detailed guide below on how to install third-party extensions on the Quetta browser.
How to install third-party extensions on mobile browser
Step 1: Download the Quetta browser for free for Android or iPhone.
Step 2: Once done, open the browser and tap on the three-dot menu and tap on the extensions icon. Now, on the extension page, tap on the Manage Extensions button.
Step 3: Now search for the Tampermonkey extension. In the search results, find the extension and tap on Install. Now go back to Manage Extensions, tap on the Tampermonkey extension
Step 4: Now, from the options, tap on Create a new script and paste the script you created here. From here, tap on the file option and click on Save, and that’s it.
Step 5: Now, visit the website; the changes should be applied automatically.
Method 2: Customize Websites Using Browser Extensions
If you don’t want to use Tampermonkey, you can also create your own extension to make changes to any website. This is a recommended method for beginners.
Unlike Tampermonkey, which depends on user scripts, an extension is easier to access and manage. Moreover, you can also easily disable and enable extensions when you want. Plus, if you are an expert, you can also add additional features to the extensions, which is sometimes not possible with user scripts.
One catch here is that you need to build the extensions. You don’t need a programmer to do that. You need to pay for one of the tools, such as OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini, or Claude. If you are a programmer, you can build it yourself, but I wouldn’t recommend it, as using those AI tools makes it easier and faster to create any extensions.
For this guide, I am using Claude Code to create an extension. You can use any other AI model to do the same.
How to Add Your Custom Extension to Chrome
Step 1: First, open the Claude app on your Mac and switch to the Code tab.
Step 2: Under the Projects folder, create a new project folder named Extensions. Once created, simply enter the prompt for the extension you want to create.
Step 3: Here, I am creating a simple extension that allows me to increase or decrease the font sizes on any web page.
Step 4: The extension will be created in the same folder. But remember that there is a high chance that it does not work on the first attempt. You need to iterate and fix the issues that come up to get the desired output you want.
Step 5: Now, open the folder and find the extension folder.
Step 6: Now, to add the extension to your browser (let’s say for Google Chrome): Open settings, go to manage extension settings, and from here, enable developer options. Once enabled, tap on Load unpacked and select the extension folder. That’s it; the extension will be added to your extensions.
Remember, you can follow the same process on mobile too, using Quetta Browser (which you can watch in the detailed step-by-step video below).
To pin it, tap on the extensions icon at the top, select your extension, and tap on the pin option. If it doesn’t work, go back to Claude and review the extension instructions.

What Argentina gets right about youth soccer — and what the U.S. gets wrong
ROSARIO — Newell's Old Boys is one of the most popular soccer clubs in Rosario — Argentina's third-largest city. It also runs one of the country's most successful youth academies.
Every week, around 700 kids ages 4 to 12 train at its facilities in the center of the city, where black and red murals depict famous alumni such as Argentine soccer superstar Lionel Messi.
The most promising young players at Newell's "baby football" academy receive scholarships to train for free. The rest pay around $25 a month to train twice a week with coaches who are mostly former professionals. On weekends competitive matches are held against other squads from around the city.
"Here you get good coaching," says Carlos Gil a fencing contractor, who takes his eight year-old son to practice at Newell's every week.
"You have the chance that your child can develop his skills," Gil says. He shakes his head and chuckles after learning that in the United States, parents pay between $1,000 and $3,000 a year for the kind of instruction his son gets at Newell's.
"If you did that here, almost nobody could play," he said of the fees at U.S. youth soccer clubs. He also says that if Argentine clubs charged their young players thousands of dollars each year, the country's status as a global soccer powerhouse might be at risk.
"Our best players tend to come from low income backgrounds," Gil said. "Where would they train?"
With the World Cup still fresh in the minds of many Americans, a debate has resurfaced online and on television over how to make youth soccer more affordable in the United States and whether the pay-to-play model that prevails in U.S. soccer is preventing America from reaching its true potential — at least on the men's side.
Argentina is one country that has managed to keep youth soccer affordable while churning out a steady stream of world-class players. And some coaches say its soccer structure could be an example for the United States to follow.
Newell's — where Lionel Messi played from ages 6 to 13 — is one of dozens of clubs in Argentina that subsidize the training of their young players.
Its survival does not depend on tuition payments or donations from local companies.
The club's professional team competes in Argentina's top division and generates revenue from ticket sales and broadcasting rights.
It also makes significant sums of money when its best young players are transferred to other clubs in Argentina or abroad.
"The kids that we are training today are what sustains this institution," said Gustavo Tognarelli, the head of youth development at Newell's.
In the United States, youth clubs have been largely excluded from transfer payments.
That's because teams in Major League Soccer, the country's top professional league, are not obliged by the U.S. soccer federation to give youth clubs a share of the transfer fees they get for elite players.
In Europe and South America, youth clubs regularly get a cut of a professional player's transfer fee if they coached that player from ages 12 to 23, through systems known as training compensation and solidarity payments.
Major League Soccer (MLS) has been slow to adopt this way of doing business, fearing it might violate U.S. laws.
But many coaches say that the lack of training compensation puts U.S. youth clubs at a disadvantage.
"In the United States, if you train a player and they go to a better situation or a bigger club, you get nothing for that," said Rory O'Neill, a coach for an under-13 team in Pennsylvania, who also runs a YouTube channel where he discusses coaching tactics and the state of U.S. soccer.
O'Neill said that youth clubs in the U.S. have very limited revenue streams, relying largely on payments from parents to cover their expenses. He believes they could improve their economic prospects if U.S. soccer transitions to what is known as an open ecosystem.
Currently, only 30 teams can play in MLS because it's a closed league that charges teams hundreds of millions of dollars to join.
But in an open system, the worst teams are relegated to lower divisions, while teams that perform well are promoted to the top flight.
O'Neill says that kind of arrangement would give hundreds of teams around the country a greater incentive to improve and invest in youth academies because reaching the top division and benefiting from the financial rewards that come with it would be a real possibility.
"You would have almost any millionaire start investing in clubs," O'Neill said.
Filippo Silva, a business owner and coach in Orlando agrees.
"If we do have an open system and it's merit-based, I do think you're going to open the doors for more small investors trying to get things done," he said. "More people would be willing to put more money into soccer if there was something you could get out of it."
In Argentina, where soccer has long operated with promotion and relegation, there are thousands of clubs around the country that have a shot at making it to the nation's top division.
Though some will never make it, many clubs invest in youth development in hopes of climbing the nation's football pyramid or making money from player transfers and solidarity payments.
Newell's, one of the top clubs in Argentina, funds the training and education of about 400 players ages 12 to 18 who practice up to six times a week.
Some of the younger children, who practice twice a week, receive training scholarships, including Dastan Gil, Carlos Gil's eight-year-old son.
Gil says driving his son to training every week is a challenge. He lives in a small town 120 miles away from Rosario, where he fixes fences for big farms and cattle ranches.
But even though being a soccer dad can be difficult, Newell's, with its scholarships and low fees, is helping ease the burden.
"In Argentina, we might not have so much money," Gil says. "But in some areas we have better quality of life."

‘Where the hell are you guys…’: CJP’s Dipke recalls moment when he was ‘mad’ at Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka
Abhijeet Dipke said the crowd grew impatient and wanted to proceed with the march, while he lacked the energy to lead them.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder and convenor Abhijeet Dipke on Sunday recalled being “mad” at his spokespersons Ashutosh Ranka and Sourav Das over their unavailability during the ‘Sansad Chalo’ march on July 20.
In an interview with BBC, Dipke said that during the ‘Sansad Chalo’ march on July 20th, when he was on the third day of his hunger strike, Ranka and Das were called by BJP leaders for a discussion. He added that the two were kept at the venue for around five hours, although the meeting lasted only 10 minutes.
“Sourav and Ashutosh went to the meeting. They (BJP delegation) called them, they kept them for five hours, and the meeting happened just for 10 minutes.”
Also Read: Vijeta Dahiya to make a comeback in CJP? Abhijeet Dipke says ‘will think about it but…’
Meanwhile, Dipke said the crowd grew impatient and wanted to proceed with the march, while he lacked the energy to lead them as it was the third day of his hunger strike. He added that he tried calling Ranka and Das multiple times, but their phones were unreachable. He said he was “pissed off” at the two as he was unable to address the crowd.
“And during all this time, I was so pissed off at both of them because I did not have the energy to address the crowd, and the crowd was getting impatient that they wanted to march.”
"We will march, but we will march with responsibility. We are not going to do anything that will create problems for anybody here. And I just kept calling Sourav and Ashutosh, "Where the hell are you guys?" and the phone was just not reachable. I really got mad at them,” Dipke said.
‘Didn’t know what to do during hunger strike’: Dipke
Asked if he would have done anything differently that day, amid police action against some protesters and criticism that CJP leaders were not present when it happened, Dipke said he would have asked Ranka and Das not to attend the meeting.
He added that he was unaware of what one should or should not do during a hunger strike and had continued to address and engage with the crowd the first two days, leaving him extremely weak by the third day.
“I was on the third day of my hunger strike. I did not have any energy left because, me being naive, I did not know what to do when you are on a hunger strike. So during all the hunger strike, I was addressing the crowd, I was engaging with them, and on the third day—on the day of the march—I was too weak. I even fainted early in the morning, and that is why I had to get on a truck because I was not able to walk.”
He added that if Das and Ranka had been at Jantar Mantar, it would have been much easier for him to manage the crowd and lead the march.
July 20 march
Dipke led the ‘Sansad Chalo’ march on July 20, which was also the first day of Monsoon session of the Parliament. CJP's march was part of a 37-days-long agitation that called for the resignation of then union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities in the NEET UG exam.
Demonstrators spread from Jantar Mantar to Parliament, Raisina Road, Janpath, Connaught Place and India Gate as repeated clashes broke out between protesters and police in the attempt to reach Sansad.
Pradhan submitted his resignation on July 25, prompting the protest to be called off.

The Terrible Movie That Chinese Audiences Can’t Stop Watching
Viewers are flocking to a new film that captures the pleasure of bad art.
One of the only compliments I can offer the new Chinese animated film Niu Lai is that it certainly qualifies as a film. There is sound. The pictures move. But beyond the basics of what makes a movie a movie, Niu Lai, which translates to “The Ox Comes,” contains little artistic merit. The plot, about a calf coming of age with the help of a leopard, a bird, and his mother, is thin, and the characters have been so nightmarishly rendered on a rudimentary computer program that they might as well be sleep-paralysis demons.
Yet Niu Lai has become a bona fide box-office hit in China. Since a small distributor unceremoniously dumped it in theaters in early August, the film has become one of the most lucrative movies in Chinese history, making more than $7 million off a reported budget of no more than $500 and outperforming recent blockbusters such as The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Much of its success is thanks to Chinese social media, where clips of it first went viral: Some users have embraced Niu Lai as a meme, purchasing tickets so they could ridicule the baffling work with an audience. Others have championed the project as anti-AI art, arguing that it deserves to be appreciated as a purely human creation. As flawed as Niu Lai may be, to the fans, it’s at least better than AI slop.
I’m not so sure about that. Watching a bootleg version of Niu Lai felt painful but apt: What better way was there to see a jankily made film than in potato quality on my computer at home? Instead, what’s distinctly human about Niu Lai comes from everything around it: how it was made, how it became a sensation, and how it has inspired further creativity in turn. Theater workers have drawn posters by hand to help advertise the movie. Businesses have made plush toys of the bovine hero. Fans have donned cow masks for screenings, and although the film isn’t available in the United States, underground viewings have popped up in major cities. As such, Niu Lai is the rare passion project that has attracted audiences not because it’s so bad that it’s good, but because it’s an occasion to celebrate the ability to have an original idea at all.
Never mind that the idea was apparently underdeveloped from the start. The first-time director, Xin Yumeng, explained in an interview that he wanted to write about an ox because that’s his father’s zodiac symbol; the year he began working on it also happened to be 2021, the year of the ox. Production took five years, as the then-29-year-old Xin and his mother, Sun Lifang, wrote the screenplay together and made up the entire crew and cast: Sun sang the theme song, and Xin animated the 86-minute film frame by frame on SketchUp, an architectural-modeling program. The process was grueling, Xin said, adding that he kept going in part because he saw the story as a way to inspire viewers to not tang ping, or “lie flat,” referring to a societal trend in 2021 where young people in China rejected overworking by cheekily glorifying the act of lying down.
In some ways, the movie is a deeply Chinese phenomenon: Fuzzy cartoon characters tend to become popular in the country—Zootopia 2 is the highest-grossing Hollywood film ever released there—and the words niu lai could also refer to the coming of a bull market, which has led some Chinese stock investors to purchase tickets for good luck. Plus, Niu Lai’s threadbare plot is rooted in the principle of filial piety, as the titular protagonist learns to respect and care for his mother.
The Niu Lai phenomenon also seems to embody a phrase that’s gained traction lately in China: huo ren gan, which, translated literally, means “alive-human feeling.” The film expresses this quality, but not only because Xi didn’t use AI to help create it. What makes Niu Lai stand out most is its unabashed sincerity. It is an earnest attempt to tell a fable about a naive cow, and the story of its making is deeply charming: Here is a mother-son duo, total outsiders to the entertainment industry, trying their best to turn their quixotic idea into reality. Making a movie anywhere requires overcoming so many hurdles that have nothing to do with art or creativity; there are budgets to be balanced and business expectations to be met. But Niu Lai is a modest reminder that any film simply begins with an idea and an irrepressible urge to see it through.

A Greenlandic commission is to present a highly anticipated report Friday to determine whether Denmark's forced contraception of thousands of the Arctic island's indigenous Inuit constituted a "genocide".
The forced contraception campaign between the 1960s and 1990 is one of the darkest chapters in Greenland's history with its former colonial master, Denmark.
Once the conclusions are presented, Greenland's government will decide how to move forward.
"For us, it's about trying to understand our history," Naaja Nathanielsen, a member of parliament representing Greenland in Denmark's parliament, told AFP.
"Others may feel that we should simply keep quiet about this and try to be conciliatory, because of the United States' aggressiveness toward Greenland."
Nathanielsen announced the creation of the commission, tasked with shedding light on the legal implications of the campaign, in August 2024 when she was Greenland's minister of justice and gender equality.
During the 1960s to 1990, more than 4,000 Greenlandic women were forced to wear a contraceptive coil -- or intrauterine device (IUD) -- in the vast majority of cases without their consent or that of their parents if they were minors.
Greenland, a Danish colony for three centuries and now an autonomous territory, still has a complicated relationship with Copenhagen.
Despite many thorny issues between them, both Copenhagen and Nuuk have presented a united front rejecting US President Donald Trump's threats to take over Greenland.
He has repeatedly accused Denmark of treating Greenland badly.
"Everything that is happening between Denmark and Greenland now is scrutinised," said historian Astrid Andersen, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS).
"There's this pressure on the relationship so of course, when we start talking about genocide, that increases the pressure.
"But everyone in Greenland has been very clear that this tragic case should not be used to legitimise other political purposes internationally."
The commission's four appointed experts were unable to agree on which approach to take and ended up writing two reports, submitted nearly six months behind schedule.
Not just about history
One of the victims, Henriette Berthelsen, told AFP the conclusions, regardless of what is decided, were skewed from the start since no Greenlandic Inuit were appointed as experts.
"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life, and my right to self-determination," she said.
"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."
The campaign affected girls as young as 12, some of whom were never able to have children afterwards.
Nuuk and Copenhagen are also shedding light on several other painful chapters from the past, including children adopted without parental consent or torn from their families.
On Thursday, the Danish parliament agreed that women affected by the forced contraception campaign can claim compensation from Copenhagen, an initiative pushed by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen who presented Denmark's official apology last year.
Beyond imagination
Media coverage of the case has revived trauma that had been buried for decades.
"I realised everything it had cost me -- all those hospitalisations, those surgeries, the schooling I missed and, above all, those pains I had never associated with that damn IUD," said Kirstine Najarak Berthelsen.
"It was buried so deeply in my subconscious... Everything that happened to people is beyond imagination if you haven't experienced it yourself," she added.
By the late 1970s, one in two Greenlandic women of childbearing age -- at least 4,070 women -- had been fitted with an IUD, according to an investigation presented in September 2025.
The scandal came to light when one of the victims spoke out in the media about the trauma she experienced.
A podcast series in 2022 then revealed the full extent of the campaign.
Henriette Berthelsen has called for a "Truth and Reconciliation" commission to be established. The Danish government is considering the idea.
According to the 68-year-old psychologist, that would make it possible to "acknowledge what happened".
"I believe that only then will we be able to begin to heal and move forward -- not as adversaries, but as human beings and as peoples equal in dignity."

Ecuador intelligence chief and five Americans killed in Kenya helicopter crash
- Published
Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter that crashed at Mount Ololokwe in central Kenya.
Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, and his wife, fashion designer Stephany Hollihan, 42, were among the group of seven people - six tourists and the pilot - killed in Samburu county at approximately 09:13 (06:13 GMT) on Wednesday.
Five of victims were Americans, a US State Department spokesperson said. The Reuters news agency reports that Hollihan also held US citizenship.
The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) said the helicopter was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy in Loisaba to Ewaso Nyiro, a river that flows along several national reserves.
Samburu county is a popular tourist destination with many private wildlife conservancies and is renowned for its stunning landscape.
Images from the scene show smoke at the wooded crash site on Mount Ololokwe, as members of the Kenya Red Cross approach the still-burning wreckage.
Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa named Sensi-Contugo director of the country's Centre of Strategic Intelligence (CIES) in January 2024.
The office of the president and Ecuador's National Assembly expressed their condolences over his death and that of Hollihan.
The Italian-Ecuadorean businessman had had close links to Noboa even before he was chosen to lead the intelligence service and was considered a close ally of the president.
Shortly before being named head of the CIES, he had served for four months as a minister in his cabinet.
Noboa has declared three days of national mourning starting on Thursday.
Newspapers in Ecuador have also run obituaries of Hollihan. The Guayaquil-based designer founded Sensi Studio, a brand praised for incorporating traditional Ecuadorean elements and materials in its designs.
Lady Lori Helicopters, which operated the Eurocopter EC130 B4 aircraft, said it was "deeply saddened" by the accident.
"Our deepest sympathies are with the guests, crew, their families and loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic accident," a statement read.
According to a memo seen by the BBC's US partner CBS News, external one of the Americans killed in the crash was NBCUniversal journalist José Alberto Suárez.
In the memo, NBCUniversal called Suárez "a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague.
"José was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many," the memo read.
Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte was among the Americans killed in the crash, according to local and US media.
Commenting on his death on X, US Rep Carlos Antonio Gimenez wrote: "Our prayers are with their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. May their memories be a blessing."
The other victims have not yet been identified.
Helicopter crashes are not uncommon in Kenya.
In February, a helicopter crash in the Rift Valley county of Nandi killed six people, including a member of parliament.
In 2024, the military chief, Gen Francis Omondi Ogolla, died after an army helicopter that was carrying 11 people crashed in the west of the country, with only two survivors.
In June 2021 at least 10 soldiers were killed when their helicopter crashed while landing near the capital, Nairobi.
