How much do you hate typing? The advent of large language models has rapidly advanced voice-to-text technology. Whether it's Wispr Flow joining your meetings to summarize discussions or Google debuting smarter on-device dictation in its latest Pixel smartphone, these tools do far more than transcribe: They intelligently strip filler words, clean up unscripted thoughts on the fly, and seamlessly mediate multilingual conversations.
Now, a new startup is entering the fray. Unlike its software-focused peers, Relay is building a dedicated, portable microphone for high-fidelity voice-to-text anywhere. Based in London, Relay was founded by two former Nothing employees: Cookie Xu, who was Nothing's head of AI and services, and Raymond Zhu, a hardware product manager. While the company is debuting its software today, the hardware—what it calls the Relay Q—won't be available until early 2027.
Zhu says when he and Xu worked at Nothing, they used Wispr Flow's transcription software to “type” most of their messages at work. He says it greatly helped with thinking out ideas, but they kept running into an issue: talking loudly in an office.
“In the office, we never really could get the right volume for input,” Zhu tells WIRED. “If I whisper too quietly, the Mac wouldn't be able to pick it up; too loud and my coworker next to me can hear. Sometimes I would actually pull out my earbud and go like this,” he says over a video call, holding an earbud in front of his mouth to demonstrate. “It calls for dedicated hardware.”
Relay is exclusive to macOS at launch, though the company has plans to bring it to Windows, iOS, and Android. It's starting with the desktop because Zhu believes conversations are most complex there. Chats with friends and family are simple on phones, but at work in front of a computer, you're sharing ideas, brainstorming, and using varied tone and formality.
Though the microphone is still months away from being ready, I've been using a beta version of Relay's macOS app, which works with or without the dedicated mic.
During setup, you'll need to choose a hotkey that will trigger Relay in any text field—the default is Fn. Press and hold the key while your cursor is in any text field, and Relay activates and handles the voice dictation. The voice-to-text engine is powered by Google's Gemini models.
It can also perform contextual actions—dubbed Skills—like asking it to message a colleague in Slack, which prompts Relay to launch the app, find the recipient, and draft the text. I had some trouble with this Slack skill, though it didn't have trouble crafting a calendar event in Google Calendar. Relay has some preset skills you can enable for popular apps like WhatsApp and Gmail, but you can make your own and connect other apps.
That automation requires sweeping system permissions. Relay needs access to your microphone, but you can grant it access to record a snapshot of your screen anytime it's activated, which is how it can execute those Skills. The company says it stores data locally on the user's device, where users can manually edit or delete it. When the data is sent for processing, it passes through Relay's servers in transit to Google's servers, but Relay does not retain the data. Still, granting AI models eyes on your operating system adds inherent privacy and security trade-offs, like with Microsoft's Recall.
Relay's transcription isn't nearly as impressive as what I've recently tried with Google's Rambler feature on its Pixel 11 series. It doesn't capture every word perfectly and can mess up punctuation sometimes. It can similarly understand when you misspeak and restate sentences, cutting the parts that don't matter. And yes, it can insert emoji for you, though it did this inconsistently in my tests. When I asked it to add a heart emoji, for example, it did it flawlessly. But when I tried to tack that on at the end of the sentence, it just wrote out “heart emoji.” How romantic.
It generally knows when you want it to perform an action that's separate from the message. For example, I sent a message via Relay to my wife saying I really want to eat at a particular restaurant, and in the same breath, I asked Relay to provide a Google Maps link to the spot—and it did. This can be a little hit or miss, though. I'll chalk it up to the beta.
I haven't used it long enough for the software to adapt to my way of speaking, but you can add notes in the Relay app to make it follow certain patterns. For example, I rarely end a sentence with a period in my Slack messages, so I told it to avoid adding periods, and it followed the rule. There's a good deal of customization for specific people that you regularly speak with, which it detects, so you can ensure your messages to your boss sound professional, while messages to your friends are casual. Or you can even set it so that messages to a coworker living in a different country are translated into their language.
I'm relying on a Mac Mini and the microphone in Apple's Studio Display monitor—some of these accuracy issues could be resolved once Relay's hardware arrives. For instance, right now there's a small delay when I press the function key on the keyboard and when Relay activates, but that delay would be far shorter with dedicated hardware.
Speaking of, the Relay Q is a cylindrical gizmo with a microphone at the end. You can hold down the top as you speak to trigger Relay on your computer or phone—exactly like the hot key—or take the button off the cylinder and clip it to a shirt if you don't want to hold it all the time. (Viewed from the top, the microphone looks like the letter Q, hence the name.) A double-tap can send the message. You can hold it up to your mouth and whisper as quietly as you'd like, and Zhu says it should be able to pick up what you say.
“One question was always in our mind when building this product,” Zhu says. “How long can you go with your workday without touching your keyboard?”
The idea of having a microphone—even a wearable one—for far more accurate voice-to-text isn't new. Last year, a startup called Sandbar unveiled the Stream Ring, and months later, Pebble showed off its own take, the Index 01. Both are rings designed for you to whisper your thoughts into them, and both are starting to ship right about now to initial buyers. Zhu says Relay considered a ring but ultimately decided against it, especially since so many smart rings are already on the market.
The Relay Q will come with a charging dock so you can neatly keep it on your desk when it's not in use. The company is also creating a separate MagSafe grip you can attach to the back of an iPhone or Qi2-enabled device where the Relay Q can attach, allowing you to press the button easily while using a phone to trigger Relay's voice-to-text on mobile, which it plans to launch alongside the Relay Q in the first quarter of 2027.
The Q will cost $150 and includes a year of the software, which will cost $15 per month afterward. (You don't need to buy the Relay Q to use the software.)

A video showing Union defence minister Rajnath Singh and his Japanese counterpart Shinjiro Koizumi signing what appears to be a diplomatic agreement has gone viral on social media. Users have circulated this clip with the claim that India and Japan have signed a contract to allow for “50 million Hindus to settle in Japan.”
X user @CoinMarginalX posted the viral claim on August 21. (Archive)
NEW: Japan and India signed a contract to allow 50 millions Hindus to settle in Japan.🇯🇵🇮🇳 pic.twitter.com/cHao8wTGC9
— CoinMarginalX (@CoinMarginalX) August 21, 2026
Another X user, Hindu hero, (@SuperBrahmin) posted the same claim. (Archive)
Shesh Paul Vaid (@spvaid), the former director general of police (DGP) of Jammu and Kashmir, amplified this viral claim, calling it an unique agreement. His tweet was viewed 92,000 times at the time of publication. However, it was later deleted by the user.
Fact Check
First, we ran relevant keyword searches to see if there were any credible news reports on the alleged contract, but could find none.
Instead, the keyword search led us to this article published by Business Standard on August 20. It reports that Indian defence minister Rajnath Singh had met his Japanese counterpart, Shinjiro Koizumi, in New Delhi, to discuss bilateral strategic partnership. The discussion was largely focused on the Indo-Pacific region, and saw the two signed a “memorandum of arrangement” on maritime security. The report does not mention any “contract” that allows 50 million Hindus to settle in Japan.
News on Air, the news service of All India Radio, also reported on the meeting, on August 20. Citing growing vulnerabilities and efforts to stifle freedom of navigation, the memorandum had reportedly been signed as a strategic imperative between the two countries to ensure co-operation in the Indo-Pacific region.
On further investigation, Alt News came across an Associated Press report, published in August 2025, which states that at the India-Japan Economic Forum in Tokyo, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi had signed a total of 11 documents, and released a “joint vision” of cooperation for the next decade in areas spanning security, defense, clean energy, technology and space.
Further, the Union ministry of external affairs (MEA) also published a media release on the discussed points on August 29, titled “Action Plan for India — Japan Human Resource Exchange and Cooperation”. Reportedly, the MEA and the Japanese foreign ministry agreed to promote the efforts of various entities in government, industry, and academia to “…increase the number of skilled personnel and potential talents from India to Japan by 50,000 over the next five years.” The proposed plan covers students, researches, skilled professionals, easing worker visas, boosting Japanese-language training in India, and setting up support systems for Indians in Japan.
Nowhere in the AP report or in the press release is it mentioned that the two countries had signed a “contract” allowing 50 million Hindus to settle in Japan. In other words, a video from the aforementioned meeting between Singh and Koizumi is being circulated with an entirely fabricated claim.

Purple Style Labs, the parent company of luxury-fashion platform Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop (PPUS), is heading to the public markets. The The initial public offering (IPO) will launch on August 31, 2026. Ahead of the commencement of the bidding for its public issue, the company has raised nearly ₹306 Cr from anchor investors. The company filed its red herring prospectus (RHP) for an IPO last week comprising a fresh issue of up to 1.18 Cr equity shares aggregating up to ₹680 Cr. There is no offer-for-sale (OFS) component, with the proceeds instead going into the business. Purple Style Labs has raised close to $78 Mn to date, most recently a $40 Mn Series E in March 2025, but it has never had a large institutional anchor. As per the DRHP, Agarwal held 27.10% and the biggest institutional shareholder, Enam Holdings, held 2.9%. Agarwal also sold shares worth ₹45 Cr to three investors in August 2025, a month before the draft papers were filed. At the upper end of the price band, the IPO values Purple Style Labs at around ₹4,600 Cr. A significant portion of the proceeds, ₹371.1 Cr, will go towards lease liabilities of its Experience Centers and back-end offices, while another major chunk will be used for sales and marketing, which we will come to later. The timing is interesting because Purple Style Labs is not coming to market after completing its growth journey or reaching profitability. Instead, it is entering the public markets after making a deliberate strategic shift, from pursuing breadth across designers, customers and geographies to focusing on its most valuable segments. The IPO-bound company’s consolidated net loss for the year ending March 31, 2026 (FY26) widened by 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr compared to a loss of ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous year. Operating revenue for the fiscal increased by about 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in the previous fiscal year. The company now has 1,109 active designer brands, 208,490 SKUs and 14 Experience Centers, including 12 in India, one in London and one in New York. It served 66,713 customers and processed 95,565 orders in FY26, while its online platforms recorded 19.14 Mn unique visitors. PPUS GMV rose 22.7% YoY to ₹721.6 Cr in FY26, while AOV jumped 34.6% to ₹75,505. But the number of customers and orders has fallen over the past two years as the company deliberately moved away from lower-value business. That leaves Purple Style Labs with a very different question from the one it faced when it started. The first challenge was to prove that India’s luxury-fashion market could support a scaled multi-brand platform. The next was to build that platform. Now, after deliberately narrowing the business, the challenge is whether its premiumisation strategy and large-format store bet can translate scale into a more sustainable financial model. From A ₹44 Cr Business To An Omnichannel Luxury Platform Purple Style Labs was founded by Abhishek Agarwal in 2015 with a broad thesis around India’s luxury market. Agarwal spent around two-and-a-half years understanding the sector before making its biggest early bet, acquiring Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop in 2018, he told Inc42. At the time, Pernia’s was primarily an online business. Purple Style Labs soon began building physical Experience Centers, opening eight locations within its first two years, including one in London. That became the foundation of its omnichannel model. The company subsequently expanded across major Indian luxury markets, opened larger stores and entered markets such as Ahmedabad and Hyderabad. Revenue grew from around ₹44 Cr in FY20-21 to more than ₹500 Cr by FY24, according to Agarwal. The strategy was based on a relatively simple insight: luxury customers often want more than digital discovery. They want to see products, try them, receive styling assistance and customise purchases. The numbers suggest physical retail has become increasingly important. Indian Experience Centers generated an AOV of ₹90,651 in FY26, compared with ₹38,753 online. Experience Centers contributed 74.72% of PPUS GMV during the year. Purple Style Labs has consequently moved well beyond being an online designer marketplace. Its stores now range from conventional luxury formats to 20,000–60,000 sq ft Large Format Experience Centers, including locations in Mumbai, Delhi, Hyderabad and New York. The company has also built an unusual inventory model around this physical expansion. Rather than holding deep inventory across every SKU, it focuses on breadth — displaying a wide assortment while using outright inventory, consignment and back-order models. The RHP says this allows PPUS to offer a wider selection while reducing the need to hold deep inventory across products. This combination of physical experience, online discovery and a broad designer network is now the core of Purple Style Labs’ proposition. PSL The Strategic Reset: Fewer Brands, Higher-Value Customers The most consequential shift in Purple Style Labs’ recent history has been its decision to do less, but focus more sharply on what works. After crossing ₹500 Cr in revenue in FY24, Agarwal says the company spent the next two years figuring out what they did not want to do. That meant cutting the long tail of the business. The designer base fell from around 1,900 to 1,100, marketing expenditure dropped from ₹54 Cr to ₹30 Cr and business below the ₹35,000 price point declined from ₹160 Cr to ₹85 Cr. “Instead of trying to go wider, deeper, more geographies, wider customer, cheaper price point, we focused on the top designers, top geographies and top customers,” he said. The result is visible in the company’s customer metrics. Customers fell from 92,672 in FY24 to 66,713 in FY26, while orders also declined. Yet AOV increased from ₹45,513 to ₹75,505 and PPUS GMV rose from ₹588.1 Cr to ₹721.6 Cr. Management’s argument is that this is not deterioration in demand but a deliberate shift in the quality of demand. The top 50,000 customers accounted for 97.19% of PPUS GMV in FY26, compared with 91.16% in FY24. The top 10,000 customers alone generated ₹406 Cr of GMV, or 56.27% of total PPUS GMV. The designer side is becoming similarly concentrated. Agarwal says the top 10 designers now contribute around 30% of sales, while the top 100 account for roughly 78%. In some cases the designer relationship has been built through strategic acquisitions. Purple Style Labs acquired the late Wendell Rodricks' label in 2020 and counts Hemant Trivedi among its owned brands, alongside Pernia's itself. An owned label cannot leave for a rival marketplace so this could become a strong moat for the parent company. The strategy, therefore, is no longer to maximise the number of brands or customers on the platform. It is to build deeper relationships with its highest-value customers and designers and drive greater GMV through there. That raises an important question for the next phase: how much growth can Purple Style Labs generate by going deeper before it needs to widen the funnel again? For now, management believes there is enough room to grow through its existing designer ecosystem. The company has also become significantly more India-focused. India contributed 79.71% of PPUS GMV in FY26, up from 64.93% in FY24. International GMV fell to 20.29%, although Purple Style Labs continues to operate in London and recently opened its New York Experience Center. The reset has therefore produced a more focused business but also one where growth is increasingly dependent on a relatively concentrated set of customers, designers and cities. “While the company does not have any listed peers, which gives it a strong proposition as a new category, the shift in its business direction could also raise questions among retail investors about whether the fundamentals are still evolving and the company is yet to fully figure out its business model. As a result, many investors may prefer to wait and watch for four to five listed quarters before taking a long-term investment call,” an analyst at a leading brokerage firm said. PSL GMV The IPO Test: Can Premiumisation Translate Into Profitable Scale? The ₹680 Cr IPO now puts this strategy under the scrutiny of public-market investors. The fresh capital will largely support the infrastructure Purple Style Labs has already committed to. Of the proceeds, around ₹371 Cr will go towards lease liabilities, while ₹139 Cr will fund sales and marketing. This high allocation sits awkwardly against the cutback seen in the marketing spend in the past two years. The earmarked amount from the IPO is more than four times the current annual spend for Purple Style Labs. This is particularly relevant because the company’s physical expansion is still relatively recent. Four large Experience Centers, two in Mumbai, one in Delhi and one in New York, were opened during FY26. Their ability to mature and generate stronger economics will be critical to the next phase. The company has demonstrated that physical stores can command significantly higher AOVs. What remains to be established is whether that higher ticket size can ultimately translate into sufficient operating leverage after accounting for rentals, employees, marketing and other costs. The RHP also shows that net working capital has increased from ₹43.1 Cr in FY24 to ₹86.9 Cr in FY26, partly reflecting upfront costs associated with new Large Format Experience Centers. This is where the IPO story becomes more nuanced. Purple Style Labs has already proven that it can build scale in Indian luxury fashion. It has created a network of more than 1,000 designers, built a sizeable online discovery engine and established physical stores that generate much higher ticket sizes. But the company remains loss-making, while its physical-store footprint creates ongoing lease and operating commitments. The management’s answer is that the heavy lifting has already been done. The stores have been opened, the designer network has been curated and the customer base has been narrowed towards higher-value cohorts. The next phase is about allowing those investments to mature. For investors, however, the question is whether premiumisation can become operating leverage. “The company’s recent strategy suggests it does not necessarily need to return to its earlier model of aggressive customer and brand expansion. If the top customers continue to spend more, Purple Style Labs could potentially grow GMV without proportionately increasing its customer base or marketing expenditure. But that also means the company will have to prove that its more concentrated model is durable. Hence, the IPO will be more favourable for IPO gains rather than long-term investing,” the analyst quoted above said. Purple Style Labs began with Agarwal spending years trying to understand a fragmented luxury market. The acquisition of Pernia’s gave it the platform to build an omnichannel business, while the following years were about scaling stores, designers and customers. Now the IPO marks the next test. The question is no longer whether Purple Style Labs can grow. It is whether it can make its growth increasingly valuable and turn a ₹700 Cr-plus GMV luxury-fashion platform into a business capable of generating sustainable returns on the physical and financial capital it has deployed. The charge against a man accused of shooting a Melbourne father has been upgraded to murder following the discovery of a body last week.
Mohammed Aboueid, 56, was initially charged with intentionally causing serious injury after an alleged dispute unfolded at a home in Wildwood, north-west of the city, on August 19.
During that dispute, police allege Mr Aboueid shot 37-year-old Khaled Malas, who was then reported missing.
Police conducted a large-scale search for Mr Malas, which came to an end last Wednesday, when human remains were discovered.
Police said his body was found covered in grass on Havelock Road in Clarkefield, about 15 kilometres from Wildwood.
Mr Aboueid has been remanded in custody and will face the Melbourne Magistrates' Court in November.
Friends remembered Mr Malas as a "humble, hard-working man who loved his young family" and someone who was deeply respected by his community.

A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.
Rajendra Dawadi decided to halt classes and order children to higher ground after receiving warnings about the scale of the flooding heading their way.
Dawadi, the headteacher at Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot, which has 1,600 pupils, said he had received four warnings from different people within minutes, including one from Betrawati, a town directly upstream.
This prompted him to take immediate action. “I decided I shouldn’t delay any more,” he told the BBC. “Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day’s classes.”
Dawadi said during the evacuation of the school he saw a hostel building about 100 metres from the river being engulfed by the torrent of flood water.
“If we had made the decision 10 minutes later, all of us, including the students and me, would not be able to speak to you today,” he said.
One student said Dawadi’s decision had saved their lives with moments to spare. Yunisha, 16, told reporters: “I, along with my friends, survived by just 10 seconds.”
She described the children running up a muddy path to escape as water and debris inundated the town. “Within no time, the bazaar was swept away in front of my eyes,” she said. She was reunited with her family three days later.
At least 69 schools have been destroyed or damaged by the floods, affecting nearly 19,000 children, according to the charity Save the Children.
In Dhading, one of the areas worst hit by the floods, a group of schoolchildren survived the disaster when they left their classroom for their lunch break.
Others in the area escaped when teachers told them to quickly evacuate classrooms just before the waters came crashing in.
The mother of one child told the Associated Press that teachers had warned students: “There is a flood and you should leave bags and tiffins. That’s how they managed to survive.”
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. The country said on Sunday 2,502 people, including 592 foreigners, were out of contact. It reported an updated death toll of 781 people.
The disaster, which struck the Nepal-Tibet border region of the Himalayas on Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a wall of water and debris cascading downstream, the US Geological Survey said.
Nepal’s foreign minister has called for a global response to the climate crisis, saying the Nepali people had disproportionately become “major victims of climate change” despite having contributed a fraction of the planet’s fossil fuel emissions.

Michele Spagnuolo, the Google engineer arrested in May by US authorities for alleged insider trading on Polymarket, is making a new bold bet. On Wednesday, his legal team filed a motion to dismiss the charges against him. Spagnuolo isn’t outright denying that he made money using internal information from Google. Instead, his legal team says that the wagers were not financial instruments subject to regulation by the United States’ Commodities Exchange Act but rather good old-fashioned international betting that the US has no authority over.
Spagnuolo, who has been placed on leave from Google, is accused of committing commodities fraud, wire fraud, and money laundering. Using the alias “AlphaRaccoon,” he allegedly made a series of wagers on Polymarket’s flagship platform that resulted in profits totaling over $1.2 million. According to the criminal complaint, “AlphaRaccoon” correctly wagered that the singer D4vd, who gained notoriety for his suspected connection to a grisly killing, would be Google’s most-searched person of the year in 2025. (D4vd was later charged with murder; he pleaded not guilty.)
You might not expect the lawyers defending someone accused of felonies to agree with state prosecutors, but the vicious legal infighting over prediction markets is creating strange alliances. Across the United States, state attorneys general and regulators are battling against both the federal government and prediction markets over whether event contracts should be considered “swaps” and therefore have to follow the Commodities Exchange Act, or instead be categorized as gambling, which is regulated by states.

Spagnuolo’s lawyers argue that defining swaps to include wagers like who the most-searched person on Google will be each year “would fly in the face of the statute’s purpose and history” and lead to “absurd results.” They say it would make it so that any wager in the world, from a charity raffle to a local Ping-Pong match, could be classified as a financial instrument. “Spagnuolo is basically making the same argument as the states that are suing prediction markets,” says a financial services regulation expert Todd Phillips. “This is the issue that will likely go up to the Supreme Court.”
In addition to disputing the idea that prediction markets offer swaps, Spagnuolo’s legal team argues that the US government had no jurisdiction over him in the first place because he’s a non-US citizen who was wagering on a non-US platform. Although Polymarket is headquartered in New York, the company’s flagship prediction market is banned in the United States and technically is administered by an ostensibly Panama-based entity known as Adventure One QSS.
Spagnuolo was living in Zurich, Switzerland, when he allegedly made the Google-related trades on Polymarket. “The extraterritorial argument is interesting and raises the question of whether the US should be the world’s prediction markets cop,” Philipps says. Spagnuolo’s team also claims that the charges should be dismissed because the internal information he supposedly leveraged did not have any commercial value to Google. Google did not respond to requests for comment.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency tasked with regulating prediction markets, and Spagnuolo’s legal team also did not respond to requests for comment. CFTC chairman Michael Selig previously told WIRED that the agency has the ability to pursue extraterritorial jurisdiction in cases involving offshore platforms in “extreme circumstances.”
Spagnuolo was the second person publicly charged with alleged insider trading on Polymarket in the US. A month prior to Spanguolo’s arrest, Special Forces soldier Gannon Ken van Dyke was charged with allegedly making more than $400,000 from wagers on Polymarket connected to the raid on former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. Van Dyke’s defense team is also arguing for the charges to be dismissed because they say his activity should be classified as gambling and therefore not subject to federal commodities law.
Earlier this week, the CFTC—which filed a separate civil lawsuit against Van Dyke—repeatedly stressed in an amicus brief for the criminal case that his Polymarket events contracts were, indeed, swaps. It won’t be surprising if the CFTC does something similar in Spagnuolo’s case. By mounting this type of defense, the alleged insider traders have now inserted themselves directly into a much larger existential showdown over prediction markets.

Monza memories - Italian GP in pictures through the years
ByAlan Jewell
BBC Sport
Published
2 hours ago
The Italian Grand Prix takes place this weekend at Monza, arguably the most historic venue on the calendar.
Monza has hosted Formula 1 races more times than any other circuit, staging grands prix in all but one year since the inaugural season in 1950.
The only time Monza was absent was 1980, when it was being renovated.
Located in a royal park and surrounded by woodland, it is known as the 'cathedral of speed'. It is the spiritual home of Ferrari and the devoted tifosi who adore the Italian team.
It is all but impossible to imagine F1 without Monza - it was where the first world championship was decided 76 years ago and where, last year, Red Bull's Max Verstappen set the fastest lap in F1 history during qualifying.
Throughout the years, Monza has been the scene of thrilling finishes, Ferrari glory, title wins, controversy and tragedy. Its story is F1's story.
Here is a selection of images through the years...
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
A picture from the 1950 Italian Grand Prix, the final race of Formula 1's first season. The race and inaugural drivers' title was won by Italian Giuseppe Farina, in an Alfa Romeo. Farina is the only driver to win the title in his home country.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Ferrari's Giuseppe Farina (nearest the camera), Maserati's Juan Manuel Fangio and Ferrari's Alberto Ascari, on the far side, line up before the start of the 1953 race. These three men shared the first eight Formula 1 world championships. Fangio won this race but Ascari took the title that year.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Juan Manuel Fangio is followed by Stirling Moss and Peter Collins on the steep banking during the 1956 Italian Grand Prix. The banking was used up until the 1961 race and remains in place at Monza. Maserati's Moss won the race. Ferrari pair Fangio and Collins shared second place, after the Briton handed over his car to his Argentine team-mate. The points ensured Fangio won the fourth of his five world titles.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Italian Maria Teresa de Filippis, the first woman to compete in F1, drove for Maserati at her home race in 1958.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Ferrari's Wolfgang von Trips was on the verge of winning the world championship when he collided with Jim Clark's Lotus on the second lap of the 1961 race. His car flew into a crowd of people on an embankment, killing him and 14 others. The German is pictured before that fateful race.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Spectators inside a grandstand watch the action through the Lesmos corners in 1962.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Scotsman Jim Clark is presented with a garland after winning the 1963 grand prix to secure his first of two drivers' championships for Lotus.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Lotus' Graham Hill adjusts his race helmet and visor in the pits before the 1967 race. Gathered around the Englishman is his family, including wife Bette and his children. The 1996 world champion Damon Hill, six years old when this picture was taken, is standing at the front.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Before chicanes were installed, Monza's layout ensured races were a battle of slipstreaming with regular changes of position. Here, in 1969, Matra's Jackie Stewart crosses the line to win just ahead of Jochen Rindt's Lotus, Matra's Jean-Pierre Beltoise and Bruce McLaren, representing his own team. The top four were separated by less than two tenths of a second.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Nina Rindt sits in the pits, timekeeping for her husband Jochen during a practice session in 1970. Shortly after this picture was taken, the Austrian driver was killed on the approach to the Parabolica corner, almost certainly because of a suspension failure on his Lotus. A few weeks later, Rindt became F1's only posthumous world champion.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Another thrilling finish as BRM's Peter Gethin crosses the line to win in 1971, just ahead of Lotus' Ronnie Peterson, Tyrrell's Francois Cevert, Mike Hailwood in a Surtees and BRM's Howden Ganley. There was just six tenths of a second between the top five.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Drivers and team members set off on a race around the circuit in 1973, organised by team owner Frank Williams. At the front of the pack is James Hunt but it would be Williams - who can be seen behind the bare-chested runner - who won and took the £750 prize.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Niki Lauda shows the scars of his near-fatal accident at the 1976 German Grand Prix at the Nurburging. The Austrian Ferrari driver returned to action just six weeks later at Monza, in significant pain, to continue his title battle with McLaren's James Hunt. Lauda finished fourth in Italy to extend his lead over the British driver but Hunt ultimately prevailed by a single point at the end of the season.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Behind the leaders, there is a multi-car accident at the start of the 1978 Italian Grand Prix. The Lotus driver Ronnie Peterson was trapped in his wrecked Lotus with serious leg injuries and had to be freed by other drivers, but his injuries did not appear life-threatening. After significant delays in getting him treated, the Swede died from an embolism the following morning. His team-mate Mario Andretti won the world title on the day of Peterson's accident and after his death remarked: "Unfortunately, motor racing is also this."
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
The Italian Grand Prix was the only race not won by McLaren in 1988. It would have been a clean sweep if Jean-Louis Schlesser, deputising for Nigel Mansell at Williams, had not punted off Ayrton Senna as the Brazilian attempted to lap him with two laps to go. Senna's misfortune meant Ferrari finished one-two, with Gerhard Berger leading home team-mate Michele Alboreto in front of a thrilled home crowd. The joy was tinged with poignancy - the victory was just a few weeks after team founder Enzo Ferrari had died.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
At the same chicane where Senna was hit by Jean-Louis Schlesser in 1988, the Brazilian comes together with another Williams, this time driven by Damon Hill, at the start in 1993. Both drivers were able to continue and Hill recovered to win the race.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
The Minardi of Christian Fittipaldi is upside down and somersaulting through the air after colliding with team-mate Pierluigi Martini on the approach to the line in 1993. Both drivers were unhurt and Fittipaldi crossed the finish line through his forward momentum when his car landed on the track. He took eighth place, a position behind Martini.
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
McLaren's Mika Hakkinen is in tears after spinning off while in the lead in 1999, fearing it might be a decisive blow to his title hopes. However, the Finn would eventually beat Ferrari's Eddie Irvine to the drivers' championship.

The Ferrari tifosi congregate on the start-finish straight to celebrate Michael Schumacher's victory in 2000. It was a key race on the way to the first of his five consecutive drivers' titles for the team.

The first chicane is frequently the scene of contact and cars going off track as drivers jostle for position. Many are facing in unorthodox directions here at the start in 2011.
Image source, Getty Images

The tumultuous 2021 season had many flashpoints between title contenders Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton. Monza was one of them with the two drivers coming together at the first chicane as they battled for position. The rear of Verstappen's Red Bull landed on Hamilton's Mercedes, and the importance of the halo head protection device can be seen here. It possibly saved the Briton from serious injury.

Charles Leclerc takes in the acclaim from the tifosi below him after winning for Ferrari in 2024 - his second victory at Monza after success in 2019.

- GTA 6 preview suggests that the game will run at only 30 FPS on consoles at launch.

According to YouTuber Davy Jones, GTA 6 is reportedly confirmed to run at 30 FPS on PS5 and Xbox consoles at launch. The Brazilian creator, in an official video, revealed that Rob Nelson, co-studio head at Rockstar North, told the press that GTA 6 is locked at 30 FPS on consoles during the game’s development.
Davy Jones was one of the content creators invited to Rockstar North. He got an exclusive sneak peek at GTA 6 ahead of the GTA 6 Extended Look premiere on Netflix earlier today.
Following the Extended Look, Davy Jones talked about his time at Rockstar North and his chance to play GTA 6 during a YouTube livestream. During his visit, Nelson revealed that GTA 6 is running at only 30 FPS on consoles during development. The YouTuber also revealed that there will be no first-person mode in GTA 6 at launch.
Earlier, several leaks suggested that GTA 6 will feature Quality and 60 FPS performance modes at launch. However, in line with previous Rockstar titles like RDR2 and GTA 5, GTA 6 will reportedly only feature a 30 FPS mode at launch.
In addition, numerous reports in the past suggested that GTA 6’s 60 FPS performance mode may be added later, and that is the case at the moment.

'Like fighting a dinosaur': Sydney woman recalls how she punched shark during attack
- Published
A Sydney woman who survived a shark attack has described the moment she came face-to-face with a 4m great white before repeatedly punching it.
Leah Stewart, 34, was dragged under the water at Coogee Beach in June as the shark bit into her thigh and arms, leaving her with extreme blood loss and injuries so severe that doctors had to amputate her left arm.
In an interview which aired on Sunday, the mother-of-one said she was determined to live for the sake of her baby daughter.
"In my head, I was like, ... 'You are not taking me away from my daughter', and I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again - it was like fighting a dinosaur".
Moments earlier, Stewart had just finished her regular Saturday morning swim and was heading back to shore when she was alerted to danger.
"I heard a girl behind me… a shrill shriek. I turned and there was a huge, huge fin behind her. It was massive," she told Nine Network's 60 Minutes.
"I looked at the size of it and I realised that's not a dolphin."
Stewart turned around and realised the shark was "right there … and it just was getting closer and closer and closer."
The shark's face was "horrific" with "black little beady eyes" and its "teeth and its mouth was massive".
"We were looking face-to-face," Stewart said, and at one point, the shark was just 30cm from her own.
Even in that moment, Stewart's thoughts remained calm.
"I'm right-handed, so I thought 'let's do a left hook'," she said.
"I just kind of throw my left arm and it just grabs onto my forearm and rips, rips away my skin, my muscle, everything... there's a big gap between my forearm and the hand."
The shark started to pull Stewart under the water, grabbing her leg.
"I had the thought, 'this is it, this is how I die' and then I just thought of [my daughter] August and I thought she's not going to have a mum, she's gonna grow up without a mum," she said, fighting back tears.
"I just knew I couldn't leave her... I know it sounds strange but I sort of willed myself back."
Fighting the shark felt "like punching a brick wall" but she kept going.
"I must have got a really good one in and so it let me go. It was the hardest thing in the world, but I fought my way out of there."
Stewart was pulled to the shore by other swimmers and rushed to hospital, where she was placed in an induced coma and underwent almost a dozen surgeries.
Despite her harrowing experience, Stewart said she doesn't want to be remembered as "a girl that got mauled on the beach".
"I'm the woman that punched the shark in the face," she said.

One person died and about 15 people were missing or unaccounted for after a major flash flood swept through the Grand Canyon national park in Arizona on Saturday afternoon, according to the National Park Service.
The flash-flood event occurred in the area of Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch, where park staff and the Arizona department of public safety had evacuated more than 60 people as of Sunday morning.
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the park service said, without providing additional details.
“Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground, the Phantom Ranch Canteen and cabins, and the entire North Kaibab Trail from the North Kaibab Trailhead to Phantom Ranch are closed until further notice,” the statement said.
Park officials announced the number of people who remain missing or unaccounted for in a separate statement, requesting the public to notify the government agency of information they may know about “hikers or backpackers who were in the inner canyon along the Bright Angel Creek corridor” on Saturday, as well as “anyone who had a campground reservation in the affected corridor”.

Getting an 'iPhone Unavailable' message? Here's how to fix it
You'll need your old passcode or Apple Account password.
Getting an "iPhone Unavailable" message on your lockscreen is never a welcome sight. The issue is a common one, caused by entering an incorrect passcode too many times. It's a system meant as a safeguard against unwanted access, but it can just as easily be triggered by unintentional pocket presses or plain old forgetfulness. Thankfully, there are several ways to get access to your iPhone again, though some are a bit more labor-intensive, depending on the circumstances of your lockout.
How to fix an iPhone Unavailable message
Your options for an iPhone Unavailable error vary slightly depending on your iOS version, if you've changed your passcode recently and what other technology you have available.
Use Passcode Reset
If you're using iOS 17 or later and have reset your phone's passcode within the last 72 hours, you have the option to revert back to your old passcode to solve the issue.
- 
After five incorrect passcode attempts, the iPhone Unavailable screen will appear, and you can select the Forgot Passcode option in the lower righthand corner
- 
Select Enter Previous Passcode
- 
After entering your previous passcode and unlocking your phone, you'll immediately need to reset the passcode to a new number
Reset your iPhone without a computer
To reset your iPhone without a computer, you'll need to be using iOS 15.2 or later, have Find My previously enabled, have an active cellular or Wi-Fi connection and know your Apple Account and password. Apple recommends that, if you're using an eSIM on iOS 16 or later, you should contact your carrier before following these steps, as they may be able to give you a QR code that allows you to set up your eSIM again.
- 
From the iPhone Unavailable screen, select Forgot Passcode
- 
Select iPhone Reset
- 
Enter your Apple Account password to sign out of your account
- 
Select Erase iPhone, which will delete all your data and settings. If you're using an eSIM and iOS 17 or later, you'll have the option to keep your eSIM but erase your data, or delete both your data and eSIM
- 
Your phone will restart; from there follow the instructions to set up your device again
Reset your iPhone with a computer
To reset your iPhone with a computer (either PC or Mac), you'll need a cable to connect your phone to your computer and an internet connection. On PC, you'll also need the Apple Devices app, which can be found on the Microsoft Store. After resetting your iPhone, you'll only be able to restore it if you have an existing iCloud backup.
- 
Turn off your iPhone by holding down the side button and volume down button, then using the power slider
- 
Connect the cable to your computer, then plug in your iPhone and quickly hold down the side button
- 
Keep holding the button when the Apple logo appears, and continue holding until the image of a computer and cable appears; this means your phone is in recovery mode
From here, the directions differ slightly depending on if you're using a PC or Mac.
Resetting an iPhone on PC
- 
Open the Apple Devices app and select your phone from the sidebar
- 
If needed, opt to trust the device, then select General
- 
Choose Restore and follow the instructions
- 
Once your iPhone has been restored, you can disconnect the phone from your PC and set up your iPhone
Resetting an iPhone on Mac
- 
Open Finder and select your phone from the sidebar
- 
If necessary, allow the accessory to connect to your Mac
- 
A window will pop up stating there's a problem with the phone that requires it to be updated or restored; choose Restore
- 
Once restored, you can disconnect your iPhone and set it up again
Apple notes that you may need to update your iPhone before you can finish the restoration process; if your phone restarts during this process, you'll need to shut your phone off and repeat the steps for entering recovery mode.

Mount Fuji pics, life-changing ramen and a weak yen - why young Brits are going to Japan
- Published
As I open up Instagram, I see another person in their late-20s has been to Japan.
It shouldn't come as a surprise any more.
"I cannot scroll through TikTok or Instagram without seeing videos of people in [convenience store] 7-11 and trying all the different skincare and trying all the snacks and the viral sandwiches and the viral drinks and going to all the viral restaurants," says Alex Baker, who has been to Japan three times.
There's been growing hype about Japan as a travel destination among young British people.
Data from the Japanese National Tourism Organization, external shows that 483,157 British tourists visited Japan in 2025, up 24.8% on 2024 and up 40.8% on 2019, the benchmark year used by travel companies to compare with pre-pandemic trends. Provisional data for 2026 suggests numbers are continuing to grow.
This reflects the boom in total tourism to Japan since the pandemic, with a record number of foreign visitors in 2025.
The Brits in their 20s and 30s I spoke to gave a long list of reasons for wanting to go to Japan - the cityscapes, food, anime, nature, history, gaming, temples. But they largely agreed that social media was the main driving force behind so many young people heading there.
When Maitri Sanghvi scrolled through TikTok, "Japan just kept popping up," she says.
It was a big reason why Maitri, 24, and her boyfriend went for three weeks earlier this year. "Seeing [Japan] on social media restarted my urge of wanting to go," she says.
Search #japantravel on TikTok or Instagram and you'll see countless videos of Mount Fuji, bowls of steaming ramen, itinerary suggestions, small villages in the Japanese Alps, the Fushimi Inari torii gates in Kyoto, the neon lights of Osaka's Dotonbori, and the chaos of Shibuya Crossing.
"Seeing other people's Japan videos definitely influenced my decision to go," says Aden Ibrahim, 29.
Since he went with friends last July, Aden has posted dozens of TikToks of his trip, and he's still uploading them more than a year later. One captioned "Japan made it out the group chat" has 1.1 million views.
Travelling to Japan isn't cheap - return off-peak flights with a layover in China start at about £450 with a budget airline. But the yen is weakening, making it cheaper for tourists when they're actually out there - even as rising prices hit residents. In July, the yen fell to a 40-year low.
"You can literally get a bowl of life-changing ramen for £3/£4 compared to a rubbish one here for like £20," says Faye Jawad, 26, who reviews restaurants on TikTok and visited Japan last year.
"When the yen was weakening, I thought 'actually this is a good time to go, things are going to be cheap'," says Vivek Haria, 26, who has a trip planned for this autumn. His interest in Japanese culture means he's wanted to visit for years - he has been learning the language and even sings in the UK-Japan Choir - but he says the value of the yen made it even more attractive.
The low prices have led to many tourists splashing out on souvenirs when they're out there. Videos of people showing off their Japan "haul" of flavoured KitKats, stationery and clothes have become popular on social media.
When Sam Corbett, 23, was in Japan in May he bought so many souvenirs - including snacks, matcha, clothes and skincare - that he had to buy an extra suitcase, which he stuffed full. Everything was "really affordable," he says.
Almost all the Brits I spoke to had stuck to the same route known as the Golden Route: Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, often with day trips to nearby destinations like Nara, Hiroshima and Mount Fuji.
It's easy to see why so many tourists pick this route. These cities are easy to travel between and packed with some of Japan's biggest attractions.
But complaints about badly-behaved tourists are sparking debate about overtourism.
Chiyuki Izumii, a tour guide for the Japan Guide Agency, feels tourist behaviour has got worse in recent years. She says that while her customers are respectful, she's seen other tourists jumping queues for buses, blocking space on board with big suitcases, carving their initials on trees in Kyoto's bamboo forest, speaking in loud voices at night and entering restricted areas to take pictures.
Some authorities are cracking down. Fujikawaguchiko, a town near Mount Fuji, cancelled this year's cherry blossom festival after repeated issues with misbehaving tourists, while Tokyo's Shibuya ward, home to the famous Shibuya Crossing, started issuing on-the-spot fines for littering in June.
In July, Japan increased its international tourist tax, external - typically incorporated into flight and boat tickets for people leaving Japan - from 1,000 yen (£4.60) to 3,000 yen, which it says will be spent on things like improving public transport and restoring historic sites.
Some visitors were surprised just how crowded major cities in Japan were.
"I was prepared for it to be busy but I didn't expect it to be as busy as it was," says Millie Dring, a huge anime fan who went in November with a friend to celebrate her 21st birthday.
The DisneySea theme park near Tokyo was so busy that Millie and her friend only went on one ride, which had a three-hour queue, and felt overwhelmed by the crowds.
Sam blames some of the crowds at tourist hotspots on social media hype and he says he regrets going to some places just because they were popular online. One dessert spot he went to in Kyoto after seeing it "all over social media" was very busy "and there wasn't a single local person in the queue," he says.
Sites like the Hakone torii gates and Arashiyama bamboo forest had huge crowds of people trying to get Instagram-perfect photos, he says.
But for some visitors, the hustle and bustle of the tourist destinations are all part of the attraction.
"I think there's a snobbiness around being a tourist over the past couple of years where people want to avoid looking like one," says Laura McGregor, 29, who's spending two weeks in Tokyo and Osaka in November for her honeymoon. Her plans include going to Disney and Universal, attending a sumo event, visiting Fuji and Hiroshima, and hiring go-karts to drive around Tokyo.
"Of course I want to experience an authentic side of Japan but I'm excited to embrace the tourist side too and go along with it," she says.

Iceland EU referendum on a knife edge as counting continues
- Published
Iceland's closely fought referendum on whether to resume membership talks with the European Union is going down to wire, with the result too close to call.
Based on the first 153,197 votes counted of the 270,000 voters eligible, 50.1% rejected the government's proposal, while 49.9% said yes, public broadcaster RUV said, with just 435 votes splitting them.
Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government promised to hold a referendum by 2027, but brought it forward because of international tensions, including US President Donald Trump's threats against Greenland.
However, debate in this island nation of almost 400,000 people centred more on its fishing industry rather than security concerns.
Already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone, EU membership would bring Iceland into the customs union and eventually the euro.
Iceland began its application to join the EU in 2009 in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system.
Its application was already well advanced when a eurosceptic government came to power in 2013 and put talks on hold. Fishing rights was the biggest obstacle then - as it remains today.
Fish and marine industries account for almost 40% of Iceland's exports and many No voters feared they would cede some control of their lucrative fishing grounds under the EU's common fisheries policy.
The referendum campaign has fuelled debate about Iceland's place in the world, Frostadottir said after casting her ballot in the capital on Saturday.
"This is a great day, we've been waiting for this for years to be able to have a vote," Frostadottir said, adding that her government would continue its work regardless of the outcome.
The question on the ballot was: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"
A Yes vote would not be a final decision on joining the EU, but a move towards an accession agreement, which would then have to be approved by a second referendum.
Equally, the No vote would not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.
While economic issues dominated the referendum campaigns, security concerns also featured.
Iceland is a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.
The country has backed Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have been alarmed by Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island.
Trump's expressed interest in taking over Greenland has also raised concerns.

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

The Spider-Man star likened her energy to that of soul singer James Brown, who he called the "hardest working man in showbusiness".
"She's not only an incredible performer... songwriter and musician, but also an incredibly kind and giving person and a real deal activist."
Kidjo is a Unicef and Oxfam goodwill ambassador, and is the co-founder of the Batonga Foundation, which helps vulnerable young girls and women in Benin.
At the Los Angeles gathering she was also praised by Harvey Mason Jr, the CEO of Recording Academy - the organisation that also oversees the Grammy awards.
"She's connected cultures, she's crossed borders, she's reminded audiences everywhere that while we may come from different backgrounds, her music unites in a way that few other things can," he said.
During her interview with the BBC, the musician's phone kept ringing with those wanting to congratulate her.
"Yesterday I received the call of the president of Benin," she said.
"Today I received the call of Chris Blackwell, the founder of Island Records, the producer of Bob Marley, the maker of U2 and so on and so forth."
Kidjo explained how fundamental Blackwell, who signed her in the 1990s, had been to her success - launching her breakthrough album Logozo.
"I said to him at that moment… 'Can I do the music I want to do and keep my cultural identity without anyone imposing any other music on my shoulder?' He said… 'It's no brainer.'"
Kidjo joins Charlize Theron, a white South African actress, in representing Africa on the Walk of Fame, which comprises more than 2,800 stars.
She said she was amazed to hear a year ago that she had been nominated for a Hollywood star, telling Focus on Africa she did not believe the news given to her by her husband until she said she had seen it on the BBC.
And when asked about the significance of becoming the first African musician with a star, she replied: "Changes that last take time."

Four areas in Sarawak record 'hazardous' air quality; East Malaysian state prepares for possible haze emergency
Sarawak’s Serian district recorded the worst Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of 475 at 9am on Monday (Aug 31). But moderate air quality in Putrajaya enabled Malaysia’s National Day celebration in the administrative capital to proceed as scheduled.
KUALA LUMPUR: Four areas in Sarawak recorded “hazardous” air quality on Monday (Aug 31), the second day running that Malaysia has hit such levels as it continues to grapple with haze linked to forest fires in neighbouring Indonesia.
Air quality in the country began to reach hazardous levels over the weekend.
Sarawak’s Serian district recorded the worst Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of 475 at 9am on Monday, followed by Samarahan at 334, Sri Aman at 330 and Kuching at 324.
Another three areas in the East Malaysian state – Sarikei, Sibu and Mukah – recorded “very unhealthy” air quality, with API readings of 271, 219 and 214 respectively.
Another 14 locations in the country – in Sarawak, Kedah, Penang, Labuan, Sabah and Perak – observed “unhealthy” air quality, the Department of Environment, under Malaysia's Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability, said in a statement posted on Facebook.
Under Malaysia’s API scale, readings above 300 are classified as hazardous. Readings up to 50 are classified as good, 51 to 100 as moderate, 101 to 200 as unhealthy, and 201 to 300 as very unhealthy.
The Department of Environment said air quality across the country has deteriorated, including in parts of the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia as well as in Sarawak, Sabah and Labuan due to the “movement of haze from various directions”.
Areas with unhealthy air quality included Taiping in Perak with an API of 150, Seberang Jaya in Penang (156) and Sungai Petani in Kedah (157).
In Sabah, the Kota Kinabalu Polytechnic monitoring station recorded an API of 111 while Tawau registered 153.
Citing an Aug 30 report by the Singapore-based ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre, the Department of Environment said satellite images showed 324 hotspots in Kalimantan and 42 in Sumatra.
Only two hotspots were detected in Malaysia - one each in Perak and Sarawak.
Moderate to dense transboundary smoke was observed over West and Central Kalimantan, Brunei and western and central Sarawak, while moderate smoke from hotspot clusters in North Kalimantan was seen moving into southern Sabah, said the department on Monday.
“Moderate to dense smoke was also observed coming from hotspot clusters across much of Kalimantan and central and southern Sumatra,” it added.
On Sunday, Sarawak’s deputy premier Douglas Uggah Embas said the state was prepared to declare an emergency should air quality reach a critical level, local media reported.
“Should the Air Pollutant Index exceed 500, the applicable guidelines provide for the closure of government and private-sector offices and workplaces, except essential services, pending declaration of a disaster emergency by the national committee on disaster management,” he was quoted as saying by the Borneo Post.
A haze emergency was previously declared in Kuching in September 1997 when an air pollution reading of 650 was recorded.
Air quality in Sarawak is also believed to be at its worst since 2019, when a monitoring station in Miri recorded an API reading of 442, according to the Borneo Post.
Sarawak premier Abang Johari Openg announced on Sunday that the state-level National Day celebrations, which had been scheduled to take place in Kapit, were cancelled due to the haze affecting large parts of the state.
Over on the peninsula, air quality in Putrajaya was moderate at 79 as of 7am on Monday and did not affect the main National Day celebrations.
The parade and procession were reported to proceed as scheduled, with Malaysians beginning to fill the area around Dataran Putrajaya as early as 4am on Monday, New Straits Times reported.
On Sunday, Indonesia’s National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB) found that smoke from forest and land fires in Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan was drifting towards the Malacca Strait and Natuna Sea, raising the risk of transboundary haze affecting Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei, Bernama reported.

లోక్సభలో ప్రతిపక్ష నేత రాహుల్ గాంధీకి సంబంధించిన ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ఈ వీడియోలో ఆయన మహిళలు, అత్యాచారాలకు సంబంధించి వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసినట్లు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు. వైరల్ వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ, “80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణం. భారతదేశంలో అత్యాచారాలు జరుగుతాయి, కానీ ‘భారత్’లో అత్యాచారాలు జరగవు.” అని చెప్పినట్లు వినిపిస్తోంది. అయితే, ఈ వీడియో నిజంగా రాహుల్ గాంధీ చేసిన వ్యాఖ్యలను చూపిస్తుందా? ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో వెనుక ఉన్న నిజమేంటో ఈ కథనంలో తెలుసుకుందాం.
క్లెయిమ్: లోక్సభలో ప్రతిపక్ష నేత రాహుల్ గాంధీ “80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణం. భారతదేశంలో అత్యాచారాలు జరుగుతాయి, కానీ ‘భారత్’లో అత్యాచారాలు జరగవు” అని అంటున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోను ఎడిట్ చేశారు. అసలు వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలు చేయలేదు. ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్, మాజీ హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ గతంలో చేసిన వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలను ప్రస్తావిస్తూ, వారి అభిప్రాయాలను రాహుల్ గాంధీ విమర్శించారు. అయితే, వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఆయన ఎవరి వ్యాఖ్యలను ప్రస్తావిస్తున్నారో చెప్పిన భాగాన్ని తొలగించి, ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలు రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా చేసినట్లుగా చూపించారు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీలక ఫ్రేమ్లను ఉపయోగించి రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, కాంగ్రెస్ పార్టీ అధికారిక యూట్యూబ్ ఛానల్లో 22 ఆగస్టు 2026న అప్లోడ్ చేసిన అసలు వీడియో మాకు లభించింది. అదే రోజు పుణెలో జరిగిన కాంగ్రెస్ “ఛాత్రోన్ కీ గూంజ్” కార్యక్రమానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియో ఇది. అసలు వీడియోలోని 1:00:12 టైమ్స్టాంప్ వద్ద వైరల్ క్లిప్లోని దృశ్యాలు కనిపిస్తాయి. అయితే, అసలు వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలను స్వయంగా చేయడం లేదు. ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్, మాజీ హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ గతంలో చేసిన వ్యాఖ్యలను ఆయన ప్రస్తావించాడు. అత్యాచారాలు “ఇండియా”లో జరుగుతాయి కానీ “భారత్”లో జరగవని మోహన్ భగవత్ చెప్పారని, 80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణమని మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ వ్యాఖ్యానించారని రాహుల్ గాంధీ పేర్కొన్నారు. అనంతరం, ఇలాంటి వ్యాఖ్యలు తాము వ్యతిరేకిస్తున్నానని ఆయన తెలిపారు.
మోహన్ భగవత్, మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ పేర్లను ప్రస్తావించిన భాగాన్ని వీడియో నుంచి తొలగించారు. ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలను రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా చేసినట్లుగా కనిపించేలా వైరల్ వీడియోను రూపొందించారు. దీంతో వైరల్ వీడియోను ఎడిట్ చేసినట్లు స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
తదుపరి, గూగుల్లో కీవర్డ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) ఉన్న వీడియోలు లభించాయి. వీటి ప్రకారం, 4 జనవరి 2013న ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్ అసోంలోని సిల్చర్లో పర్యటించిన సమయంలో అత్యాచార ఘటనలపై వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేశారు. “ఇండియా”లో ఇలాంటి నేరాలు ఎక్కువగా జరుగుతాయని, “భారత్”లో తక్కువగా జరుగుతాయని ఆయన చెప్పినట్లు వార్తలు వచ్చాయి. ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలు అప్పట్లో వివాదానికి దారితీశాయి. తర్వాత అప్పటి ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ అధికార ప్రతినిధి రామ్ మాధవ్ వివరణ ఇచ్చారు. మహిళలను గౌరవించే భారతీయ సంప్రదాయాల గురించి మోహన్ భగవత్ మాట్లాడారని, ఈ విలువలకు దూరమైనవారు నేరాలకు పాల్పడే అవకాశం ఉందని ఆయన చెప్పినట్లు రామ్ మాధవ్ వివరించారు.
అదేవిధంగా, 2018 నవంబర్లో అప్పటి హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ అత్యాచారం, వేధింపుల ఘటనలపై వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేశారు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). వార్తా కథనాల్లో ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలకు సంబంధించిన వివరాలు ఉన్నాయి. అత్యాచారం, వేధింపుల ఘటనల్లో 80–90 శాతం వరకు ఒకరికొకరు తెలిసిన వ్యక్తులే ఉంటారని ఖట్టర్ అన్నారు. అలాగే, కొన్నిసార్లు చాలా కాలంగా సంబంధంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తుల మధ్య వివాదాలు తలెత్తిన తర్వాత ఇలాంటి ఘటనలు జరుగుతున్నాయని ఆయన సూచించారు.
చివరిగా, అత్యాచారం, మహిళలపై రాహుల్ గాంధీ వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసినట్లు చూపిస్తున్న ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో ఎడిట్ చేసినది.

New Zealand's government introduced legislation on Monday to ban under 16s from using social media, joining a number of countries seeking to keep youngsters off sites such as Instagram and TikTok.
Australia implemented world-first legislation banning children from social media in December, with the UK, France and others following suit.
Under New Zealand's proposed law, firms like Meta could be fined up to 10 percent of their global revenue if they fail to comply.
"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said.
"One in three children aged between 13 and 17 are now spending at least five hours on social media a day," he said.
"Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with, and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education."
Luxon specifically called out platforms Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook, saying they would be required to take "reasonable steps to check users are over the age of 16".
They would have to use "existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services and formal ID" to verify age.
Platforms would also be required to assess the risks they pose as well as report on how those dangers are being reduced, with penalties slapped on companies that fail to comply.
Education Minister Erica Stanford said the Bill "places legal obligations on platforms".
"No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers," Stanford said.
It's unclear whether the bill will pass, as both National Party's coalition partners, the libertarian ACT party and populist NZ First, have said they oppose it.
In a statement, the populist NZ First said they could not support the law given the "colossal failure" of the legislation in Australia, while ACT said they believed the law "won't work" and that teenagers would easily get around the ban.
The main opposition party Labour has submitted a list of dozens of questions it wanted answered before deciding whether it would offer support, including how age verification will work and which platforms will be affected.
"We take this legislation very seriously," spokesman Reuben Davidson said.
"The safety of young people in Aotearoa New Zealand is at stake and the risks they face in increasingly complex online environments are significant," he added, using the Maori-language name for the country.
Australia banned under 16s last year from the likes of Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, in a crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and "predatory algorithms".
A team of Australia-based researchers in a peer-reviewed study published in June found little evidence to suggest teenagers have turned away from social media as a consequence, however.

Former Indian cricketer Ravichandran Ashwin had another tough day as Edinburgh Castle Rockers defeated his side Dublin Guardians by four wickets in the eighth match of the European T20 Premier League 2026 at The Hague on Sunday.
Guardians skipper Ashwin won the toss and opted to bat first. However, his team was dismissed on 109 in 18 overs.
The 39-year-old Ashwin scored eight runs in 12 balls without hitting any boundaries.
In response, the Castle Rockers chased down the target in just 13.4 overs. Off-spinner Ashwin bowled an economical spell, conceding only 20 runs in his four overs, but he did not manage to pick a single wicket. He did help Josh Little remove Castle Rockers’ opener J J Smuts by taking a catch.
New Zealand’s left-arm spinner Mitchell Santner was named the Player of the Match for his figures of five for 16 during the Guardians’ innings.
On Saturday, in the Guardians’ 33-run loss to Glasgow Cosmic, Ashwin had conceded 43 runs in his four-over spell, which included the wicket of Moises Henriques. With the bat too, he disappointed with a two-ball duck.

About 1,600 federal employees who work at the General Services Administration have been forced to relocate from their office on F Street in Washington, DC, to the Theodore Roosevelt Federal Building, roughly two blocks away. Workers say the new building, which also houses staff from the Office of Personnel Management has mice, a caved-in bathroom ceiling, and drinking water that needs to be run for five to 10 seconds before it is clear.
The federal workforce has been rocked by changes made by Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) since January 2025. DOGE effectively fired tens of thousands of workers and forced those who remained to commit to in-person schedules and, in some cases, zero-based budgeting. GSA, the agency in charge of the federal government’s IT services and real estate assets, was hit early by DOGE, and in addition to major workforce cuts also rolled out plans to sell hundreds of federal office buildings. A year after the cuts, GSA announced it planned to hire about 400 workers.
“We’ve all been through a lot, but this really made me finally understand that they don’t care about us,” says one GSA employee who asked to remain anonymous, as they aren’t authorized to speak to the press. “We’re left wondering what else is going to collapse or break—do we need to look at the ceiling before going to the bathroom? Can we actually trust the water is safe to drink?”
Photos obtained by WIRED show a toilet in a men’s room on the third floor covered in debris from the ceiling, a gaping hole in said ceiling, and a dead mouse caught in a trap. Workers said the mouse wasn’t “entirely shocking” since many federal buildings allegedly have vermin, but the ceiling pushed them over the edge. An additional sign in the office recommends workers filling up water bottles to “run the water without your bottle for 5-10 seconds and wait for the water to run clear.”
GSA and OPM did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
GSA leadership, including administrator Ed Forst, has told employees they should expect to work in the OPM building—which is slated for “accelerated disposition,” or a quick building sale—until December 2028. Their prior building, located at 1800 F Street, is undergoing extensive renovations. The initiative is part of a “government-wide effort to reduce underutilized space and fortify the federal real estate footprint,” according to a GSA press release.
While Musk himself has stepped back from his public role in the Trump administration, DOGE affiliates have continued working in government, embracing austerity measures and AI initiatives. Others have gone back to the private sector, working in AI, data centers, and manufacturing.
