On his role with Century Cricket, Ponting - head coach of Punjab Kings in the IPL and Washington Freedom in the US-based Major League Cricket - added: "To be involved with a platform like this that I can use as a coaching and talent-identification tool and to get down to growing the game in the US is the major reason I am involved.
"Cricket hasn't grown as rapidly as I would have thought in the US, but with what we have been able to create, it will allow people of all ages to sample what the game is all about skill-wise.
"It's a platform like I've never seen before. The technology is second to none and I can't wait to watch."
Training can be pre-set for particular deliveries, bowlers and match scenarios, with Century Cricket's global CEO Chris Millard adding: "It really is a global platform that can change cricket for the better.
"People can face a Jasprit Bumrah or a Moeen Ali in whatever setting they want. We have the data to pull that off and if we are able to scale that globally we will be starting the future of cricket."

The census questionnaire is perhaps the most comprehensive manuscript of a nation’s social, economic and political evolution. Far from being a neutral statistical exercise, it is also a record of the state’s priorities and anxieties at a given moment. Every new question added, and every old one dropped, offers clues about what a society values, what policymakers seek to measure, and how governments perceive their citizens.
The evolution of census questionnaires across the world reflects this intimate relationship between statistics and statecraft. The population enumeration phase of the Census, scheduled to begin next month, will have 13 new or modified questions compared with the 2011 Census, including details of a person’s father and mother and their places of birth. These questions were also part of the National Population Register schedule notified in 2020, sparking a political debate, with opposition questioning the government’s motive.
Australia, which conducts a census every five years, included eight questions on heritage and migration backgrounds in its latest census, completed in August 2026. The emphasis is unsurprising in a country where immigration remains one of the defining political debates and where over a third of the population was born overseas. The questionnaire reflects not merely demographic realities but also contemporary political concerns.
India’s census forms tell a similar story. As “Population Census in India: A Futuristic Perspective” by Seema Jain and Madhav Shyam shows, changes in the census schedule over the past century and a half mirror India’s transition from a colonial possession to a developmental state, and later to a society increasingly concerned with welfare delivery, urbanisation, financial inclusion and social identity.
Popularly, 1872 census is considered to be the first for the Indian subcontinent, though it covered only the tracts that were under British rule. The questionnaire framed by the imperial government was shaped by colonial imperatives. Religion, caste and community formed the backbone of enumeration because understanding and categorising Indian society was critical to colonial governance. Educational qualification, taken for granted in modern surveys, appeared only in the 1941 census.
One of the most significant shifts occurred after Independence with the rise of planning. The demands of the Five-Year Plans exposed major gaps in information about housing, infrastructure and living standards. Until 1951, states followed their own houselisting formats, making nationwide comparisons difficult. The introduction of a uniform houselisting schedule in 1961 represented more than administrative standardisation; it reflected a state increasingly interested in measuring the material conditions of its population.
The evolution of the houselisting schedule over subsequent decades maps India’s development trajectory. The 1961 schedule focused on basic housing characteristics such as building material, tenure status and number of rooms. By 1991, it had expanded to include drinking water, electricity, sanitation and cooking fuel, reflecting a growing focus on basic services and rural infrastructure. The shift became even more pronounced in 2001 and 2011, when questions on bathrooms, kitchens, drainage connections, household assets, electricity sources and access to banking facilities moved the census beyond counting houses to assessing quality of life. The census was increasingly measuring developmental outcomes rather than merely recording demographic facts.
The treatment of work in the census offers another window into changing economic thinking. Early censuses employed relatively narrow definitions of work. By 1991, unpaid labour on family farms and enterprises was recognised as work, signalling a broader understanding of economic contribution in a largely agrarian society. The introduction of categories such as main workers, marginal workers and non-workers reflected the state’s growing concern with labour participation and underemployment rather than simple occupational classification.Migration provides a similar example. From 1981, the forms started recording birth and the last place of residence, to capture the data on migration.
The evolution of questions relating to family and gender also reveals changing social attitudes. Marital status classifications gradually expanded from a simple distinction between married, unmarried and widowed persons to include separated and divorced persons. The introduction of age at marriage in 2001 reflected increasing policy attention to gender, reproductive health and social development. Likewise, the recognition of a category other than male and female in 2011, and the subsequent adoption of the category “transgender person”, marked an acknowledgement of identities that earlier census frameworks had erased.
Urbanisation emerged as another major concern. The dedicated enumeration of slum populations in 2001 and the expansion of such coverage in 2011 reflected growing awareness that India’s urban story could not be understood without accounting for informal settlements. The decision to collect more detailed slum data was itself a recognition that urban poverty had become a central development challenge.
Seen in totality, the history of the Indian census questionnaire is the history of the Indian state itself.

'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis
- Published
"If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you."
The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back.
"They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service.
It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom.
Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people."
About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima.
She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.
Fatima is one of an estimated 800,000 Nigerians who the UN says have been displaced in the country's north-west. One of the main reasons people have left their homes is violence.
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by gangs, locally referred to as bandits, who often move around on motorcycles and attack quickly then ride away, escaping before security forces arrive.
Thousands of people have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fight, and the BBC spoke to one who said his armed group had killed many bandits.
But the gangs keep attacking in what appears to be a deteriorating pattern of violence and abductions that is spreading southwards.
Fatima says when the bandits attacked her home, she ran into the nearby forest with other villagers to hide: "The forest became our sanctuary. We ran with our kids, if you couldn't find your child you'd take your neighbour's child."
She says people slept in the forest before moving on to the state capital, Gusau, "where we found a little bit of peace".
Fatima now lives in an informal camp in Gusau with her seven children, who are aged between nine and 30.
Dozens of women sit in groups on the dusty ground of the makeshift compound, many wearing brightly coloured hijabs. More than 1,000 people are here, she believes.
Conditions are tough with "no proper place to even lay your head". Food is scarce and assistance arrives irregularly.
Fatima describes two occasions where "good Samaritans" brought rice or potatoes. Children are sent out to gather firewood to sell so families can buy food, but 22 have been kidnapped by bandits, she says.
Gesturing towards a nearby building, Fatima says that there "you will find 100 or more women… maybe just two or three have had breakfast.
"When we had peace, we had our own wealth, but now the tables have turned and we have become beggars."
Her eyes fill with tears and she cries for a few minutes, wiping her face with her hands.
Despite being 16 miles (25km) from her village, the threat Fatima fled has not disappeared.
When she first arrived at the camp, the sound of gunshots kept her awake at night. Things have since quietened, she says, crediting patrols by the army and government-backed vigilantes, but the atmosphere is still tense.
The bandits are mostly people from the Fulani ethnic group, who traditionally make their living by raising animals. Some of them have swapped cattle trading for kidnapping and extortion, which is seen as a faster, easier way to make money.
They attack towns and villages or ambush travellers, abducting people for ransom, stealing whatever they want - and sometimes killing those who resist. They also force communities to pay protection money, only allowing farmers into their fields if they hand over large sums of cash.
Attacks are now more frequent than ever. In the bandit heartlands of north-west Nigeria, the number of incidents recorded by the international conflict monitoring group Acled rose 78% in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025.
One security consultancy estimates that kidnappers across Nigeria collected nearly $5.8m (£4.3m) in ransoms over the past year as the number of abductions surged. SBM Intelligence estimates that 7,825 people were kidnapped between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase on the previous year.
The increase in bandit activity appears to be a key driver in this trend.
Malik Samuel at Good Governance Africa, a research and advocacy non-profit group, says that "there is no region in northern Nigeria currently that does not experience one form of mass abduction or the other".
Nigeria's battle with bandits is just one part of a more complex security situation facing the country.
As well as the bandit gangs in the north-west, there is an Islamist insurgency in the north-east, separatist unrest in the south-east and clashes in central regions, where the main grievance is over access to land and water for grazing and farming and where ethnic and religious elements have also fuelled some of the unrest.
Most analysts agree that armed groups have waged campaigns of violence that affect all communities, regardless of background or belief.
- The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria 
  - Published28 November 2025
Schools are a common target. When the Islamist Boko Haram militant group infamously kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from the north-eastern village of Chibok in 2014, it made global headlines.
At the time the group forced its captives into sexual slavery, domestic servitude or used them as suicide bombers.
But a range of groups across Nigeria now use kidnapping to raise funds, focusing on soft targets such as schools, churches, mosques and remote villages.
This was mainly confined to the Boko Haram strongholds of the north-east or the bandit zones of the north-west - areas that are largely Muslim.
Then, in May this year, gunmen on motorcycles attacked three schools in Oyo state, south-west Nigeria, one of the few regions that was previously considered relatively safe. Thirty-nine children, the youngest just two years old, were abducted along with seven teachers. One teacher was killed during the raid, another's murder was filmed and shared online.
After 56 days, the remaining 44 hostages were released. The government said it refused to pay a ransom and that the children were released after an operation by security forces. Three men were sentenced to life in prison for the attacks and confessed to being members of an affiliate of Boko Haram.
The abduction spread fear throughout the south-western town of Oriire, with parents in the community pulling their children out of school.
"There is fear because many residents have run away and are yet to return," says the traditional ruler of the area, Oba Tajudeen Abioye, whose niece was among the kidnapped children.
"And for those of us who are left here, we are relying on the security officials, the soldiers" who were sent to protect the community, he says.
Nigeria already has one of the highest numbers of out-of-school children in the world: the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) estimates the number is about 19 million.
The multiple, overlapping security issues mean Nigeria's military and police are overstretched and as a result struggle to tackle the violence.
A 2025 UN report said that police stations were often underfunded and not fully operational, citing independent sources that accused officers of lacking skills in hostage negotiation and forensic investigation.
President Bola Tinubu's administration has allocated the largest defence and security budget in the country's history, raising it by 10% in December 2025 compared to one year before. He has recently approved the recruitment of 28,000 new soldiers.
In the meantime communities are still suffering and in Zamfara thousands of residents have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fill the gaps in security.
But there are concerns about their involvement. In 2020 Zamfara banned a large vigilante group over concerns that extrajudicial killings were driving more violence, according to AFP.
The authorities say the new vigilantes are better trained, but Samuel, from Good Governance Africa, calls them a "time bomb waiting to happen".
"If citizens arm themselves how do you control them at the end of the crisis, how are you able to disarm them?" he asks.
One of the vigilantes meets us outside his group's headquarters, a single-storey concrete building, and agrees to speak on the condition of anonymity during our visit in July.
He perches on his motorcycle, an AK-47 slung over his shoulder, a scarf across his face as a makeshift balaclava, gold and silver skull rings on his fingers.
"We are some of the people the governor hired to protect the community," he says, explaining that they are sometimes told where the bandits are and "with the help of God we fight them and defeat them".
"Let the bandits understand that when they attack a place and kill, they can also be killed," he adds.
He estimates he has fought bandits at least 20 times and says the calls for his group's help keep coming.
"It's hard to go a week without these reports," he says. "There are regions that became safer… but there are other regions where the same cannot be said."
He calls on the state governor, whom he supports, to hire and arm more people to take on the bandits. "These people won't be afraid of you unless you have proper weapons to fight them," he says.
Fatima also calls for more action: "These kidnappers are in every nook and cranny.
"I am not saying the government has failed but even if it is trying, it needs to do more. There are problems and we think with more effort and more security agents, villages will be peaceful."
She wants to return home, but is doubtful that will happen as she has heard her village has now been turned into a camp for the gunmen that attacked it.
The local bandit leader has become the de facto authority, and that families look to him to solve domestic disputes, she says.
Another nearby village "is completely empty, not even a chicken lives there… empty villages like that are countless", Fatima says.
"Even if you go back to our area, it's just difficulty you will face. There's nothing there, no food… you farm and when you go to harvest, they stop you or kidnap you."

India’s growth to stay at 7% despite global uncertainties: Nirmala Sitharaman
Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said India’s economy will sustain 7% growth despite wars, tariff uncertainty and disruptions to global energy and fertiliser supplies.
India’s economy has been growing at 7% or more since the Covid-19 pandemic and is expected to maintain the momentum despite global uncertainties, Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said while addressing the Indian diaspora in Chicago.
Sitharaman said India had “recovered well” from the pandemic and continued to sustain growth at 7% or more, even as global uncertainties have multiplied due to wars, tariff issues and disruptions to energy and fertiliser supplies through the Strait of Hormuz. “We thought, we saw the worst when we went through Covid,” she said.
“This year too, our growth will be at that range,” she said, pointing to global uncertainties caused by two wars, tariff issues and the situation at the Strait of Hormuz, which is disrupting global supplies of energy, fertilisers and other essential commodities.
The finance minister’s statement came close on the heels of the Reserve Bank of India’s latest growth projection on August 5. According to the RBI, India’s real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 2026-27 is projected at 6.7%.
The RBI increased its latest GDP growth rate projection by 10 basis points from its June estimate as the economy weathered the storm generated by a turbulent global geopolitical environment, trade-related uncertainties and an unpredictable monsoon in the first quarter of 2026-27.
Sitharaman said notwithstanding the breakdown of global energy and fertiliser supply chains, the government shielded its citizens. Despite the Hormuz crisis—which the finance minister termed a “big challenge”—India kept itself “well provisioned” to meet the fertiliser requirements of farmers without any additional cost, and energy was made available to every household.
India imported nearly 80% of the fertilisers it consumed through Hormuz, including urea, diammonium phosphate (DAP) and potash, she said. As a result, Indian farmers were left without fertilisers, which she recalled as an “unthinkable” situation. But the government arranged fertilisers through various routes and the country is “adequately” stocked.
While the crisis has been managed, the government paid a huge price to procure fertilisers for farmers from global suppliers, she said. The government continues to give urea at ₹300 per bag to Indian farmers, while its procurement cost is ₹3,000 per bag, she said. “So, ₹2,700 is the subsidy we give per bag of fertilizer,” she said, adding that “there is no shortage” of fertilizer for farmers and no burden of the cost is shifted to them.
The finance minister said irrespective of global uncertainties, India is marching on the reform path with its focus on bilateral trade and investment cooperation with several economies and accelerating the domestic engine of growth through capital investments for their multiplier effects. “So, reforms continue. We are also talking with several countries for bilateral investment treaty and also bilateral trade agreements because multilateral institutions are very slow…, she said.
Talking about fiscal management, she said, “We have set ourselves a certain target, which is to bring the borrowing down to the 50% level of GDP by 2030. Therefore, I will be working on that path. There are advanced economies whose debt is well over 200% of their GDP even now. We have given ourselves a fiscal discipline path on the fiscal deficit as well. We have fulfilled the trajectory. The last mile that had to be reached by 2025-26, we have reached,” she added.
“The world has witnessed the fiscal prudence of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi when he was Chief Minister of Gujarat and when he is the Prime Minister of the country. Our credit ratings are improving. But that’s not by cutting corners. That’s not by stopping the resources which have to go for social welfare. It is through proper management of the economy,” she said.
She said 2047 is the target year set for achieving Viksit Bharat. “It’s hardly 20 years from now. So, the speed and scale with which the reforms are happening require a lot more support. Lots more support from people who are talented and have exposure. Lots more support from people who can give ideas for us to carry it forward. And, above all, support in terms of capital, which is so required for a country to meet all its aspirations,” she added.

Early backers continue to dilute their shareholding in Lenskart. Alpha Wave Ventures has now offloaded 2.94 Cr shares of the omnichannel eyewear giant in multiple block deals for ₹1,856.8 Cr. As per NSE data, the venture capital (VC) firm sold the shares at ₹630 apiece to rake in the amount. The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by National Pension System (NPS) Trust, Bajaj Life Insurance, BofA Securities, Edelweiss, Goldman Sachs, HDFC Life Insurance, Kuwait Investment Authority, Morgan Stanley, Societe Generale, Susquehanna, among others. The NPS Trust emerged as the biggest buyer and purchased 78.6 Lakh Lenskart shares for nearly ₹495 Cr, while ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund bought 60.3 Lakh shares for ₹380 Cr. Meanwhile, Whiteoak Capital MF also bought shares worth nearly ₹100 Cr, Redwheel (via multiple entities) lapped up Lenskart stock worth ₹65 Cr and Morgan Stanley acquired shares worth ₹69.3 Cr. With this, Alpha Wave Ventures has offloaded nearly 1.7% stake in Lenskart. The VC firm held 3.42% stake, or 5.9 Cr. shares in the eyewear giant at the end of June 2026. Alpha Wave Ventures is not the first early backer to sell its stake in the listed company in the past couple of months. Just days ago, Japanese tech giant SoftBank dumped Lenskart shares worth ₹2,887.9 Cr, while Temasek also offloaded 2.05% stake in the omnichannel eyewear company last month for ₹1,934 Cr. In June, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) also sold 4 Cr shares of the company in a block deal worth ₹1,960 Cr. The stake sales come as early backers look to book profits amid an uptick in Lenskart stock price. Shares of the company have jumped 14.6% in the past month and are up 41.2% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. This has come on the back of multiple brokerages raising their target prices on the eyewear giant after its healthy Q1 FY27 results. While Jefferies raised its target price for Lenskart to ₹680 from ₹600, Macquarie raised its target price to ₹675 from ₹625. Goldman Sachs raised its target price to ₹715 from ₹625 and Citi raised its target price to ₹650 from ₹600. The positive outlook came as the omnichannel eyewear giant’s consolidated net profit surged 273% to ₹228.4 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹61.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue jumped 43% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹2,714.2 Cr. Shares of Lenskart closed Friday’s trading session 0.54% lower at ₹636.15 on the BSE.

Amid growing concerns over analogue paneer, Zomato has announced a zero-tolerance policy against the sale of dishes containing analogue dairy products on its platform. It has also warned restaurant partners that non-compliance would result in their delisting. The company said that, with immediate effect, it has removed dishes that restaurant partners had declared as containing analogue dairy from its platform. Analogue dairy products are substitutes designed to mimic conventional dairy products such as cheese, butter or milk and use vegetable oils, starches and other non-dairy ingredients. Under the new policy, restaurants have been asked to either transition to natural dairy products or remove items containing analogue products from menus if an immediate transition is not feasible. Restaurant partners have also been directed to review product labels and ingredient declarations provided by suppliers to verify the ingredients being used and ensure that food items are accurately represented on Zomato. “At Zomato, our core mission is better food for more people, and that means safeguarding customer health and upholding clear standards for what's listed and served by our restaurant partners,” Zomato CEO Aditya Mangla said. The move is aimed at improving transparency and food quality for consumers, Zomato said, adding that the policy is part of its broader push towards healthier food choices and greater disclosure around the food being sold through its platform. The development comes as food delivery platforms face increasing scrutiny over food quality, ingredient disclosure and the accuracy of claims made by restaurants and food brands listed on their platforms. The crackdown also sheds light on the growing focus of regulators on food quality, hygiene and transparency as online platforms increasingly become a key channel through which consumers purchase food and grocery products. Earlier this month, the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) suspended the licences of 14 food establishments linked to Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart following a statewide inspection drive that uncovered food safety and hygiene violations. The regulator had inspected 86 dark stores and also issued 60 improvement notices.

Topline
The northern lights could be visible from some northern U.S. states on Sunday night, according to a forecast from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, although forecasters are currently not expecting any space weather that typically makes the lights visible further south.
Key Facts
NOAA is forecasting a Kp index of four out of nine on Sunday night, meaning the aurora could appear brighter with more “motion and formations” in some places.
Forecasters at NOAA were not expecting any space weather events that could impact the aurora on Sunday night, according to the agency’s most recent three-day forecast, however, the agency did issue an alert for the higher expected Kp index on Sunday afternoon.
Where Could the Northern Lights Be Visible?
The aurora has a “low” likelihood of visibility for several states along the U.S.-Canadian border, according to NOAA’s forecast map. These include northern Washington, Idaho, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. The lights also have a high likelihood of visibility from most of Alaska. However, the sun sets very late in Alaska during the summer months, meaning the night sky might not get dark enough for the aurora to become visible.
What’s the Best Way to View the Northern Lights?
Experts at NOAA recommend viewers travel as far north as possible to catch a glimpse of the aurora. Viewers should then position themselves on an ideal vantage point with a good view of the sky facing north, ideally as far away as possible from cities or other sources of bright lights. The aurora is most active in the hours just before and after midnight, according to NOAA, so viewers should try to search for the aurora between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.
What’s the Best Way to Photograph the Northern Lights?
A photographer who spoke to National Geographic said viewers can take quality photos of the northern lights using smartphone cameras, provided they use the right equipment and settings. Photographers should remember to bring a tripod and remote timer when trying to capture images of the lights, as all cameras need to be held still for long periods of time to capture the aurora in the dark night sky. Smartphone users should also remember to turn off their flash settings, turn on night mode and shoot using RAW image format if possible.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction as rivers including the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli overflowed and swept away homes, roads, bridges, and other infrastructure. Experts said the disaster was likely triggered by the collapse of a glacier and a massive ice-and-rock avalanche in the Himalayas, which sent huge amounts of debris and water into the river systems. As of 28 August 2026, the death toll in Nepal had risen to 469, according to Nepal Police, while nearly 1,000 people remained missing as search and rescue operations continued (here, here, and here).
Amid the disaster, multiple visuals are being shared on social media with the claim that they show visuals of the August 2026 Nepal floods. Let’s verify the truth behind these visuals in this article.
Claim: The visuals show the August 2026 Nepal floods.
Fact: None of the videos are related to the Nepal floods in August 2026. They are either old videos from other locations or AI-generated videos that are being shared as visuals of the disaster. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
This video is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows a Chinese helicopter reaching the site where a glacier had broken, causing a massive amount of water to be released and resulting in widespread destruction in Nepal.
In our investigation, we found that the video was originally uploaded (archived) on the Instagram account of Leigh Coates, an American commercial helicopter pilot based in Valdez, Alaska. She posted the video on 22 August 2026 and specifically identified the location as Columbia Glacier in Alaska. She explained that a Jökulhlaup, also known as a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), occurs when water trapped by glacier ice suddenly finds a way out, causing the water to drain rapidly beneath the glacier and rush downhill with immense force. She further stated that such events have been occurring annually at Columbia Glacier since 2014, although they are rarely captured because they generally occur in remote areas.
Video 2
The video is being shared on social media with claims that it shows the largest lake in the mountains whose embankment breached, causing the massive Nepal-Tibet floods.
We found that the video was uploaded by Leigh Coates on her official YouTube channel on 16 August 2026, before the Nepal floods. The video is titled “Before and After a Jökulhlaup Glacial Outburst Flood” and shows an example of the glacial outburst flood that occurred in Juneau, Alaska. This confirms that the video is unrelated to the August 2026 Nepal-Tibet floods.
Video 3
The video (here, here, and here) is being shared with claims on social media that it shows vehicles and buildings being swept away by flash floods in Nepal.
However, we found (archived) that this video has been available on the internet since 04 August 2026, at least 22 days before the Nepal floods. Moreover, upon examining the video, we noticed that the movement of the water and vehicles appeared unnatural.
We also analysed the video using AI detection tools such as Hive, which indicated that the video was AI-generated.
Video 4
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows vehicles being swept away by heavy floods during the August 2026 Nepal disaster.
We found that this video is related to the flash floods that occurred in the Chamoli region of Uttarakhand on 10 August 2026. Media reports (here, here) from the time also carried the same visuals and reported that vehicles were swept away after a bridge collapsed amid the flooding.
Video 5
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a mudslide rapidly turning into a torrent of muddy floodwater during the August 2026 Nepal floods.
We found that the video is not related to the August 2026 Nepal floods. The video was actually recorded in Hpakant, Myanmar, in January 2024 (here, here).
Video 6
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows water and debris rushing down from a mountainous area and sweeping away homes during the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal.
We found (here, here, and here) that this video is from Dharali village in Uttarkashi, Uttarakhand, and dates back to August 2025. It shows flash floods that occurred following a cloudburst in the upper catchment area of the Kheer Ganga River. The resulting floodwaters, debris and silt surged through Dharali, washing away houses and other structures. At least four people were confirmed dead, while more than 50 others were reported missing.
Video 7
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a massive landslide occurring during the August 2026 Nepal floods.
We found (here, here) that this video has been available on the internet since at least 11 August 2026, predating the recent Nepal floods. Several users have claimed that the landslide was triggered by an earthquake that struck Colombia on 10 August 2026.
Video 8

Russia is rattling NATO’s nerves, but how far will Moscow go?
Incursions may be aimed at testing Western military alliance's resolve
It would be fair to say this summer has been the season of fear and loathing in Eastern Europe, as more signs emerge that Russia could be ready to further test NATO solidarity in the hopes of breaking it.
Poland and Romania have witnessed a series of Russian drone intrusions and at least one missile strike since the spring.
The idea that the Kremlin is preparing some kind of incursion drove speculation surrounding the CIA director's surprise visit to Moscow last week.
What is worrying officials in Poland and the Baltic states is not the prospect of Russian armoured divisions suddenly crossing the frontier.
The concern is that Moscow may believe it can carry out a deliberately ambiguous, limited act of violence — large enough to frighten or destabilize NATO, but small and deniable enough to make invoking the Western military alliance's self-defence clause, Article 5, politically difficult.
In late July, a Russian cruise missile crashed into Poland's Lublin province after travelling deep into Polish territory during a massive strike against Ukraine. Multiple drones have also approached or tested Polish airspace in the weeks since.
A Polish defence expert who specializes in the Russian military and politics said the war in Eastern Europe is rapidly approaching a critical turning point where the Kremlin has reached the conclusion that the only way to defeat Ukraine is to politically break NATO.
"There is frustration [over the] inability to break Ukrainian armed forces and to defeat Ukrainians in the field," said Withold Rodkiewicz, a security expert at the Center for East European Studies at the University of Warsaw.
The Russian "elite," as Rodkiewicz calls them, know they're not winning the war, and Ukraine's increasingly effective attacks on oil and commercial infrastructure have the potential to destabilize the Kremlin's grip on power.
"The analysis that's around in Moscow is that the main reason that Ukrainians are able to resist is because they are supplied from the West," he said, adding that nothing short of total victory in Ukraine will satisfy the Kremlin.
"They're not looking for a way out. They are not looking for … an off-ramp," he said. "When they are thinking what to do next, an escalation is an obvious thing."
Rodkiewicz said he believes the time will be right for Moscow sometime in September, either before or after Russia's parliamentary elections.
There is mounting evidence of Russian risk-taking, but there is no consensus that Russian President Vladimir Putin has decided to start a conventional war with NATO. Estonia’s foreign intelligence service, for example, still assesses that Russia does not presently intend to attack a NATO country militarily in the coming year.
Do I think they'll do something that is so clearly aimed at shaking NATO decision-making and political cohesion? Absolutely.- Kerry Buck, Canada's former ambassador to NATO
At the same time, throughout the summer, U.S., Polish and Baltic warnings about a provocation have become considerably more specific.
In late June and July, reporting emerged that Western intelligence services had picked up indications that Russia could be preparing some form of action against Poland or the Baltic states, designed specifically to test NATO cohesion.
The Guardian newspaper in the U.K. reported that intelligence received by Latvia pointed toward a possible Russian military provocation, and subsequent reporting said the United States had warned Poland about the possibility of an armed incident on Polish territory.
By early August, the warning sharpened even further. U.S. intelligence was reportedly telling Poland and the Baltic countries that Putin could be prepared to authorize provocative action against NATO while the Ukraine war is still underway, rather than waiting for Russia to regenerate its conventional forces after the war.
That is a significant change in the threat conversation.
Canada's former ambassador to NATO, Kerry Buck, said Russia has been out to destroy the alliance since its invasion of Crimea in 2014, and the conditions have only improved since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to power last year.
The constant berating of allies, the new fiscal demands placed on them, the cutting of U.S. forces earmarked for an emergency, and now Washington's review of American troop posture in Europe have created the conditions for a major political crisis, should there be a provocation.
It is, Buck said, "a window of opportunity where Russia was emboldened to poke NATO more, poke NATO territory, airspace and space more."
While she doesn't believe an outright attack on NATO is in the offing, she also believes Russia is prepared to try something ambiguous.
"Do I think they'll do something that is so clearly aimed at shaking NATO decision-making and political cohesion? Absolutely," Buck said.
Trump told reporters last week that he's "not concerned at all" about Russia attacking NATO territory. He said he's spoken to Putin and has been assured he "is not going to be attacking a NATO territory."
At a meeting of the North Atlantic Council in Brussels last week, U.S. defense policy chief Elbridge Colby insisted Washington is not abandoning Europe. He said it wants a new vision of NATO built around European-led conventional defence.
Buck said most of what Russia is likely planning falls below the threshold of a direct attack. She also accepts at face value what Colby has said. Rather, her concern lies within the reality of NATO politics.
In the past, whenever there's a crisis, the U.S. has stepped up to organize the allied response. Will that happen under the current administration?
"All signs from President Trump are that they are not as committed as they used to be, so who would step in and lead the preliminary response?" Buck asked.
"And would it be held up by U.S. reluctance? So we're dealing not just with a lack of U.S. leadership, but potentially U.S. reluctance to fall into whatever it is NATO is doing or might contemplate doing."
Just recently, Lithuanian intelligence raised another disturbing possibility: Russia using captured Ukrainian drones in a false flag operation against a Baltic country.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said that intelligence indicated Russia might employ captured Ukrainian UAVs in an operation intended to look as though Ukraine had attacked NATO territory.
The objective would be political rather than military, creating confusion inside the alliance and undermining support for Kyiv. Russia dismissed the allegation.
But that scenario becomes more plausible because something very similar happened in Latvia last spring.
Ukrainian strike drones have repeatedly wandered into NATO airspace, apparently in some cases because Russian electronic warfare has disrupted their navigation.
The incident in Latvia caused a political crisis that cost the defence minister his job, and eventually cost the prime minister her job.
Buck said there's a range of disturbing scenarios for Moscow to make mischief.
"It's in their interest to do it now," she said. "And I don't think NATO's quite ready to respond in a way, particularly because of the uncertainty about the U.S. response."

The story so far: The Union Health Ministry this past week tightened controls on all fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) containing chlorpheniramine maleate and phenylephrine hydrochloride, requiring manufacturers to carry a clear warning that they must not be used in children below four years of age.
What are these two drugs?
Chlorpheniramine is an antihistamine. It can reduce allergy symptoms such as a runny nose and sneezing. Phenylephrine is a decongestant, intended to relieve a blocked nose.
An FDC puts both ingredients into one medicine. Such combinations are commonly encountered in cold/allergy preparations.
The government’s action does not mean every medicine containing either ingredient individually has been banned. The specific regulatory action concerns FDCs containing the two ingredients together.
What has changed now is the rule where manufacturers must put the warning. “Fixed Dose Combination shall not be used in children below four years of age” — on the label, package insert and promotional literature. The restriction covers manufacture, sale and distribution of these FDCs.
This expands an earlier action. In 2023, India’s Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) had already directed manufacturers of a particular chlorpheniramine + phenylephrine formulation to warn against use below four.
In April 2025, restrictions were imposed on certain FDCs. The August 2026 notification extends the warning requirement to all such formulations.
Why are children under four the focus?
Young children are more vulnerable to medication-related adverse effects because their bodies process medicines differently from adults and because dosing errors can have proportionally larger consequences.
The government’s Expert Committee and Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) concluded that these combinations could pose risks to children below four and that safer alternatives are available.
There is also a broader international concern around giving young children multi-ingredient cough-and-cold medicines. The US FDA, for example, warns that decongestant- or antihistamine-containing cough/cold products can cause serious adverse effects in very young children and notes the risk of accidental overdose when several ingredients are combined.
Does this mean cold medicines don’t work?
Not necessarily. These drugs can relieve symptoms, but they don’t cure the underlying viral infection. Most childhood colds resolve on their own. What doctors have been saying is that while parents may understandably want to make a congested or coughing child comfortable, but more medication isn’t automatically better.
For nasal congestion, relatively simple measures such as saline nasal drops/spray, fluids and a cool-mist humidifiercan help.
The key message is don’t self-medicate a child under four with a chlorpheniramine + phenylephrine combination, even if the product is marketed as a children’s cold medicine.
Check the active ingredients, not just the brand name. Many cold preparations contain several ingredients, creating a risk of accidentally giving the same drug twice through different products.
For fever or discomfort, parents should use medicines such as paracetamol/acetaminophen or ibuprofen only according to age/weight-appropriate instructions and medical advice.

Health insurance enrollment through the Affordable Care Act is plummeting.
How Obamacare changed healthcare
Affordable Care Act enrollment is plummeting. What happened?
Nearly 3 million fewer Americans now have insurance through the program, popularly known as Obamacare, compared to last year, according to federal data released in June. After congressional Republicans allowed enhanced subsidies for the program to expire in January, many Americans saw their health insurance premiums spike by an average of about 30 percent.
As a result, many Americans have been forced to drop their coverage entirely.
With affordability among the top concerns on voters’ minds heading into the midterms, healthcare costs have become a central issue for candidates.
“A lot of policy experts say, look, when you raise the price of something, demand goes down. And that’s what’s happening here,” KFF Health News senior correspondent Julie Appleby told Today, Explained. “It’s the prices — people are dropping out.”
Appleby has been reporting on healthcare policy for decades, and she joined Today, Explained co-host Noel King to break down the latest changes to the Affordable Care Act, why enrollment is plummeting, and how the ACA crisis is teeing up healthcare as a central issue in the upcoming midterms.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Sixteen years ago, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act into law. Julie, what was the situation at the time that made it feel so necessary? What did the Affordable Care Act aim to do?
There was a lot going on. We had a lot of people who were uninsured. We had premiums going up. Many times in the past there had been some effort to do some kind of health reform, but nothing ever really passed. We had Medicare and Medicaid in the ’60s, but no major legislation since then.
People had employer coverage, like they do now, but there were a lot of people who were on their own and buying in what’s called the individual market.
The individual market was really tough. They could tell people, “Hey, you’ve got a health condition, we’re not taking you.” They could you could sign up for an individual plan and later, if you did get some kind of health condition, they could go back through your medical records and see, “Hey, did they tell us about every single thing that had happened to them in the past five or ten years?” And if not, they could retroactively cancel your plan.
What did the Affordable Care Act do exactly?
It allowed young people to stay on their parents’ insurance plan up to age 26, and that was a really big deal and also a very popular provision in the Affordable Care Act.
It created these subsidies to help people purchase coverage on the individual market. It pays for part of your premium. After you pay a certain percentage of your household income, the subsidies kick in and it picks up the rest, up to a certain up to a certain income level.
“They used to be able to charge women more than men. They can’t do that anymore.”
It did some other things, like they can’t tell you, “You have a preexisting condition, so we’re not going to take you.” They’ve got to take you.
It created a benefit package that covers all these essential things like hospitalization and drug costs and maternity care, which might not have been in plans before. They used to be able to charge women more than men. They can’t do that anymore.
What was the conversation around passing the Affordable Care Act? Remind us how and why it got so toxic and pitched.
It was super polarized, kind of like what we have now. There was a lot of discussion around whether this is going to be too much government or if it was just the right amount. A lot of people thought, “No, this is terrible, it’s gonna destroy things.”
And I think polls reflected that for the first four or five years or more of the Affordable Care Act. It was pretty evenly divided, when you looked at opinion polls, between people who thought it was a good thing and people who didn’t think it was a good thing.
In more recent years, that has changed and the favorability ratings have gone up for the Affordable Care Act and now majorities do favor the Affordable Care Act.
If you had told me that 16 years ago, I would not have believed you. Here we are. And how is the Affordable Care Act doing?
To use medical terminology, is it on life support? No, it’s actually doing fairly well. But there are some symptoms that there are problems.
Remember at the end of last year, there was all the discussion about these things called enhanced premium tax credits and whether they were going to be extended or not. The government shut down over this. Those were not extended. As a result, it costs more this year for most people in the plan, and what we’ve seen is during open enrollment last year we had about a million people fewer sign up and that was about a five percent drop.
That was 5 percent just in signups at the end of last year. Since then, the first few months of the year, we’ve seen about 3 million people drop off. Some people are finding that they can’t afford it and they are not paying their bills and they are getting dropped. A 3-million-person drop-off is pretty substantial.
There’s also a group of folks, particularly conservatives and Republicans, who say, “You know what, the numbers were inflated.” There was all this improper enrollment. People were getting these zero-premium plans and so there was fraud, there was improper enrollment, the subsidies were too generous or there were other factors that led to some fraudulent activity. And so these drop-offs just represent people who were fraudulently enrolled dropping out for one reason or another.
There’s this real split right now between what are the reasons for the drop off. But most policy folks, most people who study the situation here say the main reason is people just aren’t able to afford it.
Why is it so expensive? Why are healthcare costs so high?
That’s the $64,000 question, right?
And if you get it right, you win. You’re in charge.
That’s been the question since I’ve been covering this debate. Look, it’s not just Affordable Care Act costs going up. Employer plans are going up. Everything’s going up.
Generally, healthcare costs go up faster than inflation and that’s driven by a lot of things. It’s driven by drug costs, it’s driven by hospital costs, it’s driven by labor costs. So all of those things go into the mix with the Affordable Care Act. But also this year, there’s this additional factor of the subsidies that went away.
Insurers were looking at that saying, “You know what, the subsidies are going down. We expect to have lower enrollments next year. The people most likely to stay enrolled are the ones who have health problems because they don’t want to take the risk of being uninsured.” So insurers were calculating that in when they set their premium rates for this year: We might have sicker people in our pool that we’re gonna have to cover.
That’s part of what we’ve seen with costs in the Affordable Care Act. But everybody is seeing health inflation go up right now and that’s affecting premiums.
Here we are 16 years after the passage of the Affordable Care Act. Has it accomplished what it set out to do?
You have to look at that in a number of ways. It aimed to expand coverage and reduce the uninsured. I think the answer there is yes, the number of uninsured has gone from 13 or 14 percent to as low as just under 8 percent a couple of years ago. It’s ticked up a little bit since then.
Did it control costs? That’s a harder one to answer. And it’s back to that $64,000 question. How do you do that? Costs have continued to go up. Premiums are definitely higher than they were pre-ACA. To be fair, the plans are very different. They cover more, they’re more generous, they’re better coverage, but they are more expensive.
The big question is: What is going to be put forward as an alternative and how palatable will that be to consumers, lawmakers, the healthcare industry? It’s going to be challenging, but I think we’re going to hear a lot more discussion this year. Whether or not we see actual proposals that could pass, I think that’s a little more questionable.

Venus Williams loses 15th match in row in 2am finish
- Published
Venus Williams lost her 15th singles match in a row as she was beaten by fellow American Sofia Kenin in a 2am finish at the US Open.
The 46-year-old very nearly took the first-round match into a deciding set, but 2020 Australian Open champion Kenin saved seven set points to win 6-2 7-6 (8-6).
The match did not begin until 00:13 local time in New York as it followed Mariano Navone's five-set victory over Novak Djokovic on Arthur Ashe Stadium.
It was the latest starting match in US Open history, and there was barely 1,000 spectators left by the end.
"It's not ideal," Williams - who was given a wildcard to play her home Grand Slam tournament - said about the midnight start.
"I would have preferred something else definitely. I think it wasn't great for either of us, so I think we both tried our best.
"I just don't know any other sport where you have to start that late. I definitely think there's room for improvement there.
"I just kept pushing myself to try to find my best tennis and to find my rhythm. It's not easy to do in the first round. It's not easy to do it at 1am or 2am in the morning."
- Djokovic in tears during US Open first-round exit 
  - Published1 hour ago
- Fighting to stay No 1 - Sabalenka's US Open mission 
  - Published1 day ago
Seven-time major singles champion Williams proved highly competitive in the second set, but lost the last six points of the match having led the tiebreak 6-2.
The former world number one is ranked 618th in the world and the wildcard she received into the tournament was her 12th of the season so far - leading to some questioning whether she deserves one.
But there is no limit to the number of wildcards a Grand Slam champion can receive and, for many tournaments, having a Williams sister on site still makes commercial sense.
"I think it's good for tennis to have these generational icons," said Karl Hale, the tournament director who offered Williams a wildcard for this month's WTA 1000 event in Toronto.
"That they are still allocating wildcards for them says something to their intrinsic value to the tournaments."
Former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash does not think Williams should be taking wildcards away from younger players, but understands the enduring pull of the iconic American.
"That makes complete sense. You need a draw card, a legend to come out and play in these smaller tournaments," Cash said during BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra's US Open coverage.
"The Grand Slams sit on their own. It's up to Venus whether she thinks she's good enough to play and play well enough.
"I personally don't think she should be taking a wildcard away from a young player after she's had a great career."
- Samuel breaks more new ground with first win at a Slam 
  - Published9 hours ago
- How to follow US Open on the BBC 
  - Published8 hours ago
Two-time US Open singles champion Williams has not qualified for a Grand Slam by ranking since Wimbledon 2021, which is also where she recorded her most recent singles win at a major.
Williams was a doubles quarter-finalist at last year's US Open, but the first round defeat by Kenin was her 19th loss in 20 singles matches. The only bright spot has been a win over Peyton Stearns in Washington in July 2025.
And yet this year alone tournament directors in New Zealand, Australia, Spain, Germany and Canada - as well as the United States - have wanted Williams at their events.
Eight of the 128 spots in a Grand Slam singles draw are assigned to wildcards, and usually between four and eight at WTA and ATP events depending on the size of the field.
"The way we looked at Venus is that her legacy is phenomenal," Hale told BBC Sport.
"She's done so much for the sport and is really popular here in Toronto and our markets specifically - so we thought it was really good to announce it early that we have a Williams sister coming.
"Venus played opening day. She kicked off our tournament, so it added a lot of value."
One sporting event which has reduced the opportunity for past champions to return is golf's Open Championship.
Twenty years ago, any champions under 65 could play whenever they wished. Now, winners only get the chance to return until they are 55, which could open up the odd place in the field to younger, more highly ranked professionals.
Golfers can be competitive for much longer, but there are no limits in tennis. Martina Navratilova was given a wildcard for both the 2004 French Open and Wimbledon - and won a round on the grass - when she made a comeback aged 47.
Williams now turns her attention to the women’s doubles, where she will play alongside her sister Serena.
And she was non-committal when asked whether she has thought about her future in the sport.
"I don't think I should have to,” she said.
“I mean, my mind is fully focused on that (the doubles). So I'm going to recover from this completely insane evening and get ready for the next one."

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

Story so far: The Supreme Court on August 20, 2026, has ruled that the police cannot independently investigate offences relating to illegal prenatal sex determination under the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994. The responsibility lies primarily with the Appropriate Authority, a specialised body constituted under the law. In a judgment authored by a Bench of Justice Sanjay Karol and Justice Nongmeikapam Kotiswar Singh, it settles a long-standing disagreement among High Courts over whether the police could register FIRs and investigate such offences because they are classified as “cognisable” and “non-bailable”.
What was the case about?
The case arose from an allegation of illegal sex determination of a foetus at a hospital in Bulandshahar, Uttar Pradesh.
The District Magistrate, who was the Appropriate Authority under the Act, received information about the alleged practice. A Tehsildar was authorised to conduct a decoy operation. Following the operation, a raid was conducted at the hospital, and an FIR was registered against the doctor and others.
The FIR included offences under the Indian Penal Code as well as the sex-determination law. The accused approached the Allahabad High Court seeking to quash the chargesheet.
The High Court noticed that courts had taken different views on the role of the police in such cases and referred the issue to the Supreme Court.
There were essentially three questions before the Supreme Court: Can the police register an FIR for an offence under the Act? Can they investigate it? And can a Magistrate take cognisance of the offence on the basis of a police chargesheet?
Who is the Appropriate Authority?
The Appropriate Authority is the specialised authority created under the law to enforce the ban on sex selection and regulate the use of prenatal diagnostic techniques.
Section 17 of the Act specifically gives it the responsibility of investigating complaints of violations and taking action.
According to the section, when appointed for the whole of the State or the Union territory, it should consist of the following three members i) an officer of or above the rank of the Joint Director of Health and Family Welfare Chairperson; ii) an eminent woman representing women’s organisation; and iii) an officer of Law Department of the State or the Union territory concerned.
The functions of the appropriate authority includes to grant, suspend or cancel registration of a Genetic Counselling Centre, Genetic Laboratory or Genetic Clinic; to enforce standards prescribed for the Genetic Counselling Centre, Genetic Laboratory and Genetic Clinic; to investigate complaints of breach of the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder and take immediate action and to seek and consider the advice of the Advisory Committee.
The Supreme Court therefore held that the law has deliberately placed the investigation of such offences with this specialised authority.
So, can the police register an FIR?
Not for the purpose of independently investigating a violation of the Act.
The complication came from Section 27 of the law, which says that every offence under it is “cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable.” A cognisable offence ordinarily allows the police to investigate without first obtaining permission from a court.
But the Supreme Court said that Section 27 cannot be read on its own. It has to be read along with the provisions that specifically give the Appropriate Authority the power to investigate and Section 28, which lays down how a court can take up an offence under the Act.
The Court said, “The language of the statute, more particularly Sections 27 and 28 of the Act when read together, in light of the other provisions and the socially beneficial nature of the Act as also the requirement of sensitivity along with medical and technical know-how, indicates that the police are not meant to be the investigators for the purpose of this Act. This is further made clear by the fact that an FIR once registered cannot be taken to its logical conclusion as per the procedures of this Act. The restriction applies only to offences under this Act and does not restrict the police’s power to investigate or prosecute independent offences disclosed under substantive criminal law (IPC/BNS)”.
The Court held that allowing the police to independently investigate would undermine this specialised system.
It said, “the police are not meant to be the investigators for the purpose of this Act.”
The police can, however, assist the Appropriate Authority when their help is necessary. Rule 18A(3)(iv) says that police involvement should be avoided “as far as possible”. The Court held that this rule has statutory force.
The phrase does leave room for police assistance, but not for an independent police investigation. The Court said that, when involved, the police would have to act “strictly in a supplemental or aiding capacity.”
What happens if there is also another crime?
The Supreme Court has not said that the police have no role whenever a suspected sex-determination offence is involved. The police can investigate a separate offence under the IPC, BNS or another criminal law, even if it arises from the same incident.
For example, if the facts disclose both a violation of the sex-determination law and an independently constituted offence under general criminal law, the two investigations can proceed separately.
The Appropriate Authority would investigate the offence under the special law. The police would investigate the independent criminal offence.
But the police cannot use the existence of another offence as a way of taking over the sex-determination investigation. The Court’s concurring opinion makes the distinction clear: the police cannot use a general criminal offence “as a gateway to take over the PC & PNDT inquiry.”
Similarly, the special law cannot be used to prevent the police from investigating a genuinely separate criminal offence.
Can a Magistrate act on a police chargesheet?
No. This was the third question before the Supreme Court, and the Court’s answer was categorical.
Section 28 says that a court cannot take cognizance of an offence under the Act except through the complaint mechanism specified in the provision. A police chargesheet therefore cannot, by itself, give the Magistrate jurisdiction to take cognizance of a PC &PNDT offence.
The Appropriate Authority has to follow the procedure prescribed under the Act.
The Court concluded that there is a “complete statutory embargo” on taking cognizance except in the situations provided under Section 28.
What is the takeaway?
The immediate impact is on how a suspected illegal sex-determination case moves through the criminal justice system.
If information received by a police station discloses only a violation under the Act, the police should record the information and send it, along with the relevant material, to the Appropriate Authority. They should not independently investigate the offence.
If the information also reveals an independent cognizable offence under the IPC, BNS or another general criminal law, the police can investigate that offence while sending the sex-determination component to the Appropriate Authority.
The Supreme Court has also made clear that a police investigation cannot simply end with a chargesheet for the offence under the Act. Section 28 creates a separate route for bringing such a case before a court.
The ruling does not weaken the prohibition on prenatal sex determination. Instead, it clarifies who is responsible for enforcing it.

Chess.com has done one thing, and one thing very well, for almost 20 years, but now it’s going beyond its domain name. The biggest name in online chess quietly launched its first companion site in beta back in May: Gambit, a free online poker website where players can learn the game without risking any real money. Now Gambit’s ready to really get the ball rolling with its first livestreamed event and collaborations with content creators, and Chess.com is planning to branch out into even more games from here.
Chess.com launched a poker site and is planning even more classic games
Chess.com’s Albert Cheng says AI helped get Gambit off the ground with just a two-person team.
Chess.com’s chief growth officer, Albert Cheng, told The Verge the company chose poker for its first companion site because, like chess, it has learning and social elements on top of just playing the game. He also promised there will never be real-money gambling on Gambit, saying, “Real money is the problem we built Gambit to get away from, the whole industry makes money when beginners lose. We’d rather build a place where people can actually learn.”
Gambit will look familiar to anyone who’s used Chess.com. It borrows the same design style and includes similar play modes, like bot matches, games with friends, tournaments, a review mode for studying your past games, and a learning mode. Gambit even includes Chess.com’s bot characters, with matching skill levels — I immediately recognized “Martin,” the lowest skill level bot from Chess.com, who is also the lowest skill level bot on Gambit.
Chess.com also developed its own Elo-style rating system for Gambit. Cheng explained in an interview with The Verge that the rating system serves as the main motivator for players to improve: “You’re not gambling your own hard-earned money necessarily, so the stakes are lower from that standpoint, but you need something to counterbalance it that you care about, and that keeps the ecosystem in play, and keeps the poker that’s on Gambit reasonably high-quality.”
The rating system is also the backbone of Gambit’s paid subscription for access to premium learning features, following the same model Chess.com uses. “Our primary business model of Chess.com is a subscription, but most people play Chess.com for free,” Cheng said. “They subscribe to get unlimited access to review their games and to get unlimited puzzles, lessons, et cetera.” A reliable rating system allows players to track their improvement, potentially motivating them to pay for those premium features.
Rating systems are also at the heart of Chess’s next move. Chess.com is now looking to expand into even more classic games, including go, backgammon, and mahjong. Like Gambit, Chess.com is developing Elo-style rating systems for these games, as well. Cheng didn’t say when the new sites will launch but that “development is moving quite rapidly” on them, using the same playbook he used for Gambit.
AI is a key reason Chess.com was finally able to expand into other games after nearly 20 years, according to Cheng. He and one other employee took Gambit from prototype to launch within a year, partly with help from AI, mainly for coding tasks. “I think the biggest advantage that it’s provided is essentially being able to read our existing codebase and our design system and apply consistent patterns to how we develop Chess.com over to a different platform and do so quickly,” Cheng said.
He went on to add that there were also a lot of areas where AI struggles, such as brand and feature design. “I think that’s the best ultimate use of AI is that ultimately it’s going to be a blend, right?” Cheng said, adding, “Just because code is easier to write doesn’t mean that you just let it run on its own, but it certainly is a superpower in getting things off the ground.” Cheng also said the version of Gambit that’s live at the time of writing has “zero or close to zero” AI-created assets, which were used in early prototypes.
According to Cheng, without help from AI, getting another site up and running would have required a bigger team or “would have been a lot more disruptive to the status quo of building and growing Chess.” Now that a “small, scrappy” team can get a new platform off the ground much faster, it’s opened the door for Chess.com to dip into more games, starting with poker.
As Chess.com plans its next move, Cheng says they’re focusing on games with “both that classic durability plus the community around it,” like chess. Now that Gambit has launched, Cheng’s leaning into the community and social side of the platform more, following Chess.com’s lead, and getting content creators more involved. On August 31st at 12PM ET / 9AM PT, Gambit’s livestreaming its Gambit Cup for the first time on Twitch and YouTube with Chess.com co-founder Danny Rensch and chess content creator Alexandra Botez.
