Capital, SBI Capital Markets, DAM Capital Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026 Amagi Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services. The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price. Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr. Aye Finance Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO. In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses, listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. Fractal Founded in 2000 by Srikanth Velamakanni, Pranay Agrawal, and Ashwath Bhat, Fractal is a SaaS unicorn that offers AI-powered analytics solutions to enterprises globally. Backed by TPG Capital, Khazanah Nasional, and Apax Partners, the startup has raised $800 Mn to date. It achieved unicorn status in 2022 and was last valued at more than $2 Bn. In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI, and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025. The company’s ₹2,833.9 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,023.54 Cr and an OFS worth up to ₹1,810.4 Cr. The public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.66X, with investors placing bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 1.86 Cr on offer. Fractal’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the exchanges and listed at ₹876 on the NSE, a discount of 2.7% to the issue price of ₹900. On the BSE, the shares listed flat at ₹900. On the financial front, Fractal’s profit declined about 3% YoY to ₹70.9 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹1,559 Cr. Kissht Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a digital lending platform that offers personal and business loans up to ₹5 Lakh. It uses AI and machine learning to assess creditworthiness. It also offers health insurance products and credit against property. The startup has secured over $140 Mn till date from investors such as Vertex Growth, Brunei Investment Agency, Endiya Partners, and Ventureast. The lending tech startup filed its DRHP in August last year and received SEBI’s nod to proceed with its public listing in January 2026. As per its RHP, its IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹850 Cr and an OFS component of up to 44.4 Lakh shares. It had set a price band of ₹162-₹171 for the public issue, which was oversubscribed 9.5X. Subsequently, Kissht made a stellar debut on the bourses on May 8. The lending tech startup’s shares listed at ₹191 a piece on the BSE, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price of ₹171. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹190, up 11.1% from the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹199.3 Cr in 9M FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹1,569.9 Cr during the period under review. Klassroom Founded in 2016 by the mother-sons trio of Alka, Dhruv, and Dhumil Javeri, Klassroom is an edtech startup that operates at the intersection of offline and online coaching. It operates 30 offline partner centres that cater to both academic and skill-development needs. It also collaborates with state governments, private companies and education institutions to deliver academic and skilling programmes. The edtech startup also offers an AI-powered education OTT app that features over 100 courses for classes 8 to 12, and claims to have a footprint of over 4 Lakh registered users across the country. The startup raised over $2 Mn in private rounds from the likes of actor Suniel Shetty, ah! Ventures, LetsVenture, CPT Family Trust, Growth Sense and others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in February 2026, Klassroom filed its DRHP with the BSE for an SME IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to 19.89 Lakh shares and an OFS component of up to 4.66 Lakh shares. The startup subsequently received the in-principle approval from BSE to move ahead with its public offering in May 2026. It had set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for the issue, looking to raise ₹39 Cr at a valuation of ₹148.1 Cr. Subsequently, the startup’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 1.46X. Shares of Klassroom listed on the BSE SME on August 7 at ₹170, a premium of 6.92% to the issue price of ₹159. With this, the company became the second listed edtech startup in the country, after PhysicsWallah. On the financial front, Klassroom posted an operating revenue of ₹23 Cr in FY26, up 128% from around ₹10 Cr in the year prior. Meanwhile, net profit jumped nearly 162% to ₹7.6 Cr from ₹2.9 Cr in FY25. LEAP India A brainchild of Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions through asset pooling, enabling companies to share pallets, containers, and other assets. Founded in 2013, the platform also offers inventory management, transportation, returnable packaging and tool repair. It also sells electric and fossil fuel-powered forklifts through its subsidiary TRON. LEAP India has raised over $184 Mn till date from investors like KKR and Sixth Sense Ventures. The startup first attempted to list on the bourses in 2022, eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr listing. But the plan was later shelved amid market volatility. Reigniting its IPO plans, the logistics tech startup then filed its DRHP with SEBI in August 2025, and received SEBI’s nod in December 2025. In August 2026, the company filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹480 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹2,000 Cr. The company then set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for its public issue, which eventually closed with an oversubscription of 8.38X as investors bid for 96.32 Cr shares as against 11.49 Cr shares on offer. Shares of LEAP India eventually made their debut on the bourses on August 14, listing at a premium of about 4.4% to the issue price of ₹159. The stock got listed at ₹166 on the BSE and ₹165.90 on the NSE. Financially, LEAP India’s net profits zoomed 65.3% to ₹62.3 Cr in FY26 as against ₹37.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue climbed 56.4% to ₹729.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹466.5 Cr in FY25. SEDEMAC Founded in 2007 by IIT-Bombay professor Shashikanth Suryanarayana and his students Pushkaraj Panse, Amit Dixit, and Manish Sharma, SEDMAC designs electronic control systems for mobility and industrial applications. The deeptech company produces motor control units, integrated starter generators, fuel injection systems, genset controllers, and small industrial powertrains. Backed by Xponentia Capital Partners, A91 Partners, and 360 ONE Asset, SEDMAC has raised over $107 Mn to date. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the deeptech company filed its DRHP with SEBI in November 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in February 2026. Its public issue comprised solely an OFS component of up to 80.43 Lakh shares. The IPO was oversubscribed 2.68X, with investors cumulatively bidding for 1.51 Cr shares against 56.32 Lakh shares on offer. Shares of the company made a stellar debut on the exchanges on March 11, listing at a premium of 13.5% on the NSE. The stock opened at ₹1,535 as against the issue price of ₹1,352 per share. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹1,510, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price. SEDEMAC reported a net profit of ₹71.4 Cr in the first nine months of FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹770.66 Cr during the period under review. Shadowfax Founded in 2015 by Vaibhav Khandelwal and Abhishek Bansal, Shadowfax is a logistics company that offers hyperlocal and on-demand delivery solutions for businesses. Competing with the likes of Delhivery, LoadShare and Pickrr, the logistics major is backed by names such as Flipkart, Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India), IFC, Nokia Growth Partners, Qualcomm and Trifecta Capital. Shadowfax pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 for an IPO, and received markets regulator's nod in October 2025. It filed its updated DRHP with SEBI in November 2025. The company’s IPO comprised a fresh issue worth ₹1,000 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹907 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.72X, receiving total bids for 24.23 Cr shares against 8.9 Cr on offer. Subsequently, shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on January 28. The stock listed at ₹112.60 apiece on the NSE, a discount of 9.19% to the issue price of ₹124. On the BSE, shares of the logistics unicorn debuted at ₹113, down 8.87% below the issue price. In H1 FY26, the logistics unicorn’s net profit more than doubled to ₹21 Cr from ₹9.8 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue surged 68.4% YoY to ₹1,805.6 Cr during the period. Shiprocket Founded in 2017 by Saahil Goel, Vishesh Khurana, Akshay Gulati, and Gautam Kapoor, Shiprocket aggregates third-party logistics providers. It claims to partner 17 courier firms like Delhivery, FedEx, Aramex, Xpressbees, DTDC, and Shadowfax and serves over 24,000 pin codes across India. The logistics unicorn has raised over $323 Mn to date from investors like Temasek, Bertelsmann, Tribe Capital, Lightrock, and Zomato. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the Zomato-backed unicorn in May 2025 confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI and received the regulator’s approval in October 2025. Shiprocket then filed its RHP with the markets regulator in August 2026. The logistics major’s ₹1,617 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹885.5 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹732 Cr. Subsequently, in mid-August 2026, Shiprocket’s public issue opened to healthy market response and closed with an oversubscription of 99.38X, receiving bidding for 938.53 Cr shares against 9.44 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a strong debut on the D-Street on August 19. The stock listed at ₹131 on the NSE, marking a premium of 35.05% to the issue price of ₹97. On the BSE, it debuted at ₹129.50, a premium of 33.51%. On the financial front, Shiprocket’s operating revenue rose 24% to ₹2,024 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,632 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, net loss widened over 6% to ₹79.2 Cr during the fiscal from ₹74.5 Cr in FY25. Turtlemint Founded in 2015 by Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and Anand Prabhudesai, Turtlemint operates an insurtech platform that enables financial advisors to distribute car, bike, health, and term life insurance to their customer networks. The startup has raised more than $197 Mn to date from investors such as Amansa Capital, Jungle Ventures, Peak XV Partners, Vitruvian Partners, and Nexus Venture Partners. In September 2025, Turtlemint pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI, and secured market regulator’s approval three months later in December. Subsequently, the insurtech unicorn filed its RHP in June 2026. The IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹660.7 Cr and an OFS of 1.46 Cr shares. Its public issue opened on June 19 and closed on June 23, with an oversubscription of 1.2X. Despite this, the startup made a muted debut on the bourses on June 29. Shares of the insurtech startup listed at ₹134.90 on the NSE, a discount of 11.25% to the issue price of ₹152. Atomberg Founded in 2012 by Manoj Meena and Sibabrata Das, Atomberg began as a B2B supplier of energy-efficient BLDC fans before entering the D2C segment in 2016. It has since expanded to manufacture mixer grinders, water purifiers, and small appliances. The startup designs and manufactures its products in India and sells them via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. Backed by names such as Steadview Capital, Jungle Ventures and A91 Partners, Atomberg has raised over $126 Mn in funding to date. Taking the first step towards its public listing, the D2C appliance brand, in July 2026, converted into a public entity and changed the name of its parent entity from Atomberg Technologies Pvt Ltd to Atomberg Technologies Ltd. In August 2026, the startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹450 Cr and an OFS of up to 7.65 Cr shares. On the financial front, Atomberg’s losses widened 26.5% to ₹149 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹117.8 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 34.8% to ₹1,293.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹959.5 Cr in FY25. AVPL International (AITMC Ventures) Founded in 2016 by Preet Sandhuu and Deep Sisai, AITMC sits at the intersection of agriculture and drones. In July 2025, AITMC once again kicked off its IPO plans as the company’s board approved a proposal to increase the fresh issue size of its IPO to ₹200 Cr from ₹125 Cr previously. AITMC then filed its draft papers with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in October 2025. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. That earlier plan was shelved after AITMC signed a term sheet in January 2025 for a strategic merger with BSE SME-listed DroneAcharya, a deal that ultimately fell through. On the financial front, AITMC Ventures’ net profit climbed 59% to ₹14 Cr in FY25 from ₹8.8 Cr a fiscal earlier, while operating revenue zoomed 87% to ₹87.5 Cr as against ₹46.8 Cr in FY24. boAt Founded in 2016 by Aman Gupta and Sameer Mehta, boAt is a D2C consumer electronics brand that sells headphones, smartwatches, speakers, and other audio wearables. In October 2025, boAt filed its updated DRHP for an ₹1,500 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to ₹500 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹1,000 Cr. C5i Founded in 2000 by Ashwin Mittal, C5i (formerly known as Course5 Intelligence) is an enterprise AI company that helps large businesses automate tasks and turn data into actionable insights. The platform first attempted to go public in 2022, targeting a ₹600 Cr IPO, but later shelved the plans due to weak market conditions. Reigniting its IPO ambitions, the startup once again filed its DRHP with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in July 2026. C5i is now looking to raise about ₹1,000-1,200 Cr via the public issue. On the financial front, C5i’s consolidated net profit declined 15% to ₹48.3 Cr in FY25 as against ₹56.7 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile its operating revenue surged 26% to ₹545.3 Cr from ₹431.4 Cr in FY24. Curefoods Founded in 2020 by Ankit Nagori, Curefoods is a cloud kitchen unicorn that manages brands like EatFit, CakeZone, Nomad Pizza, Sharief Bhai Biryani, and Frozen Bottle. It claims to operate over 200 cloud kitchens and offline outlets across 70 Indian cities. The startup has raised over $175 Mn from backers including Iron Pillar, Accel, Three State Ventures, Chiratae Ventures, and ASK Finance. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, Curefoods filed its DRHP with SEBI in late June 2025 and received markets regulator’s approval in late October. As per the DRHP, the proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to ₹800 Cr and an offer-for-sale of up to 4.85 Cr equity shares. However, in June 2026, the startup took a U-turn and put its IPO plans on hold amid the turmoil in the Indian equities market and concerns over its potential valuation. As per reports, mutual funds were not aligned with the ₹4,000 Cr (about $419 Mn) valuation sought by Curefoods during its roadshows. On the financial front, Curefoods' net loss remained steady at ₹169.9 Cr in FY25 as against ₹172.6 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 27.4% to ₹745.8 Cr compared to ₹585.1 Cr in FY24. ESDS Software Solution Founded in 2005 by Piyush Somani, ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. It operates five data centres in Navi Mumbai, Nashik, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Noida. The data centre company claims to have served 2,501 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with an average revenue per customer of around ₹19 Lakh. Backed by ace investor Ashish Kacholia, ESDS Software Solution has raised nearly $47.3 Mn in funding to date. ESDS first attempted to go public in September 2021 but the plan failed to materialise due to aftershocks of the pandemic. The company then refiled its papers in March 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in December 2025. As per its RHP, ESDS Software Solution’s public issue consists entirely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹720 Cr. It also set a price band of ₹408 to ₹429 per share for its IPO, valuing the company at ₹5,028 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. Its public issue opened for subscription on August 28 and was subscribed 2.1X on the first day of bidding, receiving bids for 2.60 Cr shares against 1.24 Cr shares on offer. The IPO will now close on September 4. On the financial front, the company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹120.8 Cr in FY26, up 117% from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25. Fibe Founded in 2015 by Akshay Mehrotra and Ashish Goyal as EarlySalary, Fibe initially offered salary advances and small-ticket personal loans to young working professionals. Today, it offers personal loans and purpose-driven financing solutions across sectors such as education, insurance, healthcare, rooftop solar and travel. It claims to operate a merchant network spanning 10,387 touchpoints across India, and claims to have ₹8,603 Cr in assets under management as of March 2026. On the financial front, Fibe saw its net profit more than double to ₹257.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹113.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue surged 31% to ₹1,584.6 Cr from ₹1,208.9 Cr in FY25. Garuda Aerospace Founded in 2015 by Agnishwar Jayaprakash and Rithika Mohann, Garuda Aerospace manufactures over 30 types of drones, while also offering drone-as-a-service (DaaS) solutions. It claims to have trained over 1 Lakh drone pilots, serving more than 100 government agencies along with over 500 enterprises. Backed by cricketer MS Dhoni, Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle and Ocgrow Ventures, Garuda Aerospace has raised more than $37.1 Mn in funding to date. Eventually in April 2026, the Chennai-based dronetech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. While the exact size of the IPO is yet to be determined, the company’s board, in March, approved a proposal to raise up to ₹750 Cr via fresh issue of shares and an undisclosed OFS component. The startup bagged SEBI’s approval for its IPO in August 2026. On the financial front, Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹11 Cr in H1 FY26 against an operating revenue of ₹41.2 Cr. InCred Holdings Founded in 2016 by Bhupinder Singh, InCred Group runs three distinct business verticals. InCred Holdings reported a 5.3% jump in net profit to ₹290 Cr in 9M FY26 from ₹275.5 Cr during the same period last fiscal. Operating revenue also surged 38.6% to ₹1,848.9 Cr from ₹1,333.9 Cr in 9M FY25. Infra.Market Founded in 2016 by Souvik Sengupta and Aaditya Sharda, Infra.Market runs a B2B marketplace that helps customers procure construction materials like concrete, steel, pipes, fittings, and chemicals. The startup has raised over $415 Mn till date from investors such as Tiger Global, Accel, and Nexus Ventures. Kuku Founded in 2018 by Lal Chand Bisu,Vikas Goyal and Vinod Kumar Meena, Kuku is an audio-centric OTT platform that hosts audiobooks, podcasts, and original shows under Kuku FM in multiple Indian languages. It also operates a vernacular short-video app under Kuku TV brand and a microlearning platform Guru. MakeMyTrip Launched in 2000 by Keyur Joshi, Rajesh Magow, and Deep Kalra, MakeMyTrip is an online travel aggregator (OTA) that operates an end-to-end platform for booking flights, hotels and holiday packages. It also offers ancillary services such as forex cards and travel insurance. In Summary
- A decade ago, Indian brands commanded a large chunk of the Indian smartphone market. In Q2 2016, three of the top five smartphone brands were Indian ones.
- The arrival of Chinese brands and changes in the market led to the decline and exit of many Indian phone brands. Today, while brands like Lava and AI+ exist, their market shares are nothing compared to Indian brands of the past.
- Rising smartphone prices and memory costs seem to have opened the door for Indian smartphone brands, with new brands emerging and old ones looking to make a comeback, with encouragement and support from the Government. But is this just a temporary phase, or will Indian brands win back the market dominance they lost almost a decade ago?
When I first started covering technology, the Indian smartphone market looked extremely different from what it does today. Today, there are barely any Indian brands among the major smartphone brands in the Indian market – Counterpoint’s report on Q2 2026 showed not a single Indian brand among the top eight smartphone brands in the Indian market. Yes, some Indian smartphone brands do exist, such as the persistent Lava and the newcomer AI+, but they do not command significant market shares.
The story was extremely different a decade ago.
It may be hard to believe, especially for those who have started following smartphone trends in India since 2017, but in mid-2016, Indian tech brands were not just surviving but ruling the smartphone charts. IDC’s report for Q2 2016 placed three Indian brands in the top five smartphone brands in the country – Micromax, Intex and Reliance Jio (this was around the time of the 4G revolution).
And this was not because of a lack of competition. The Indian market was home to a number of high-profile foreign smartphone players like Apple, Samsung, HTC, BlackBerry, LG, Sony, and Motorola were very much present in the Indian market, and the likes of OnePlus, Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo had also arrived in the market. Still, Indian brands like Micromax, Intex, Spice, and Karbonn dominated sales charts for multiple and sometimes even consecutive quarters. In fact, in Q2 2014, Micromax even overtook Samsung to be the number one smartphone brand in the country in terms of shipments. It was a time when we carried a story on how Micromax deserved to be shown more respect.
Ghosts of the Indian smartphone market past: Why Indian brands ruled, and how the Chinese brands beat them
There was a reason for this dominance. At that point of time, Indian smartphone brands mainly catered to the budget segment, mostly under Rs. 15,000 (or even Rs 10,000), which comprised a large chunk of the smartphone market. While international brands had tried to enter this segment, they had very limited success, as they could not match the price-to-spec ratio that the Indian brands were offering. Big displays, big batteries, and decent processors (often from the more affordable MediaTek) and a small price tag made phones from the likes of Micromax, Intex, and Karbonn the perfect pick for anyone looking to pick up an entry-level smartphone. The likes of Apple, Samsung, HTC, Sony, and BlackBerry were largely operating in the mid/ upper mid and premium segment.
The tech climate changed as Chinese brands began to make their presence felt. Xiaomi, OnePlus, Vivo, and Oppo all stepped into the Indian market in 2014. Oppo and Vivo seemed to be playing in the premium segment, while brands like Xiaomi and OnePlus initially seemed to focus on flagship killers (a term OnePlus popularised). However, given India’s demography, it did not take a long time for these brands to realize that real numbers were actually in the budget and mid segment.
Even as Indian brands struggled with inventory issues as the 4G revolution hit India, the Chinese brands shifted focus and brought in smartphones with prices and spec combinations that matched and, in many cases, even eclipsed what Indian brands were offering. That was not all.
With the mobile Internet becoming more accessible thanks to extremely affordable 4G rates (pioneered mainly by Reliance Jio), these brands also opted for a very unconventional plan of action, going for flash sales, online only sales, often with little to no advertising in mainstream media, and building communities online. These not only cut expenses, but built greater brand loyalty (something Indian brands had been unable to do, as they had focused mainly on price). This combination of pricing and communications affected all the other brands in the market, but hit the Indian brands particularly hard, as it took away their biggest USP – a low price tag. The years that followed saw not just Indian brands fade, but even the likes of LG, Sony and HTC bid farewell to the Indian market.
The Indian Smartphone Market Today: Rocked by a steep price rise
In the last ten years, the Indian smartphone market has changed completely. Many Indian brands that had seemed almost invincible have packed their bags and left, although some like Lava have managed to stick around, in spite of not being the force they once were. But the tech stars in the tech universe move in different ways, and the way in which they have been aligning in recent times makes me think that the time is ripe for Indian smartphone brands to make a comeback in their own market.
Hear me out before you think I am talking through my hat. We have seen a very steady shift happening in the tech world in 2026. Many brands that earlier ruled the budget, mid, and lower-mid segments have been climbing up the price ladder for a while now, seeking larger profit margins. Indeed, the number of phones available in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment has been shrinking in recent times, with many brands seemingly inching towards vacating it altogether.
The likes of Motorola, OnePlus and Xiaomi are also no longer organizations with lean portfolios and small, focused teams but have become tech behemoths with large-scale operations, huge marketing budgets, multiple sub-brands and extensive product portfolios. This has, of course, affected their ability to offer the extremely competitive price-spec combo that made them popular in the first place.
The dramatic increase in the price of memory has now made it even more difficult for existing brands to offer good devices at lower price points. Devices with specs that used to be seen in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment are now being seen at prices in the range of Rs 25,000 or more. Options at lower price points are either vanishing or are coming with relatively modest specs.
And Indian brands are suddenly appearing on the horizon again.
Guess who’s back, back again… Indian smartphone brands
White Lava had never left; it seems to have got a new lease of life. AI+ is increasingly aggressive, and Fire-Boltt, a brand known more for its wearables and hearables, has entered the smartphone market. Even as this is being written, Mivi, a mainly audio brand, has announced plans for a smartphone with a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor for under Rs 15,000, and there is also talk of Micromax returning to the market, and Boat (which, like Fire-Boltt, is known mainly for audio and wearable products) is also planning to sail in smartphone waters. And from what we know, all these brands are targeting the sub-Rs 15,000 market, from which many brands have moved products to higher price points and/ or releasing new devices with much more modest specs in the past.
The Indian Government is also making efforts to build a smartphone brand that it can call its own. On August 21, it officially sent out a notification, as per which the Union Cabinet approved a budget of Rs. 62,500 crore for a Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) to build globally competitive, native smartphone brands. The scheme offers a number of incentives and rewards for Indian brands. To qualify, a company must be registered in India, keep its ownership and trademarks in India, have more than 51 percent Indian shareholding, be controlled in India, and have its products designed locally without outsourcing. This is a massive push and is likely to encourage more Indian entrepreneurs to enter the smartphone market.
Welcome back, Indian brands, but this time, please stay!
But making a comeback will not be enough. The smartphone world has changed a fair bit since the time Indian brands ruled the charts. And the new ones or those making a comeback would need to adopt a fundamentally different approach to ensure that the second innings of Indian brands in the smartphone market is a long one, and does not end as abruptly as the first. Being an ‘Indian brand’ has to have a different connotation than it did in the past.
Indian brands have struggled with offering good after-sales service and good software, and have tended to compete mainly on price and specs. That needs to change. The new and not-so-new native brands have to ensure they not just deliver a smartphone at a competitive price, but follow through on the whole process that comes after. Easy access to repairs and spare parts, timely OS updates, and improved, new-age marketing strategies are all necessities for these brands to actually establish themselves in this competitive market for the long run.
Native brands also need to shed their image of merely assembling and/or importing devices from outside and rebranding them for the Indian market. Authentic and good quality products backed up with a solid sales and service system are both needed to make consumers associate Indian brands not just with low prices, but also with high quality.
As of now, Indian brands are knocking on the door of their nation’s smartphone market once again. Just how well they will do, only time will tell. While I am hoping their second coming will be a successful one and they will win back lost ground (more local brands are always welcome in any market, and the big five out there need competition), there is no way of knowing how things will actually work out. Who knows, if I am still here, covering tech a decade later, I might be telling you a completely different story altogether.
A decade is a VERY long time in tech. Stay tuned.

Lights out, Instagram off? The changes to Meta for teens could be a big deal
Meta settlement means new restrictions on nighttime and school-time scrolling for kids
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The social media company Meta has agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion in a settlement in a federal lawsuit alleging the company's social media platforms have harmed children and teens. The company denies the allegations, but has agreed to make a suite of changes to its social platforms — Facebook and Instagram — to make them less compelling and potentially dangerous to minors.
This comes at a time when healthcare providers are increasingly seeing symptoms of social media addiction among youth, says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, who is the Co-Director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.
"We know that about 50% of kids are reporting at least one symptom of clinical dependency on social media," he says. "We know that kids who are having a difficult time getting off social media are also reporting more depression, loneliness, anxiety, even suicidality over time."
While Meta denies the allegations that it designed its social platforms to be addictive for kids, child safety advocates and researchers have welcomed the settlement as a major development in holding tech companies accountable.
"This settlement isn't perfect, but I do think it's a critical first step in making sure platforms are safer for our children and that our kids can grow up healthy," says Julie Scelfo, founder of the grassroots organization Mothers Against Media Addiction.
The changes Meta will have to make are intended to reduce the addictiveness of Facebook and Instagram. For example, it will have to give minors the option of having a non-personalized feed, where it doesn't use an algorithm to tailor content based on individual preferences to keep kids scrolling. The changes are detailed in a press release from California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led a coalition of 50 states and territories and the District of Columbia that settled with Meta.
The other reforms Meta has agreed to for people under 18 include:
- a default daily time limit of two hours for minors, with only parents having the ability to opt kids out.
- a default block on nighttime use from midnight to 6 a.m.
- a default block on notifications to minors – both overnight, and from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year.
- a ban on showing minors how many likes or reactions their posts receive.
- a ban on cosmetic procedure image filters.
- a better system for teens to report potentially harmful content and a commitment that Meta respond to 90% of those reports within six hours.
Meta is also promising to do a better job of verifying users' ages and has agreed to report regularly to an independent auditor.
Meta is calling on other social media companies to make the same changes, and has negotiated that $5 billion of the settlement will be paid to states if other companies join the effort. Texas negotiated an additional $1 billion settlement with Meta.
"This framework will only work if all our peers join us," Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. "Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away."
Enthusiastic reception from experts
"It is very exciting to see that a lot of the changes that are written into the settlement are very similar to what we saw scientifically," says Prinstein, who was scheduled to testify next week in the case brought by the states.
For example, he says, studies show why the design elements of Facebook and Instagram are particularly addictive for teens and pre-teens.
"By the time a kid turns around ten or 11, the part of their brain that makes them suddenly super interested in things like popularity and who sits at the lunch table are really showing a hypersensitivity to social signals," he says. And so, when kids encounter constant notifications about followers, likes, and dislikes on social media accounts, it easily leads to time spent on these platforms.
"We saw kids unable to stop themselves on these platforms," explains Prinstein. "They would tell us, 'I have tried to quit and I can't. It's interfering with my daily roles and routines.'"
So turning off notifications during school days and overnight should help lower problematic use by minors, he adds.
Making sleep a priority
Similarly, the block on nighttime use could make a big difference to teen mental health, says Dr. Jason Nagata, a pediatrician and researcher at the University of California, San Francisco.
His analysis of the longitudinal Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, where researchers have followed thousands of children as they grow up, shows that a big proportion of teens are using their cell phones between midnight and 4 a.m.
"The most used app category during this period was social media," says Nagata. "So I think that it is likely that most of these teenagers are … on social media and getting the notifications and kind of distractions that are impairing their sleep."
And sufficient sleep is key to teen brain development and mental wellness.
Implementation will be important
But Nagata and Prinstein also caution that it remains to be seen whether these changes required by the settlement actually will have the desired effect on kids' experience of social media and their mental health.
"I do think that the details of the implementation are really important," says Nagata. "What we have found, even in some of the testimony during this case, is that it's actually very hard to get some of these things to work."
He is referring to some of the changes Meta had already made on its apps, like the "Take a Break" feature on Instagram, which reminds teen users to close the app after they have been on it for a certain length of time. As Instagram head Adam Mosseri testified in court, the feature wasn't as effective as they had hoped.
"We really need to know how this is going to be implemented," says Nagata, "and then I do think that this needs to be rigorously evaluated. It's not just like we're going to make some changes and then that's it."
Prinstein agrees. "We still need research to make sure that these changes are actually helping, and they're not in some ways making kids worse or kids are finding sneaky ways around them," he says. "So we still have some work to do."
The settlement does include an agreement from Meta "to maintain, review, and improve existing teen content safety measures" and to "create enhanced parent supervision tools."

Excel Entertainment’s Mirzapur The Movie is one of the most keenly-awaited films of the year. Directed by Gurmmeet Singh, it stars Ali Fazal, Divyenndu, Pankaj Tripathi, Jitendra Kumar, Ravi Kishan, Rasika Dugal, Shweta Tripathi, Shriya Pilgaonkar, among others. The film is special since it is based on the web series Mirzapur, which is a big hit on OTT. It has had three successful seasons on Amazon Prime Video. The film is expected to take a strong opening.
Mirzapur The Movie is not the first Indian film based on a web series, this regional project did it less than a month ago
It is widely believed that Mirzapur The Movie is the first film in India to be based on a web series that will have a release in theatres. However, that is not quite the case.
In 2018, the Punjabi web series Yaar Jigree Kasooti Degree became one of the most loved shows in the language. Written, directed and created by Rabby Tiwana, it starred Pukhraj Bhalla, Karan Sandhawalia, Sukhdeep Sapra, Amrit Amby, Prateek Singh Rai and Karanvir Deol.
Yaar Jigree Kasooti Degree told the story of love, friendship and struggles of the students of a university in Punjab. It was aired on Troll Punjabi YouTube channel in September 2018 and gained popularity. Hence, the makers came up with its second season in September 2020, which released on the same YouTube channel.
Following the success and popularity of its two seasons, the makers of the show announced a theatrical film on the show also titled Yaar Jigree Kasooti Degree in 2025 with the same cast and some new names. Interestingly, the film released in theatres just earlier this month on August 7, which is less than a month before the release of Mirzapur The Movie on September 4.
Therefore, Yaar Jigree Kasooti Degree became the first Indian theatrical film based on a web series. However, one can’t deny that Mirzapur The Movie is the first time that a Hindi web series has been made into a theatrical film.

India’s sovereign-backed private investor National Investment and Infrastructure Fund Ltd. (NIIF) has raised ₹19,000 crore, or $2 billion, in the first close of its NIIF Infrastructure Fund II from large global and domestic institutional investors.
The firm is targeting $3.2 billion in total commitments and expects some of its marquee investors to allocate an additional $950 million towards co-investment opportunities, it said in a statement.
The capital will be deployed across core infrastructure sectors including energy, transport and digital infrastructure, while expanding into emerging themes such as urban infrastructure and electric mobility.
Broader mandate
“The strategy for fund two will remain the same. In addition to investing in sectors such as transportation, energy, and digital, we are looking at adding EV and urban sectors to the deployment plan for Fund 2” said Vinod Giri, managing partner, infrastructure at NIIF, in an interview with Mint.
“The opportunity set in India across sectors has scaled up in a very significant manner. We are looking at investing at least on the opportunity set just two and half times of what you have done investing into infrastructure over the last five to seven years,” he added.
Anchored by the government of India, the fund saw global investors such as AustralianSuper, CPP Investments, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan and Temasek come in as limited partners, or LPs.
Large domestic institutional investors such as ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, Axis Bank, Kotak Life Insurance and HDFC Life Insurance have also committed capital to the fund.
Co-investment pool
Alongside the Fund, NIIF expects to mobilize approximately ₹9,000 crore ($950 million) in co-investment capital, enabling investors to participate at scale in select transactions, the firm said. Its first fund did not have co-investment built into it.
“The first close is with existing investors of Fund One. Majority of our existing investors are reupping their commitments. That's a big sign off on India infrastructure and the execution track record that NIIF has executed in originating the right transaction, managing and exiting it well. We are looking at a sizeable co-investment pool to be able to be exercised alongside the fund. So, this is India's largest infrastructure-focused fund,” Giri said.
The firm will soon start deploying from the second fund, having built a strong pipeline of opportunities it has lined up, said Giri.
Infrastructure Fund II builds on NIIF’s first infrastructure fund, which raised ₹16,000 crore ($2.34 billion) and has invested across renewables, transmission, distribution, battery storage, roads, ports and logistics, airports, data centres and smart metering. The first fund, says Giri, is “fully committed and significantly deployed.”
First fund track record
Through the first fund, the firm has invested in companies such as Hindustan Infralog Private Limited and Hindustan Ports Private Ltd through its operating partner DP World; in road platform Athaang, which is wholly owned by NIIF; in airports sector firms such as MOPA Airport and Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport through its operating partner GMR Group; in data centre firm Digital Edge; in wireless solutions provider iBus Networks; its renewable energy platform Ayana Energy; smart metering platform IntelliSmart, among others.
The firm has also successfully exited its investments in Ayana and is in the last leg of a deal to sell its stake in IntelliSmart. Within its road platform, it has sold some of its select road assets too to deliver close to 50% DPI (distributed to paid-in capital), a key performance metric in private equity that measures the actual cash returned to investors against the investments received.
“We currently are at a DPI of close to 50%, and our DPI should improve once the smart metering transaction (exit) is consummated. So good exit track record as well,” Giri said.
“Publicly listed infrastructure InvITs are really emerging as a very attractive opportunity for investors like us to monetize our investments. And the way you see large commercial ReITs operating in the country, having a good track record on cash distribution and performance, I would see InvIT emerging as a very attractive asset class for investors like us.”
Including the infrastructure fund, NIIF manages more $7 billion in equity capital commitments across four strategies such as private markets, growth equity and climate investments.

Retired Bengal couple returns from Nepal, recounts narrow escape
The group turned back from around one-and-a-half hours driving distance from Rasuwa, which the flood tore through on August 26, the couple told reporters.
A couple from Basirhat in West Bengal's North 24 Parganas district, who had been in the vicinity of the flash flood-affected area in Nepal, came back home on Sunday and recounted days of anxiety before their safe return.
Retired schoolteachers Anukul Poddar and his wife Reba Roy Poddar, who were in a group of 17 pilgrims on the Mansarovar Yatra with a travel agency, said their tour manager received the news of the disaster and the driver reversed the vehicle in the nick of time.
The group turned back from around one-and-a-half hours driving distance from Rasuwa, which the flood tore through on August 26, the couple told reporters.
Deep Dive
"We had set out around 6:30 am in a convoy of vehicles carrying Bengali and South Indian tourists. About two hours into the journey, our driver spotted water cascading down a hillside at a distance, followed by what looked like white smoke moving down a river," Reba said.
"We could see people running, children crying. That is when we realised something terrible had happened," she said.
The driver moved the vehicle to higher ground before their manager learnt over the phone that a bridge on the route to the immigration office had been washed away in the flash flood, cutting off further travel.
"We saw shops quickly downing shutters and schoolchildren running uphill," he said.
Anukul said they had planned to cross into Tibet on August 27, but instead reached Birgunj, a Nepal town bordering Bihar on Friday on the way home.
While the administration of Basirhat sub-division had advised them to fly to Kolkata from Patna, they said they did not have the courage to travel from Raxaul to Patna, and chose to return with the rest of the group by train.
They reached Howrah station on Sunday aboard the Mithila Express and were received by a team of the Basirhat police station, which escorted them home under state government arrangements.
Another retired couple from Basirhat - Swapan Mondal and Mou Mondal - who were also on the trip but with a different travel agency, remain untraced.

Suvendu Adhikari outlines Bengal govt's big moves after last year's Lionel Messi tour chaos
Suvendu Adhikari told sports minister Indranil Khan to ensure that football players and other sportspersons from the state participate in world tournaments.
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday called upon sports minister Indranil Khan to ensure that representatives from the state become part of the national football team.
Addressing a programme to mark National Sports Day in Kolkata, Adhikari referred to the Lionel Messi event at Salt Lake Stadium on December 13 last year, describing the episode as a "big scandal". He said that around 33,000 young football fans were deprived of the opportunity to see the Argentine star despite paying high ticket prices.
"I have started an internal process to give an international feel to football lovers," he said, without elaborating.
Adhikari told Khan to ensure that football players and other sportspersons from the state participate in world tournaments such as the Commonwealth Games and South Asian Federation (SAF) Games.
Suvendu says previous governments ‘politicised’ sports
Claiming that the previous governments in West Bengal had politicised sports, Suvendu Adhikari said sports organisations and federations should not be controlled by politicians.
"No sports organisation and federation should be influenced by and helmed by politicians. MPs and MLAs should not run the show. Why should sports organisations have politicians at the top?" he asked.
He directed sports minister Indranil Khan to “change the system”.
Adhikari said his government had earmarked ₹400 crore for sports in the budget and would spend more.
"We are here for only 110 days," he said, apparently referring to the tenure of his government.
He said the BJP government would introduce indoor stadiums in all 294 Assembly constituencies, with each facility to be named after Sri Aurobindo.
Adhikari said the files of budding sportspersons who received appointment letters and cheques at the event had allegedly remained pending in the Chief Minister's Office for years during the previous government.
"When we see neighbouring Odisha, Jharkhand and Haryana making the country proud with the feats of their athletes and other delegations at international meets, we must also recognise the immense possibilities of our sportspersons and introspect on how to nurture them," he said.
"We have to see where West Bengal lacks. What is the reason behind the fallen motivation of our sporting talents so far?" Adhikari said.
Lamenting the alleged lack of support, inspiration, and initiative from previous governments, he said that appointment letters and financial assistance would motivate young talent to bring laurels to the country at international competitions.

Guinea-Bissau votes in a referendum on granting the president expanded powers
Guinea-Bissau is voting in a referendum to decide on granting new presidential powers
BISSAU, Guinea-Bissau -- BISSAU, Guinea-Bissau (AP) — Guinea-Bissau was voting Sunday in a referendum to decide on granting new presidential powers ahead of December's general election, which will return the West African nation to democracy after its latest coup.
There was a low turnout across many voting stations after the opposition urged voters to boycott the referendum, saying it would make the head of the military government more powerful.
The military government seized power in November of last year following a disputed election in which former President Umaro Sissoco Embaló and opposition candidate Fernando Dias both claimed victory.
If passed, the new constitution by the self-styled National Transitional Council will grant more powers to the president and reduce parliamentary representation, among other issues.
The authorities argue that a parliament trimmed from 102 to 65 seats would allow for easier and more robust debates, while new presidential powers would underline the higher authority of the president over the prime minister, which they claim is a source of political instability in the country. Opposition groups reject the claim.
“In a community, there is only one leader. No community or village can have two leaders. We revised the constitution to avoid constant conflict between the president of the republic and the prime minister. We clarified the law and helped the public understand that the president of the republic is the national symbol. It is the president who stands for election in presidential polls,” Gen. Tomás Djassi, the head of the armed forces, said.
But the opposition has called on voters to boycott the referendum, saying it is a path for the head of the military government to amass power and calling it a "source of political instability at all levels".
“This constitution significantly weakens the prime minister and the government, subordinates the National People’s Assembly and political parties, and devalues — or even ignores — the popular will expressed at the polls, carrying all the attendant risks of political and social division and tension,” Muniro Conté, spokesperson for the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde, told The Associated Press.
Last year's coup in Guinea-Bissau worsened West Africa's democratic crisis, adding it to a growing number of countries in the region under military rule.
Leaders on the continent branded it a “staged” takeover after the military allowed the former president to host a press conference to announce he was being deposed and allowed to leave the country in seemingly favorable circumstances. Skeptics say Embaló had given up the seat to the military after seeing he was losing the election.
Since it gained independence from Portugal in 1973, the only Portuguese-speaking country in West Africa has been rocked by several coups and attempted coups. Before last year’s coup, a failed coup was reported only a month before.
The tiny country of around 2.2 million people has the highest proportion of natural wealth per capita in West Africa, according to the World Bank, but more than half of the country lives in poverty. The country is a hub for drug trafficking between Latin America and Europe, an issue experts say fuels its political instability.
Nearly 915,000 voters are registered to vote in the referendum, but the majority say the constitution is not a problem.
Bacar Camará, a high school teacher in the capital, Bissau, said he would not be voting and disapproves of the referendum, citing a fraught political and social environment.
“The transitional government should focus on creating conditions for better understanding and reconciliation among Guineans,” he said.
Another resident in Bissau, Carolina Djeme, said the constitution is unfamiliar to her.
"I’ll go vote on Sunday. However, I’ll vote ‘no’ because — honestly, and I think this is the case for many other citizens — I don’t know this new constitution well, so I can’t vote ‘yes’,” she said.
Analysts say the military government lacks the legitimacy to change the constitution, which has sparked discontent among the citizens.
“The fundamental question is: Who drafted this constitution, and on whose behalf? To protect which interests or institutions? Who stands to benefit from this constitution?” Paulino Quadé, a Guinean political analyst, said.

Singapore's young table tennis team confident but face 'uphill battle' at Asian Games
"The standard of competition at the Asian Games will be exceptionally high," said STTA president Poh Li San.
SINGAPORE: After a number of encouraging performances, Singapore's young table tennis team will depart for the upcoming Asian Games confident but aware of the magnitude of the task ahead.
Speaking at a squad announcement press conference at OCBC Arena on Monday (Aug 31), Singapore Table Tennis Association (STTA) chief Poh Li San said that the 10-member contingent faces an "uphill battle" in Japan.
"As we head out to Aichi-Nagoya with confidence, we are cognizant that it's an uphill battle. Asia is home to many of the world's strongest table tennis nations, the standard of competition at the Asian Games will be exceptionally high," said Ms Poh, who was re-elected unopposed as STTA president last week. She is also MP for Sembawang West SMC.
"Competition will be even steeper than in the Olympics right from the start. But iron will sharpen iron, and I'm sure our athletes will savour every moment of this very precious experience, compete fiercely and give their 120 per cent for Singapore."
At next month's Games, Singapore will be fielding a team with an average age of 22.
Coached by Gao Ning, the men's team comprises Izaac Quek, Clarence Chew and Koen Pang, with Josh Chua and Ellsworth Le making their Games debut. The women's team is made up of Zeng Jian and Ser Lin Qian, along with debutants Tan Zhao Yun, Chloe Lai and Loy Ming Ying. They will be led by Jing Junhong.
"They are young, they are courageous, they are fearless, hardworking, disciplined," said Ms Poh of the debutants. "And they have been working every hard in the months leading up to the Asian Games."
The team will depart on Monday for a centralised training camp in Shimada, Shizuoka, before making the trip to Nagoya. The Games will be held from Sep 19 to Oct 4.
'WE DON'T SET ANY GOALS FOR OUR TEAM'
After clinching at least one table tennis medal from the 2002 to 2018 edition of the Games, Singapore's streak ended at the last edition of the Games in Hangzhou, China.
"This question is always asked at every press conference, and my answer will be consistent: we don't set any goals for our team. All we want, especially for this very young team, is to go out there, do their very best, go out there to fight for every point," said Ms Poh, when asked what targets STTA had set for the contingent.
"Because at the end, it's more important that they are able to make their own breakthrough, able to play their very best game in this competition. And the results will follow."
Singapore's table tennis players have registered some creditable results in recent times. The women's team clinched a joint-bronze at last year's Asian Table Tennis Team Championships, with the men taking home three golds at the 2025 SEA Games.
Speaking to reporters, Quek said he wanted to progress at least a round further than he did at the previous Games. In Hangzhou, he was eliminated in the men's singles round of 32, and the men's doubles round of 16.
Quek won three golds at the 2025 SEA Games, and along with Pang is ranked 10th in the world for men's doubles.
Said the 20-year-old: "At the Asian Games level, each opponent is extremely strong. I hope we can fight hard as a team."

Mondelez India Foods, maker of Bournvita and Cadbury products, has withdrawn health and nutrient-comparison claims flagged by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), along with related advertisements from e-commerce platforms, as the regulator steps up action against misleading food claims.
The action is part of a wider drive in which FSSAI has issued more than 150 notices to food companies over misleading advertisements, false claims and labelling violations. Nestlé India, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola India, Abbott India, Red Bull India, Danone India, Monster Energy India, Ferrero India and Kenvue are among companies named by the regulator.
Bournvita had come under scrutiny in 2023 over its sugar content and nutritional claims, particularly its marketing to children.
The latest corrective-action drive has also prompted Amway India to remove “100%” from its “100% Pure Coconut Oil” packaging and promotional material and drop the “Energy Drink” descriptor from its caffeinated XS range. Keralam-based Juza Foods has agreed to withdraw claims including “boost immunity”, “support stronger bones” and comparative calcium claims from its baby-food products.
The action follows FSSAI’s May 2025 advisory asking food businesses to discontinue the use of “100%” on labels, packaging and promotional material, arguing that the term could imply absolute purity or superiority.
The FSSAI has also widened enforcement to e-commerce platforms and food-service establishments, issuing 12 notices to e-commerce companies and more than 30 to food-service establishments, including major restaurant chains.
The regulator’s latest action underlines its focus on ensuring that food claims are substantiated and do not mislead consumers. The challenge, however, will be to ensure sustained compliance after companies withdraw or modify the claims.

The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison. Unfolding in observational vignettes, Pankaj Johar and Sunaina Kapoor’s thought-provoking documentary centres on Vidya Mutth, a prestigious Hindu school in the holy city of Varanasi, India, where sectarian beliefs are drilled into its students, all in the name of cultural preservation.
The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.
For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.
Moreover, though fanatically strict on its Hindu teachings, the school pays little attention to the mental and physical wellbeing of the pupils. Scenes of the school’s lavish celebration of its leader’s birthday are intercut with the students’ ramshackle living quarters. Even more shocking than this are the changes we observe in the boys over the course of mere months. Once a fresh-faced youth with a gentle demeanour, Hari soon starts to parrot the guru’s intolerant ideology with terrifying conviction. Laying bare the mechanism of indoctrination, Johar and Kapoor’s film sounds an urgent alarm for a new generation growing up under the spell of extremism.

There’s a new kind of gadget on shelves, designed for you to ignore it 99 percent of the time—it only needs attention when its battery is low. I'm talking about the screen-free wearable. You rarely look at it or touch it, yet it collects health stats day and night so you can view them later on in an app, when you get the time—if you can find the time. No pressure.
They have been exploding of late and are only set to grab more attention in the coming months, with the promise of demanding less of your attention once you actually buy one. Today there’s the Garmin Cirqa, Google Fitbit Air, Polar Loop, the Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Whoop series, the original pioneer of this category. Apple is considering its own version of the concept, according to Bloomberg. One answer to that big question of why? Many of us are sick of attention-hoarding tech and social media, not least realizing it is probably doing us no good.
I have reviewed wearables since they went mainstream the first time around with the early waves of Fitbits from 2009 and onward. In some ways this new generation of trackers feels like a callback to those days. Back when I used the Fitbit Ultra, a 2011 tracker that clipped to your jeans, I paid so little attention to it that two days passed before I realized I’d lost it somewhere on the streets of Zagreb, Croatia. While, like many, I fell for the sub-Tamagotchi little cartoon faces of the 2012 Fitbit Zip’s screen, it—like a Fitbit Air—wasn't something you were meant to pay attention to more than a couple times a day, max.
Over the last few years, though, I’ve spent most days referring to a Garmin, Samsung, Fitbit, Coros—the list goes on—dozens or hundreds of times a day. WhatsApp messages and emails buzz on their little screens and my wrist reflexively raises to see what’s up. When I wear a Garmin watch, I’m also lulled into the rhythm of checking evening and morning “reports,” and pathologically looking at my sleep score as soon as I wake up. And let’s not even get into the move alerts, an eye-rolling nag wearables have had for years now.
What Wearables Have Become
Part of the sell-in of new-breed wearables is that they're, in some ways, the antithesis of what other watches have grown into. Fitness watches are more smartwatch-like than ever. OLED screens are near-ubiquitous even in health trackers; hardcore running wearables let you communicate with AI assistants. And this is all even though smartwatches have never really fulfilled the original promise of a life-changing app or feature beyond what people used the first Apple Watch for back in 2015: not much.
Sure, Apple Watches may have saved a life or two, but that’s not necessarily what you’re buying them for. I waited years to report on smartwatch apps that would change things and instead saw entire wearable app ecosystems wither like neglected houseplants. Screen-free wearables want to hit “reset” on the entire category.
The most interesting factor isn't that bands like the Fitbit Air exist now, but why this is all happening now, in 2026. These wearables are largely a case of design subtraction. They are much like a normal fitness tracker—heart rate sensor, battery, accelerometer, Bluetooth transmitter, and whatever other sensors are packed in on a per-case basis—with the display excised.
Whoop has made screen-free wearables since its first proper release in 2015, but the shift in what Whoop considers itself to be about mirrors the change we see in the wider market. Today a Whoop band is made for just about anyone with the spare cash to pay for its $199 annual subscription. It’s a system to “help you improve how you sleep, train, and feel—starting day one,” to use Whoop’s own words. This couldn’t be further removed from the self-serious way Whoop described itself in 2015, as a “performance optimization system exclusively designed for elite athletes and teams.” What a change a decade makes.
Even if Whoop has always been grounded in the now-common concept of “training readiness,” things have altered drastically. So while it’s tempting to say Google's Fitbit and company are playing catch-up with Whoop, that’s not quite it. It has homed in on the “low-distraction” lifestyle selling point just as the other bigger tech companies have.
On at least three fronts this can be attributed—or blamed—on AI, to some extent.
AI as the Good and Bad Guy
AI is a way for these wearable companies to upsell and make money, and on the other side, a major contributor to why a lot of us feel like we need low-distraction tech these days in the first place. While virtually every Whoop rival says it can be used without a subscription, some of these companies lean heavily on AI as an upsell.
Take Google and the Fitbit Air. Without a subscription, the app looks cute enough but is fairly spare. You get stats and charts, but if you want chatty explainers of what any of it means, you need Google Health Premium at $10 a month. Numbers and graph lines become paragraphs that reference specific quirks or events of the day because, to steal a line from humorist and podcaster John Hodgman, specificity is the soul of narrative.
And this is just the beginning. “The use of AI in monitoring and guiding health and wellness is still at the early stage of development but will likely become significantly more advanced as AI matures,” says Peter Richardson, vice president and cofounder of Counterpoint Research.
I find Google Fitbit’s chatbot ramblings quite annoying, with not-that-rare dips into the condescending, and I may even prefer the subscription-free experience. But my job has pushed me through the unenviable task of learning what VO2 Max actually means, what heart-rate variability trends indicate, and so on: not the norm.
AI could solve that long-standing issue with wearables—people glazing over data as soon as they see anything more than their daily step count. This AI use will be better represented on the phone than the watch screen, too, making the lack of screen a strength. It lets the AI shine.
Technostress
The most important influence of AI here is on the other side of the equation, though, as just the latest stage in the tech-ification of our daily lives. I’ve heard from multiple friends about how their recent work appraisals focused on higher-ups demanding greater AI use within their “personal workflow.” Perhaps you’ve had a similar experience.
Elizabeth Marsh, a doctoral researcher at the University of Nottingham who studies the dark side of the digital workplace, finds that digital tools consistently trigger a familiar cluster of harms: technostress, information overload, constant interruption, and blurred work–home boundaries.
“These appear to have become the predictable by-product of environments where the volume and pace of digital demand has risen faster than people's capacity to absorb it,” Marsh tells WIRED, noting that information overload and FOMO correlate strongly with lower well-being and higher strain.
It’s a good argument for not having notifications and alerts pop up on your wrist, phone, and work PC—and wherever else your to-do list of responsibilities takes on a digital form.
“Participants described them in visceral terms—one said the notifications “make me feel sometimes on edge and it does make me feel anxious and it affects my mental health;” another described feeling angry at the sender for taking their time, while simultaneously feeling bad for not replying immediately,” Marsh says about her study on “digital workplace technology intensity.”
But she found simply cutting off notifications wasn’t necessarily a solution either, as people worried they would miss something. Screen-free wearables are a parallel development to this kind of tech cold turkey of banishing wearables from your wrist entirely. You can still get your sleep scores and step count, but without it being advertised consciously through the day. With a Garmin Cirqa, you can even see maps of runs and walks without ever having tapped a “start workout” button. Nothing needs to buzz away or, at a simpler level, require the daily charge coddling of an Apple Watch.
This is perhaps the key. So many tech companies are making these low-distraction wearables because so many of us are close to wanting to opt out altogether, at least in the areas of tech in which we can.
Digital Mindfulness
Marsh’s suggested strategy for dealing with tech strain is what she calls “digital mindfulness,” which is all about having an “awareness of how you engage with technology, rather than operating on autopilot.” That mindless social media feed scrolling? In most cases, you won't convince anyone that’s a digitally mindful practice. Marsh says it involves three things.
“Intention—having a clear purpose for picking up the device in the first place, rather than reaching for it reflexively and then wondering where twenty minutes went,” she says. “Attention—staying with what you've chosen to do and resisting the pull of whatever else is competing for your attention. And attitude—responding to yourself with a bit of kindness and patience when it goes wrong, as self-criticism about our own tech habits tends to make the relationship worse rather than better.”
Buying a screen-free tracker like a Fitbit Air isn’t digital mindfulness in itself. But it’s more intuitively compatible with adopting that mindset than a notification-spewing, buzzing smartwatch.

‘Like Beyonce’: How ‘Rockstar’ Pope Leo XIV is energising Catholic youth
Tickets for an 80,000 seater stadium event in France sold out in less than an hour, with young people among those hoping to catch a glimpse of a very modern pontiff
Vast crowds steamed through Rome last September, to witness the historic canonization of The Catholic Church’s first millennial saint, 15-year-old Carlo Acutis.
Thousands of young people flocked to Vatican City to pay tribute to the British-Italian computer enthusiast, who used the internet to spread the word of Catholicism.
One year on, the canonization can be seen as a symbolic event, both of a church transitioning into a digital era and one that seeks to provide new role models for the young.
At the helm of this transition is Pope Leo XIV, who has has received rock star welcomes from large crowds of young people worldwide since his election in May 2025.
“At 70, Pope Leo is obviously not himself a young man,” Ruth Gledhill, assistant editor of Catholic international paper The Table, told The Independent.
“Yet he has an air of youthful vigour around him, he is sporty and fit. He also seems genuinely bereft of any ego.”
Earlier this month, tickets to see the US-born Pope in the 80,000-seat Stade de France near Paris in September sold out in less than an hour.
Among them was 21-year-old Allan, who had ten members of his family on hand trying to secure a ticket online. It was much the same kind of approach many music fans take, when trying to get into hugely popular festivals like Glastonbury.
“[It was] like it was Beyonce,” he told Le Parisien of the challenge in securing a spot at the forthcoming event.
And last August, Pope Leo brought a youth jubilee to a close by holding a mass for more than one million people. Dubbed the ‘Catholic Woodstock’ by Italian media, the Vatican said it drew young attendees from 146 different countries.
Pope Leo is regarded both as a product and a driver of the growing interest in Catholicism among young people, a candidate who was perfectly suited to the role of being a youth-facing pontiff as the amount of interest grew.
"For the first time we have a Pope who personally used social media before being elected to the Chair of Peter,” says Alessandro Gisotti, deputy director of Vatican Media. “This is a major development in the Church’s communication.”
The Pope’s understanding of the importance of digital communications is “particularly appealing to younger generations, who see in Leo XIV a Pope who is in tune with their way of communicating", he adds.
Leo is also seen by many as having a common, down-to-earth approach that might appeal to the young.
In May, he went viral for using the ‘6-7’ gesture while riding the popemobile in Madrid, and he appears to share many of the same interests of ordinary Catholics around the world from apps to sports.
Christopher Lamb, the CNN’s Vatican correspondent, writes in American Hope: “He’s a pope who understands the online world: he plays Wordle with his brother (and uses a different starter word each day), communicates with WhatsApp, and was even spotted using the Duolingo language app in the early hours of the morning.”
“His love of sports, particularly baseball, helps him connect with people, whether he’s holding a tennis racquet with Jannik Sinner or sporting the cap of his beloved Chicago White Sox.
“When passing in his popemobile he was even heard shouting,’ They lost!’ in response to someone who’d yelled, ‘Go Cubs!’, the White Sox rivals.”

Ukraine-Russia war latest: Moscow vows ‘massive strikes’ as missile attack on Belgorod kills two
Kremlin says strikes would be an ‘appropriate response’ to Ukraine’s ‘path of escalation’
Russia’s defence ministry has announced it is preparing “massive strikes” on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in retaliation for a drone campaign by Kyiv attacking warehouses and oil and gas facilities.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the move would be an “appropriate response” to Ukraine’s “path of escalation” and said that Moscow had been “fairly systematic” in attacking Kyiv’s military infrastructure.
Ukraine has targeted online retailers Wildberries - often referred to as Russia’s Amazon - and Ozon, accusing the companies of selling goods that have aided the military, claims that they deny.
This comes as a missile attack killed two people and injured 16 in the city of Belgorod close to the Russian border with Ukraine, acting governor Alexander Shuvayev said.
Sunday's deaths followed Ukraine's hit on a commercial facility, which also set ablaze seven warehouses in the city, he added.
Meanwhile, CIA director John Ratcliffe is reported to have floated a trilateral meeting between Vladimir Putin, Volodymyr Zelensky, and Donald Trump during his mysterious visit to Moscow, according to two sources briefed on the matter cited by Axios.
Talks between Ukraine and Russia were paused in February when the US invaded Iran, and little progress has been made since.
Ukraine's new defence chief seeks to close $27bn funding gap
Ukraine’s new defence minister Yevhen Khmara said the ministry has options for closing the $27bn funding gap he inherited from his predecessor, including seeking more contributions from allies.
Khmara made the remarks at his first briefing with reporters since taking the post Saturday.
His appointment followed weeks of protests after Mykhailo Fedorov's dismissal that sparked a military reset in Kyiv and culminated in a video in which Fedorov called for a new presidential election.
Khmara's comments were released for publication on Sunday.
Khmara, a former special forces officer, takes over as Kyiv's war effort faces mounting financial pressures.
He said a priority will be avoiding battlefield shortages while ensuring soldiers are paid and other essential needs are met.
The ministry is considering bringing forward part of a €90bn (£76.9bn) European loan planned for next year, and has identified partners for separate talks on financing specific defense needs, he said.
“Ukraine will show its partners a clear vision and a clear plan,” he vowed, adding he planned to preserve much of the existing ministry team.

Navy tracks Russian warships in English Channel during ‘intense’ operation
Russian warships have been tracked by the Navy through UK waters in an “intense” 72-hour operation.
A task group was shadowed by Type 45 destroyer HMS Duncan, Type 23 frigate HMS St Albans and patrol vessel HMS Severn as it made its way from the North Sea through the English Channel.
Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko was watched escorting sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta, with a Merlin helicopter extending the UK’s surveillance as the ships approached the Strait of Dover.
In response to the tracking, Russia deployed other military resources including the Neustrashimy frigate to guard the illegal shipment, UK officials said.
First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said there was “no room for complacency” as shadow fleet vessels continue to pose “an unacceptable risk” to maritime security and the environment.
“Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose. That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required,” he said.
