On the road with pro-independence Albertans, one small town at a time
Road trip talking independence was unexpectedly met by law enforcement
Chris Scott sat in the driver’s seat of his 2001 Monaco Dynasty motorhome last week, bumping along the network of rural highways in southern Alberta.
The vehicle creaked a bit. Some leather-covered furniture was cracking, and some cabinet drawer latches didn’t work anymore.
It’s like Alberta, Scott said: you can ignore problems and let them get worse, or you can pay attention to them and fix them.
“I see there's a lot of things going on with Alberta that need some care and attention,” said Scott.
The restaurant owner, who gained prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic, has hit the road this summer to talk independence, travelling with a group of people who also support the idea of Alberta becoming its own nation.
CBC News recently spent a day aboard the “Let’s Talk Alberta” bus, speaking with passengers about what motivates them at a time when Albertans are weighing their vote in an Oct. 19 referendum.
Earlier this summer, CBC spent time with volunteers helping the pro-Canada group Forever Canadian, talking to them about their efforts and why they wouldn’t be voting to have a future referendum on whether Alberta should stay in the country.
Federalist and separatist groups have been a common sight this summer, fundraising and shaking hands with voters at events like the Calgary Stampede. Voter mobilization efforts are expected to ramp up considerably with less than two months to go to the referendum.
On the bus
On a recent weekday in August, Scott’s bus hit the road for a 10-stop tour through the southern part of the province.
Scott’s passengers included Jasper Smit, a friend from the Netherlands who runs a social media channel called CommonSense TV.
Leaning on a countertop in the back of the motorhome, Smit studied the packaging of a snack purchased from a highway gas station. He read it aloud: roasted grilled pepperoni cheesesteak.
“Mystery meat!” called out another rider.
The wrapping on the bus’ exterior was less ambiguous.
The vehicle is emblazoned with the “Let’s Talk Alberta” decal, framed by provincial viewscapes: the hoodoos of Drumheller flowing into sweeping mountains and rivers, topped by an expansive prairie sky. It was an Alberta postcard, designed with artificial intelligence and then smoothed out by a designer.
On the back of the vehicle, a Bible verse printed in script: Jeremiah 29:7 — "Seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you into exile. Pray to the Lord for it, because if it prospers, you too will prosper."
It was Scott who procured the motorhome to criss-cross the province.
With a full standup shower and decent-sized bed in the back, Scott could spend days on the bus if he needed to.
Increasingly, he has been, as he’s travelled to all corners of the province with the clock running down to voting day.
He carries with him his experiences from the pandemic.
He was charged and later acquitted for breaching public health restrictions during COVID-19 related to his Whistle Stop Cafe in east-central Alberta.
Scott was highly critical of politicians that he viewed as allowing laws that "strip our fundamental rights and freedoms away." His reputation has made him something of a folk hero amongst those who share his views in these small towns.
“I just learned that if there's something that's wrong, you need to stand up for yourself,” Scott said of his experience.
When the bus pulls into a town, it’s often greeted with supporters. Some caught word of the trip on social media.
In Rosemary, Alta., with a population of little more than 350, a lone man who came out to get a lawn sign said he heard news of the trip on a Facebook group entitled, “Bassano Bitching or Bragging.”
“The whole thing is really not about separation, in my opinion,” said Bassano resident Tom Schaffer.
“It's about making the government wake up and go, hey, these guys might want to separate. Maybe we should actually do something and listen to them?”
Tanya Clemens, co-leader of a separate Alberta independence group, Let Alberta Decide, was on the bus too, as was John Bolton, a former Calgary radio host who now provides emcee services at various independence events, and Patti Vold, a mother of nine and a grandmother of 15.
There was also Sandy Duguay, who was born and raised in Montreal, where she lived through two referendums as an English speaker. Duguay also spent 26 years in Victoria, where her husband was a chaplain at a prison on Vancouver Island.
Duguay was never involved in politics before, but was motivated to become political after the COVID-19 pandemic hit, which evolved into helping the Alberta independence signature drive. She’s now travelling full-time on the bus.
“I feel very close to these people,” Duguay said, who turns 72 in a few weeks.
As the bus weaved its way along the route, the conversation snaked through the group’s motivating complaints with the federal government. Some, like frustration with the federal equalization program or Ottawa’s approach to firearms, have been kindling for alienation for years.
The cultural divide at play quickly came into focus, too. Certain federal bills, perhaps less familiar to the broader Canadian public, are viewed by this group as threats to religious freedom.
“Bill C-9 especially,” Duguay said, referring to the Combatting Hate Act, which amends the Criminal Code to strengthen penalties for hate crimes. The Liberals received support from the Bloc Québécois after including a clause to remove a religious exemption from the country's hate speech laws.
The Conservatives have argued that amounts to an “assault” on religious freedoms, while Justice Minister Sean Fraser has said the new law won’t “criminalize faith.”
“Look what’s happened to Europe,” Duguay said, turning to Smit. “You were founded on Judeo-Christian principles. And you guys were the first to get rid of them."
Wearing a Let’s Talk Alberta shirt and a Whistle Stop hat, Smit, the visitor from the Netherlands, didn’t entirely agree. He said he's “not religious at all" and that embedding Christian principles into governance would set a precedent that would require adopting other religious laws whenever demographics shifted in the future.
“In all fairness, you should bring that [into] politics,” he said.
Vold, the grandmother of 15, feels Christian values have been fading from public life, which is pushing society towards moral decline.
“For many, many years, the idea was you shouldn't mix church and state, right? I disagree,” Vold said. “The state should not be in the church, but people of faith should be in the state. They should be helping to guide the country.”
Soon after this conversation, the bus arrived in Strathmore and pulled near Kinsmen Park. Scott and Smit exited. Talk of faith continued, until suddenly, Smit ran back up the bus stairs.
“The police are here.”
A heated confrontation
Outside the bus, a crowd had formed in the parking lot.
Various supporters of the independence movement who had arrived to greet the bus gathered around Scott as he was engaged in an argument. On the other side was a town official, flanked by a peace officer.
“So anyway, we'll be here for about an hour,” Scott said.
“I’m asking you to leave,” the official responded. The group was free to express its opinions, the man said, but not on the town’s property.
“But I can,” Scott responded. “It’s public property.”
The crowd grew increasingly frustrated. Scott was told that if he did not move the vehicle, the RCMP would be called.
“Well, I mean, it’s not the first time I’ve been arrested,” Scott said.
Minutes passed. Separatist influencers began to livestream from the scene. Eventually, word came that the bus was allowed to stay.
“The town respects individuals' right to peacefully express their views and participate in democratic processes,” a town spokesperson later said in an email to CBC News. “The group was able to continue gathering and expressing its views.”
The bus moved on to an Airdrie pizza place that’s become a gathering spot for the separatist movement.
Behind schedule and with three stops still to go, the Let’s Talk Alberta crew sat down and scarfed down slices, with a Toronto Blue Jays game playing on the screens above and curious onlookers surrounding the crowd of blue shirts.
One man asked what the group was doing there.
“It’s an Alberta independence bus tour,” he was told.
The man grimaced.
Polling suggests that support for independence is stronger in the rural regions, and Let’s Talk Alberta’s tour last week to smaller locales was largely met by receptive crowds.
But to win in October, the group understands it needs to make gains in the cities, where it hasn't received as friendly a welcome as it has in rural Alberta. That’s where they're headed next.
“September, October will be all cities,” Duguay said. “The cities, different cultures, different mindsets … we’ve covered just about every little town. But now, the cities.”

Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost
A volatile and unpredictable U.S. administration makes it difficult to know which levers to pull
With the Trump administration's promise to impose more tariffs on us in January, many Canadians are asking: What leverage should we use to get them to change course?
The question suggests that there are actually real things we can do to change U.S. President Donald Trump's mind — that if Canada hits back hard enough, or demonstrates its willingness to suffer enough, we will get that policy change.
Christopher Ragan, the founding director of McGill University's Max Bell School of Public Policy and former chair of Canada’s Ecofiscal Commission put it this way: "Canada is in a set of negotiations with a party that appears to be unpredictable, volatile, so I don't think anybody really knows what's going to work here."
Don Drummond, former chief economist for TD Bank, said if Canadians are willing to suffer the consequences, there are plenty of ways to punch back at the U.S.
"You first strike the things they've said are the most important to them," Drummond said. "They made it painfully clear that the only thing they want or need from Canada is oil, and maybe for a while electricity.
"We've had an export tax on oil and natural gas before and we could introduce that. We could also introduce quotas," he said.
Canada's leverage is significant when it comes to energy and fertilizer. In 2025 Canadian comodities accounted for 63 per cent of oil imported into the U.S., 81.3 per cent of imported electricity, almost 100 per cent of imported natural gas and 80 per cent of imported potash.
A number of non-tariff options
And while there's still a long way to go before Canada fully develops its critical mineral reserves, Drummond says we could notify the U.S. that they won't get preferential access when those reserves come online.
"We could also restrict American access to Canada," Drummond said. "In the extreme we could require a visa and we could be very stingy with them."
Canada could also refuse to buy the F-35 fighter jets from the U.S. and choose instead to go with the Gripen from Sweden, he said.
Canadian banks, governments, pension funds and others currently hold about $459.6 billion US in U.S. treasury bonds.
"Given that the U.S. is tormented at the moment trying to get their long-term bond yields down, if we said we were going to divest ourselves of those, or at least not buy any more, that would tick them off," Drummond said.
- Carney says trade deal became untenable when U.S. 'asked too much and offered too little'
- Carney says he'll resume negotiating when Trump team has the 'right attitude'
Drummond also said that Canada's CPP fund could divest itself of all U.S. assets (51 per cent of the $864-billion fund is invested in the U.S., compared to just 12 per cent in Canada), but that would open the door to using Canadians' retirement as a political tool and placing retirees at risk — a step he said the country should avoid taking.
"You could put back the digital services tax, for example. Why the hell did we give it away? We got absolutely nothing for giving it away," Drummond said.
He says we could also eliminate the Canadian Film or Video Production Tax Credit, which he says results in lost tax revenue of about $500 million annually, with little economic benefit for Canada.
"So it could be fairly broad-based, it could be export restrictions or export taxes, it could be any number of things," Drummond said.
Some economists warn that while employing these non-tariff measures might feel good and would certainly harm the U.S. economy, they would hurt Canada's economy more.
Long-term, short-term pain
"I think emotions are pretty high and there's just a desire to lash out, but cooler heads require us to take a moment to think about what it is we're trying to achieve," said Trevor Tombe, director of fiscal and economic policy at the University of Calgary's School of Public Policy.
Tombe says the 50 per cent tariffs on about $27 billion of Canadian goods represent a hit to Canadian GDP of about 0.4 or 0.5 per cent, and taking retaliatory action that costs Canada more than that doesn't make economic sense unless it changes U.S. behaviour.
"That's a lot easier said than done," Tombe said. "And if we do things that increase costs in the United States, that might very well play into the hands of the U.S. administration by allowing them to blame Canada."
Beyond hurting Canada's economy in the short term, there's another negative side effect: hurting it in the long term.
"Maybe we have a lot of leverage, a lot of ability to impose pain, but it comes at a huge cost for us because we are both losing revenue and we are potentially severing relationships with our best customer," said Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway Chair in Business and Trade Law at the University of Ottawa.
What if, for example, the U.S. replaced all Canadian oil with Venezuelan oil in a decade?
By way of example, Alschner says, China's export controls on critical minerals have prompted the U.S. to try to strike new deals, find new customers and build new critical mineral supply chains. Perhaps the best example of this is Canada's push to diversify in the face of the Trump administration's trade war.
"Even if you do it for a short period of time, you're sending a signal that this can be turned on and off. And so maybe the United States will not have time to mitigate that particular disruption at that moment, but it will then put measures in place to mitigate it in the future," he said.
Alschner also said bringing back concessions such as reimposing the Digital Services Tax or cancelling tax credits would be a direct provocation with an unclear dividend.
Sometimes there is only the fight
Ragan from McGill University says the U.S. would likely react strongly to export controls or taxes that drive up U.S. gas prices. That would risk turning energy scarcity caused by Canada into something that unites Americans against this country.
"That move escalates the trade war a few notches at once," Ragan said. "I say this half jokingly, but I wonder if you restricted electricity sales or oil sales or natural gas sales, whether that would lead Donald Trump to calling the troops. I'm not so sure."
Some economists say that rather than take actions that cost the Canadian economy in the short and long term, Canada should focus on how it can make up the difference with trade expansion and diversification abroad while building at home.
"Another way to think about the U.S. right now that I find kind of helpful is that they are flailing around in increasingly irrational ways and we are getting hit in the face," Tombe said.
"To the extent that their moves are crazy and not grounded in economic rationale, the best option might be to step back, try to weather the storm, and hopefully they work out their own issues domestically."
- Interprovincial trade barriers are falling. But rewriting old rules will take time
- Will auto tariffs be a permanent roadblock for a Canada-U.S. trade deal?
Tombe says that aside from the broader move to diversify our exports, sign new trade deals and build at home, Canada still hasn't liberalized internal trade, an opportunity he calls low-hanging fruit.
He says that by simply recognizing credentials across the country, Canada could boost productivity enough to offset a 25 per cent across-the-board tariff.
Alschner says the advantage Canada has right now is that the EU and other global trading partners are locked in similar trade disputes with the United States, which means they may be highly motivated to work with Canada.
"We should really use this as an opportunity to forcibly substitute U.S. imports with strategically selected non-U.S. imports," Alschner said. "We should say to the European Union, 'All right, what are the things that you can sell to us that the United States used to sell to us?'"
Tombe notes that while there are plenty of economic reasons to avoid employing non-tariff retaliatory measures in this trade fight, Canada's battle with the U.S. isn't entirely economic.
The U.S., as Prime Minister Mark Carney has said, wants to break us so it can own us, and some say a threat to our sovereignty requires an un-economic response.
"I'm getting a little tired, mainly, with fellow economists who point out that it's harmful to Canada to retaliate. I think that's pretty narrow-minded," Drummond said.
"I'd like to give that advice to the kid in the schoolyard who's getting bullied, [because] it's not much more complicated than that: If you want to stop a bully you have to be prepared to get your nose bloodied. It just eggs them on otherwise."

One year ago, we jointly submitted our resignations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Each of us had been tested as we tried to protect our communities and the agency we loved, but we realized we could no longer remain quiet under this administration.
But the political interference and scientific integrity issues we warned about were not isolated. They exposed vulnerabilities that still exist, and will remain after today’s leaders are gone. The answer is not simply to restore the CDC to what it was, but to build a stronger and more resilient public health institution for the future. That requires safeguards so that no administration, Republican or Democratic, can replace independent public health decision-making with partisan ideology.
Erica Schwartz, the new CDC director, has pledged scientific rigor and said she would disagree privately with health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. when necessary. But she has not said what she would do if directed to implement a policy that conflicts with science and data. During her confirmation hearing, she stated that vaccines do not cause autism and promised to review the CDC’s misleading webpage. Yet the page remains unchanged. She will have to determine where her line is, just as we did, and what she will do if that line is crossed. The country’s scientific safeguards, however, should not depend on the judgment or resolve of any single leader.
Here are four ways that Congress can protect the integrity of the CDC and the health of our country:
Shield science from politically driven policies
Public health decisions such as quarantine, travel restrictions, and vaccine recommendations can significantly restrict individual liberties. It is therefore essential that agencies issuing these orders explain the evidence, expected benefits, potential harms, and alternatives. Consider the CDC’s inconsistent response this spring to Americans evacuated from a cruise ship with a hantavirus outbreak. Despite CDC guidance supporting home monitoring, the acting director required some passengers to be quarantined in a government facility in Omaha, Neb., for as long as six weeks. (Other passengers were allowed to monitor for symptoms at home.) When one of them challenged the order, a CDC medical officer recommended rescinding it, but Kennedy overruled that recommendation.
Congress should require any major public health directive from an agency or its political leadership to include a scientific assessment describing the evidence, uncertainties, and why the action is proportionate to the threat. Political leaders have the authority to make policy and should be accountable for their choices. They should not be able to conceal or rewrite the underlying science or to present a political decision as the agency’s scientific conclusion. This undermining of evidence-based guidance has led health departments and clinicians to turn to U.S. medical organizations and the World Health Organization for recommendations.
Protect scientific publication
The suspension of the CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report in early 2025, the first moratorium in its 60-year history, was an early warning. The report demonstrated the effectiveness of the Covid vaccine, but Jay Bhattacharya — then acting director of the CDC — rejected it, citing methodological flaws. Previous agency protocols placed final scientific review on the weekly reports with a career scientist in the director’s office, usually the chief medical officer or principal deputy director. Both are now political roles. The rejected paper was subsequently published in the journal JAMA Network Open, after the science passed peer review.
CDC’s scientific publications and data should be protected by a statutory firewall. Once research passes established agency scientific and ethical review, political officials should not suppress it because its findings are inconvenient. Any decision to delay, alter, or block a report should be documented and made public. Americans should see where scientific review ends and political policy decision-making begins.
Restore independent expert advice
Federal advisory committees ensure that federal decisions benefit from outside expertise. However, many of these advisory bodies have been eliminated, meetings canceled, and entire panels — such as CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices — dismissed and then hastily reconstituted. Congress should strengthen the laws governing the independence of major federal health advisory committees. Members should be selected transparently based on relevant expertise, with rigorous conflict-of-interest standards, staggered terms spanning administrations, and removal only for predefined reasons. Transparent scientific disagreement strengthens trust. A panel assembled to rubber-stamp a predetermined conclusion does not.
Administer funding as directed by Congress
After federal staffing cuts in 2025, the CDC now has so-called “zombie” programs that Congress continues to fund, but are functionally dead. This is because the people who ran them — monitoring threats, supporting health departments, and translating evidence into action — are gone, laid off, or put on leave. Congress should require the Department of Health and Human Services and CDC to report whether funded programs have the capacity to fulfill their missions. The executive branch should not be able to dismantle a congressionally funded program through staffing decisions rather than legislation.
Political appointees have also directed CDC funding toward their own priorities without following standard competitive processes. Examples include a proposed study that would have delayed the hepatitis B vaccine for newborns in Guinea-Bissau, an African country with high disease rates, and grants allocating $32 million to four communities, including one where SpaceX is located, for “Great Health for America.” Congressional approval should be required for significant discretionary expenditures or those that deviate from congressional appropriations.
These reforms will not eliminate political disagreement, nor should they. Questions about government authority, spending, and competing priorities are properly the domain of our democratic process. But how diseases spread and the risks and benefits of interventions are questions for science, not for ideology.
One year ago, we resigned because we believed remaining silent would make us complicit with the secretary’s dismantling of both the agency and its long-standing evidence-driven decision-making. We walked out of the CDC, but we did not walk away from public health. Over the past year, we have continued our commitment through work in health departments, communities, universities, and direct patient care. We have continued to use our voices, sometimes at personal and professional cost, because we believe in our country and the opportunity to improve the health of our communities.
We still believe in these public health institutions and the public servants working under extraordinary pressure. But hope is not a strategy. Congress must decide whether it will protect the institutions, the people who work to keep us healthy, and the independent process, based on evidence, that has made the U.S. a global public health leader.
Debra Houry, M.D., M.P.H., was the CDC’s chief medical officer and is now a senior medical adviser for the California Public Health Network Innovation Exchange, adviser to Jimini Health, and a senior fellow at Yale University School of Public Health. Daniel Jernigan, M.D., M.P.H., was director of the National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases, and is a contributing scholar at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Demetre Daskalakis, M.D., M.P.H., was director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases and is a consultant for Sanofi, AstraZeneca, and ViiV Healthcare.

Units of the U.S. Air National Guard received guidance from Ukrainian doctors as they practiced evacuating a field hospital under attack by drones during a large exercise held this month in Alpena, Michigan.
During the multinational military training event called Northern Strike 26-2, Ukrainian doctors with frontline experience advised over 100 Air National Guard members drawn from seven units on how to care for wounded patients under siege from a mass of swarming drones.
The event marked the first test of National Guard combat medics’ abilities on a large scale under the simulation of an intense drone threat.
Protecting Patients From Drone Swarms
The harrowing scenario saw multiple small unmanned aircraft systems swarm a hospital site.
Mirroring combat situations from Ukraine, the drones simulated immediate fatal threats to service members and patients receiving treatment.
The exercise aimed to give U.S. military personnel experience at defending injured people from small unmanned systems under high stress while performing combat casualty care.
“One of the largest lessons learned here was the need to go underground more,” U.S. Air Force Col. Patrick Frank, deputy director of air staff for the Michigan National Guard Joint Forces Headquarters, said in a statement.
"The Ukrainian doctors discussed with the medics and leadership about how tents are okay, but underground is better.”
A Robot Dog Plus Drone Nets
The Guard used drone nets to fortify the hospital location. These nets were specially designed to block many variations of small unmanned aircraft while allowing humans to easily maneuver through them.
"The specific type of netting is supposed to be impenetrable by most drones, creating large tunnels that casualties could be evacuated through,” said U.S. Air Force Maj. Sarah Blackthorne, a medical planner for the Northern Strike Air Component, in a statement.
Using the nets to defend the site, Guard troops shot down swarming drones with firearms to stop them from attacking patients and evacuated wounded to a secondary fortified location in a bunker, mirroring tactics used in Ukraine.
A four-legged unmanned ground vehicle, popularly known as a robot dog, approached the destroyed drones to analyze them for troops at a safe distance.
Why Medical Skills Are Vital For National Guard Troops
Many National Guard members specialize in providing emergency medical treatment not only to fellow military service members but members of the public while responding to disasters and performing rescues.
Guard troops frequently deploy across state lines to help respond to disasters including tornadoes and hurricanes. Nearly 40% of requests for assistance received by the Emergency Management Assistance Compact, a national mutual aid system for states, specifically request Guard troops, according to the National Guard Bureau.
They are not only called upon to respond to emergencies formally but often render assistance to people in unexpected situations. This month, four members of the Illinois Army National Guard gave life-saving aid to an injured motorcyclist they found on U.S. Highway 72 highway in Michigan. Last month, three soldiers of the Pennsylvania Army National Guard stepped into help victims of a rollover crash in Texas.
With emergency medical aid forming a pillar of their expertise, National Guard troops across the country train constantly to improve their medical skills.
However, this new model of counter-drone training for National Guard units is very different from past training regimens and marks a new area for U.S. combat medicine.
A Changing World For Combat Medicine
Unmanned aircraft systems capable of striking far behind fortified areas have eliminated the concept of a frontline and have potential to strike at military medical facilities previously assumed to be safe.
These new circumstances place extra burdens on military service personnel not only to master caring for wounded people under fire from bullets but under threat from aerial attacks.
The Ukrainian doctors included in the exercise were able to share firsthand knowledge with U.S. troops about best practices for shielding injured personnel not only from isolated drones but from persistent and heavy attacks.
The drone swarm attack scenario for Guard troops sets a new benchmark for skills that U.S. combat medics will be expected to master. It draws attention to drone swarms as a defining characteristic of modern warfare and also the demands that U.S. military service members will face not only to defend themselves but save the lives of vulnerable people.

When people in India are used to buying all sorts of medicines over the counter (OTC), the challenge is the enforcement of laws which make prescription mandatory, said Hyderabad-based paediatrician Sivaranjani Santosh even as she welcomed the Centre’s decision to make all syrups, including cough syrups, as prescription-only.
Why India has restricted chlorpheniramine, phenylephrine medicines for children under 4 | Explained
Many in the pharmaceutical trade as well are uncertain how effectively the new rules can be enforced among consumers accustomed to buying medicines over the counter (OTC).
On Tuesday (June 16) the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare notified amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, ending the OTC sale of syrups, including cough syrups. Following the amendment, cough lozenges, pills and tablets will continue to be available over the counter, but syrups will require a prescription.
Dr. Santosh welcomed the move, saying concerns over overdoses, incorrect dosing and indiscriminate use of cough-and-cold preparations justified tighter controls. Many formulations contain ingredients such as terbutaline, levosalbutamol, salbutamol, chlorpheniramine maleate and phenylephrine, which could add to complications if used inappropriately, she said.
ALSO WATCH Watch: Why are prescriptions now mandatory for cough syrups? | Above the Fold | 16.06.2026
Doubts over implementation were echoed by pharmacists. Uday Kumar of Mor Chemists and Druggists said consumers increasingly expected immediate relief and questioned whether a blanket prescription requirement would work in the long run. “Everyone wants to recover instantly. If they fall sick today, they want to become well tomorrow,” he said.
Mr. Kumar argued that counterfeit, adulterated and unbranded medicines posed a bigger challenge. He added that identifying genuine and fake products was difficult and laboratory testing often took months.
Neelesh Kanodia, who runs Yash Agencies, distinguished between codeine-based cough syrups and regular formulations. “I don’t think the blanket rule will continue in the long run. But restrictions on codeine-containing syrups will continue,” he said. According to Mr. Kanodia, codeine-containing cough syrups were already largely dispensed against prescriptions only, whereas commonly used formulations had traditionally been available over the counter.
Meanwhile, the Telangana Chemists and Druggists Association (TCDA) moved quickly to inform retailers about the new rules. Krishna Kumar, treasurer of the association, said broadcast messages had been sent to pharmacies across the State immediately after the notification was issued. “We also circulated those messages in Telugu so that they reach even the remote corners of the State,” he said.
Mr. Kumar said Telangana had around 39,000 pharmacies, of which nearly 18,000 were located in Hyderabad.
A Hyderabad-based pharmacist who runs a prominent store in Panjagutta and requested anonymity said implementation was likely to vary across regions. “Large and reputed pharmacies in metropolitan cities and affluent areas would comply with the rules but enforcement in smaller localities and towns could prove more difficult,” he said.
He added that consumer behaviour is a major obstacle. Patients often reuse old prescriptions instead of returning to doctors, while consultation fees, travel costs and waiting times discourage repeated visits.

Odisha to deduct maintenance from salaries of govt employees who default: CM
The amount will then be deducted from the salary and transferred electronically to the bank account of the employee’s wife or children
The Mohan Majhi government will directly deduct court-ordered maintenance payments from the salaries of government employees who fail to pay it to their wives or children regularly, chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi said on Sunday.
A press release from CMO said the state government has directed departmental drawing and disbursing officers (DDOs) to deduct the amount specified by family courts from the monthly salaries of employees who default on maintenance or alimony payments and transfer it electronically to the bank accounts of their wives or children.
The decision follows repeated complaints received during the CM’s public grievance hearings, with two to three cases relating to non-payment of maintenance were brought at each hearing.
“There are government employees in the state who are committing contempt of court and, at the same time, doing injustice to their wives and children. This is absolutely unacceptable to the state government,” Majhi said.
Under the new guidelines, when a court orders a government employee to pay maintenance or alimony, the departmental drawing and disbursing officer will factor the court-ordered amount into the employee’s monthly salary bill.
The amount will then be deducted from the salary and transferred electronically to the bank account of the employee’s wife or children. CMO officials said the government aims to ensure that maintenance reaches the intended beneficiaries directly and that government employees cannot easily evade their obligations.
During CM grievance cell hearings, there were several such complaints of some government employees failing to comply with court orders. The CM directed that the court-ordered maintenance provisions be integrated into Odisha’s Human Resource Management System (HRMS), the automated system for managing government employees.
The integration is expected to make the process more systematic and reduce delays in implementing court orders, the CMO said. “The system would not only improve compliance with court orders but also help reduce the financial hardship faced by women and children whose maintenance payments have been withheld,” it said.
The CMO said the new mechanism would ensure that court-ordered payments are made without requiring the affected women or children to repeatedly pursue the defaulting employee.

Dolly Parton laid to rest alongside husband in Nashville

Dolly Parton has been laid to rest, the music legend's great-niece has said.
The singer had a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, following her death earlier in the week at the age of 80.
She has been placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city.
Lainey Parton posted an emotional tribute, external a day after the burial, saying: "It still doesn't feel real that she's gone. I'm going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there."
'She believed in me'
She referred to Parton as "granny" and wrote: "Because she couldn't have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers. She loved us that way, and I'll forever be grateful for that."
Lainey remembered: "From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn't do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself."

Amelia Young, a reporter for Nashville's NewsChannel 5, posted photos of flowers, external and a book of condolence at the tomb, which features a brass plaque showing Parton and Dean's names and engravings of their childhood homes.
On Saturday, one of Parton's nieces, Jada Star, performed as part of a tribute concert at Nashville's Grand Ole Opry House, regarded as the home of country music.
Star performed her song The Orchard, which she recorded with her aunt in 2024 on the album Smoky Mountain DNA: Family, Faith and Fables.

Country superstar Jelly Roll made a surprise appearance during the event's finale - a group performance of Parton's 9 to 5 - while other participants included Carly Pearce, who has gone from being a performer at Parton's Dollywood theme park to a Grammy-winning singer.

Arunachal Pradesh – A Living Treasure of Biodiversity
Arunachal Pradesh is one of India’s most biologically diverse states, where forests, rivers, wetlands, mountains and communities are part of one interconnected ecological landscape. Its extraordinary range of habitats supports thousands of plant and animal species, including several rare, endemic and threatened species.
The State’s biodiversity is shaped by its remarkable variation in altitude and climate. From tropical forests in the foothills to temperate forests, alpine meadows and high-altitude ecosystems, Arunachal Pradesh offers a continuous range of habitats within a relatively compact geographical area.
With more than 80 per cent of its geographical area under forest cover, the State plays an important role in maintaining the ecological balance of the Eastern Himalayas. It is also part of the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, one of the world’s globally recognised regions of exceptional biological richness and conservation importance.
A Landscape of Remarkable Ecological Diversity
The geographical diversity of Arunachal Pradesh is reflected in its forests. Depending on altitude and climatic conditions, the State has tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, moist deciduous forests, subtropical broad-leaved forests, pine forests, temperate forests, coniferous forests, sub-alpine vegetation and alpine meadows.
This remarkable transition from the warm foothills to the high Himalayas creates habitats for species with very different ecological requirements.
The State is home to more than 5,000 species of flowering plants, around 600 species of orchids, about 75 species of rhododendrons, 45 species of bamboo, 17 species of cane and hundreds of medicinal plants. Arunachal Pradesh is particularly renowned for its orchid and rhododendron diversity.
The forests also support a remarkable variety of mammals, including the tiger, leopard, clouded leopard, snow leopard, golden cat, marbled cat, Asiatic elephant, red panda, takin, hoolock gibbon and several other rare and threatened species.
A Paradise for Birds
Arunachal Pradesh is equally celebrated for its avian diversity. Its forests and mountain ecosystems provide habitats for hundreds of bird species, making the State one of the most important birding regions in India.
The Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary in West Kameng is one of the best examples of this extraordinary richness. Located within the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, Eaglenest is home to a wide variety of hornbills, pheasants, kingfishers and other birds. The sanctuary is also known for the discovery of the Bugun liocichla, a bird named after the Bugun community that lives in the region.
Protecting Arunachal’s Wildlife
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is protected through an extensive network of national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, tiger reserves and other conservation landscapes.
The state is home to important protected areas such as Namdapha National Park and Tiger Reserve, Kamlang Tiger Reserve, Pakke Tiger Reserve, Mouling National Park, Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary, Sessa Orchid Sanctuary, Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary and Mehao Wildlife Sanctuary, among others.
These landscapes support an exceptional range of wildlife, from high-altitude species such as the snow leopard and red panda to tropical forest species including the clouded leopard, hoolock gibbon and numerous birds, reptiles and amphibians.
Recent wildlife surveys have continued to expand scientific knowledge of these ecosystems. A 2024 WWF-India survey in Arunachal’s high-altitude rangelands recorded six wild cat species, including photographic evidence of the elusive Pallas’s cat, marking the first such photographic record from the state. The survey used 136 camera traps across 83 locations, covering approximately 2,000 sq km.
The Orchids of Arunachal Pradesh
Among the many botanical treasures of the State, orchids hold a special place.
Arunachal Pradesh has one of the richest orchid assemblages in India, with hundreds of species occurring across its varied habitats. The Sessa Orchid Sanctuary in West Kameng was established in 1979 to conserve and study orchids in their natural habitats. The sanctuary has recorded a remarkable diversity of orchid species, including epiphytic and terrestrial orchids.
The Orchid Research and Development Centre at Tipi further strengthens conservation and research efforts. Its facilities include orchid species houses, natural orchidaria, a herbarium, tissue culture laboratory, museum and hardening units. These initiatives support both ex-situ conservation and the rehabilitation of orchids in their natural habitats.
Glaw Lake: Arunachal Pradesh’s First Ramsar Site
A landmark development came in August 2026, when Glaw Lake, located within the Kamlang Tiger Reserve in Lohit district, was designated as India’s 101st Ramsar Site and became Arunachal Pradesh’s first Ramsar Site.
Situated at an elevation of around 1,168 metres, Glaw Lake covers approximately 82 hectares and forms part of the catchment of the Kamlang, Lang and Lati rivers, which flow into the Lohit River. The lake is recognised by the State Forest Department as an important repository of aquatic biodiversity.
Its Ramsar designation gives international recognition to the ecological importance of the wetland and strengthens the focus on its conservation and sustainable management. The recognition is also significant for Arunachal Pradesh’s wider efforts to protect wetlands and the ecosystems and communities that depend on them.
A State Where New Discoveries Continue
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity story is still being written.
Recent scientific discoveries demonstrate how much remains to be documented within the State’s forests and mountains. The rare plant Vaccinium piliferum, a relative of the wild blueberry that had not been documented for nearly 188 years, was rediscovered in Vijoynagar in Changlang district recently.
New orchid species have also been identified in different parts of the State, while researchers have recorded new cascade frog species from Arunachal Pradesh. In 2026, scientists also identified a new butterfly species, Euthalia zubeengargi, from Basar in Leparada district.
Such discoveries are a reminder that Arunachal Pradesh is not merely a repository of known species. Its forests and mountains continue to offer opportunities for scientific research and the discovery of life forms that may not yet be fully documented.
Biodiversity and Indigenous Knowledge
For generations, the indigenous communities of Arunachal Pradesh have lived closely with their natural surroundings. Forests provide food, medicinal plants, fibres, fuel and other resources, while traditional knowledge has helped communities understand seasonal changes, plants, wildlife and sustainable use of natural resources.
Today, this relationship is increasingly important to conservation.
A recent example comes from West Kameng, where indigenous communities are sustainably harvesting Zanthoxylum, locally known as Khagi, a wild Himalayan spice. The initiative has reportedly involved around 200 families while contributing to the protection of approximately 100 square kilometres of forest and generating livelihood opportunities.
Such efforts demonstrate that conservation and livelihoods can move together when local knowledge and sustainable practices are placed at the centre of biodiversity management.
Conservation: Protecting a Living Legacy
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is a natural asset of national and global importance. At the same time, ecosystems across the world are facing growing pressures from habitat loss, climate change, pollution, invasive species and unsustainable exploitation of natural resources.
Protecting Arunachal’s biodiversity therefore requires more than creating protected areas. It calls for habitat restoration, scientific research, responsible tourism, community participation, sustainable livelihoods and greater awareness among citizens.
The State’s protected areas, community conservation initiatives, biodiversity documentation programmes and institutions dedicated to research and conservation all contribute to this larger effort.
Looking Ahead
The story of Arunachal Pradesh is inseparable from its forests, rivers, mountains and wildlife. Its biodiversity sustains ecosystems, supports livelihoods, enriches traditional knowledge and strengthens the ecological security of the Eastern Himalayas.
From the orchids of Sessa to the forests of Namdapha, from the bird-rich landscapes of Eaglenest to the wetlands of Glaw Lake, every ecosystem adds another chapter to the State’s natural heritage.
The recent recognition of Glaw Lake as a Ramsar Site is an important milestone, but it is also a reminder of the responsibility that comes with being home to such extraordinary natural wealth.
Arunachal Pradesh is a living treasury of biodiversity and conserving it is not only about protecting nature today, but ensuring that its forests continue to breathe, its rivers continue to flow, and its remarkable species continue to thrive for generations.

Donald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel on Saturday over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the country erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting a video of him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA.
Rhetoric over the naming of Lake Ontario is the public face of an escalating trade dispute between the US and its northern neighbor involving a 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.
Trump’s order for the US government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America by Sunday had at least one prominent impact. Google Maps had changed Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America for US users to reflect the president’s executive renaming order.
Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney has flat-out rejected the renaming, explaining that Lake Ontario derives from an Indigenous Wendat word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is great” that dates back more than 400 years.
With talks to resolve the trade dispute stalled, Trump issued an executive order on Thursday directing US agencies that the lake was now Lake America.
It revived memories of a dispute earlier in his second presidency with Mexico, which saw Trump direct US agencies to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters before he signed an executive order renaming the body of water among US federal agencies.
In a statement explaining why it was acquiescing to Trump’s desired name for Lake Ontario, Google said its practice is to “reflect name changes in official government sources”. Trump’s order affects the US’s federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), “which sets the standard for official US maps”, the tech company said.
The Lake of Ontario’s name change “does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or how the rest of the world refers to the lake,” Google said in a statement. And it said “those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’” on Google Maps, “and those outside … the US and Canada will see both names.”
Google had done similarly in Trump’s executive order for the US government to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. US Google Map users for now see that body of water named as the “Gulf of America”.
Meanwhile, on Saturday, the US president raised the volume again by resorting to the kind of AI-generated imagery for which he has shown a penchant.
He posted one such video of an army of Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles in protection of Lake America. He published another of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America while he danced in his distinctive to a soundtrack of the Village People hit YMCA, which he has implemented into his public appearances for years.
Across the US’s northern border, Ontario premier Doug Ford replied with a two-stories high billboard declaring “Lake Ontario. Now and Always,” near Grimsby, Ontario. Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves”, and he argued the name would outlast the president.
“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.
In an interview with the Associated Press earlier, Ford said the late Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies.
Meanwhile, Manitoba’s premier, Wab Kinew, said Trump’s Lake America provocation was akin to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit.
“You know when, like, a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago, I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said. “Like he thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico.
“He’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad, and it’s not his best work.”
Wendat Nation grand chief Pierre Picard called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.
Lake Ontario is one of North America’s five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie. At 7,340 sq miles, Lake Ontario is the smallest of those in terms of surface area.

Apple prototyped a stylus for the foldable iPhone that we may never see
On the bright side, Apple is more certainly working on an Apple Watch overhaul.
If Apple were to create a stylus designed for a smartphone, the upcoming foldable iPhone would be the perfect opportunity. Apple seems to be well aware of that and according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the company has "internally prototyped, tested and considered launching" a modified Apple Pencil for its upcoming foldable. However, Gurman added that it was "unlikely" that Apple releases this prototyped accessory along with its first iPhone with a folding display.
Gurman reported that the prototype stylus was "stubbier" than the existing Apple Pencil models that are usually paired with iPads. Like the existing styluses in Apple's product offerings, this prototype would attach to the side of the foldable iPhone for storage and charging. Maintaining that same attachment point poses a major problem since it would get in the way when you open up the foldable but don't want to use the stylus. On top of that, Gurman added that a stylus could leave marks on the display since foldable devices tend to have more delicate screens. Even Samsung has certain S Pens that only work with its foldable smartphones. We're expecting to see the foldable iPhone makes its debut on September 9, where we will see whether or not this stylus makes it out of the prototype stage.
While this Apple stylus is highly unlikely, Gurman offers more certainty about Apple testing out white and dark gray offerings for the upcoming Apple Watch Series 12's ceramic cases. On the software side, Gurman reported that Apple is testing a new smartwatch feature that keeps the heart-rate sensor collecting data throughout the day, instead of only when you're doing something physical or at random times. On top of that new feature, Apple is reportedly revamping its fitness and health app to look more like those we see with Whoop and Oura. For anyone looking to upgrade, Gurman also said that the Apple Watch is more likely to see a big redesign next year, with the potential to be pushed back to 2028.

Which Dan Sullivan Will These Dan Sullivans Vote For?
The Alaska Senate race has become complicated by two candidates with the same name.
What in the Dan Sullivan is going on in Alaska? Senator Daniel S. Sullivan is running for reelection. Daniel J. Sullivan is one of his challengers. And former Anchorage Mayor Daniel A. Sullivan recently endorsed the senator, while also declaring himself “the OG Dan Sullivan.”
“It’s kind of hilarious,” Daniel K. Sullivan, a 33-year-old diesel mechanic and off-road fabricator from Wasilla, who is not running for Senate, told me.
“I got a chuckle out of it,” Daniel P. Sullivan, a longtime teacher from Nome, who is also not on the ballot, told me.
Control of the Senate could come down to a ranked-choice ballot that currently includes two Dan Sullivans (the Republican incumbent and the Republican challenger) and one Mary Peltola (a Democrat who was the state’s former at-large congresswoman). Republicans are worried that voters could be confused about which Dan Sullivan to select. Theories abound: Is this some sort of nefarious political plot by the Democrats? Or is it just that there are so many Dan Sullivans in the state that something like this was bound to happen?
To get at the question, I reached out to half a dozen Dan Sullivans who appear to live in Alaska.
I caught a second Daniel P. Sullivan, this one from Chugiak, while he was driving on a remote gravel road the other day. “The Dan Sullivan thing” has become a common topic of conversation, he told me, and his co-workers call him “the senator.” So many Dan Sullivans live in Alaska that his firearms purchases require a deeper background check. “So I don’t get mistaken for another Dan Sullivan,” he explained. (He said that he’s planning to move next summer so likely won’t vote for either of the Dan Sullivans: “Not really fair to vote when the outcome doesn’t affect me.”)
Daniel F. Sullivan, a registered nurse, called me back from Palmer. “I often joke that I’m the real Dan Sullivan, and those are all imposters,” he told me. He said he grew up in New York with another Dan Sullivan in his high school, who was a better student than he was: “My parents would sometimes get honor-roll letters in the mail. I always wondered if his parents got all the bad letters about skipping school.”
In Alaska, he found that his name had even greater benefits. A few years back, he had workers out to fix the electronic system in his hot tub, and the bill they promised to send never arrived. “I often wonder if the other Dan Sullivan got the bill,” he said. Whenever he’s part of a group going out to eat, the reservation is in his name in case it prompts VIP treatment. In this election, he said, he’ll probably vote but hasn’t settled on a candidate. “I won’t vote just because it’s a Dan Sullivan,” he said.
This is not the first time a ballot has featured multiple Dan Sullivans. In 2014, Dan S. Sullivan was running for Senate for the first time when Dan A. Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, was running for lieutenant governor (the Senate bid was successful; the lieutenant-governor one was not). Then, in 2016, the former mayor briefly ran for the state’s other Senate seat. Had he won, both of the state’s U.S. senators would have been named Dan Sullivan. Neither of those Dan Sullivans returned my messages.
The Dan Sullivan who has put the name into the news is Dan J. Sullivan, who lives in Petersburg, a small fishing village on an island where Sitka black-tailed deer outnumber the roughly 3,000 people. His father was named Dan Sullivan. So was his grandfather. At the moment, so is one of his sitting senators. Shortly before the June 1 deadline, he filed paperwork declaring his candidacy. “We need a Sullivan who stands up for Alaska,” his website says.
The only Dan Sullivans he personally knows, he told me in an email, are in his own family: three Dan Sullivans and four more Dans who are not Sullivans. “We all have nicknames,” he said. “Mine will never be divulged.” He says that his campaign strategy mostly consists of maintaining his website and posting on social media. “Maybe some travel, but I don’t have much money,” he told me. (He has $8,400 cash on hand in his campaign account. The other Dan Sullivan has nearly $7.3 million.)
His candidacy was immediately challenged by the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which referred to him as “Sham Candidate Sullivan,” and the Alaska Republican Party. Senator Dan Sullivan told reporters in Washington that it was “an insult” and that the challenger was “trying to trick my constituents to rig the election for Peltola.” “This is serious stuff,” he told CNN. “When people are going, Oh there’s two Dan Sullivans, isn’t that funny? No. It’s cheating.”
The senator and his allies pointed to similarities between the challenger’s logo and the senator’s: Both are navy and mustard-yellow and feature at least one gold star. They accused the other Dan Sullivan of being part of a partisan plot engineered by a Democratic consultant. The Sullivan facing those questions told me the consultant had helped set up his campaign site and provided “tips on communications and basic campaign functions,” but said “she is not currently working for me.” They questioned his party affiliation. (He was previously a member of the Alaska Independence Party, but when that disbanded late last year, he switched his affiliation to the Republican Party, which he said was in line with his conservative views.) The director of the Alaska Division of Elections, which is overseen by the state’s Republican lieutenant governor, determined in June that the newcomer’s declaration as a candidate was invalid because it had been “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.” The Sullivan in question appealed to the Alaska Superior Court.
“I am running because I am tired of sitting back and watching our current Senator routinely fail to represent the interests of ordinary Alaskans like me,” he wrote in his defense. “The fact that Senator Sullivan shares my first and last names adds insult to injury, motivating me to raise my hand as an alternative choice for Alaskans.”
Ultimately, the court determined that Dan Sullivan met all the requirements for making the ballot: It was his actual name; he did live in Alaska; he was over the age of 30. The whole experience, he told me, has been “daunting” because he feels unfairly singled out. “Typical of Sullivan to cry about it, make a nickname, and blame others,” he said, when asked about being called a “sham” candidate. Of the dozens of candidates running statewide in Alaska, he said, “only I have been accused of bad intentions (including one guy who is in jail). Seems unfair to me.”
Both Dan Sullivans were on the ballot in the nonpartisan primary earlier this month, after which the top four candidates advanced to the general election. Peltola, the Democratic candidate, got the most votes, leading the incumbent Sullivan by seven percentage points. Daniel J. Sullivan came in a distant third with 2.5 percent of the vote, qualifying him for the general election—and showing that he could be a spoiler in November.
His advancement angered Republicans, including the president. “The Crooked, Radical Left Dumocrats have put up another man named ‘Dan Sullivan,’ and they did this to take Votes away from our Great Senator of the same name,” Donald Trump wrote on social media. Senator Dan Sullivan’s early campaign ads have not mentioned the other Dan Sullivan, and when he talks in his speeches about an opponent, he references only Peltola.
But this is not the first time an election has featured similarly named candidates and accusations of political shenanigans. When John F. Kennedy ran for Congress in 1946 against a Boston city council member named Joe Russo, his allies helped recruit a janitor named Joe Russo to also run. In 2004, Representative José E. Serrano of New York was primaried by an unemployed former dockworker, Jose E. Serrano, who dropped out after being questioned about his legislative platform and not knowing what that was. In 2024, the governor’s race in Washington State featured Attorney General Bob Ferguson running against Robert Arthur Ferguson and Robert Benjamin Ferguson (the latter two Fergusons withdrew from the primary before ballots were printed).
The name Dan Sullivan is common enough. There was the offensive lineman for the Baltimore Colts in the 1960s. There was the race-car driver Danny Sullivan, who won the 1985 Indianapolis 500. There’s a theater and film director named Daniel J. Sullivan. Daniel was the ninth-most-common first name and Sullivan was the 107th-most-common last name in the United States in 2020, according to census records. There are nearly 5,300 Dan Sullivans in the country, according to the personal search aggregator Spokeo, and more than two dozen in Alaska.
In Anchorage, there’s the Sullivan Arena (named for the city’s longtime mayor, George M. Sullivan, the father of the Dan Sullivan who was the most recent mayor of Anchorage) and Sullivan’s Steakhouse (named after John Sullivan, a 19th-century boxer). “Sullivan just seems to be the big thing,” Dan Sullivan the Wasilla mechanic told me. “But I don’t know any benefits from it that I’m aware of. I don’t get any discount at the steakhouse or anything.”
The Dan Sullivan from Nome told me he would occasionally get random calls from people around the state confronting him about his campaign promises, especially when the Anchorage mayor and the U.S. senator were both Dan Sullivans. “I’d show my credit card, and they’d look at me and do a double take,” he said. “I got to meet all the Dan Sullivans. All the famous ones. I’m probably the least interesting out of all of them.” (He has since retired and has been traveling, and says he has not yet done his homework on which candidate he’ll support in the election).
For the Dan Sullivans, it can be a little disorienting when the political ads are blanketing the airwaves. “It’ll say, Dan Sullivan’s ruining the Alaska fisheries! Or Dan Sullivan voted to raise your health insurance! I’m like, No, I didn’t! It wasn’t me,” said Dan Sullivan the mechanic. “Or you’ll get an ad on the radio and it’s like, Dan Sullivan’s great for Alaska! Yeah, he is.” He’s not much into politics, so he says he’s unlikely to join the other Dan Sullivans in campaigning. He’s more conservative, so he plans to vote for the incumbent senator.
As if things couldn’t get more confusing, there’s also a Dan Sullivan who has run for Congress in Massachusetts. There are so many Dan Sullivans that, at times, my attempts to reach the ones in Alaska went awry. I messaged a Dan Sullivan I thought for sure was from Palmer, Alaska, but instead located one in Cleveland, Ohio. He politely responded that his origins are in Brooklyn and Massachusetts. “I am Daniel M. Sullivan. My dad was Daniel P. Sullivan,” he said. Although he won’t be voting in Alaska, the intrigue has caught his eye: “I have been following this story with interest.”
The Alaska race will be determined in November. At least in this election cycle, there’s room for only one Dan Sullivan in the Senate (and possibly none). But some other Dan Sullivans are getting ideas about future options.
“Maybe one of us needs to run for president,” Dan Sullivan the mechanic told me. Or perhaps two? “You can pick anybody you want. As long as it’s Dan Sullivan.”

The Great American Conflict, a 75-minute documentary produced by a Texas-based organization dedicated to converting Iran to Christianity, declares its goal right at the beginning: “to reveal the true Islam to all people, especially in the West,” Iran Alive Ministries’s founder Hormoz Shariat says. “This film is also meant to be a warning to America. There is a serious threat of Islam in our nation.”
Islamophobia is getting worse in Texas. One strange movie is helping drive it.
A documentary warns about a coming cultural conflict with Muslims in the US. It’s had surprising political influence.
Released at the start of summer and having premiered at a gathering of the Dallas County Republican Party, it’s an obscure film — you’ve probably never heard of it — but it has so far had a surprising political influence. It’s been shown at gatherings of local Republicans and conservative activists in Texas, where Islamophobic rhetoric and policy proposals have played a key role in activating the Republican base, candidates, and party leaders over the course of this year’s elections. The documentary is both a symptom and a cause of a larger trend unfolding in American politics in 2026 that is picking up steam now: the rise of a new iteration of blatant Islamophobia paired with Christian nationalist sentiment on the American right.
Iran Alive Ministries did not respond to requests for comment.
It’s no surprise who some of the backers and voices of this documentary are: Some members of this collection of right-wing, conservative, and evangelical activists are a throwback to early-2000s and 2010s Islamophobia, when some of the same figures spoke out against “radical Islamism” and “radical Islamic terror.” One of them, for instance, is the activist Brigitte Gabriel, the controversial founder of ACT for America, an early-2000s anti-Islamic extremism group. As the film makes clear, this latest version of Islamophobia in America has its roots in this post-9/11 era and borrows heavily from it, while making some modern-day tweaks.
What’s different now is how mainstream this stance is becoming in politics and how it appears to be getting only more mainstream.
“Islamophobia has passed the dinner table test. You can say things about Muslims with basic impunity today,” Nathan Lean, a researcher, assistant teaching professor at North Carolina State University and author of the book The Islamophobia Industry, told me. “And it’s institutionalized in the way that prejudice that targets other marginalized communities is not.” He pointed to the Sharia-Free America Caucus in Congress, which is composed of 68 elected members of Congress representing 25 states. He also pointed to efforts in Texas to make eliminating “sharia” law an official stance of the Texas GOP, and then the subsequent vote to recommend Gov. Greg Abbott “ban” it on the Texas 2026 primary ballot.
Now, politicians, content creators, and politically connected advocacy groups are using films like The Great American Conflict, selectively edited clips spread on social media, and investigative-style pseudo-documentaries to spread this sentiment further and wider, power more wins of right-wing candidates, and take aim in particular at Muslim candidates and politicians.
This is all playing out as antisemitism and Islamophobia are peaking during the 2026 midterm cycle, accelerated by demographic change across America, increased Muslim visibility and engagement in politics, including elections of Zohran Mamdani in New York City and the Senate campaign of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, and more Republican politicians feeling comfortable using Islam as a scapegoat and cudgel, particularly in Texas. It all paints a worrying picture of what’s to come.
What The Great American Conflict argues is coming
As a cinematic project, The Great American Conflict isn’t much of an accomplishment; it can broadly be described as a collection of testimonials from evangelical Christians and former Muslims who’ve converted to Christianity who each make a case against Islam. Though poorly organized, it starts with some rough accounting of the rise of Islam in world history, lays out the case through interviews that Islam is an ideology and not a religion, then zooms in on specific Texan communities and examples of how Muslim politicians and activists are using democratic processes to achieve “domination.”
There are broadly three core themes that these speakers come back to:
- Islam is inherently violent and imperialistic: The documentary’s interview subjects argue that true believers seek to expand the faith and establish a cross-national Islamic state. They rely on some sketchy history of the prophet Muhammed and the contemporary history of Lebanon and Iran as examples of this “violence.”
- Islam is incompatible with the American Constitution and Western liberalism: Speakers also argue that, as opposed to other religions, Islam does not tolerate diversity of thought and seeks to enforce its rules and guidelines on nonbelievers. They claim that Islam rejects the separation between church and state, and that mosques can function as political or military centers.
- There is an ongoing effort by Muslims to infiltrate American politics and replace “Judeo-Christian” America: The rise of Muslim American politicians in Congress, in New York City, and at the state and local government level are all part of an effort to whittle away religious liberty and replace American values with “Islamic” values. Liberal and progressive allies are enabling this takeover. And they interpret public calls to prayer, halal food, school prayer rooms, Ramadan accommodations, mosque construction, and Muslim residential developments as evidence that American institutions are yielding to Islamic demands.
Interspersed throughout these testimonials are fearmongering compilations of social media clips of Muslim prayers and veiled women, and short selections of purportedly Muslim speakers making inflammatory comments about 9/11, about Jews and Christians, and about Islamic domination in the West, and violent clips of terrorist actions abroad.
And though the film’s main backer, Hormoz Shariat, says at the beginning of the film that his goal is not to inspire fear or hate, that’s precisely what the speakers seem to do for an hour.
For example, the Christian pastor Shahram Hadian, the founder of Truth in Love Ministry in Tennessee, repeatedly argues that America is at a turning point. “Western societies are right now at a critical decision point. Either they’re going to maintain, preserve, [and] fight for their Judeo-Christian values, or they’re succumbing,” he says.
And he takes a natalist turn, arguing that Muslims in the US are happy to continue to raise families as Western birth rates drop. “We continue to see the demise of Christianity, of our Judeo-Christian values, family values, family ethics, marriage — one man, one woman,” he says. “They’re just waiting us out. They’ll just wait us out. They’ll aid us in our own demise and destruction.”
To drill down on this, various speakers point to demographic change in Michigan and Texas as early signs of what they see as the capitulation of the United Kingdom and continental Europe to Islam. They point to self-segregating Muslim communities in Europe being mirrored in the US, particularly focusing on a housing development project in East Plano, Texas, centered around a mosque and Islamic center, that has been a focal point for Republican politicians.
Other speakers argue against accepting Islam as a religion at all, instead casting it as a political ideology that is seeking to take over American institutions. Some, like Gabriel, allege a coordinated strategy to “infiltrate” and “dominate the West and establish an Islamic government,” tracing this back to the Muslim Brotherhood, and a supposed decades-long plan to infiltrate political parties, schools, media, and churches to use democratic institutions to establish Islamic law. She points to Mamdani as an example of this, and ropes in Reps. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota and Rashida Tlaib of Michigan as being loyal to a foreign Islamic identity rather than to the United States.
And they contrast this all with an idealized “Judeo-Christian” America defined by constitutional government, traditional marriage, Christianity, and cultural assimilation. The final call to arms is to preserve and promote this Christian vision of America, on top of defending the Constitution, religious liberty, and “American” culture against what is a coming ideological and demographic conflict.
The danger of rising Islamophobia
Iran Alive Ministries itself doesn’t seem primarily dedicated to anti-Muslim American advocacy and activism. Most of its YouTube and internet presence is focused on digital Christian evangelism, particularly in Iran. It’s not entirely hard to see how a group focused on conversions would drift into Islamophobic preaching, but it does seem like a peculiar move, Lean told me.
“There is a group of people who form a faction of this sort of anti-Muslim movement in the United States who are, by their own description, evangelical Christians,” Lean said. “And it’s no surprise that a group like Iran Alive Ministries, that is formed on the basis of, as they say, transforming Iran into a Christian nation, one soul at a time, would go there.”
Emphasizing that Christian proselytism and evangelism are not inherently Islamophobic, Lean told me that there has been a more overt merging of religious convictions with Republican politics in recent years.
“The…driving mission of the group leads to a marriage of, we want a Christian world on the one hand, versus there are active agents in the world that are potentially preventing that. And who represents that biggest threat to that right now? Well, in the eyes of these people, Muslims do,” Lean said.
Lean told me that he expects to see this momentum build as midterms approach. At the local level, it’s most visible in Texas, where the New York Times recently reported on the stunning rise in Islamophobia and fearmongering across the state, and in Michigan, where cities like Dearborn and Hamtramck have seen white nationalist and anti-Islam demonstrations.
Lean said many of these lines of Islamophobic thinking sound like familiar tropes, smears, and lies of the last couple of waves of fearmongering around Muslims. Still, as opposed to the post-9/11 era, he noted a worrying difference: the scale of Islamophobia, given its increasing presence on both social and traditional media.
Much of the growth of these sentiments is happening online, too. Since Mamdani’s election as New York City mayor, and especially since El-Sayed’s victory in the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, these kinds of views have surged online and in conservative media, while conservative activists and influencers have been pushing similar narratives of infiltration and under-the-radar Muslim “encroachment.”
A recent survey of internet discourse and activity by the research group Magnitude Media found something similar, centered on Dearborn: “Since the beginning of the month, there have been 690 posts mentioning Dearborn, generating 5.1 million engagements. Right-leaning accounts drove 88% of that engagement, compared to just 7% from left-leaning accounts,” the authors write. “The broader anti-Muslim conversation online has been substantial for months. Over the past six months, 68% of posts that either mentioned Islamophobia or contained common Islamophobic language came from right-leaning accounts. Dearborn appears less like the cause of a new Islamophobia conversation than the right’s newest focal point.”
So the documentary certainly isn’t the only cause for concern — but the fact that Texas Republicans have used it in official events, on top of strategists saying they are pivoting to “sharia” and fearmongering, suggests just how politically useful the party thinks these messages can be.
Which all suggests more ugliness to come. And as Lean told me, talking about a coming conflict and a threat to survival indicates an existential threat that should be fought by any means.
“Where does the logic of all of this take us? What’s the solution?” he said. “You can’t help but wonder when they’re issuing statements about fertility rates and these overtures are being kind of taken over, that this could very easily go to a dark place.”
